[p-251]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

**Tafsir of Surat al-Tawbah (The Repentance)**

This surah is Medinan, except for two verses: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128] to its end. It is called Surat al-Tawbah, as reported by Hudhayfah and others. It is also called al-Fadihah (the Exposer), as reported by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. It is called al-Hafirah (the Digger) because it dug out the hearts of the hypocrites. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "It kept being revealed, 'And among them, and among them,' until we thought that no one would be left." Hudhayfah said: "It is the surah of punishment." Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "We used to call it al-Muqashqishah (the Liberator)." Al-Harith ibn Yazid said: "It was called al-Muba'thirah (the Disperser)," and it is also called al-Mutheerah (the Stirrer) and al-Bahuth (the Searcher).

Abu Malik al-Ghifari said: "The first verse revealed from Bara'ah (Immunity) was ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾ [al-Tawbah: 41]." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Bara'ah was similar in length to Surat al-Baqarah."

There is a difference of opinion regarding why the line ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ (the basmalah) is missing from its beginning. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Its meanings resemble those of al-Anfal, and in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ it was called one of the two companions (al-qarinatayn). Therefore I joined them together, and I did not write ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, and I placed it among the seven long surahs." 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ is a pledge of security and good news, while Bara'ah was revealed with the sword and the repudiation of covenants. Therefore it does not begin with the pledge of security."

[p-252]

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This opinion is attributed to al-Mubarrad, but it is in fact from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him. It is like the angry addressee beginning with "Amma ba'du" (as for what follows), without praise or opening with an honorific. It is also narrated that the scribes of the Mushaf in the time of 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, disagreed about al-Anfal and Bara'ah: were they one surah or two? So they left a gap between them, out of consideration for those who said they were two surahs, and they did not write ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, out of consideration for those among them who said they were one surah. All of them were content with this.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This opinion is weakened by the consideration that the Book of Allah should not differ in such a manner. It is narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to command us to place ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ at the beginning of every surah, and he did not command us regarding this (surah) with anything, so we did not place it." It is also narrated from Malik that he said: "We have been informed that it (Bara'ah) was about the length of Surat al-Baqarah, then it was abrogated and much of it was lifted, and the basmalah (the formula 'In the name of Allah') was among what was lifted. Therefore they did not consider it appropriate to place it in a position other than its own."

Surat Bara'ah is among the last things revealed to the Prophet ﷺ. 'Imran ibn Judayr reported that a Bedouin heard Surat Bara'ah and said: "I think this is among the last that Allah revealed to His Messenger." He was asked: "Why do you say that?" He said: "I see things being annulled and covenants being repudiated."

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿A declaration of immunity from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you made covenants among the polytheists.﴾
﴿So travel freely in the land for four months, and know that you cannot escape Allah, and that Allah will humiliate the disbelievers.﴾
﴿And an announcement from Allah and His Messenger to the people on the day of the greater Hajj that Allah is free of obligation to the polytheists, and so is His Messenger. So if you repent, it is better for you; but if you turn away, then know that you cannot escape Allah. And give tidings to those who disbelieve of a painful punishment.﴾

[p-253]

"Bara'ah" is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, whose implied sense is: "These verses are a declaration of immunity." It may also be nominative as the subject, with the predicate being in His words ﴿to those with whom﴾. Beginning with an indefinite noun is permitted because it is qualified (by the following description), so it becomes definite in a general way, and it is permissible to make a predicate about it. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "Bara'atan" in the accusative, with the sense "Adhere to the declaration of immunity," so it carries the meaning of urging (al-ighra'). And "Bara'ah" means: release and disavowal from the covenants that are between you and the disbelievers who initiated the breach. You say, "I am free of such-and-such towards you" (bari'tu ilayka min kadha). So Allah the Exalted and His Messenger disavowed, by this verse, to the disbelievers, those covenants which existed and which the disbelievers had broken. The people of Najran read "Min Allahi" with a kasra on the nun.

This verse is a ruling from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to annul the covenants and truces that existed between the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and groups of polytheists, among whom a breach had appeared or was suspected. Since the covenant of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was binding upon his community, it was fitting to say "those with whom you made covenants." Ibn Ishaq and other scholars said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had made a general covenant with the Arabs that no one would be prevented from the Sacred House, and similar truces. This verse annulled that, and it set a term of four months for all of them. Whoever had a specific covenant with the Prophet ﷺ and had less than four months remaining of it, it was completed to four months. Whoever had a term longer than four months, his covenant was fulfilled for him, except if he was among those suspected of a breach, in which case he was limited to four months. And whoever had no specific covenant was given four months in which to travel freely in the land, meaning to go about in safety, like the flow of water (al-sayh min al-ma'), which is what runs and spreads out. From this is the saying of Tarafa ibn al-'Abd:

"Had I feared this from you, you would not have reached me, until we see horses before me moving freely."

This indicates that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sensed from the disbelievers a breach and a lying in wait against him, except from the excepted group.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: The first of the four months was Shawwal, and at that time the verse was revealed. Its end was at the expiry of the sacred months, which is the end of Muharram fifty days after the day of the announcement. So the term for whoever had a covenant was four months from the day the verse was revealed, and the term for the rest of the polytheists was fifty nights from the day of the announcement.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is objected to on the grounds that the term is binding only from the day it is heard, and it is possible that Bara'ah had been heard from the first of Shawwal, and then its proclamation was repeated together with the announcement on the day of the greater Hajj. Al-Suddi and others said: Rather, its beginning is the day of the announcement, and its end is the twentieth of Rabi' al-Akhir, and those (the months) are the sacred ones; the name was borrowed for them because of this sanctity and the particular security that Allah ordained and imposed in them. It is the term for all, both for one who has a covenant and is suspected of a breach, and for one who has no covenant.

Al-Dahhak and other scholars said: "Among the Arabs there were those who had no covenant at all between them and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. There were among them those who had a covenant with him and a breach was suspected from them, and there were among them those who had a covenant with him and did not break it. So His Exalted saying ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾ is a term set for the one who had a covenant and a breach from him was suspected. The beginning of this term is the day of the announcement, and its end is the completion of the first ten days of Rabi' al-Akhir. His Exalted saying ﴿When the sacred months have passed, then kill the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5] is a ruling distinct from the first, applied to the polytheists who have no covenant whatsoever. So the term of their security is fifty days, the beginning of which is the day of the announcement and the end of which is the completion of Muharram. His saying ﴿those with whom you made covenants﴾ intends those who have a covenant and did not break it, and about whom no breach is suspected. They, as it is reported, were the Banu Dhamrah of Kinanah, with whom al-Muhassir ibn Khuwaylid made a covenant. On the day of the announcement, nine months remained of their covenant."

Al-Tabari reported from a group that they said: "The term of Allah is only four months for the one whose covenant expires at its end or before it. The meaning is: say to them, O Muhammad, 'Travel freely.' As for the one whose covenant extends beyond the four months, they are the ones for whom Allah commanded fulfilment."

His Exalted saying ﴿and know that you cannot escape Allah﴾ means: know that you cannot overcome Allah or outpace Him by fleeing from His punishment. Then He informed them of His ruling of humiliation for the disbelievers, and that is certain, either in this world or in the Hereafter.

His Exalted saying ﴿And an announcement from Allah and His Messenger to the people﴾ is the verse. "Adhan" means: notification and public proclamation. "Al-nas" (the people) here is general, encompassing all creation. "Yawm" (day) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and the governing element is "adhan" (announcement). Although it has been described, the sense of the verb remains, and so it governs the adverb of time. It was said: this is not permissible, since the verbal noun has been described, and so it loses the strength of the verb. It is also possible that a verb implied by the wording governs it. It was said: the governing element is the description of the announcement. It was said: the governing element is "mukhzi" (humiliating).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is far-fetched.

"And the day of the greater Hajj": 'Umar, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn al-Musayyib and others said: it is the Day of 'Arafah. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, also held this view, and it is reported from him as well that it is the Day of Sacrifice (al-Nahr). This is also reported from Abu Hurayrah and a group, and it is reported from the Prophet ﷺ. Mundhir ibn Sa'id and others said: The people on the Day of 'Arafah were scattered, since the Hums used to stand at Muzdalifah, while the gathering was on the Day of Sacrifice at Mina. Therefore they called it "the greater Hajj," meaning in contrast to the lesser (hajj) in which they were scattered.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This ceased in the Hajj of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, because no one stood at Muzdalifah then. Al-Mahdawi mentioned that the Hums and those who followed them stood at Muzdalifah in the Hajj of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. What the hadiths agree upon in this meaning is that 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, proclaimed that verse on the Day of 'Arafah following the sermon of Abu Bakr. Then he saw that he had not informed the people by audible proclamation, so he followed them with the announcement of it on the Day of Sacrifice. On that day Abu Bakr sent with him someone to assist him in announcing it, such as Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, and others. They also followed the markets of the Arabs with it, such as Dhu al-Majaz and others. From here the opinion of Sufyan is preferred: that "yawm" in this verse means "days." For this reason a group said: "The day of the greater Hajj" is 'Arafah, since the first announcement occurred then. Another group said: it is the Day of Sacrifice, since the completion of the announcement occurred then. They also argued that whoever misses standing at 'Arafah on its day may compensate by standing on the night of the Sacrifice, so on this view the Day of 'Arafah is not the day of the greater Hajj.

[p-256]

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no proof in this. Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: The intended meaning is all the days of the Hajj, as you say "the day of Siffin" or "the day of the Camel," meaning all its days. Mujahid said: "The day of the greater Hajj" is all the days of Mina, and the gatherings of the polytheists wherever they were, at Dhu al-Majaz and 'Ukaz, when it was proclaimed among them that the Muslims and the polytheists should not gather after this year of theirs.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is like what 'Uthman said to 'Umar when he offered him the marriage to Hafsah: "I have decided not to marry on this day of mine." And like what Sibawayh mentioned: you say to a man, "What is your occupation today?" while you mean in these days of yours. It has been disputed why it was described as "greater." Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith ibn Nawfal said: because in that year the Muslims and the polytheists performed Hajj together, and it coincided with the festival of the Jews and the Christians.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak: that Allah would describe it in His Book as "greater" for this reason. Al-Hasan also said: It was called "greater" only because Abu Bakr performed Hajj in it, and the covenants were repudiated in it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the view that resembles al-Hasan's reasoning. Its explanation is that on that day the opening with truth and the leadership of Islam began, through the Prophet ﷺ sending (Abu Bakr) forward, and the covenants were repudiated in it, and religion was made mighty and polytheism was humbled. This was not so in the year eight, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ appointed 'Attab ibn Usayd over the Hajj, [p-257] rather the affair of the Arabs remained in its former state. Therefore every Hajj after the Hajj of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, is built upon it, and its due for this reason is to be called "greater."

Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and others said: "al-Hajj al-akbar" (the greater Hajj) is so called in relation to "al-Hajj al-asghar" (the lesser Hajj), which is the 'Umrah. Al-Sha'bi said: it is so called in relation to the 'Umrah performed in Ramadan, for that is the lesser Hajj. Mujahid said: "al-Hajj al-akbar" is al-Qiran (combining Hajj and 'Umrah in one ihram), and "al-asghar" is al-Ifrad (performing Hajj alone). This has nothing to do with the verse. What Mundhir ibn Sa'id mentioned has already been discussed. It is more fitting that it be described as "al-akbar" as a form of praise, not in relation to a specific "asghar." Rather, the meaning is: the greatest of all the days. So consider this carefully.

A summary of what this verse requires, according to Mujahid and others, regarding the circumstances: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Makkah in the eighth year and appointed 'Attab ibn Usayd over it. He settled the affair of Hunayn and al-Ta'if and returned to Madinah, where he remained until he set out for Tabuk. Then he returned from Tabuk in Ramadan of the ninth year and intended to perform Hajj. Then he considered that the polytheists would perform Hajj that year and circumambulate the House naked, so he said: "I do not want to see that." So he commanded Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, to lead the people in Hajj and sent him off. Then he sent 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, after him on his she-camel al-'Adba', and commanded him to proclaim to the people four things: "No polytheist shall perform Hajj after this year, no one shall enter Paradise except a believing soul (in some narrations: no disbeliever shall enter Paradise), no one shall circumambulate the House naked, and whoever has a covenant with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), it remains valid until its term." In some narrations: "Whoever has a covenant between himself and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), its term is four months during which he may travel freely. When those months are over, then Allah is free of the polytheists, and so is His Messenger."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
I say: they were proclaiming all of this. The part about the covenant-holders was for those who had a covenant and whose breach was suspected, while granting them time until the term was for those about whom no breach was known.

Al-Tabari mentioned that the Arabs said on that day: "We disavow your covenant and the covenant of your cousin, except for [those who fight with] spear-thrusts and sword-blows." Some of them blamed others and said: "What are you doing, when Quraysh has embraced Islam?" So they all embraced Islam, and no one went about touring the land (sayh).

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
At that time people entered the religion of Allah in multitudes. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had commanded 'Ali to recite to the people the first forty verses of Surat Bara'a. It was also said: thirty, and it was said: twenty. In some narrations: ten verses, and in some: nine verses, as mentioned by al-Naqqash. Sulayman ibn Musa al-Shami said: that is twenty-eight verses. 'Ali caught up with Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both, on the road. Abu Bakr said to him: "Are you an amir or one who is commanded?" He said: "Rather, one who is commanded." So they both set out until they reached the season (of Hajj). When Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, delivered the sermon at 'Arafa, he said: "Stand up, O 'Ali, and convey the message of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, stood up and did so. He said: "Then it occurred to me that not all the people had witnessed Abu Bakr's sermon, so I began to follow the tents on the day of sacrifice (al-nahr)."

Most of the reciters read "أنَّ اللهَ بَرِيءٌ" with the alif open, on the assumption of "بِأنَّ اللهَ". Al-Hasan and al-A'raj read "إنَّ اللهَ" with the alif kasra, as a fresh clause, since the proclamation (adhan) carries the sense of speech. Most of the reciters read "وَرَسُولُهُ" in the nominative, as an inchoative (mubtada') with the predicate omitted, and its implied predicate is: "and His Messenger is free of them." This, according to our shaykh, the jurist and teacher Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Badhish, may Allah have mercy on him, is the meaning of coordination with the position (al-'atf 'ala al-mawdi'). That is, he makes the first sentence, which is of the form mubtada' and khabar, a point of familiarity, and this sentence is coordinated to it. It was also said that it is coordinated to the position of the clause before the entry of "anna," which does not change the meaning of the inchoative but emphasizes it. "Idh" has also been read with a kasra, because one does not coordinate to the position of "anna" with a fatha. Consider this, for its permissibility is disputed, because the rule of "anna" is to raise the inchoative's rule, except in this position and what resembles it. This is the view of Abu al-'Abbas and Abu 'Ali, may Allah have mercy on them both. The view of our teacher, in accordance with the implication of Sibawayh's statement, is that there is no position for what "anna" enters upon, since it is declinable, and the effect of the governing word has appeared in it. Also, there is no difference between "anna," "layta," and "la'alla." The consensus is that what these enter upon has no position. It was also said that it is coordinated to the pronoun in "bari'" (the hidden subject), and what made this acceptable is that the intervening prepositional phrase served as emphasis, just as "wa la" appeared in the words of the Exalted: ﴿ما أشْرَكْنا ولا آباؤُنا﴾ (We did not associate anything with Him, nor did our fathers) [al-An'am: 148]. Ibn Abi Ishaq and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "رَسُولَهُ" with the accusative, coordinating it to the form of the written clause. With this verse Mu'awiya tested Abu al-Aswad until he laid down grammar, when he had a reader recite "وَرَسُولُهُ" with a genitive (khafd). The meaning of this verse is: He is free of their covenants and their religions, with a general disavowal that requires separation and the use of the sword.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿فَإنْ تُبْتُمْ﴾ (So if you repent), that is: from disbelief. He promised them, with the condition of repentance, and threatened them, with the condition of turning away. It was permissible for glad tidings to be included within what is disliked, since it came explicitly with that, and the difficulty is removed.

[p-251]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

This is objected to on the grounds that the term is binding only from the day it is heard, and it is possible that Bara'ah had been heard from the first of Shawwal, and then its proclamation was repeated together with the announcement on the day of the greater Hajj. Al-Suddi and others said: Rather, its beginning is the day of the announcement, and its end is the twentieth of Rabi' al-Akhir, and those (the months) are the sacred ones; the name was borrowed for them because of this sanctity and the particular security that Allah ordained and imposed in them. It is the term for all, both for one who has a covenant and is suspected of a breach, and for one who has no covenant.

Al-Dahhak and other scholars said: "Among the Arabs there were those who had no covenant at all between them and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. There were among them those who had a covenant with him and a breach was suspected from them, and there were among them those who had a covenant with him and did not break it. So His Exalted saying ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾ is a term set for the one who had a covenant and a breach from him was suspected. The beginning of this term is the day of the announcement, and its end is the completion of the first ten days of Rabi' al-Akhir. His Exalted saying ﴿When the sacred months have passed, then kill the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5] is a ruling distinct from the first, applied to the polytheists who have no covenant whatsoever. So the term of their security is fifty days, the beginning of which is the day of the announcement and the end of which is the completion of Muharram. His saying ﴿those with whom you made covenants﴾ intends those who have a covenant and did not break it, and about whom no breach is suspected. They, as it is reported, were the Banu Dhamrah of Kinanah, with whom al-Muhassir ibn Khuwaylid made a covenant. On the day of the announcement, nine months remained of their covenant."

Al-Tabari reported from a group that they said: "The term of Allah is only four months for the one whose covenant expires at its end or before it. The meaning is: say to them, O Muhammad, 'Travel freely.' As for the one whose covenant extends beyond the four months, they are the ones for whom Allah commanded fulfilment."

His Exalted saying ﴿and know that you cannot escape Allah﴾ means: know that you cannot overcome Allah or outpace Him by fleeing from His punishment. Then He informed them of His ruling of humiliation for the disbelievers, and that is certain, either in this world or in the Hereafter.

His Exalted saying ﴿And an announcement from Allah and His Messenger to the people﴾ is the verse. "Adhan" means: notification and public proclamation. "Al-nas" (the people) here is general, encompassing all creation. "Yawm" (day) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and the governing element is "adhan" (announcement). Although it has been described, the sense of the verb remains, and so it governs the adverb of time. It was said: this is not permissible, since the verbal noun has been described, and so it loses the strength of the verb. It is also possible that a verb implied by the wording governs it. It was said: the governing element is the description of the announcement. It was said: the governing element is "mukhzi" (humiliating).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is far-fetched.

"And the day of the greater Hajj": 'Umar, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn al-Musayyib and others said: it is the Day of 'Arafah. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, also held this view, and it is reported from him as well that it is the Day of Sacrifice (al-Nahr). This is also reported from Abu Hurayrah and a group, and it is reported from the Prophet ﷺ. Mundhir ibn Sa'id and others said: The people on the Day of 'Arafah were scattered, since the Hums used to stand at Muzdalifah, while the gathering was on the Day of Sacrifice at Mina. Therefore they called it "the greater Hajj," meaning in contrast to the lesser (hajj) in which they were scattered.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This ceased in the Hajj of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, because no one stood at Muzdalifah then. Al-Mahdawi mentioned that the Hums and those who followed them stood at Muzdalifah in the Hajj of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. What the hadiths agree upon in this meaning is that 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, proclaimed that verse on the Day of 'Arafah following the sermon of Abu Bakr. Then he saw that he had not informed the people by audible proclamation, so he followed them with the announcement of it on the Day of Sacrifice. On that day Abu Bakr sent with him someone to assist him in announcing it, such as Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, and others. They also followed the markets of the Arabs with it, such as Dhu al-Majaz and others. From here the opinion of Sufyan is preferred: that "yawm" in this verse means "days." For this reason a group said: "The day of the greater Hajj" is 'Arafah, since the first announcement occurred then. Another group said: it is the Day of Sacrifice, since the completion of the announcement occurred then. They also argued that whoever misses standing at 'Arafah on its day may compensate by standing on the night of the Sacrifice, so on this view the Day of 'Arafah is not the day of the greater Hajj.

[p-256]

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no proof in this. Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: The intended meaning is all the days of the Hajj, as you say "the day of Siffin" or "the day of the Camel," meaning all its days. Mujahid said: "The day of the greater Hajj" is all the days of Mina, and the gatherings of the polytheists wherever they were, at Dhu al-Majaz and 'Ukaz, when it was proclaimed among them that the Muslims and the polytheists should not gather after this year of theirs.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is like what 'Uthman said to 'Umar when he offered him the marriage to Hafsah: "I have decided not to marry on this day of mine." And like what Sibawayh mentioned: you say to a man, "What is your occupation today?" while you mean in these days of yours. It has been disputed why it was described as "greater." Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith ibn Nawfal said: because in that year the Muslims and the polytheists performed Hajj together, and it coincided with the festival of the Jews and the Christians.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak: that Allah would describe it in His Book as "greater" for this reason. Al-Hasan also said: It was called "greater" only because Abu Bakr performed Hajj in it, and the covenants were repudiated in it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the view that resembles al-Hasan's reasoning. Its explanation is that on that day the opening with truth and the leadership of Islam began, through the Prophet ﷺ sending (Abu Bakr) forward, and the covenants were repudiated in it, and religion was made mighty and polytheism was humbled. This was not so in the year eight, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ appointed 'Attab ibn Usayd over the Hajj, [p-257] rather the affair of the Arabs remained in its former state. Therefore every Hajj after the Hajj of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, is built upon it, and its due for this reason is to be called "greater."

Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and others said: "al-Hajj al-akbar" (the greater Hajj) is so called in relation to "al-Hajj al-asghar" (the lesser Hajj), which is the 'Umrah. Al-Sha'bi said: it is so called in relation to the 'Umrah performed in Ramadan, for that is the lesser Hajj. Mujahid said: "al-Hajj al-akbar" is al-Qiran (combining Hajj and 'Umrah in one ihram), and "al-asghar" is al-Ifrad (performing Hajj alone). This has nothing to do with the verse. What Mundhir ibn Sa'id mentioned has already been discussed. It is more fitting that it be described as "al-akbar" as a form of praise, not in relation to a specific "asghar." Rather, the meaning is: the greatest of all the days. So consider this carefully.

A summary of what this verse requires, according to Mujahid and others, regarding the circumstances: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Makkah in the eighth year and appointed 'Attab ibn Usayd over it. He settled the affair of Hunayn and al-Ta'if and returned to Madinah, where he remained until he set out for Tabuk. Then he returned from Tabuk in Ramadan of the ninth year and intended to perform Hajj. Then he considered that the polytheists would perform Hajj that year and circumambulate the House naked, so he said: "I do not want to see that." So he commanded Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, to lead the people in Hajj and sent him off. Then he sent 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, after him on his she-camel al-'Adba', and commanded him to proclaim to the people four things: "No polytheist shall perform Hajj after this year, no one shall enter Paradise except a believing soul (in some narrations: no disbeliever shall enter Paradise), no one shall circumambulate the House naked, and whoever has a covenant with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), it remains valid until its term." In some narrations: "Whoever has a covenant between himself and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), its term is four months during which he may travel freely. When those months are over, then Allah is free of the polytheists, and so is His Messenger."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
I say: they were proclaiming all of this. The part about the covenant-holders was for those who had a covenant and whose breach was suspected, while granting them time until the term was for those about whom no breach was known.

Al-Tabari mentioned that the Arabs said on that day: "We disavow your covenant and the covenant of your cousin, except for [those who fight with] spear-thrusts and sword-blows." Some of them blamed others and said: "What are you doing, when Quraysh has embraced Islam?" So they all embraced Islam, and no one went about touring the land (sayh).

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
At that time people entered the religion of Allah in multitudes. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had commanded 'Ali to recite to the people the first forty verses of Surat Bara'a. It was also said: thirty, and it was said: twenty. In some narrations: ten verses, and in some: nine verses, as mentioned by al-Naqqash. Sulayman ibn Musa al-Shami said: that is twenty-eight verses. 'Ali caught up with Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both, on the road. Abu Bakr said to him: "Are you an amir or one who is commanded?" He said: "Rather, one who is commanded." So they both set out until they reached the season (of Hajj). When Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, delivered the sermon at 'Arafa, he said: "Stand up, O 'Ali, and convey the message of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, stood up and did so. He said: "Then it occurred to me that not all the people had witnessed Abu Bakr's sermon, so I began to follow the tents on the day of sacrifice (al-nahr)."

Most of the reciters read "أنَّ اللهَ بَرِيءٌ" with the alif open, on the assumption of "بِأنَّ اللهَ". Al-Hasan and al-A'raj read "إنَّ اللهَ" with the alif kasra, as a fresh clause, since the proclamation (adhan) carries the sense of speech. Most of the reciters read "وَرَسُولُهُ" in the nominative, as an inchoative (mubtada') with the predicate omitted, and its implied predicate is: "and His Messenger is free of them." This, according to our shaykh, the jurist and teacher Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Badhish, may Allah have mercy on him, is the meaning of coordination with the position (al-'atf 'ala al-mawdi'). That is, he makes the first sentence, which is of the form mubtada' and khabar, a point of familiarity, and this sentence is coordinated to it. It was also said that it is coordinated to the position of the clause before the entry of "anna," which does not change the meaning of the inchoative but emphasizes it. "Idh" has also been read with a kasra, because one does not coordinate to the position of "anna" with a fatha. Consider this, for its permissibility is disputed, because the rule of "anna" is to raise the inchoative's rule, except in this position and what resembles it. This is the view of Abu al-'Abbas and Abu 'Ali, may Allah have mercy on them both. The view of our teacher, in accordance with the implication of Sibawayh's statement, is that there is no position for what "anna" enters upon, since it is declinable, and the effect of the governing word has appeared in it. Also, there is no difference between "anna," "layta," and "la'alla." The consensus is that what these enter upon has no position. It was also said that it is coordinated to the pronoun in "bari'" (the hidden subject), and what made this acceptable is that the intervening prepositional phrase served as emphasis, just as "wa la" appeared in the words of the Exalted: ﴿ما أشْرَكْنا ولا آباؤُنا﴾ (We did not associate anything with Him, nor did our fathers) [al-An'am: 148]. Ibn Abi Ishaq and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "رَسُولَهُ" with the accusative, coordinating it to the form of the written clause. With this verse Mu'awiya tested Abu al-Aswad until he laid down grammar, when he had a reader recite "وَرَسُولُهُ" with a genitive (khafd). The meaning of this verse is: He is free of their covenants and their religions, with a general disavowal that requires separation and the use of the sword.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿فَإنْ تُبْتُمْ﴾ (So if you repent), that is: from disbelief. He promised them, with the condition of repentance, and threatened them, with the condition of turning away. It was permissible for glad tidings to be included within what is disliked, since it came explicitly with that, and the difficulty is removed.

[p-251]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

**Tafsir of Surat al-Tawbah (The Repentance)**

This surah is Medinan, except for two verses: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128] to its end. It is called Surat al-Tawbah, as reported by Hudhayfah and others. It is also called al-Fadihah (the Exposer), as reported by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. It is called al-Hafirah (the Digger) because it dug out the hearts of the hypocrites. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "It kept being revealed, 'And among them, and among them,' until we thought that no one would be left." Hudhayfah said: "It is the surah of punishment." Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "We used to call it al-Muqashqishah (the Liberator)." Al-Harith ibn Yazid said: "It was called al-Muba'thirah (the Disperser)," and it is also called al-Mutheerah (the Stirrer) and al-Bahuth (the Searcher).

Abu Malik al-Ghifari said: "The first verse revealed from Bara'ah (Immunity) was ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾ [al-Tawbah: 41]." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Bara'ah was similar in length to Surat al-Baqarah."

There is a difference of opinion regarding why the line ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ (the basmalah) is missing from its beginning. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Its meanings resemble those of al-Anfal, and in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ it was called one of the two companions (al-qarinatayn). Therefore I joined them together, and I did not write ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, and I placed it among the seven long surahs." 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ is a pledge of security and good news, while Bara'ah was revealed with the sword and the repudiation of covenants. Therefore it does not begin with the pledge of security."

[p-252]

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This opinion is attributed to al-Mubarrad, but it is in fact from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him. It is like the angry addressee beginning with "Amma ba'du" (as for what follows), without praise or opening with an honorific. It is also narrated that the scribes of the Mushaf in the time of 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, disagreed about al-Anfal and Bara'ah: were they one surah or two? So they left a gap between them, out of consideration for those who said they were two surahs, and they did not write ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, out of consideration for those among them who said they were one surah. All of them were content with this.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This opinion is weakened by the consideration that the Book of Allah should not differ in such a manner. It is narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to command us to place ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ at the beginning of every surah, and he did not command us regarding this (surah) with anything, so we did not place it." It is also narrated from Malik that he said: "We have been informed that it (Bara'ah) was about the length of Surat al-Baqarah, then it was abrogated and much of it was lifted, and the basmalah (the formula 'In the name of Allah') was among what was lifted. Therefore they did not consider it appropriate to place it in a position other than its own."

Surat Bara'ah is among the last things revealed to the Prophet ﷺ. 'Imran ibn Judayr reported that a Bedouin heard Surat Bara'ah and said: "I think this is among the last that Allah revealed to His Messenger." He was asked: "Why do you say that?" He said: "I see things being annulled and covenants being repudiated."

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿A declaration of immunity from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you made covenants among the polytheists.﴾
﴿So travel freely in the land for four months, and know that you cannot escape Allah, and that Allah will humiliate the disbelievers.﴾
﴿And an announcement from Allah and His Messenger to the people on the day of the greater Hajj that Allah is free of obligation to the polytheists, and so is His Messenger. So if you repent, it is better for you; but if you turn away, then know that you cannot escape Allah. And give tidings to those who disbelieve of a painful punishment.﴾

[p-253]

"Bara'ah" is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, whose implied sense is: "These verses are a declaration of immunity." It may also be nominative as the subject, with the predicate being in His words ﴿to those with whom﴾. Beginning with an indefinite noun is permitted because it is qualified (by the following description), so it becomes definite in a general way, and it is permissible to make a predicate about it. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "Bara'atan" in the accusative, with the sense "Adhere to the declaration of immunity," so it carries the meaning of urging (al-ighra'). And "Bara'ah" means: release and disavowal from the covenants that are between you and the disbelievers who initiated the breach. You say, "I am free of such-and-such towards you" (bari'tu ilayka min kadha). So Allah the Exalted and His Messenger disavowed, by this verse, to the disbelievers, those covenants which existed and which the disbelievers had broken. The people of Najran read "Min Allahi" with a kasra on the nun.

This verse is a ruling from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to annul the covenants and truces that existed between the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and groups of polytheists, among whom a breach had appeared or was suspected. Since the covenant of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was binding upon his community, it was fitting to say "those with whom you made covenants." Ibn Ishaq and other scholars said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had made a general covenant with the Arabs that no one would be prevented from the Sacred House, and similar truces. This verse annulled that, and it set a term of four months for all of them. Whoever had a specific covenant with the Prophet ﷺ and had less than four months remaining of it, it was completed to four months. Whoever had a term longer than four months, his covenant was fulfilled for him, except if he was among those suspected of a breach, in which case he was limited to four months. And whoever had no specific covenant was given four months in which to travel freely in the land, meaning to go about in safety, like the flow of water (al-sayh min al-ma'), which is what runs and spreads out. From this is the saying of Tarafa ibn al-'Abd:

"Had I feared this from you, you would not have reached me, until we see horses before me moving freely."

This indicates that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sensed from the disbelievers a breach and a lying in wait against him, except from the excepted group.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: The first of the four months was Shawwal, and at that time the verse was revealed. Its end was at the expiry of the sacred months, which is the end of Muharram fifty days after the day of the announcement. Mujahid said: "al-Hajj al-akbar" is al-Qiran (combining Hajj and 'Umrah in one ihram), and "al-asghar" is al-Ifrad (performing Hajj alone). This has nothing to do with the verse. What Mundhir ibn Sa'id mentioned has already been discussed. It is more fitting that it be described as "al-akbar" as a form of praise, not in relation to a specific "asghar." Rather, the meaning is: the greatest of all the days. So consider this carefully.

A summary of what this verse requires, according to Mujahid and others, regarding the circumstances: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Makkah in the eighth year and appointed 'Attab ibn Usayd over it. He settled the affair of Hunayn and al-Ta'if and returned to Madinah, where he remained until he set out for Tabuk. Then he returned from Tabuk in Ramadan of the ninth year and intended to perform Hajj. Then he considered that the polytheists would perform Hajj that year and circumambulate the House naked, so he said: "I do not want to see that." So he commanded Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, to lead the people in Hajj and sent him off. Then he sent 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, after him on his she-camel al-'Adba', and commanded him to proclaim to the people four things: "No polytheist shall perform Hajj after this year, no one shall enter Paradise except a believing soul (in some narrations: no disbeliever shall enter Paradise), no one shall circumambulate the House naked, and whoever has a covenant with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), it remains valid until its term." In some narrations: "Whoever has a covenant between himself and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), its term is four months during which he may travel freely. When those months are over, then Allah is free of the polytheists, and so is His Messenger."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
I say: they were proclaiming all of this. The part about the covenant-holders was for those who had a covenant and whose breach was suspected, while granting them time until the term was for those about whom no breach was known.

Al-Tabari mentioned that the Arabs said on that day: "We disavow your covenant and the covenant of your cousin, except for [those who fight with] spear-thrusts and sword-blows." Some of them blamed others and said: "What are you doing, when Quraysh has embraced Islam?" So they all embraced Islam, and no one went about touring the land (sayh).

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
At that time people entered the religion of Allah in multitudes. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had commanded 'Ali to recite to the people the first forty verses of Surat Bara'a. It was also said: thirty, and it was said: twenty. In some narrations: ten verses, and in some: nine verses, as mentioned by al-Naqqash. Sulayman ibn Musa al-Shami said: that is twenty-eight verses. 'Ali caught up with Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both, on the road. Abu Bakr said to him: "Are you an amir or one who is commanded?" He said: "Rather, one who is commanded." So they both set out until they reached the season (of Hajj). When Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, delivered the sermon at 'Arafa, he said: "Stand up, O 'Ali, and convey the message of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, stood up and did so. He said: "Then it occurred to me that not all the people had witnessed Abu Bakr's sermon, so I began to follow the tents on the day of sacrifice (al-nahr)."

Most of the reciters read "أنَّ اللهَ بَرِيءٌ" with the alif open, on the assumption of "بِأنَّ اللهَ". Al-Hasan and al-A'raj read "إنَّ اللهَ" with the alif kasra, as a fresh clause, since the proclamation (adhan) carries the sense of speech. Most of the reciters read "وَرَسُولُهُ" in the nominative, as an inchoative (mubtada') with the predicate omitted, and its implied predicate is: "and His Messenger is free of them." This, according to our shaykh, the jurist and teacher Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Badhish, may Allah have mercy on him, is the meaning of coordination with the position (al-'atf 'ala al-mawdi'). That is, he makes the first sentence, which is of the form mubtada' and khabar, a point of familiarity, and this sentence is coordinated to it. It was also said that it is coordinated to the position of the clause before the entry of "anna," which does not change the meaning of the inchoative but emphasizes it. "Idh" has also been read with a kasra, because one does not coordinate to the position of "anna" with a fatha. Consider this, for its permissibility is disputed, because the rule of "anna" is to raise the inchoative's rule, except in this position and what resembles it. This is the view of Abu al-'Abbas and Abu 'Ali, may Allah have mercy on them both. The view of our teacher, in accordance with the implication of Sibawayh's statement, is that there is no position for what "anna" enters upon, since it is declinable, and the effect of the governing word has appeared in it. Also, there is no difference between "anna," "layta," and "la'alla." The consensus is that what these enter upon has no position. It was also said that it is coordinated to the pronoun in "bari'" (the hidden subject), and what made this acceptable is that the intervening prepositional phrase served as emphasis, just as "wa la" appeared in the words of the Exalted: ﴿ما أشْرَكْنا ولا آباؤُنا﴾ (We did not associate anything with Him, nor did our fathers) [al-An'am: 148]. Ibn Abi Ishaq and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "رَسُولَهُ" with the accusative, coordinating it to the form of the written clause. With this verse Mu'awiya tested Abu al-Aswad until he laid down grammar, when he had a reader recite "وَرَسُولُهُ" with a genitive (khafd). The meaning of this verse is: He is free of their covenants and their religions, with a general disavowal that requires separation and the use of the sword.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿فَإنْ تُبْتُمْ﴾ (So if you repent), that is: from disbelief. He promised them, with the condition of repentance, and threatened them, with the condition of turning away. It was permissible for glad tidings to be included within what is disliked, since it came explicitly with that, and the difficulty is removed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 4–5:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Except those with whom you made a treaty among the polytheists, and who have not failed you in anything nor backed anyone against you; so fulfil their treaty to them until their term. Indeed, Allah loves the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿And when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them, and seize them, besiege them, and lie in wait for them at every ambush. But if they repent, establish the prayer, and give the zakat, then let them go their way. Indeed, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.﴾

(p-260) This is the exception mentioned earlier, concerning those polytheists whose treaty had nine months remaining and who had fulfilled the covenant as it should be fulfilled. Qatada said: they are the Quraysh who concluded a covenant with the Muslims at the time of Hudaybiyya.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is rejected, since the Quraysh embraced Islam at the conquest (of Makkah), before the proclamation of all this. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿until their term﴾ means: until the four months mentioned in the verse.

The majority read "yanqusukum" with an unpointed ṣād. 'Ata' ibn Yasar, 'Ikrima and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read "yanqudukum" with a ḍād, from al-naqḍ (breaking), which is appropriate with the covenant; but it is awkward in its transitivity to the pronoun. What makes it acceptable is that breaking (naqḍ) is breaking of fidelity and a right of the one with whom the covenant is made. Likewise "atimmū" is transitive with "ilā" because the covenant is in the sense of what is discharged and what one is released from by it, as though they are demanding the covenant. "Yuẓāhirū" means "yu'āwinū" (they assist), for ẓahr is the helper; it derives from ẓahr (back), as though one supports his back against the other, and the other likewise. His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the God-fearing﴾ is an indication that fulfilling the covenant is part of taqwa (God-consciousness).

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And when the sacred months have passed﴾ — the verse. Insilākh (inslākh, "stripping away") is the departure of a thing from that which it was clothed in, like the skin's stripping from a sheep or a man's removal from his garments; from it is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We strip from it the day﴾ [Yasin: 37]. Thus the passing of the months with their names and rulings from time is likened to this. The discussion of those who made the end of the sacred months a term has already been given, and what is meant by "the sacred months" has been covered, so there is no need to repeat it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿kill the polytheists﴾ is a command to fight the polytheists. The command came in the form "uqtulū" as encouragement and strengthening of the soul, i.e., this is how your command toward them should be. This verse (p-261) abrogated every truce in the Qur'an, or armistice, and what is similar to that. According to what has been mentioned, it abrogates one hundred and fourteen verses. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Suddi and 'Ata' said: this verse is abrogated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then either release them as a favour or ransom them﴾ [Muhammad: 4]. They said: it is not permitted to kill a captive at all in cold blood; either he is shown favour or he is ransomed. Qatada, Mujahid and others said: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then either release them as a favour or ransom them﴾ [Muhammad: 4] is abrogated by this verse, and they said: it is not permitted to show favour to a captive or to ransom him; there is nothing but killing. Ibn Zayd said: both are muhkam (established, not abrogated).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He (Ibn Zayd) did not explain more than this, and his saying is the correct one. The two verses do not resemble each other in meaning, because this verse—His saying, ﴿kill the polytheists﴾, and ﴿seize them and besiege them﴾—are actions that apply only to the fighting enemy who is in the field, and there is no mention or ruling in them concerning a captive. When the unbeliever is taken, he leaves the ranks of this verse and passes to the ruling of the other verse, and that verse has no application except to the captive. Therefore Ibn Zayd's saying is the correct one. His saying, ﴿seize them﴾ means: capture. His saying, ﴿every ambush﴾ means: at places of inattention where they are watched. al-Nabigha said:

*O blamer, indeed folly is part of a young man's pleasure, and indeed death lies in wait for souls.*

The accusative of "kull" (every) is adverbial of place, the preference of al-Zajjaj, or by dropping the preposition, the sense being: "in every ambush" or "at every ambush." Sibawayh related: "He struck the back and the belly."

(p-262) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But if they repent﴾ means: from disbelief; so it includes faith. Then he joined to it the establishment of the prayer and the giving of zakat, as an indication of the place of prayer and zakat in the Sharia. His saying, ﴿then let them go their way﴾ is a grant of safety.

Anas ibn Malik said: this is the religion of Allah with which the messengers came, and it is among the last things revealed before the divergence of desires. Concerning it the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever dies, sincere to Allah, obedient to Him, meets Allah while He is pleased with him." Then He promised forgiveness in the form of a statement about His attributes.

(p-263) His words, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And if any of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection until he hears the words of Allah, then deliver him to his place of safety. That is because they are a people who do not know.﴾ ﴿How can there be a covenant with the polytheists in the sight of Allah and in the sight of His Messenger, except those with whom you made a covenant at al-Masjid al-Haram? So long as they remain upright toward you, be upright toward them. Indeed, Allah loves those who are mindful of Him.﴾

In this verse, after the command to fight the polytheists, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded that whenever a polytheist requests a covenant by which he may be safe, so that he may hear the Qur'an and witness the state of Islam, he should be given that; this is ijara (protection), which derives from jiwar (neighbourhood).

Then he was commanded to convey him to his place of safety if he does not accept Islam and is not guided to it. Al-Hasan said: it is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated), a sunnah until the Day of Resurrection. Mujahid, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: this is mansukh (abrogated) by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then kill the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5]. Others said: the ruling of this verse applied only during the period of the four months which were set as a term for them.

His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿until he hears the words of Allah﴾ means the Qur'an. This is an idafa (construct) of an attribute to the thing described, not an idafa of a creation to its Creator. The meaning is: until he understands its rulings, its commands and its prohibitions. Hearing through the ears is mentioned because it is the path to understanding, and hearing is sometimes used in the speech of the Arabs in the sense of understanding, as when you say to one whom you addressed and who did not accept from you: "You have not heard my words," meaning: you have not understood them. This occurs in the Book of Allah Exalted in a number of places. "Ahad" (anyone) in this verse is in the nominative, governed by a verb which is explained by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿sought your protection﴾; the inceptive construction is weak here because the verb is governed by "in" (if). His saying, Exalted is He: "That" refers to this gentleness in granting protection, in making him hear, and in conveying him to his place of safety. "They do not know" negates their knowledge of the paths of right guidance in following Muhammad (ﷺ).

(p-264) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿How can there be a covenant with the polytheists in the sight of Allah﴾, and so on.

This is an interrogative form, used in the manner of wonder and remote likelihood; that is: in what manner can there be a covenant for the polytheists, when they have broken their pledges and openly transgressed? Then He excepted from the general category of polytheists the people with whom a covenant was made at al-Masjid al-Haram, that is, in its vicinity and direction. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said, as is related from him: what is meant here is Quraysh. Al-Suddi said: what is meant is the Banu Judhayma of al-Dil. Ibn Ishaq said: they are the tribes of Banu Bakr, who had entered, at the time of al-Hudaybiyya, into the truce that existed between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Quraysh; there was no breach except by Quraysh and the Banu al-Dil of Banu Bakr, so the Muslims were commanded to complete the covenant for those who had not broken it. Some said: what is meant is Khuza'a; this was said by Mujahid, but it is rejected by the fact that Khuza'a embraced Islam in the year of the Conquest. Some of those who said that they were Quraysh said: this verse was revealed and they did not stand upright, but rather broke their covenant, so their term of four months was set after that. al-Tabari related this view from Ibn Zayd, and it is weak and self-contradictory, because at the time of the proclamation of the four months, none of Quraysh remained except a Muslim, and that was a year after the Conquest of Makkah; likewise Khuza'a, as al-Tabari and others have said.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who are mindful of Him﴾ means by it those among the believers who fulfil the covenant; therefore it came with a definite expression for the fulfilment of the covenant, implying faith.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 8–10:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿How (can there be a covenant), when if they gain the upper hand over you they will not observe any tie of kinship or covenant regarding you? They please you with their mouths, but their hearts refuse, and most of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾ ﴿They have traded the signs of Allah for a small price, and they have turned (people) away from His way. Evil is what they have been doing.﴾ ﴿They observe neither tie of kinship nor covenant regarding a believer, and it is they who are the transgressors.﴾

After "kayfa" (how) in this verse there is necessarily an elided verb, which is indicated by what precedes it. So it is good to supply: "How can they have a covenant?" Similar to it is the saying of the poet:

*"And tell me that death is in the villages, / so how (can it be)? Here are a hill and a sand dune."*

In "kayfa" here there is an emphasis on the disapproval (istib'ad) found in the first occurrence. "La yarqubu" means: they do not observe and do not guard. The root of *irtiqab* is looking with the eye, and from it comes *al-raqib* (the watcher) in gambling and other things. Then it was said of everyone who guards something and observes it: *raqabahu* and *irtaqabahu*.

Most of the readers read "illan" (إلًّا). 'Ikrima, the client of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "iylan" (إيلًا) with a *ya'* after the hamza, with a light *lam*. A group read "allan" (ألًّا) with a fatha on the hamza. As for those who read "illan," it may be intended to mean Allah, may He be exalted and glorified; this was said by Mujahid and Abu Mijlaz. It is His name in Syriac, Arabicized. From this is the saying of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, when he heard the speech of Musaylima, and said: "This is speech that did not come out of *Il*." It may also be intended to mean the covenant. The Arabs say *illun* for covenant, kinship, protection and similar meanings. From this is the saying of Abu Jahl:

*"For Il over us there is an obligation that we do not neglect, / its strength firm, its cord not broken."*

It may also be intended to mean kinship, for in the language of the Arabs kinship is called *ill*. From this is the saying of Ibn Muqbil:

*"Corrupt people have been ruined by successors who succeeded (their fathers), / they cut the ill and the roots of the womb."*

Abu 'Ubayda recited it as evidence for kinship, and its apparent meaning is that it refers to covenants. From this is the saying of Hassan:

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 11–12:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿But if they repent, establish the prayer, and give the zakat, then they are your brothers in religion. And We detail the verses for a people who know.﴿ ﴿And if they break their oaths after their covenant and revile your religion, then fight the leaders of disbelief, for they have no oaths, so that they may cease.﴾

"Tābū" (repented): they returned from their state, and their repentance includes faith. Then the Exalted joined to their faith the establishment of the prayer and the giving of zakat. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, said: this verse made sacred the blood of the People of the Qibla (the Muslims). Ibn Zayd said: Allah joined the prayer with zakat and was not pleased with one of them without the other.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Upon this, Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, acted at the time of the apostasy (ridda).

Brotherhood in religion is the brotherhood of Islam. The plural of "akh" (brother) in this sense is "ikhwan," while its plural in the sense of blood kinship is "ikhwah," as stated by some philologists. It has also been said that the blood-brother is likewise pluralized as "ikhwan" (p-269), and this is evident from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nor is there any blame upon yourselves that you eat from your houses or the houses of your fathers or the houses of your mothers or the houses of your brothers or the houses of your sisters﴾ [An-Nur: 61]. What clarifies this is His saying at the end of the verse: ﴿or your friends﴾ [An-Nur: 61]. Likewise His saying in this surah: ﴿Say: If your fathers and your sons and your brothers and your spouses...﴾ [At-Tawbah: 24], the verse. As for the brother by affection, the Book of Allah says: ﴿The believers are only brothers﴾ [Al-Hujurat: 10].

Abu Hurayrah said in al-Bukhari: "My brothers from among the Emigrants were occupied by trading in the markets," so from all of this it is established that "akh" is pluralized as "ikhwah" and "ikhwan," whether by blood or by affection. "Tafsil al-ayat" means their explanation and clarification.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if they break their oaths﴾, the verse. Nakth means breaking, and its origin is in everything that was tied and then untied; it is used figuratively for oaths and covenants. His saying ﴿and revile your religion﴾ means by disparagement, by war, and other things that the polytheist does; this is a metaphor. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ when he appointed Usama: "If you revile his command, you had already reviled the command of his father before him," the hadith.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is fitting here to mention something of the reviling of religion by a dhimmi. The well-known position of the school of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, is that if he does any such thing, such as denying the Shari'ah or cursing the Prophet ﷺ and the like, he is killed. It has also been said: if he disbelieves and declares what is known of his creed and disbelief, he is disciplined for the declaration and left alone; and if he disbelieves in something that is not part of his known disbelief, such as cursing and the like, he is killed. Abu Hanifa said in this matter that he is asked to repent (yustatab). (p-270) It was disputed if a dhimmi cursed the Prophet ﷺ and then became Muslim out of fear of being killed. The well-known position of the school is that he is left alone, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Islam erases what came before it." In al-'Utbiyya it is stated that he is killed and does not have a better status than a Muslim.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿then fight the leaders of disbelief﴾ means their heads and notables who lead the people to it. Qatadah said: what is meant by this is Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, and others.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This view—unless it is interpreted as their being mentioned by way of example—is weak, because the verse was revealed long after Badr. It is reported from Hudhayfah that he said: "These have not yet come."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He means: they have not died out; they will live forever and be killed. The most correct thing said in this is that no specific individual is meant; rather the command to fight the leaders of those who break covenants among the disbelievers has been issued until the Day of Resurrection without specification. The circumstances of the disbelieving Arabs and the opponents of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ required that the reference to them first be by His saying: ﴿leaders of disbelief﴾, and they were included under the term at that time, since the one who undertakes fighting the Prophet ﷺ and resisting at the outset of his Shari'ah is the leader of everyone who disbelieves in that Shari'ah until the Day of Resurrection. Then in every generation of disbelievers there come leaders specific to each generation.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr read: "A'immah" (أيِمَّةَ) with a single hamza followed by a kasra-vowelled ya; it is also reported from Nafi' that he lengthened the hamza, and Ibn Abi Uways narrated from him: "A'immah" (أئِمَّةَ) with two hamzas. Its original form is "a'immah," its pattern is af'ilah, the plural of imam, like 'imad and a'midah. The vowel of the mim was moved to the hamza which is the fa' of the verb, the two mims were assimilated, and the hamza was changed to ya' because of its kasra and because two hamzas came together in one word. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read: "A'immah" (أئِمَّةَ), with the same reasoning, except that they did not change the hamza to ya'. Al-Musayyabi from Nafi' read: "A'immah" (آيِمَّةَ) with a long hamza, and Hisham from Abu 'Amir read with a long vowel between the two hamzas. The great majority of people read: "La aymana lahum" (لا أيْمانَ لَهُمْ), in the plural of yamin, and the intended meaning is not the negation of oaths in general, but rather: they have no oaths that are fulfilled and kept. This meaning is close to the verse. Al-Hasan, 'Ata', and Ibn 'Amir alone among the seven read: "La iman lahum" (لا إيمانَ لَهُمْ). This admits of two meanings; the first: there is no belief (taṣdiq). Abu 'Ali said: this is not strong, because it is a repetition, since he has already described the leaders of disbelief as having no faith. So the reading with the kasra of the alif is that it is a verbal noun from amanahu iman, and from it is His saying: ﴿who gave them security from fear﴾. The meaning is that they are not granted security as the People of the Dhimma, the People of the Book, are granted it, since the polytheists had nothing except Islam or the sword. Abu Hatim said: al-Hasan explained his reading as: "There is no Islam for them."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The repetition from which Abu 'Ali fled is valid, because it is an explanation of the ambiguous matter that makes their killing obligatory.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if they break their oaths﴾, the verse. Nakth means breaking, and its origin is in everything that was tied and then untied; it is used figuratively for oaths and covenants. His saying ﴿and revile your religion﴾ means by disparagement, by war, and other things that the polytheist does; this is a metaphor. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ when he appointed Usama: "If you revile his command, you had already reviled the command of his father before him," the hadith.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is fitting here to mention something of the reviling of religion by a dhimmi. The well-known position of the school of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, is that if he does any such thing, such as denying the Shari'ah or cursing the Prophet ﷺ and the like, he is killed. It has also been said: if he disbelieves and declares what is known of his creed and disbelief, he is disciplined for the declaration and left alone; and if he disbelieves in something that is not part of his known disbelief, such as cursing and the like, he is killed. Abu Hanifa said in this matter that he is asked to repent (yustatab). (p-270) It was disputed if a dhimmi cursed the Prophet ﷺ and then became Muslim out of fear of being killed. The well-known position of the school is that he is left alone, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Islam erases what came before it." In al-'Utbiyya it is stated that he is killed and does not have a better status than a Muslim.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿then fight the leaders of disbelief﴾ means their heads and notables who lead the people to it. Qatadah said: what is meant by this is Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, and others.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This view—unless it is interpreted as their being mentioned by way of example—is weak, because the verse was revealed long after Badr. It is reported from Hudhayfah that he said: "These have not yet come."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He means: they have not died out; they will live forever and be killed. The most correct thing said in this is that no specific individual is meant; rather the command to fight the leaders of those who break covenants among the disbelievers has been issued until the Day of Resurrection without specification. The circumstances of the disbelieving Arabs and the opponents of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ required that the reference to them first be by His saying: ﴿leaders of disbelief﴾, and they were included under the term at that time, since the one who undertakes fighting the Prophet ﷺ and resisting at the outset of his Shari'ah is the leader of everyone who disbelieves in that Shari'ah until the Day of Resurrection. Then in every generation of disbelievers there come leaders specific to each generation.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr read: "A'immah" (أيِمَّةَ) with a single hamza followed by a kasra-vowelled ya; it is also reported from Nafi' that he lengthened the hamza, and Ibn Abi Uways narrated from him: "A'immah" (أئِمَّةَ) with two hamzas. Its original form is "a'immah," its pattern is af'ilah, the plural of imam, like 'imad and a'midah. The vowel of the mim was moved to the hamza which is the fa' of the verb, the two mims were assimilated, and the hamza was changed to ya' because of its kasra and because two hamzas came together in one word. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read: "A'immah" (أئِمَّةَ), with the same reasoning, except that they did not change the hamza to ya'. Al-Musayyabi from Nafi' read: "A'immah" (آيِمَّةَ) with a long hamza, and Hisham from Abu 'Amir read with a long vowel between the two hamzas. The great majority of people read: "La aymana lahum" (لا أيْمانَ لَهُمْ), in the plural of yamin, and the intended meaning is not the negation of oaths in general, but rather: they have no oaths that are fulfilled and kept. This meaning is close to the verse. Al-Hasan, 'Ata', and Ibn 'Amir alone among the seven read: "La iman lahum" (لا إيمانَ لَهُمْ). This admits of two meanings; the first: there is no belief (taṣdiq). Abu 'Ali said: this is not strong, because it is a repetition, since he has already described the leaders of disbelief as having no faith. So the reading with the kasra of the alif is that it is a verbal noun from amanahu iman, and from it is His saying: ﴿who gave them security from fear﴾. The meaning is that they are not granted security as the People of the Dhimma, the People of the Book, are granted it, since the polytheists had nothing except Islam or the sword. Abu Hatim said: al-Hasan explained his reading as: "There is no Islam for them."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The repetition from which Abu 'Ali fled is valid, because it is an explanation of the ambiguous matter that makes their killing obligatory.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verse 13–15:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths, and resolved to expel the Messenger, and they began (the hostility) against you first? Do you fear them? God has more right that you fear Him, if you are believers.﴾ ﴿Fight them; God will punish them at your hands, and disgrace them, and give you victory over them, and heal the breasts of a believing people,﴾ ﴿and remove the rage of their hearts. And God relents toward whomever He wills. God is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Will you not fight﴾ is an exhortation and urging (taḥḍīḍ). His saying: ﴿and they resolved to expel the Messenger, and they began (the hostility) against you first﴾. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: the intended meaning is "from Medina." This holds good, as in the battles of Uhud, the Confederates (al-Aḥzāb), and others. Al-Suddi said: the intended meaning is "from Mecca." So on this reading the meaning is: they resolved and acted; or it is said they resolved to expel him by their hands, but they did not reach that, rather he went out by the command of God, the Mighty and Majestic. This is consistent with the Prophet's ﷺ rejection of Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith's saying:

"He drove me away for God's sake, from one I drove away in every driving."

Expulsion is not attributed to them except when the speech is in the context of blaming them, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿and expelling its people from it is greater in the sight of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217], and His saying: ﴿from your town which has expelled you﴾ [Muhammad: 13]. The first (interpretation) holds that what they did to him was among the causes of expulsion, which is expulsion itself.

His saying: ﴿first time﴾ — it is said that it refers to their actions in Mecca against the Prophet ﷺ and the believers. Mujahid said it refers to what Quraysh initiated by aiding the Banu Bakr, their allies, against Khuza'ah, the allies of the Messenger of God ﷺ; so this was the beginning of the breaking (of the treaty). Al-Tabari said: it means their action on the day of Badr. His saying: ﴿Do you fear them?﴾ is an interrogative in the sense of affirmation and rebuke. His saying: ﴿God﴾ is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿has more right﴾ is its predicate (khabar). ﴿That you fear Him﴾ is either an apposition (badal) to the name of God, a badal of inclusion (ishtimal), or in the accusative position by dropping the preposition, its estimate being: "in that you fear Him." It is also permissible that "God" is a subject, "has more right" is a second subject, and "that you fear Him" is the predicate of the second, and the whole clause is the predicate of the first. His saying: ﴿if you are believers﴾ is like your saying: "Do such-and-such if you are a man," i.e., a complete man. So its meaning is: if you are believers of complete faith, for their faith had already been firmly established.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Fight them; God will punish them﴾ — the verse. The preceding verses established the deeds of the disbelievers, then He urged fighting, linking it to their sins, so that zeal would be stirred along with it. Then in this verse He firmly commanded fighting them, coupled with a promise and a decree that includes victory over them and triumph against them. His saying: ﴿will punish them﴾ means: by killing and capture, and all of that is punishment. ﴿And disgrace them﴾ means: He humiliates them for their sins. It is said: "khaziya al-rajul yakhza khizyan" when a man is humiliated by falling into shame, and "akhzāhu ghayruhu" when another causes it; and "khaziya yakhza khizāyatan" when he feels shame.

As for His saying: ﴿and heal the breasts of a believing people﴾, the speech may be understood to mean the community of believers in general, since everything that removes disbelief is a healing for the grief in the breasts of believers. It may also be understood to specify a particular group of believers. It is narrated that they were Khuza'ah; this was said by Mujahid and al-Suddi. The reason for specifying them is that they were the ones against whom the covenant was broken and upon whom war fell, and there were many believers among Khuza'ah at that time. This is supported by the saying of the Khuza'i about seeking the Prophet's ﷺ aid:

"...then we became Muslims, and a hand was not withdrawn..."

And at the end of the rajaz he says:

"...and they killed us while bowing and prostrating."

The majority of readers recited "and remove the rage of their hearts" with the verb ascribed to God, the Mighty and Majestic. A group recited "and the rage of their hearts will go away" with the verb ascribed to the rage. The majority recited "and He relents" with the nominative (raf'), as a resumption (qaṭ') from what precedes it, the meaning being that the verse begins a fresh statement that He may relent toward some of these disbelievers whom He commanded to be fought. Abu al-Fath said: this is an existing matter whether they are fought or not, so there is no basis for including repentance in the conditional response of the imperative "fight them" in the accusative reading; rather the correct reading is the nominative, as a resumption and a cutting off. Al-A'raj, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Isa al-Thaqafi, Amr ibn Ubayd, and Abu 'Amr (according to what is narrated from him) recited "and that He relents" with the accusative, with the estimate "and that He relents." This, in my view, is sound if one holds that repentance here is intended to mean that killing the disbelievers and striving in the way of God is a repentance for you, O believers, and a perfection of your faith; thus repentance enters, on this view, into the condition of fighting.

And ﴿All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾ [al-Anfal: 71] are two attributes whose relation to the verse is clear.
