Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 16–17:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Or do you think that you will be left alone while Allah has not yet known those among you who strove and did not take, other than Allah and His Messenger and the believers, any intimate friend (walija). And Allah is Aware of what you do.﴾ ﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah while bearing witness against themselves of disbelief. Those, their deeds have become worthless, and in the Fire they will abide eternally.﴾

"Am" (أم) in this verse is not the equalizing particle (al-mu'adilah). Rather, it is the intermediate one in speech (al-mutawassit fi al-kalam). According to Sibawayh, it is the one that implies a turning away from the wording and not its meaning, and an interrogation. So it takes the place of "bal" (rather) together with the interrogative alif. It is the one in the saying: "Innaha la-ibilun am sha'" (Indeed it is camels, or sheep?), the implied meaning being: "Bal ahiya sha'?" (Rather, is it sheep?). His words ﴿an tutraku﴾ (that you will be left) take the place, according to Sibawayh, of the two objects of "hasiba" (to think). Al-Mubarrad said: "An" and what follows it is the first object, and the second is omitted.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It seems its implied meaning is: "unattended" (muhmalin), or "aimless" (suda), or something similar.

His words, Exalted is He: "wa-lamma" (وَلَمّا) is "ma" joined to "lam", and in it there is emphasis. The meaning of the verse: (p-275) Do you suppose that you will be left without testing and trial? So "lamma" in this verse is like the words of the poet:

By the hands of men who have not wiped clean their swords, * and in which the slain have not multiplied when they were drawn.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The intended meaning of His words ﴿wa-lamma ya'lam﴾ (and Allah has not yet known) is: He has not yet known that as existing, as He knew it from eternity on the condition of existence; and your action and acquisition on which reward and punishment fall has not yet manifested. So there is figurative usage (tajawwuz) in the expression. Otherwise, it is certain that Allah had known from eternity those whom He described with this attribute, their existence being conditional, and knowledge does not newly arise for Him, exalted is He above that.

And ﴿walija﴾ means: intimate friend (bitanah) and confidant (dakhilah). 'Ubada ibn Safwan al-Ghanawi said:

Their intimates in every open and gathering * ... to everyone who is hoped for and everyone who is feared.

It is derived from "al-wulud" (entering), so the meaning is: a hidden matter of what the truth disapproves of.

This verse addresses the believers, and its meaning is that there is necessarily their testing. It is like His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the example of those who passed away before you?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214], and like His words: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 1] ﴿Do people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tried?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 2]. In this verse there is a criticism of the hypocrites who took intimate friends, especially when fighting was prescribed. The majority of readers recited "wa-Allahu khabirun bima ta'malun" (and Allah is Aware of what you do) with the "ta" (second person address), while al-Hasan, and Ya'qub in the narration of Ruways, and Salam recited with the "ya" (third person), as a report about an absent party.

(p-276) His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿It is not for the polytheists...﴾ the verse. Its meaning: it is not for the polytheists, by right of entitlement, to maintain (ya'muru) [the mosques]. This is what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, negated. Otherwise, they had maintained His mosques in the past and in the present, by domination and oppression. Hammad ibn Abi Salamah, from Ibn Kathir, and al-Jahdari recited "masjid Allah" in the singular in both places. Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-A'raj, Shayba, Abu Ja'far, Mujahid, Qatadah, and others recited "masajid" in the plural in both places. Ibn Kathir also, and Abu 'Amr, recited "masjid" in the singular in the first place and "masajid" in the plural in the second, as if he first mentioned the specific occasion of that time, then generalized the mosques in the second place in the ruling that remains as long as the world lasts. The plural form implies the generality of all mosques, and it is possible that by it is meant the Sacred Mosque alone in both places, on the basis that each place of prostration is considered a mosque and then they are collectively referred to in the plural. The singular form in both places implies the specificity of the Sacred Mosque alone, and it is possible that by it is meant the genus, so it encompasses all mosques. Its being in construct form does not prevent this, as was held by one who has no insight. Abu 'Ali said: the second in this reading is meant as the first, and all other mosques have the same ruling as the Sacred Mosque.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿bearing witness against themselves of disbelief﴾ refer to their state, since their statements and actions require acknowledgment of disbelief and adornment with it. It was also said: the reference is to their saying in the talbiyah: "Except a partner who is Yours, You own him and what he owns," and the like. Al-Tabari related from al-Suddi that he said: the reference is to the Christian saying, "I am a Christian," and the Jew likewise, and the idolater says, "I am a polytheist."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This has not been transmitted. Then Allah, Exalted is He, judged against them that their deeds have become worthless (habitat), i.e., have become void. I do not know that this root is used except in striving and working. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 16–17:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Or do you think that you will be left alone while Allah has not yet known those among you who strove and did not take, other than Allah and His Messenger and the believers, any intimate friend (walija). And Allah is Aware of what you do.﴾ ﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah while bearing witness against themselves of disbelief. Those, their deeds have become worthless, and in the Fire they will abide eternally.﴾

"Am" (أم) in this verse is not the equalizing particle (al-mu'adilah). Rather, it is the intermediate one in speech (al-mutawassit fi al-kalam). According to Sibawayh, it is the one that implies a turning away from the wording and not its meaning, and an interrogation. So it takes the place of "bal" (rather) together with the interrogative alif. It is the one in the saying: "Innaha la-ibilun am sha'" (Indeed it is camels, or sheep?), the implied meaning being: "Bal ahiya sha'?" (Rather, is it sheep?). His words ﴿an tutraku﴾ (that you will be left) take the place, according to Sibawayh, of the two objects of "hasiba" (to think). Al-Mubarrad said: "An" and what follows it is the first object, and the second is omitted.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It seems its implied meaning is: "unattended" (muhmalin), or "aimless" (suda), or something similar.

His words, Exalted is He: "wa-lamma" (وَلَمّا) is "ma" joined to "lam", and in it there is emphasis. The meaning of the verse: (p-275) Do you suppose that you will be left without testing and trial? So "lamma" in this verse is like the words of the poet:

By the hands of men who have not wiped clean their swords, * and in which the slain have not multiplied when they were drawn.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The intended meaning of His words ﴿wa-lamma ya'lam﴾ (and Allah has not yet known) is: He has not yet known that as existing, as He knew it from eternity on the condition of existence; and your action and acquisition on which reward and punishment fall has not yet manifested. So there is figurative usage (tajawwuz) in the expression. Otherwise, it is certain that Allah had known from eternity those whom He described with this attribute, their existence being conditional, and knowledge does not newly arise for Him, exalted is He above that.

And ﴿walija﴾ means: intimate friend (bitanah) and confidant (dakhilah). 'Ubada ibn Safwan al-Ghanawi said:

Their intimates in every open and gathering * ... to everyone who is hoped for and everyone who is feared.

It is derived from "al-wulud" (entering), so the meaning is: a hidden matter of what the truth disapproves of.

This verse addresses the believers, and its meaning is that there is necessarily their testing. It is like His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the example of those who passed away before you?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214], and like His words: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 1] ﴿Do people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tried?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 2]. In this verse there is a criticism of the hypocrites who took intimate friends, especially when fighting was prescribed. The majority of readers recited "wa-Allahu khabirun bima ta'malun" (and Allah is Aware of what you do) with the "ta" (second person address), while al-Hasan, and Ya'qub in the narration of Ruways, and Salam recited with the "ya" (third person), as a report about an absent party.

(p-276) His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿It is not for the polytheists...﴾ the verse. Its meaning: it is not for the polytheists, by right of entitlement, to maintain (ya'muru) [the mosques]. This is what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, negated. Otherwise, they had maintained His mosques in the past and in the present, by domination and oppression. Hammad ibn Abi Salamah, from Ibn Kathir, and al-Jahdari recited "masjid Allah" in the singular in both places. Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-A'raj, Shayba, Abu Ja'far, Mujahid, Qatadah, and others recited "masajid" in the plural in both places. Ibn Kathir also, and Abu 'Amr, recited "masjid" in the singular in the first place and "masajid" in the plural in the second, as if he first mentioned the specific occasion of that time, then generalized the mosques in the second place in the ruling that remains as long as the world lasts. The plural form implies the generality of all mosques, and it is possible that by it is meant the Sacred Mosque alone in both places, on the basis that each place of prostration is considered a mosque and then they are collectively referred to in the plural. The singular form in both places implies the specificity of the Sacred Mosque alone, and it is possible that by it is meant the genus, so it encompasses all mosques. Its being in construct form does not prevent this, as was held by one who has no insight. Abu 'Ali said: the second in this reading is meant as the first, and all other mosques have the same ruling as the Sacred Mosque.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿bearing witness against themselves of disbelief﴾ refer to their state, since their statements and actions require acknowledgment of disbelief and adornment with it. It was also said: the reference is to their saying in the talbiyah: "Except a partner who is Yours, You own him and what he owns," and the like. Al-Tabari related from al-Suddi that he said: the reference is to the Christian saying, "I am a Christian," and the Jew likewise, and the idolater says, "I am a polytheist."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This has not been transmitted. Then Allah, Exalted is He, judged against them that their deeds have become worthless (habitat), i.e., have become void. I do not know that this root is used except in striving and working. It may be that it is from "al-habat," which is a fatal disease that afflicts grazing livestock when they eat, a harmful thing (p-277) and it is what is in his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Indeed, among what spring rain makes grow is what kills by habat or causes distress," the hadith...

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 18–19:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Only those maintain the mosques of Allah who believe in Allah and the Last Day, establish prayer, give zakat (obligatory alms), and fear none but Allah. It is they who may be among the guided.﴾ ﴿Do you consider the providing of water for the pilgrims and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque equal to one who believes in Allah and the Last Day and strives in the way of Allah? They are not equal in the sight of Allah. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

The meaning of this verse: "Only those maintain the mosques of Allah" with what is right and obligatory for them. The wording of this verse is a statement of fact, but within it is an instruction to the believers to maintain the mosques. Some of the early pious predecessors (al-salaf) said: "When you see a man who maintains the mosques, think well of him." Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you see a man who frequents the mosques, then testify for him that he has faith." The discussion of the reading of "masajid" has already been given earlier.

His saying, ﴿and the Last Day, establish prayer and give zakat﴾, includes faith in the Messenger, since these things are only received from him. His saying, ﴿and fear none but Allah﴾: the alif has been dropped from "yakhsha" (fear) for the jussive mood (jazm). Sibawayh said: "Know that when the final letter is pronounced with sukun in the nominative (raf'), it is dropped in the jussive, so that the jussive does not become the same as the nominative." He means the fear of reverence, worship and obedience. This is the rank of justice among people. Without doubt, a person fears others and fears worldly dangers, but he should fear, in all of that, the decree of Allah and His disposal of affairs. And "'asa" (perhaps) from Allah is binding wherever it occurs in the Qur'an. Allah does not hope for guidance except for those who have attained this great rank of justice. In this is a powerful exhortation to piety.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read: "Do you consider the siqaya (providing water) of the pilgrims and the 'imara (maintenance) of the Sacred Mosque..." Ibn al-Zubayr, Abu Hamza, Muhammad ibn 'Ali, and Abu Ja'far al-Qari read: "Do you consider the saqat (water-carriers) of the pilgrims and 'amarat (caretakers) of the Sacred Mosque..." Ibn Jubayr also read it in this way, except that he put "al-masjid" in the accusative, intending the tanwin (nunation) on "'amara" (the caretaker). Al-Dahhak, Abu Wajza, and Abu Ja'far al-Qari read: "siqaya" with a damma on the sin, and "'amara." As for those who read "siqaya" and "'imara," then in the sentence, according to them, something is elided, either at its beginning or at its end. Either one estimates: "Do you consider the people of the provision of water..." or one estimates: "like the deed of one who believes in Allah..." As for those who read "saqat" and "'amara," their reading is straightforward. As for the reading of al-Dahhak, it is the plural of "saqin" (water-carrier), except that he gave its first letter a damma, as they said: "'urq" and "'uraq" (root and roots), and "zi'r" and "zu'ar" (a suckling mother-camel and its young). Its analogy would be to say "suqa'" but if it is feminine, as the plurals "hijara" (stones) and others are made feminine.

The provision of water for the pilgrims was held by the Banu Hashim, and al-'Abbas was in charge of it. Al-Hasan said: "When this verse was revealed, al-'Abbas said: 'I think I will only leave the siqaya.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Remain in charge of it, for it is good for you.'"

As for the 'imara of the mosque, it was said: it is guarding it from injustice within it, or it is said: (keeping it free from) abuse (hujr). This was entrusted to al-'Abbas. It was also said: it is al-sadana, the service of the House specifically, and it was held by the Banu 'Abd al-Dar. 'Uthman ibn Talha ibn Abi Talha (the name of Abi Talha being 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza ibn 'Abd al-Dar) and Shayba ibn 'Uthman ibn Abi Talha, the one mentioned, were in charge of it. These are the two to whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) handed the key of the Ka'ba on the second day of the Conquest, after al-'Abbas and 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with them both) had requested it. "The Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'Uthman and Shayba: 'A day of fidelity and righteousness. Take it, eternal and inherited; no one will dispute it with you except a wrongdoer.'"

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He means the sadana. People differed regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse. It was said: the disbelievers of Quraysh said to the Jews: "We provide water to the pilgrims and maintain the House. Are we better, or Muhammad (ﷺ) and his religion?" The rabbis of the Jews said to them: "Rather, you are." So the verse was revealed concerning that. It was also said: the disbelievers boasted with this, so the verse was revealed concerning that. al-Tabari reported on the authority of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir that he said: "I was near the pulpit of the Prophet (ﷺ) with a group of his companions. One of them said: 'I wish for nothing after Islam except to be the one who gives water to the pilgrims.' Another said: 'Except to be the servant of the House and its maintainer.' The third said: 'Except to be a fighter in the way of Allah.' 'Umar ibn al-Khattab heard them and said: 'Be silent until I enter upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and ask him for a ruling.' He entered and asked him, and the verse was revealed concerning that." Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: the Muslims reproached the prisoners of Badr for their disbelief. Al-'Abbas said: "Rather, we are the water-carriers of the pilgrims and the caretakers of the House." So the verse was revealed concerning that. Mujahid said: they were commanded to emigrate, and al-'Abbas said: "I give water to the pilgrims," and 'Uthman ibn Talha said: "I am the chamberlain of the Ka'ba, so we will not emigrate." So the verse was revealed: ﴿Do you consider the providing of water for the pilgrims...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿until Allah brings His command﴾ [al-Tawba: 24]. Mujahid said: all of this was before the Conquest of Mecca. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: al-'Abbas, 'Ali and 'Uthman ibn Talha boasted, so al-'Abbas said: "I am the water-carrier of the pilgrims." 'Uthman said: "I am the maintainer of the House, and if I wished, I could stay the night in it." 'Ali said: "I am the companion in fighting the disbelievers with the Prophet (ﷺ), and I believed and emigrated earlier." So the verse was revealed concerning that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 20–23:

His the Mighty and Majestic's saying:

﴿Those who have believed and emigrated and struggled in the way of Allah with their wealth and their lives are greater in rank with Allah. And those are the attainers of success.﴾ ﴿Their Lord gives them good tidings of a mercy from Him and approval and gardens for them wherein is enduring pleasure.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein forever. Indeed, Allah has with Him a great reward.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, do not take your fathers and your brothers as allies if they prefer disbelief over faith. And whoever of you allies with them, then it is those who are the wrongdoers.﴾

When Allah, Exalted is He, decreed in the preceding verse that the two groups are not equal, He clarified that in this last verse and made it explicit. He enumerated faith, emigration, and struggle with wealth and self, and ruled that the people of these qualities are greater in rank with Allah than all of creation. Then He ruled that they will attain success through His mercy and His approval. Success (al-fawz) is the attainment of the desired aim, either in obtaining a wish or in being saved from destruction. The hadith that came in regard to the meaning of this verse is relevant: "Leave my companions to me, for if one of you were to spend gold equal to Uhud, it would not reach a mudd of one of them, nor half of it."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Because the men of these qualities, it is upon their swords that Islam was established, and they returned people to the Sharia.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Their Lord gives them good tidings﴾ to the end of the verse, this is a verse of promise. The recitation of the people is "yubashshiruhum" with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the shīn, shaddated. Al-A'mash, Talha ibn Musarrif, and Humayd ibn Hilal recited "yabshuruhum" with a fatha on the yā', a sukun on the bā', and a damma on the shīn, lightened. Al-Tabari transmitted through Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: I have given you something better than this. They say: Our Lord, what thing is better than this? He says: My approval." And in al-Bukhari, in the Book of the Sunnah from it: "So I will never be displeased with you ever."

The majority recited "wa-ridwanun" with a kasra on the rā'. 'Asim and 'Amr recited "wa-ruḍwanun" with a damma on the rā'. Al-A'mash recited with a damma on both the rā' and the ḍād. Abu Hatim said: this is not permissible.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take your fathers﴾ to the end of the verse.

The apparent address of this verse is to all believers without exception, and its ruling remains in effect until the Day of Resurrection. A group has related that this verse was revealed only to urge emigration and to renounce the lands of disbelief. Thus the address, according to this view, is to the believers who were in Makkah and other lands of the Arabs, who were addressed not to take as allies their fathers and brothers, lest they follow them into dwelling in lands of disbelief. The sons were not mentioned in this verse, because it is most common among people that sons are the followers of their fathers. "Al-ikhwan" in this verse is the plural of the brother by lineage, and likewise in His saying: ﴿or the houses of your brothers﴾ [al-Nur: 61].

Ibn 'Umar's reading... (Isa ibn 'Umar recited "an istahabbu" with a fatha on the alif of "an", and the majority recited "in" with a kasra on the alif, as a conditional. "Istahabbu" here implies the meaning of "preferred and chose," and for this reason it takes "ʿalā.")

Then Allah, Exalted is He, ruled that whoever allies with them and follows them in their aims, then he is a wrongdoer, meaning one who places a thing other than its proper place. This is the wrongdoing of disobedience, not the wrongdoing of disbelief.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verse 24:

His words, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, your kinsfolk, the wealth you have acquired, the commerce you fear may decline, and the dwellings you are pleased with are dearer to you than God and His Messenger and striving in His cause, then wait until God brings about His command. And God does not guide the defiant people.﴾

This verse strengthens the view of those who held that it and the one before it are aimed at urging emigration (hijrah). Within His words ﴿So wait﴾ is a clear threat. As for His words "bi-amrihi" (His command), al-Hasan said: it refers to a punishment or chastisement from God. Mujahid said: it refers to the conquest of Makkah. The meaning is: when God brings His command, you will not have secured what would have earned you reward and standing in Islam.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The sons are mentioned in the verse because love brings them to mind, and sons are foremost in love. They are not like this in that their fathers follow them in their opinions, as in the preceding verse. The majority of people read ﴿wa-'ashiratukum﴾ (and your kinsfolk, singular). 'Asim alone read it with a variant from him, and Abu Raja', Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and 'Ismah read ﴿wa-'asheeratukum﴾ (plural). This plural reading is良 (good) because every person has a clan (ʿashīra) specific to him. The singular is also良 because Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash said: the Arabs form the plural as "'asha'ir" and hardly say "'asheerat." ﴿Iqtaraftumuha﴾ means: you have earned them. The root of iqtiraf and muqarafah is: approaching a thing. ﴿And commerce you fear may decline﴾ is clear regarding types of wealth. Ibn al-Mubarak said: (p-283) it refers to daughters who do not marry and for whom no suitor is found. "Masakin" is the plural of "maskan" with a fatha on the kaf; it is a pattern (mafal) from al-suknā (dwelling), and whatever of this type has a weak initial radical (mu'tall al-fa') comes on the pattern mafil with a kasra on the ʿayn, like "mawʿid" and "mawṭin." "Masakin" means palaces and houses. "Ahabba" is the predicate of kana (was). Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf used to read it as "ahabbu" with a damma. He had an account concerning this with Yahya ibn Ya'mar. Al-Hajjaj asked him: "Do you hear me making a grammatical error?" He said: "Yes, in this letter." He mentioned to him the nominative "ahabbu," and he denied it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

That is permissible in Arabic on the basis that the pronoun of the matter and situation (ḍamīr al-amr wa-al-shaʾn) is implied in kana, but it was not read that way. His words, exalted is He: ﴿And God does not guide the defiant people﴾ is a general wording intended to be particular, applying to those who die in their defiance, or it is an absolute generality meaning that there is no guidance from the standpoint of defiance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 25–27:

His the Exalted and Majestic's saying:

﴿Allah has already given you victory in many battlefields, and on the day of Hunayn, when your great number pleased you but it availed you nothing, and the earth, spacious as it is, became confining for you, then you turned back in retreat.﴾ ﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and sent down hosts you did not see, and He punished those who disbelieved. And that is the recompense of the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿Then Allah relents after that to whom He wills. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

This is an address to all the believers, in which Allah enumerates His blessings upon them. "Mawatin" is the plural of "mawtin" (with a kasra on the ta'), and the mawtin is the place of residence or dwelling, because it is the first of residence. The battlefields referred to are Badr, the Trench, al-Nadir, and Qurayza. "Mawatin" is not declined (lam yunsaraf) because it is a plural and a plural of a plural's final form (nihayat jam'). "Yawm" is conjoined either to the place of "fi mawatin" (i.e., in grammatical position) or to the wording with the implied phrase "and in the day of," so the preposition is elided. "Hunayn" is a valley between Makkah and al-Ta'if, near Dhu al-Majaz. It is declined when it is intended as a place and location; if it were intended as a plot of land, it would not be declined, as the poet said:

*They gave victory to their Prophet and strengthened his back*
*at Hunayn, on the day when heroes were devoured by one another.*

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿when your great number pleased you﴾, it is narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, when he saw his army of twelve thousand: "We will never be defeated today due to small numbers." And it is narrated that a man among his companions said it, and Allah willed to show their weakness, so it appeared when the people fled; then destiny turned back with His victory.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and the earth became confining for you despite its vastness﴾, meaning: to the extent that it is spacious and wide, due to the severity of the situation and its hardship; so "ma" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya).

As for His saying: ﴿then you turned back in retreat﴾, it refers to the people fleeing from the Prophet ﷺ.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The summary of this story is that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ conquered Makkah, he had ten thousand of his companions, and two thousand of the Tulaqa' joined him, so he became twelve thousand. The disbelieving Arabs heard of this and it grieved them. Hawazin and their allies gathered against him, led by Malik ibn 'Awf al-Nasri, and Thaqif, led by 'Abd Yalil ibn 'Amr, and mixed groups of people joined them until they were thirty thousand. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out to them until they gathered at Hunayn. When the people lined up, the polytheists charged from the sides of the valley, and the Muslims were routed. Qatada said: It is said that the Tulaqa' from the people of Makkah fled and intended to spread defeat among the Muslims. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was on a white mule, and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Fihri said: "I was with the Prophet ﷺ that day, and he was on a horse, surrounded by al-'Abbas, his uncle, and his cousin Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, and before him was Ayman ibn Umm Ayman—and he was later killed, may Allah have mercy on him. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw the severity of the situation, he dismounted from his mule to the ground—so said al-Bara' ibn 'Azib—and sought victory from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. He took a handful of dust and pebbles and threw them at the faces of the disbelievers, saying: 'Shahat al-wujuh' (may the faces be disfigured)." Abu 'Abd al-Rahman said: he stretched from his horse and took a handful of dust, and the angels descended to aid him, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called out: "O for the Ansar!" and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered al-'Abbas to call out: "Where are the companions of the tree? Where are the companions of Surat al-Baqara?" So the people returned as one body and the polytheists were routed. Ya'la ibn 'Ata' said: "Their sons narrated to me from their fathers, saying: None of us remained except that some of that dust entered his eyes." The full account of this story is in the books of biography (al-siyar).

The apparent meaning of al-Nahhas's words is that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was with fourteen thousand, and this is an error. His saying "mudbirin" is an accusative of the emphatic circumstantial type (hal mu'akkida), like His saying: ﴿and it is the truth, confirming﴾ [al-Baqara: 91]. The emphatic circumstantial is the one whose preceding context indicates it, as the meaning of "tawalli" indicates "idbar."

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquility﴾ and so on, "thumma" here retains its original sense of sequence. "Sakina" is the victory in which souls and circumstances find rest. The reference to "the believers" is to the Ansar according to what has been narrated, since "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called out on that day: 'O assembly of the Ansar!'" So they returned and repelled the defeat. "Junud" are the angels and terror. Abu Hajir Yazid ibn 'Amir said: "There was in our insides something like the striking of a stone in a basin from terror." The punishment of those who disbelieved is the killing that spread among them and the capture that befell their families, and Malik ibn 'Awf al-Nasri had brought the people out with their dependents and children so they would fight for them. Durayd ibn al-Simma criticized him for this, and said to Malik ibn 'Awf: "Shepherd of sheep! Will anything turn back the one who has fled?" On that day Durayd ibn al-Simma was killed in his famous death, killed by Rabi' ibn Rafi' ibn Uhban al-Sulami—it is also said Ibn al-Dughunna.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then Allah relents after that to whom He wills﴾, it is an announcement that whoever of the disbelievers who escaped that day embraces Islam and repents, they are accepted, Muslims, promised forgiveness and mercy.

The punishment of those who disbelieved is the killing that spread among them and the capture that befell their families, and Malik ibn 'Awf al-Nasri had brought the people out with their dependents and children so they would fight for them. Durayd ibn al-Simma criticized him for this, and said to Malik ibn 'Awf: "Shepherd of sheep! Will anything turn back the one who has fled?" On that day Durayd ibn al-Simma was killed in his famous death, killed by Rabi' ibn Rafi' ibn Uhban al-Sulami—it is also said Ibn al-Dughunna.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then Allah relents after that to whom He wills﴾, it is an announcement that whoever of the disbelievers who escaped that day embraces Islam and repents, they are accepted, Muslims, promised forgiveness and mercy.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verse 28:

His the Exalted's saying:

﴿O you who have believed, the polytheists are only impure, so let them not approach al-Masjid al-Haram after this year of theirs. And if you fear poverty, Allah will enrich you from His bounty, if He wills. Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾

Qatada, Ma'mar ibn Rashid, and others said: The description of the polytheist as "impure" (najas) is only because he is in a state of janabah (major ritual impurity), since his washing from janabah is not a valid washing. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: Rather, the meaning of polytheism is what made him impure, like the impurity of wine. al-Hasan al-Basri said: Whoever shakes hands with a polytheist, let him perform wudu'.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Whoever said "because of janabah" made washing obligatory for one who shakes hands with polytheists, while whoever held the other view did not make washing obligatory. The whole school (madhhab) holds the view that washing is obligatory, except Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, who said: It is not obligatory.

Abu Hayawa read "nijs" with a kasra on the nun and a sukun on the jim.

(p-287) Allah the Exalted, in this verse, specified the polytheists and the Sacred Mosque. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and others analogized all disbelievers, from the People of the Book and others, to the polytheists, and analogized all mosques to the Sacred Mosque, and prohibited all of them from entering all mosques. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz likewise wrote to his governors, and cited this verse in his letter. The saying of the Exalted supports this: ﴿in houses which Allah has permitted to be raised﴾ [al-Nur: 36]. al-Shafi'i said: It is general regarding disbelievers, but specific to the Sacred Mosque, so he permitted Jews, Christians, and idolaters to enter the other mosques. Among his proofs is the hadith of the tying of Thumama ibn Uthal. Abu Hanifa said: It is specific to idol-worshippers and to the Sacred Mosque, so he permitted Jews and Christians to enter the Sacred Mosque and other mosques, and idol-worshippers to enter all other mosques. 'Ata' said: The description of the mosque as "sacred" and the prohibition of approaching it requires their prohibition from the entire Haram.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The strength of His saying ﴿so let them not approach﴾ requires that the Muslims prevent them. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and Qatada said: No polytheist may approach the Sacred Mosque except one who is a holder of the jizya or a slave of a Muslim. Idol-worshippers are polytheists by consensus.

There is disagreement regarding the People of the Book. The position of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar and others is that they are polytheists, while the majority of scholars said: They are not polytheists. The benefit of this disagreement becomes clear in the jurisprudence of their marriages, their slaughtered animals, and other matters.

His the Exalted's saying ﴿after this year of theirs﴾ means: after the year nine of the Hijra, which was the year Abu Bakr led the people in Hajj and 'Ali proclaimed the surah of Bara'a. (p-288) As for His the Exalted's saying ﴿and if you fear poverty﴾, 'Amr ibn Fa'id said: The meaning is: "and when you fear".

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a non-Arabic usage (ujma), and the meaning is excellent with "wa-in". When the Muslims were prevented from the polytheists' seasonal gathering, and they used to bring food and trade goods, Satan cast into their souls the fear of poverty, and they said: From where will we live? So Allah promised them that He would enrich them from His bounty. al-Dahhak said: He opened for them the door of taking the jizya from the protected people (ahl al-dhimma), through His saying ﴿Fight those who do not believe﴾ [al-Tawba: 29] up to His saying ﴿while they are humbled﴾ [al-Tawba: 29]. 'Ikrima said: He enriched them by abundant rain upon them.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The Arabs embraced Islam, so their Hajj and trade continued, and Allah enriched them from His bounty through jihad and dominance over the nations.

Al-'ayla (poverty) means destitution. It is said: "'ala al-rajul ya'ilu 'aylatan" when he became poor. The poet said:

"The poor man does not know when his wealth will come, and the wealthy man does not know when he will become poor."

'Alqama and others among the companions of Ibn Mas'ud read "ā'ila(tan)", which is a verbal noun like al-qa'ila from qala yaqilu, and like al-'aqiba and al-'afiya. It may also be an adjective for an omitted noun, its estimated form being "ḥālan 'ā'ila(tan)". al-Tabari related that it is said: "'ala ya'ulu" when one becomes poor.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verse 29:

His the Exalted, the Majestic, saying:

﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day, and do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, and do not adopt the religion of truth from among those who were given the Book, until they give the jizyah willingly while they are humbled.﴾

This verse includes the fighting of the People of the Book, from among the Jews and the Christians, until they either are killed or pay the jizyah (the poll tax levied on non-Muslim subjects). Mujahid said: When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ set out to campaign against the Romans and marched toward Tabuk. Whoever considers the People of the Book to be polytheists, this verse abrogates for him (naskh) by what it contains of taking the jizyah, due to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then kill the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5]. He denied them faith in Allah and the Last Day because they abandoned the law of Islam, which it is obligatory for them to enter. Thus all that they have regarding Allah, Exalted and Majestic, and regarding the Resurrection, is of imaginings and beliefs that have no meaning, since they received them from other than their proper source. Also, their beliefs were not sound, because they split into sects and said: ʿUzayr is the son of Allah, and Allah is the third of three, and other than that. They also hold many opinions regarding the Resurrection, such as buying houses in Paradise from the monks, and the saying of the Jews about the Fire: "We will remain in it for a number of days," and the like.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden﴾, it clarifies and explicitly states their opposition to Muhammad ﷺ. As for His saying: ﴿and do not adopt﴾, its meaning is: do not obey and comply. From this is the saying of ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her: "I did not become aware of my parents except that they were adopting the religion (yadinani al-din)." The word al-din (religion) in the language is a shared term (lafẓa mushtaraka), and here it means the sharia (sacred law), as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Al ʿImran: 19]. As for His saying: ﴿from among those who were given the Book﴾, it is explicit regarding the Children of Israel and the Romans, and the people are agreed on this. As for the Magians, Ibn al-Mundhir said: I know of no disagreement that the jizyah is taken from them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is related that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Treat them as you treat the People of the Book (sunnu bihim sunnata ahl al-kitab)." Many of the scholars said: its meaning is in taking the jizyah from them, and they are not People of the Book. According to this, the comparison does not extend to their slaughtered animals or their marriages, and this is what Ibn Habib mentioned in al-Wadiha. Some scholars said: its meaning is: treat them with the practice of the People of the Book, since they are People of a Book, and according to this the comparison extends to their slaughtered animals and other matters. The first view is the opinion of Malik and the majority of his companions. It is also reported that a prophet named Zaradusht had been sent to the Magians. As for the Arab Magians, Ibn Wahb said: no jizyah is accepted from them, and there is no alternative to fighting or Islam. Sahnun, Ibn al-Qasim and Ashhab said: the jizyah is taken from the Magians of the Arabs and from all nations. As for the idol-worshippers of the Arabs, Allah did not exempt them from the jizyah, and no human being of them remains on the earth. Ibn Habib said: for them there is only fighting or Islam, and this is the view of Abu Hanifa.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is found attributed to Ibn al-Qasim that the jizyah is taken from them, and that is also in al-Tafriʿ of Ibn al-Jallab, but it is a possibility, not an explicit text. As for the People of the Book from among the Arabs, Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, held that the jizyah is taken from them, while Abu Hanifa indicated prohibition of that. As for the Samaritans and the Sabians, the majority hold that they are of the Jews and Christians, the jizyah is taken from them, and their slaughtered animals are permitted. A group said: their slaughtered animals are not permitted, and according to this the jizyah is not taken from them. Some prohibited the slaughtered animal while permitting the taking of the jizyah from them. As for the worshippers of idols, fire and other than these, the majority of scholars hold that the jizyah is accepted from them, and this is the view of Malik in al-Mudawwana. Al-Shafiʿi and Abu Thawr said: "The jizyah is not taken except from the Jews, Christians and Magians only." The position of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, is that the jizyah is not taken except from adult free sane men, and this is the view of al-Shafiʿi and Abu Hanifa. It is not imposed on children, women, the insane, nor on the monks of the monasteries and hermitages who have withdrawn. Malik said in al-Wadiha: "But if it had been imposed on them and then they withdrew after that, it does not drop from them." As for the monks of the churches, it is imposed on them. The matter is disputed regarding the aged decrepit man. Whoever considers that its purpose is humiliation (al-idhlal) enforces it on all. Al-Naqqash said: "The legal punishment is in property and in bodies, and the jizyah is among the punishments upon property."

As for its amount, Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and many of the people of knowledge followed what ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, set, which is four dinars for the people of gold and forty dirhams for the people of silver. ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, also imposed hospitality, provisions and clothing. Malik said in al-Wadiha: "This is lifted from them today on account of the obligations upon them." This is one of what is reported from ʿUmar, and Malik took by it. Sufyan al-Thawri said: "Various taxes have been reported from ʿUmar."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

I think that this was according to his, may Allah be pleased with him, judgment regarding their ease and hardship.

Al-Shafiʿi and others said: the amount of the jizyah is one dinar per head, and the evidence for this is the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ command to Muʿadh with it, and his taking the jizyah of Yemen in this way, or its value in Maʿafir, which are garments. Many people of knowledge said: there is no fixed limit for this in the sacred law; rather it is left to the judgment of the ruler at every time and according to each people. All of this concerns the case of conquest (ʿanwa). As for settlement (sulh), it is what they are settled upon, whether small or large. The school disagreed regarding a slave whom a dhimmi or a Muslim frees: is the jizyah obligatory on him or not? Ibn al-Qasim said: no one is reduced below four dinars, whether poor or rich. Ashhab said: the poor is reduced according to what is seen of his condition. Ibn al-Majishun said: nothing is taken from the poor.

The jizyah, in its form, is a fiʿla from jazā yajzī, when one repays for what was done to him; as if they gave it as a recompense for the security they were granted. It is like the qiʿda and the jilsa. From this meaning is the saying of the poet:

Yajzīka aw yuthnī ʿalayka, wa-inna man ∗∗∗ athnā ʿalayka bimā faʿalta ka-man jazā

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿ʿan yadin﴾ admits of several interpretations. Among them: that it means the dhimmi's bringing it with his own hand, not through a messenger, so that there is humiliation in that for him. Among them: that it means "from a blessing from you upon them" in accepting it from them and granting them security, and yad in the language means blessing and a good favor. Among them: that it means "from a strength of yours over them" and a subjugation, such that they have no banner or stronghold remaining with them; and yad in the speech of the Arabs means strength, as one says: "So-and-so has a yad (power)," and "I have no yad for such-and-such," meaning no strength. Among them: that it means that they should pay it in cash and not delay it, as you say: "I sold it yadan bi-yad" (hand to hand). Among them: that it means "from a submission on their part and compliance," in the manner of their saying: "So-and-so cast his yad" when he becomes helpless and surrenders.

His saying: ﴿and they are humbled﴾ is a term that encompasses aspects that cannot be enumerated because of their multiplicity. Mentioned among them, from ʿIkrima, is that the receiver is seated while the one paying from the people of the dhimma is standing; and this and the like calls to their humiliation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verse 30:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And the Jews say, "Ezra is the son of Allah," and the Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of Allah." That is their saying from their mouths; they imitate the saying of those who disbelieved before them. May Allah fight them; how are they deluded?﴾

What is well known in the books of the people of knowledge is that a group of the Jews said this statement, and it is narrated that none said it except Finhas. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: four of their rabbis said it: Salam ibn Mishkam, Nu'man ibn Abi Awfa, Shas ibn Qays, and Malik ibn al-Sayf. Al-Naqqash said: no Jew remains who says it, for they have died out.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

If one of them says it, it follows that the group may be held responsible for the monstrousness of the statement because of the prominence of the speaker among them, and the sayings of the eminent are always widely known among people and are cited as evidence. From here it is correct that the group is said to have spoken the saying of their prophet.

Asim and al-Kisa'i read "Ezra ibn Allah" with tanwin on "Ezra" (ʿUzayrin). The meaning, according to this reading, is that "ibn" is the predicate of an inchoative (mubtada') about "Ezra," and this is the soundest of the views, because it is the meaning being censured in them. "ʿUzayr" and the like are diptote whether foreign or Arabic. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "ʿUzayru ibn Allah" without tanwin on "ʿUzayr." Some of them said: "ibn" is the predicate about "ʿUzayr," and the tanwin was dropped from "ʿUzayr" because of the meeting of two consonants (ijtima' al-sakinayn). Similar to it is the reading of one who reads "Ahadu Allahu al-Samad." Abu 'Ali said: this is common in poetry, and al-Tabari recited in this regard:

"You will find me with the commander, righteous, and with the spear, thrusting and charging, when ʿUtayf al-Sulami flees."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Thus, the alif, according to this reading and interpretation, is retained in "ibn."

Some of them said: "ibn" is an attribute (sifa) of "ʿUzayr," as you say "Zayd ibn ʿAmr," and the attribute and the attributed are placed in the position of one name, and the tanwin is dropped when two consonants come together as if they met within one word. The meaning: "ʿUzayr ibn Allah is our worshipped one and our god," or the meaning: "Our worshipped one or our god is ʿUzayr ibn Allah."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The analogy of this reading and interpretation would be that the alif of "ibn" be dropped, but it is retained in the script of the Mushaf. From all of this it follows that the reading with tanwin on "ʿUzayr" is the strongest.

Al-Tabari and others related that the Children of Israel were struck by trials and calamity (and it was said: sickness), and Allah took away the Torah from them in that, and they forgot it. Their scholars had buried it at the first sign of that calamity. When the period grew long, the Torah was entirely lost, so Allah preserved it for ʿUzayr as an honor from Him to him. He told the Children of Israel: "Allah has preserved the Torah for me," and they began to study it from him. Then the buried Torah was found, and it was found to be identical to what ʿUzayr had been studying. They then went astray and said: "This could not have come about except that he is the son of Allah." The apparent meaning of the Christians' saying "The Messiah is the son of Allah" is sonship of begetting (bunuwwat al-naslu), as the Arabs said about the angels. This is also what the saying of al-Dahhak, al-Tabari and others implies, and this is more monstrous in disbelief. Abu al-Ma'ali said: the Christians unanimously agree that the Messiah is a god and that he is the son of God.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is said that some of them believe it to be sonship of tenderness and mercy, and this meaning also does not permit that sonship be applied to him, and it is disbelief because of the problem that enters from the direction of procreation. Likewise the Jews disbelieved in their saying "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah" and their saying "We are the sons of Allah." Sonship is metaphorically used in Arabic speech to express kinship and close association between things, when the matter is not problematic and the matter of begetting is impossible. An example is the saying of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwan: "War has pressed us and we have pressed it, so we are its sons and it is our mother," meaning close association. Among such is the saying of Huraith ibn Mihsan:

"The sons of glory, whom their mothers did not keep sitting, and whose fathers are sons of truth, so they were noble."

Among such also: "Ibn Na'sh," "Ibn Ma'," "Ibn al-Sabil," and the like. From it is the saying of the poet:

"And the earth carries us, and it was our mother."

From it is one of the interpretations of his saying ﷺ: "The son of adultery does not enter Paradise," meaning one who is constantly attached to it. The other interpretation: that a matter of doubt does not enter it. The two interpretations regarding the saying of the Christians, "The Messiah is the son of Allah," are as previously mentioned regarding the attribute and the predicate, except that the difficulty of the tanwin is removed here. ʿUzayr is a prophet from the prophets of the Children of Israel.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿by their mouths﴾ includes two meanings. One: to bind them to the statement and to emphasize it, as He said: ﴿They write the Book with their own hands﴾ [al-Baqara: 79], and like His saying: ﴿nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38]. The second meaning in His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿by their mouths﴾, that is, it is bare, having no proof or evidence; the utmost of its clarification is that it is said by the mouths, a mere statement, a bare claim.

"Yudahi'una" (they imitate) is the reading of the majority, and its meaning: they imitate, match, and resemble. ʿAsim alone among the Seven, and Talha ibn Musarrif, read "yuḍāhi'ūna" with hamza, on the basis that it is from "ḍāha'a," which is the dialect of Thaqif, with the meaning of "ḍāhā."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

As for one who said that this is derived from their saying "imra'a ḍahyā'" (a woman who does not menstruate), and it was said: one who has no breast, named so for her resemblance to men, his statement is erroneous, as Abu 'Ali said, because the hamza in "ḍāha'a" is original, while in "ḍahyā'" it is additional, like "ḥamrā'." If the pronoun in "yuḍāhi'ūna" refers to both the Jews and the Christians together, then the indication in His saying ﴿those who disbelieved before them﴾ is either to the polytheists of the Arabs, when they said "the angels are the daughters of Allah," and they were the first disbelievers, which is the saying of al-Dahhak; or to earlier nations before them; or to the earliest generation of disbelieving Jews and Christians, and "yuḍāhi'ūna" would then refer to the contemporaries of Muhammad ﷺ. If the pronoun in "yuḍāhi'ūna" refers to the Christians alone, then the indication of "those who disbelieved before them" is to the Jews, and on this basis al-Tabari interpreted, and al-Zahrawi related it from Qatada.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿May Allah fight them﴾ is a general curse upon them encompassing all kinds of evil, and it is known that whoever Allah fights is the defeated and the slain. al-Tabari related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the meaning is: "May Allah curse them." And ﴿how are they deluded?﴾ its intent: how do they turn, and how do they go? In place of this verb of intent is put a verb of evil that befalls them. This is eloquent in speech, as you say: "May Allah curse the disbeliever, how he perished," as if you are decreeing his destruction. It is as if a decree is upon them in this verse that they are deluded, and its meaning: they are deprived and turned away from good. A "ma'fūka" land is one that has not been struck by rain. Abu 'Ubayda said: "yu'faku-na" means "yuḥaddūn" (they are deprived).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He means: from your saying "a man who is maḥdūd," that is, one who is deprived and does not attain good. It seems to derive from "ifk," which is falsehood, so the one deluded is one whose hopes deceive him, so he finds no good. It is also possible that His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿how are they deluded?﴾ is an opening of reproach, that is: by what cause and from what direction are they turned away from the truth after it has become clear to them?

"Qātala" in this verse has the meaning of "qatala" (to kill), and it is a form of mufa'ala from one party, and all of this is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verse 31–33:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah, and [also] the Messiah, son of Mary. Yet they were commanded only to worship one God. There is no god but Him. Glory be to Him above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths, but Allah refuses except to perfect His light, though the disbelievers dislike it.﴾ ﴿It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, to make it prevail over all religion, though the polytheists dislike it.﴾

The singular of "al-aḥbār" is ḥibr (scholar), with a kasra on the ḥa'. It is also said ḥabr with a fatḥa on the ḥa'; the first is more eloquent. From it comes midād al-ḥibr (ink). Al-ḥabr with a fatḥa means "the learned scholar." Yūnus ibn Ḥabīb said: "I have only heard it with a kasra on the ḥa'." Al-Farrā' said: "I heard both the fatḥa and the kasra on the ḥa' for the scholar." Ibn al-Sikkīt said: "al-ḥibr with a kasra is the ink, and al-ḥabr with a fatḥa is the scholar." Al-Ruhbān is the plural of rāhib, who is one who fears, from al-rahba (fear). He called them lords, though they did not worship them, but because they received the lawful and the unlawful from them, and this is a matter that is received only from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Ibn 'Abbās, Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Yamān and Abu al-'Āliya said something similar. Al-Ṭabarī related that 'Adī ibn Ḥātim said: "I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while there was a gold cross around my neck. He said: 'O 'Adī, throw this cross from your neck.' I heard him reciting: ﴿They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, [but] we did not worship them!' He said: 'Do you not make lawful what they made lawful and make unlawful what they made unlawful?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'That is it.'" "Al-Masīḥ" is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon "al-aḥbār" and "al-ruhbān." (p-298) "Subḥānahu" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and the verb governing it is implied from the meaning, since there is no verb from the word "subḥān"; the implied sense is: "I glorify Him with glorification," so the meaning of "subḥānahu" is: glorification of Him. Those who say that the People of the Book are polytheists have argued with His saying: ﴿above what they associate﴾, while others say that taking these lords is a kind of association, and it is said of the hypocrite (al-murāʾī) that he has associated, and there are reports regarding this.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah﴾, the verse. The light of Allah in this verse is His guidance proceeding from the Qur'an and the Sharia established in the hearts of people. Thus, from the fact that He called it light, He named the attempt to corrupt it and to obstruct it a "extinguishing." A group said: the light is the Qur'an.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no sense in restricting the light to any one of the things that fall under the intended meaning. His saying: ﴿with their mouths﴾ is an expression of the weakness and feebleness of their stratagem. He informed about them that they attempt to resist a mighty matter with a feeble effort, so the extinguishing was by blowing with the mouths. It may also be meant: with statements that have no proof, which do not pass beyond the mouths to the understanding of a listener. His saying: "wa-yaʾbā" is an affirmative that is sometimes followed by "illā," because it occupies the place of a negated verb, since the sense is: "and Allah does not want except to perfect His light." Al-Farrā' said: "It is an affirmative containing an element of negation," and al-Zajjāj objected to this expression, and its explanation is what we have said.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth﴾, the verse. "His Messenger" refers to Muḥammad (ﷺ). His saying "with guidance" encompasses the Qur'an and the entire Sharia. His saying "and the religion of (p-299) truth" is an indication of Islam and the community (milla) in its totality, which is the ḥanīfiyya. His saying "to make it prevail" — Abū Hurayra, Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, and Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh said something to the effect that: the pronoun refers to the religion, and its prevailing is at the descent of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam and the return of all religions to the religion of Islam; that is its prevailing.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It seems that this group viewed the prevailing in its most complete aspects, namely, so that no other religion remains alongside it. Another group said: ﴿to make it prevail over the religion﴾ means to make it the highest and most manifest; if other religions exist alongside it, they are below it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verse 31–33:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah, and [also] the Messiah, son of Mary. Yet they were commanded only to worship one God. There is no god but Him. Glory be to Him above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths, but Allah refuses except to perfect His light, though the disbelievers dislike it.﴾ ﴿It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, to make it prevail over all religion, though the polytheists dislike it.﴾

The singular of "al-aḥbār" is ḥibr (scholar), with a kasra on the ḥa'. It is also said ḥabr with a fatḥa on the ḥa'; the first is more eloquent. From it comes midād al-ḥibr (ink). Al-ḥabr with a fatḥa means "the learned scholar." Yūnus ibn Ḥabīb said: "I have only heard it with a kasra on the ḥa'." Al-Farrā' said: "I heard both the fatḥa and the kasra on the ḥa' for the scholar." Ibn al-Sikkīt said: "al-ḥibr with a kasra is the ink, and al-ḥabr with a fatḥa is the scholar." Al-Ruhbān is the plural of rāhib, who is one who fears, from al-rahba (fear). He called them lords, though they did not worship them, but because they received the lawful and the unlawful from them, and this is a matter that is received only from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Ibn 'Abbās, Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Yamān and Abu al-'Āliya said something similar. Al-Ṭabarī related that 'Adī ibn Ḥātim said: "I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while there was a gold cross around my neck. He said: 'O 'Adī, throw this cross from your neck.' I heard him reciting: ﴿They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, [but] we did not worship them!' [p. 300]

The Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿O you who believe, indeed many of the rabbis and the monks devour the wealth of people unjustly and turn them away from the way of God. And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in the way of God, give them tidings of a painful punishment, on a Day when it will be heated in the fire of Hell and their foreheads, their sides and their backs will be branded with it: "This is what you hoarded for yourselves, so taste what you used to hoard."﴾

The purpose of this verse is to explain the faults of those mentioned, and the prohibition to the believers from those faults is implied within that. The lam in "la-yaakuloona" (they indeed devour) is the lam of emphasis. The form of this devouring is that they take from the wealth of their followers taxes and obligations in the name of churches, temples and other things, making them believe that giving to these is part of the Law and a means of drawing near to God. Meanwhile, they hoard that wealth, like the one that Salman mentioned in the Book of Biographies (Kitab al-Siyar) concerning the monk whose treasure was dug up. It was also said: they used to take from them, from their produce and wealth, taxes in the name of protecting the religion and upholding the Law. It was also said: they used to accept bribes in judgments, and the like.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

His saying, ﴿unjustly﴾, encompasses all of that. As for His saying "yasuddoona" (they turn away), the more apt reading here is that it is transitive, i.e., they turn others away. This preference is only because of the prominence of their positions among their people. "Sadda" is used both intransitively and transitively, and from its use is the saying of the poet:

"You turned the cup away from us, O Umm 'Amr,
and the cup had been flowing to the right."

"The way of God" is Islam and the Law of Muhammad (peace be upon him). It is possible that it means: they turn away from the way of God by their devouring of wealth unjustly; but the first is more preferable. His saying "wal-ladheena" (and those who) begins a new clause, and its predicate is "fa-bashshirhum" (so give them tidings). It is permissible that "alladheena" be coordinated with the pronoun in His saying "yaakuloon" (they devour), according to a certain view, since the pronoun was not emphasized. Abu Hatim attributed to 'Ilba' ibn Ahmad that he said: When 'Uthman ordered the copying of the Mushaf, he wanted to omit the waw in "wal-ladheena yaknizoona" (and those who hoard), but Ubayy ibn Ka'b refused that and said: "You must include it, or I will place my sword on my shoulder," so he kept it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

In accordance with 'Uthman's intention runs the saying of Mu'awiya: that the verse concerns the People of the Book. Abu Dharr disagreed with him and said: "Rather, it concerns us." So he complained about him to 'Uthman, who summoned him from Syria, and then he went out to al-Rabadha. What appears from the wording is that when He mentioned some of the rabbis and monks who devour wealth unjustly, He then mentioned the statement about the condemnation of those who hoard and withhold the due of wealth.

Talha ibn Musarrif recited: "alladheena yaknizoon" without the waw. "Yaknizoon" means: they gather and keep in containers. From its use is the saying of al-Munakhkhal al-Hudhali:

"May my own goodness not be good if I feed their hungry
while the stored wheat is mine, hoarded (maknooz)..."

That is, kept safe in its containers. Burying is not a condition of hoarding (kanz), but it became common among those who keep wealth to bury it, so that the term "kanz" came to be recognized for what is buried. From the same root is their saying: "a man of compact build (mukatnaz al-khalq)," i.e., gathered together. From it is the saying of the rajiz (rajaz poet):

"Upon a firm one whose flesh is compact (kinaz),
he spent the night pressing me upon the stages (awfaz)."

The threat regarding hoarding is only directed at withholding the rights due from it. For this reason, many scholars said: "kanz" is wealth whose zakat is not paid, even if it is on the surface of the earth. As for what is buried, if its zakat is paid, it is not hoarding, as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whatever wealth you have paid its zakat for is not hoarding." These words are well known from Ibn 'Umar (may God be pleased with him and his father), and this view is narrated from 'Ikrima, al-Sha'bi, al-Suddi, Malik, and the majority of scholars. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may God be pleased with him) said: "Four thousand dirhams or less is provision (nafaqa), and what exceeds it is hoarding, even if you pay its zakat." Abu Dharr and a group with him said: "What exceeds a man's need from his wealth is hoarding." These two views imply that the blame is for locking up wealth, not only for withholding its zakat. But 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz (may God be pleased with him) said: it is abrogated (mansukha) by His saying: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ [al-Tawba: 103], so the obligation of zakat came to encompass all of this.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

The implicit meaning of the verse was: "Do not gather wealth lest you be punished," and this was abrogated (naskh) by the affirmation in His saying: ﴿Take from their wealth﴾ [al-Tawba: 103]. The pronoun in His saying "yunfiqoonaha" (they spend it) may refer to the wealth and hoards implied by the meaning, and it may refer to gold and silver, since they are two kinds. It was also said: it refers to silver, and the pronoun of one is sufficient in place of the pronoun of the other when the meaning conveys it. This is like the saying of the poet:

"We are content with what we have, and you with what you have,
but opinions differ."

And like the saying of Hassan:

"Indeed the prime of youth and the hair
of beauty, if not disobeyed, is madness."

Sibawayh disliked this usage in speech. Many exegetes have compared this verse to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when they see trade or amusement, they scatter toward it﴾ [al-Jumu'a: 11], but it is not similar, because "aw" (or) separated trade from amusement and made it proper for the pronoun to refer to one of them without the other.

Gold is grammatically feminine and may be treated as masculine, though the feminine is more common. It is narrated that the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God has condemned the acquisition of gold and silver. So if we knew which wealth is best, we would acquire it." 'Umar (may God be pleased with him) said: "I will ask the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about that for you." So he asked him, and he said: "A remembering tongue, a grateful heart, and a wife who helps the believer in his religion." It is also narrated that when this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Ruin to gold, ruin to silver," and then his Companions became fearful and said what was mentioned before.

The fa' in His saying ﴿fa-bashshirhum﴾ (so give them tidings) is the response to what is in His saying "wal-ladheena" (and those who) of the sense of a condition. The tidings came with the punishment once the punishment was explicitly stated, because tidings are qualified by good or evil; when they are unqualified, they are understood only as good. It was also said: rather, it is always for good, so when it is qualified with evil, the meaning is: "Deliver to them as tidings a painful punishment." This is like the saying of the poet:

"And horses I charged upon with horses...
their greeting among them is striking and painful (wajee')."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿On a Day when it will be heated﴾ — the verse. "Yawma" (on a Day) is an adverbial phrase of time, and the governing element in it is "aleem" (painful). The majority of readers recited "yuhma" with a ya', meaning: "the fuel will be heated." Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan recited "tuhma" with a ta' from above, meaning: "the fire will be heated." The pronoun in "'alayha" refers to the hoards or the wealth, as previously mentioned.

Some people read "jibahuhum" with assimilation and gave the sound of a damma to the ending, as Abu Hatim reported.

Many hadiths have come with the same sense as this verse of threat, but they are explained as concerning only withholding zakat, not the acquisition and preservation of lawful wealth. The condition of the Companions and their wealth (may God be pleased with them) supports this. Among those hadiths is his saying (ﷺ): "Whoever leaves behind after him a hoard for which he did not pay zakat, it will be made a bald-headed, two-spotted snake for him on the Day of Resurrection," and the hadith. Al-Tabari reported, saying: "The sword-hilt of Abu Hurayra was of silver, and Abu Dharr forbade him, saying: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever leaves gold or silver will be branded with it.'" He also reported from Abu Umama al-Bahili, who said: "A man of the People of the Suffa died, and a dinar was found in his cloak, so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'A brand.' Then another died, and two dinars were found for him, so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Two brands.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

This is either because the two were living on charity while possessing gold ingots, or because this was in the early period of Islam, after which the Law established the regulation of wealth and the payment of its due. Had the regulation of wealth been prohibited, its due would be that all of it be given out, not only its zakat; and there is no one in the Community who obligates this.

His saying ﴿This is what you hoarded﴾ is a reference to the wealth with which they are branded. It is also possible that it refers to the act that befalls them, meaning: "This is the recompense for what you hoarded." Ibn Mas'ud said: "By God, no dinar touches a dinar; rather, the skin is stretched so that it is branded with every dinar and every dirham." Al-Ahnaf ibn Qays said: "I entered the mosque of Medina and there was a man of rough appearance and tattered dress, going around the circles and saying: 'Give the good news to the owners of hoards of branding on their foreheads, their sides and their backs.' Then he left, grumbling and saying: 'What might you do against Quraysh?'"
