But 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz (may God be pleased with him) said: it is abrogated (mansukha) by His saying: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ [al-Tawba: 103], so the obligation of zakat came to encompass all of this.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

The implicit meaning of the verse was: "Do not gather wealth lest you be punished," and this was abrogated (naskh) by the affirmation in His saying: ﴿Take from their wealth﴾ [al-Tawba: 103]. The pronoun in His saying "yunfiqoonaha" (they spend it) may refer to the wealth and hoards implied by the meaning, and it may refer to gold and silver, since they are two kinds. It was also said: it refers to silver, and the pronoun of one is sufficient in place of the pronoun of the other when the meaning conveys it. This is like the saying of the poet:

"We are content with what we have, and you with what you have,
but opinions differ."

And like the saying of Hassan:

"Indeed the prime of youth and the hair
of beauty, if not disobeyed, is madness."

Sibawayh disliked this usage in speech. Many exegetes have compared this verse to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when they see trade or amusement, they scatter toward it﴾ [al-Jumu'a: 11], but it is not similar, because "aw" (or) separated trade from amusement and made it proper for the pronoun to refer to one of them without the other.

Gold is grammatically feminine and may be treated as masculine, though the feminine is more common. It is narrated that the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God has condemned the acquisition of gold and silver. So if we knew which wealth is best, we would acquire it." 'Umar (may God be pleased with him) said: "I will ask the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about that for you." So he asked him, and he said: "A remembering tongue, a grateful heart, and a wife who helps the believer in his religion." It is also narrated that when this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Ruin to gold, ruin to silver," and then his Companions became fearful and said what was mentioned before.

The fa' in His saying ﴿fa-bashshirhum﴾ (so give them tidings) is the response to what is in His saying "wal-ladheena" (and those who) of the sense of a condition. The tidings came with the punishment once the punishment was explicitly stated, because tidings are qualified by good or evil; when they are unqualified, they are understood only as good. It was also said: rather, it is always for good, so when it is qualified with evil, the meaning is: "Deliver to them as tidings a painful punishment." This is like the saying of the poet:

"And horses I charged upon with horses...
their greeting among them is striking and painful (wajee')."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿On a Day when it will be heated﴾ — the verse. "Yawma" (on a Day) is an adverbial phrase of time, and the governing element in it is "aleem" (painful). The majority of readers recited "yuhma" with a ya', meaning: "the fuel will be heated." Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan recited "tuhma" with a ta' from above, meaning: "the fire will be heated." The pronoun in "'alayha" refers to the hoards or the wealth, as previously mentioned.

Some people read "jibahuhum" with assimilation and gave the sound of a damma to the ending, as Abu Hatim reported.

Many hadiths have come with the same sense as this verse of threat, but they are explained as concerning only withholding zakat, not the acquisition and preservation of lawful wealth. The condition of the Companions and their wealth (may God be pleased with them) supports this. Among those hadiths is his saying (ﷺ): "Whoever leaves behind after him a hoard for which he did not pay zakat, it will be made a bald-headed, two-spotted snake for him on the Day of Resurrection," and the hadith. Al-Tabari reported, saying: "The sword-hilt of Abu Hurayra was of silver, and Abu Dharr forbade him, saying: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever leaves gold or silver will be branded with it.'" He also reported from Abu Umama al-Bahili, who said: "A man of the People of the Suffa died, and a dinar was found in his cloak, so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'A brand.' Then another died, and two dinars were found for him, so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Two brands.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

This is either because the two were living on charity while possessing gold ingots, or because this was in the early period of Islam, after which the Law established the regulation of wealth and the payment of its due. Had the regulation of wealth been prohibited, its due would be that all of it be given out, not only its zakat; and there is no one in the Community who obligates this.

His saying ﴿This is what you hoarded﴾ is a reference to the wealth with which they are branded. It is also possible that it refers to the act that befalls them, meaning: "This is the recompense for what you hoarded." Ibn Mas'ud said: "By God, no dinar touches a dinar; rather, the skin is stretched so that it is branded with every dinar and every dirham." Al-Ahnaf ibn Qays said: "I entered the mosque of Medina and there was a man of rough appearance and tattered dress, going around the circles and saying: 'Give the good news to the owners of hoards of branding on their foreheads, their sides and their backs.' Then he left, grumbling and saying: 'What might you do against Quraysh?'"

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verse 36:

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months in the Book of Allah, the day He created the heavens and the earth; of them four are sacred. That is the correct religion. So do not wrong yourselves therein, and fight the polytheists all together as they fight you all together. And know that Allah is with those who are mindful of Him.﴾

This verse, and the one that follows it, contain what the Arabs had legislated in their pre-Islamic age: the making sacred of the months of permissibility and the making permissible of the months of sanctity. When what the Arabs used to do is stated explicitly, the meaning of the verses becomes clear. What is confirmed by the narrations and emerges from the totality of what people have mentioned is that the Arabs, most of whom had no livelihood except through raids and the use of their weapons, found it hard, when the months of Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and al-Muharram came in succession, and they ran out of resources. The Banu Fuqaym of Kinanah were a people of religion among the Arabs and adhered to the law of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. So al-Qalammas, who was Hudhayfah ibn 'Abd Fuqaym, was appointed from among them, and he postponed (nasa'a) the months for the Arabs. Then he was succeeded in this by his son 'Abbad ibn Hudhayfah, then his son Qal' ibn 'Abbad succeeded him, then his son Umayyah ibn Qal' succeeded him, then his son 'Awf ibn Umayyah succeeded him, then his son Abu Thumamah Junadah ibn 'Awf, and upon this Islam came. Al-Tabari and others mentioned that the matter was in 'Udwan before the Banu Malik ibn Kinanah. The form of their practice was that when the Arabs finished their pilgrimage, whoever wished from among them came to him gathered, and they said: "Postpone (ansi') for us a month," that is, delay from us the sanctity of al-Muharram and place it in Safar. Then al-Muharram would be made permissible for them, so they would raid in it and make their living. Then they would observe the sanctity of Safar so as to match the number of the four months. Mujahid said: "They would call that Safar 'the sacred al-Muharram'." Then they would call Rabi' al-Awwal "Safar," and Rabi' al-Akhir "Rabi' al-Awwal," and so on through the rest of the months; they would begin their year from the al-Muharram appointed for them. Thus, on this basis, the ruling of the sacred month that had been made permissible for them falls away, and the year comes to thirteen months: first the permissible al-Muharram, then the al-Muharram which is in reality Safar, then the beginning of the year as we have mentioned. Concerning this, Allah, Exalted and Majestic, said: ﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months﴾, that is: they are not thirteen months. Al-Tabari said: Ibn Wakic related to me from 'Imran ibn 'Uyaynah, from Husayn, from Abu Malik, who said: "They used to make the year thirteen months." Mujahid said: "Then they would perform the pilgrimage in each month for two consecutive years, then after that they would change it, so they would perform the pilgrimage for two consecutive years, and so on, until the pilgrimage of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, fell in Dhu al-Qa'dah in reality, and they called it Dhu al-Hijjah. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed the pilgrimage in the tenth year in Dhu al-Hijjah in reality." That is His saying: "Indeed, time has returned to its form on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth. The year is twelve months, of which four are sacred: Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, al-Muharram, and Rajab Mudar, which lies between Jumada and Sha'ban."

In the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ delivered a sermon during the Farewell Pilgrimage, and he related the hadith and said in it: "The first of them is Rajab Mudar, which lies between Jumada and Sha'ban; then Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and al-Muharram."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Most books state that they used to make the sanctity of al-Muharram fall in Safar, and they remain silent about the completion of the account. What we have mentioned is its explanation. As for al-Muharram being the first month of the Arabic year, whereas by right, since the calendar is from the Hijrah, the year should begin in Rabi' al-Awwal, that is what is reported, because 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, compiled the register of the Muslims (diwan) and made its date al-Muharram, since before it the season and the pilgrimage conclude, so the pilgrimage was the end of the year. He counted the year of the Hijrah even though some of its beginning had been lost. And since the Arabs' year was lunar, the year began from the first of the month; it was not at the twelfth of Rabi' which is the day the Prophet ﷺ entered Madinah, nor at the completion of the pilgrimage, because that falls in a fraction of a month. As for the four sacred months, they are: Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, al-Muharram and Rajab. The meaning of the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "and Rajab Mudar, which lies between Jumada and Sha'ban" was to distinguish it from what all the tribes of Rabi'ah used to do, for they would make their Rajab Ramadan and make it sacred as an innovation of their own. Quraysh and those among the tribes of Mudar who followed them in that were upon the truth. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ confirmed that and attributed it to Mudar, since its ruling and its sanctity came from Quraysh. In the Mufaddaliyyat, by one of the poets of the pre-Islamic age:

"The month of the Banu Umayyah and the offerings..." 

The verse continues. Al-Asma'i said: he means Rajab. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' recited "ithna 'ashara shahran" with the 'ayn sukun, and that is a lightening to avoid a succession of vowels. Likewise he recited "ahada 'ashara" and "tis'ata 'ashara."

As for His saying, ﴿in the Book of Allah﴾: that is, in what He wrote and established in the Preserved Tablet or elsewhere. It is a description of an act, like His creating and His providing, and it does not mean His decree and His determination, because those are before the creation of the heavens and the earth. The Book, which is the source, is the operative element in "the day" (yawm), and "in" in His saying ﴿in the Book of Allah﴾ is connected to "established" or "fixed" or the like. It is doubtful that the Book here means the Qur'an; consider this. "In" is not connected to "the number" ('iddah), so as to separate the relative clause from the predicate of "inna." His saying ﴿of them four are sacred﴾ is a textual indication of the preference of these four and their honouring. Qatadah said: "Allah chose from among the angels and humankind messengers, and from among the months al-Muharram and Ramadan, from among the places the mosques, from among the days Friday, from among the nights the Night of Power, and from among speech His remembrance; so what Allah has magnified should be magnified."

His saying ﴿That is the correct religion﴾: a group said its meaning is the upright reckoning; Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said, as related by al-Mahdawi, its meaning is the upright judgement.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view the most correct is that "the religion" here is in its most well-known sense, that is, that law and obedience to Allah. "The correct" (al-qayyim) means the upright, the straight, and it is from "qama yaqumu," in the pattern of "sayyid" from "sada yasudu," its original form being "qayyum." His saying ﴿So do not wrong yourselves therein﴾: the pronoun refers to "the twelve months," that is, do not wrong yourselves through sins throughout the entire time. Qatadah said: the pronoun refers to "the four months," and the prohibition against wronging oneself in them is to honour them by specification and mention, even though it is forbidden at all times. The grammarians assert that the Arabs use "fihinna" for what is fewer than ten months, and "fiha" for what is more than ten. It is related from al-Kisa'i that he said: "I am amazed at this practice of the Arabs." Likewise they say for fewer than ten nights "khalawna," and for more than ten "khalat." Al-Hasan said: the meaning of "fihinna" is "because of them" and "on account of them," in that you make their sanctity permissible and replace it with what has no sanctity. Al-Mahdawi related that it was said: "do not wrong yourselves therein by fighting." Then it was abrogated by the obligation of fighting at all times. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said, in the book of al-Tabari: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to forbid fighting in the sacred months, by what Allah revealed concerning that, until Bara'ah was sent down."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

His Exalted saying ﴿and fight the polytheists﴾: its meaning is, in them, and therefore all the more so outside them. His saying ﴿all together﴾ means collectively; it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial state. Al-Tabari said: like "al-'aqibah" and "al-'afiyah," so on this it is like your saying "specially" and "generally." It also appears that it is from "kaffa yakuffu," meaning a body that restrains whoever opposes it; and likewise we say "al-kaffah," meaning it restrains whoever opposes it, so the word on this view is an active participle. Some people said: its meaning is that some of them restrain others from lagging behind. What we have presented first is more general and better. Some people said: the obligation in this verse was originally directed at every individual, then it was abrogated afterwards and made a collective obligation (fard kifayah).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What they have said has never been known from the law of the Prophet ﷺ to have obligated the whole community to go forth together. The meaning of the verse is rather the exhortation to fight them, to unite against them, and to unite the word; then He restricted it by His saying, glorified is He, ﴿as they fight you﴾. So in proportion to their fighting and their gathering against us, our obligation to gather against them is determined. As for the jihad to which one is encouraged, it is a collective obligation: when some of the community undertake it, it is lifted from the rest.

His saying ﴿And know that Allah is with those who are mindful of Him﴾ is a statement which contains within it a command to taqwa and a promise of victory and support for it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verse 37:

His words, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿Indeed, the postponing (al-nasi') is an increase in disbelief, by which those who disbelieve are led astray. They make it lawful one year and make it unlawful another year, to match the number of what Allah has made sacred, so that they make lawful what Allah has made unlawful. The evil of their deeds is made attractive to them. And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾

"Al-Nasi'" (النَسِيءُ) is on the pattern fa'il and is a verbal noun (masdar) meaning postponement (al-ta'khir). The Arabs say: "Allah postponed (ansa'a) your term" and "he postponed (nasa'a) your term." From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever wishes that his term be prolonged and his provision be expanded, let him keep the ties of kinship (fal-yasil rahimahu)."

This is the reading of the majority of people and of the Seven Readers. Ibn Kathir, as transmitted from him, and a group with him, read in the irregular reading: "al-nasiyy" with a doubled yaa. Ja'far ibn Muhammad and al-Zuhri, as transmitted from them, read "al-nasi'" (as above). It is also transmitted from him that he read "al-nas'" on the pattern of "al-nas'" (with a sukun on the 'ayn). A group read "al-nasy." As for "al-nasi'" with the madd and the hamza, Abu 'Ali said: it is a masdar like "al-nakir," "al-nadhir," and "'adhir al-hayy," and it cannot be fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, because the meaning would then be: "Indeed, the postponed (month) is an increase," and the postponed thing is the month, and a month cannot be an increase in disbelief.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Abu Hatim said: it is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, and the objection of Abu 'Ali is answered by supposing an elided noun, as if the meaning were: "Indeed, the causing of postponement of the postponing..." Al-Tabari said: it is from the meaning of increase, i.e., their increasing the months. Abu Wa'il said: "al-Nasi'" was a man from the Banu Kinana.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak. As for "al-nasy," it is the same first form with the hamza lightened; it was said that the hamza was changed to a yaa and the yaa was assimilated into the yaa. As for "al-nas'," it is the masdar of "nasa'a" when he postponed. As for "al-nasy," it was said to be the lightening of the hamza of "al-nas'," and this is against analogy. Al-Tabari said: it is a masdar of "nasiya yansa" when he abandoned.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Al-Nasi' is the Arabs' practice of postponing the sanctity (of the sacred months). And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿an increase in disbelief﴾ means: it continues alongside their disbelief in Allah and their opposition to the truth. So disbelief is multiplied by this act, which is itself false in its essence.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Among what is found in their poetry on this meaning is the saying of one of them:

"And among us is the postponer of the month, al-Qalammas."

And another said:

"They postponed the months by it, and they were its people, before you, while glory had not changed."

And from this is the saying of Jidhl al-Ti'an:

"Ma'add knows that my people are generous, noble people, and that they have generosity.
So which people have come to us with an odd (unpaired) one? And which people have not had their bridle restrained by us?
Are we not the postponers over Ma'add, making the months of lawfulness unlawful?"

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "yudallu" with a fatha on the yaa and a kasra on the daad. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada and 'Amr ibn Maymun read "yudillu" with a damma on the yaa and a kasra on the daad. This is either in the sense of "Allah misguides," or in the sense of "by it those who disbelieve mislead their followers." In the first interpretation, "alladhina" is in the accusative position; in the second, it is in the nominative position. 'Asim also read, and Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Ibn Mas'ud (as transmitted from him): "yuḍallu" with a damma on the yaa and a fatha on the daad, as the passive form, and this is supported by His saying ﴿zuyyina﴾ for the sake of consistency in the wording. Abu Raja' read "yadallu" from "dalla yadallu," on the pattern of "fa'ila" with a kasra on the 'ayn with "yaf'alu" with a fatha, and these are two dialects: it is said "dalla yadillu" and "dalla yadallu." The pattern we have mentioned distinguishes between them. Likewise the saying of the Prophet ﷺ is transmitted: "until a man does not know how many (rak'ahs) he has prayed" (yadilla / yadalla), with a fatha and a kasra on the daad.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they make it lawful one year and make it unlawful another year﴾ means: a year among the years. It does not mean that this rotation was in one specific month, such that one year is lawful and one year is unlawful.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Some people have interpreted the story to mean that when the consecutive sacred months were burdensome to them, they would make the sacred month lawful for them and make Safar unlawful in its place. Then the months would proceed in their known names. When the next year came, they would make the sacred month unlawful in its proper time and make Safar lawful, and the months would proceed in order. This group thought that this was the state of the people.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What we mentioned earlier is more fitting to the wording of the verses. Mujahid and Abu Malik have explained it so, and it is what is implied by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed, time has revolved (istadara)," although the whole matter has already passed. And Allah knows best which of these it was.

His saying: ﴿li-yuwati'u﴾ means: that they may agree. Al-muwati'a is agreement; "tawati'a al-rajulan 'ala kadha" means the two men concurred upon it. The meaning of ﴿li-yuwati'u 'iddata ma harrama Allah﴾ is: that they may preserve, in every year, four months in number.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

They removed the distinction which Allah had granted to the sacred months alone, comparable to someone who breaks the fast of Ramadan and fasts another month of the year without illness or travel. His saying "zuyyina" may be attributed to Allah, exalted and glorified, meaning that He created their disbelief, let them persist in it, and made it beloved to them. It may also be attributed to those who mislead and misguide them, from among humans and jinn. Then He, exalted is He, informed that He does not guide them or lead them aright. This is a general statement whose meaning is particular to those who die in it, or it is an absolute generality, but there is no guidance for them insofar as they are disbelievers.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Abu 'Ali al-Baghdadi mentioned concerning the matter of al-nasi' that when the people departed from Mina, a man called Nu'aym ibn Tha'laba would stand up and say: "I am the one who is not blamed, and my judgment is not rejected." So they would say: "Postpone for us a month," meaning: postpone for us the sanctity of the Muharram and make it in Safar.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The name Nu'aym is not known in this, and I think it is only like what al-Naqqash related from the Banu Fuqaym, who were called al-Qulamis, and their leader was Qalammas. They used to issue rulings to the Arabs at the season; their eldest would stand in the Hijr, another would stand at the door, and another at the Corner, and they would issue rulings.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So they were, on this account, a number: among them Nu'aym and Safwan, and among them the descendants of al-Qalammas, Hudhayfa and others.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is no contagion, no owl (hama), and no Safar." Some people said: by his saying "no Safar" he means this postponement (al-nasi'). It was said otherwise.

(p-314) His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿O you who have believed, what is [the matter] with you that when you are told, "Go forth in the cause of Allah," you adhere heavily to the earth? Are you satisfied with the life of this world rather than the Hereafter? But the enjoyment of worldly life, compared to the Hereafter, is but little.﴾ ﴿If you do not go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment and replace you with another people, and you will not harm Him at all. And Allah is over all things competent.﴾

This verse is, without any disagreement, a rebuke concerning the failure of those who stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the expedition of Tabuk. It was in the ninth year after the Hijrah, one year after the Conquest. In it he (ﷺ) campaigned against the Romans with twenty thousand men, both mounted and on foot. Groups of people stayed behind from him, along with many of the believers and hypocrites. So the rebuke in this verse is directed at the tribes and at the believers who were in Medina. He singled out three men—Ka'b ibn Malik, Murarah ibn al-Rabi', and Hilal ibn Umayyah—for this severe censure, in keeping with their standing in companionship, since they were of the people of Badr and among those who are followed as examples. Their staying behind was without any excuse, as will come.

His saying: ﴿What is [the matter] with you?﴾ is an interrogative used to mean affirmation and reproach. His saying: "It was said" refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), but the change of the verb to one whose subject is not named implies a certain harshness and roughness.

Al-nafr is moving quickly from one place to another for a matter that occurs. It is said of a human being: nafara ila al-amr, yanfiru, nafiran and nafran. It is said of an animal: nafarat, tanfuru, with the fa' vowelled with a damma, nufuran. His saying: ﴿ithaqaltum﴾ originally was tathaqaltum; the ta' was assimilated into the tha', so the hamzat al-wasl was needed, as in His saying: ﴿fa-idda'aratum﴾ [al-Baqarah: 72], and as you say "izzayyana," and as the poet said:

"She turns away the clamor when she sips, slender-waisted, sweet of taste, when she draws in the kisses."

Al-A'mash—as related by al-Mahdawi and others—read "tathaqaltum" in the original form. Abu Hatim mentioned it as "tatathaqaltum" with two ta's and then a thа' with three dots, and said: it is an error or a mistake. He preferred "tathaqaltum" with one ta' and a thа' with three dots, if it were to be recited with it. His saying: ﴿ithaqaltum ila al-ard﴾ is an expression for their staying behind, their holding back, their abandonment of the campaign in favor of dwelling in their homes and clinging to their palms and shades, and it is similar to: akhlada ila al-ard (he inclined to the earth). His saying: "Are you satisfied" is an affirmation: Are you satisfied with the meager worldly life in exchange for the weighty Hereafter and its most fortunate portion? Then he informed, saying: the world, in comparison with the Hereafter, is little and meager. So the force of the speech gives the sense of wonder at the error of one who is content with the meager instead of the abundant and lasting.

His saying: ﴿If you do not go forth﴾ (the verse)—﴿If you do not go forth, He will punish you﴾ is a conditional with its response. His saying: "He will punish you" is a general term that encompasses all kinds of punishment of this world and the Hereafter, and the threat through its generality is more frightening. A group said: he means: He will punish you by withholding rain from you. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called a tribe to march out, and it sat down, so Allah withheld rain from it and punished it with that." And "painful" (alim) means "paining" (mu'lim), like the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib:

"Is it from Rayhanah, the one who calls, the one who hears..."

His saying: ﴿and replace you with another people﴾ is a threat that He will substitute for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) a people who will not sit back when he calls them to march out. The pronoun in His saying: ﴿and you will not harm Him at all﴾ refers to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, meaning: that does not diminish His might or the might of His religion. It is also possible that it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), and this is more fitting. ﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾ means: over every thing that is within capability; and their replacement by Him is not an impossible, unattainable matter.

(p-314) His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿O you who have believed, what is [the matter] with you that when you are told, "Go forth in the cause of Allah," you adhere heavily to the earth? Are you satisfied with the life of this world rather than the Hereafter? But the enjoyment of worldly life, compared to the Hereafter, is but little.﴾ ﴿If you do not go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment and replace you with another people, and you will not harm Him at all. And Allah is over all things competent.﴾

This verse is, without any disagreement, a rebuke concerning the failure of those who stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the expedition of Tabuk. It was in the ninth year after the Hijrah, one year after the Conquest. In it he (ﷺ) campaigned against the Romans with twenty thousand men, both mounted and on foot. Groups of people stayed behind from him, along with many of the believers and hypocrites. So the rebuke in this verse is directed at the tribes and at the believers who were in Medina. He singled out three men—Ka'b ibn Malik, Murarah ibn al-Rabi', and Hilal ibn Umayyah—for this severe censure, in keeping with their standing in companionship, since they were of the people of Badr and among those who are followed as examples. Their staying behind was without any excuse, as will come.

His saying: ﴿What is [the matter] with you?﴾ is an interrogative used to mean affirmation and reproach. His saying: "It was said" refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), but the change of the verb to one whose subject is not named implies a certain harshness and roughness.

Al-nafr is moving quickly from one place to another for a matter that occurs. It is said of a human being: nafara ila al-amr, yanfiru, nafiran and nafran. It is said of an animal: nafarat, tanfuru, with the fa' vowelled with a damma, nufuran. His saying: ﴿ithaqaltum﴾ originally was tathaqaltum; the ta' was assimilated into the tha', so the hamzat al-wasl was needed, as in His saying: ﴿fa-idda'aratum﴾ [al-Baqarah: 72], and as you say "izzayyana," and as the poet said:

"She turns away the clamor when she sips, slender-waisted, sweet of taste, when she draws in the kisses."

Al-A'mash—as related by al-Mahdawi and others—read "tathaqaltum" in the original form. Abu Hatim mentioned it as "tatathaqaltum" with two ta's and then a thа' with three dots, and said: it is an error or a mistake. He preferred "tathaqaltum" with one ta' and a thа' with three dots, if it were to be recited with it. His saying: ﴿ithaqaltum ila al-ard﴾ is an expression for their staying behind, their holding back, their abandonment of the campaign in favor of dwelling in their homes and clinging to their palms and shades, and it is similar to: akhlada ila al-ard (he inclined to the earth). His saying: "Are you satisfied" is an affirmation: Are you satisfied with the meager worldly life in exchange for the weighty Hereafter and its most fortunate portion? Then he informed, saying: the world, in comparison with the Hereafter, is little and meager. So the force of the speech gives the sense of wonder at the error of one who is content with the meager instead of the abundant and lasting.

His saying: ﴿If you do not go forth﴾ (the verse)—﴿If you do not go forth, He will punish you﴾ is a conditional with its response. His saying: "He will punish you" is a general term that encompasses all kinds of punishment of this world and the Hereafter, and the threat through its generality is more frightening. A group said: he means: He will punish you by withholding rain from you. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called a tribe to march out, and it sat down, so Allah withheld rain from it and punished it with that." And "painful" (alim) means "paining" (mu'lim), like the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib:

"Is it from Rayhanah, the one who calls, the one who hears..."

His saying: ﴿and replace you with another people﴾ is a threat that He will substitute for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) a people who will not sit back when he calls them to march out. The pronoun in His saying: ﴿and you will not harm Him at all﴾ refers to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, meaning: that does not diminish His might or the might of His religion. It is also possible that it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), and this is more fitting. ﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾ means: over every thing that is within capability; and their replacement by Him is not an impossible, unattainable matter.

[p. 316] This too is a conditional clause (*shart*) with its response (*jawab al-shart*, the apodosis of the conditional). The response is in the *fa'* of His words "then indeed" (*faqad*) and what follows it. Al-Naqqash said: "This is the first verse revealed from Surat al-Tawba." The meaning of the verse is: if you abandon helping him, Allah has undertaken to help him, for He already helped him in a situation of few numbers, isolation, and the great number of his enemies. So His help for him today is more fitting than it was then.

His words ﴿when those who disbelieved drove him out﴾ mean that they did the deeds that led to his departure. He attributed the expulsion to them because the purpose is to blame them. Since the aim of Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith in his saying, "I have expelled every one who is expelled," was boasting, the Prophet (ﷺ) did not approve of it. The reference is to the departure of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from Makkah to Madinah, and Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, was in his company. The summary of the story is: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was waiting for the command of Allah, mighty and majestic, regarding the migration from Makkah. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, when he had given up the protection of Ibn al-Dughunna, wanted to leave Makkah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him, "Be patient, for perhaps Allah will make the companionship easy." When Allah permitted His Messenger to leave, he prepared himself from the house of Abu Bakr, and they both went out and remained in the cave that is on the mountain of Thawr, to the west of Makkah, for three nights. The polytheists went out following their trail until they reached the cave, but the trail was obliterated for them. Abu Bakr said to the Prophet (ﷺ), "If one of them looked at his foot, he would see us." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him, "What do you think of two whose third is Allah?"

It is narrated that a spider spun a web over the entrance of the cave. It is also narrated that a dove nested near the entrance of the cave. It is also narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, to place *thumam* (a kind of grass) at the entrance of the cave, and the polytheists imagined it to be growing plants and Allah turned them away from it. It occurs in *al-Dala'il* in a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) that a *ra'a* plant (a kind of desert plant) grew over the entrance of the cave, which Allah had commanded to do so at that moment. Al-Asma'i said: its plural is *ra'*, and it is one of the plants of the plains.

It is also narrated that when Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, entered the cave, he tore his cloak and used it to block the holes of the cave, lest there be in them some creature that would harm the Prophet (ﷺ). It is narrated that one hole remained, so he blocked it with his foot, and Allah, exalted is He, protected him. Amir ibn Fuhayra, the freedman of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, used to bring them milk in the evenings.

[p. 317] His words ﴿the second of two﴾ mean: one of two. This is like "the third of three" and "the fourth of four." But when the wording differs, as when you say *rabi'a thalatha* (the fourth of three), the meaning is that he made the three into four by himself. Most reciters read *thaniya ithnayn* with a *fatha* on the *ya'* of *thani*. Abu Hatim said: nothing other than this is known. A group recited *thani ithnayn* with a *sukun* (no vowel) on the *ya'* of *thani*. Abu al-Fath said: this was transmitted by Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala', and its basis is that he made the *ya'* quiescent, treating it like the *alif*.

The author, Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is like the reading *ma baqiya mina al-riba* (what remains of usury), and like the verse of Jarir:

*He is the caliph, so be content with what he chooses for you,*
*firm in resolve, in whose judgment there is no injustice.*

His companion is Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. It is narrated that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq said one day while on the pulpit: "Who among you memorizes Surat al-Tawba?" A man said, "I do." He said, "Recite." So he recited, and when he reached His words, exalted is He, ﴿when he said to his companion, "Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us"﴾, Abu Bakr wept and said, "By Allah, I am his companion." Al-Layth said: No one accompanied the prophets like Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, was exempted by this verse from the reproach contained in His words, exalted is He, ﴿If you do not help him﴾.

The author, Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

I say: rather, everyone who witnessed the expedition of Tabuk and did not stay behind was exempted from it. The reproach is only for those who stayed behind. Nevertheless, this verse honours Abu Bakr and establishes his precedence and early acceptance of Islam, may Allah be pleased with him.

His words ﴿Indeed Allah is with us﴾ mean by it help, deliverance, and kindness. As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿then Allah sent down His tranquility upon him﴾ and the rest of the verse, Habib ibn Abi Thabit said: the pronoun in "upon him" [p. 318] refers to Abu Bakr, because the Prophet (ﷺ) was always calm in soul and trusting in Allah, mighty and majestic.

The author, Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the view of one who understands tranquility (*sakina*) only as calmness of the soul and steadiness of heart. Most scholars said: the pronoun refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), and this is stronger. In my view, tranquility is only what Allah sends down upon His prophets of protection for them and special qualities that are fitting only for them, like His words, exalted is He, ﴿In it is tranquility from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 248]. It is possible that His words ﴿then Allah sent down His tranquility﴾ to the end of the verse mean what Allah did for His Prophet up to the time of Tabuk of victories and conquests, and not that this verse is specific to the story of the cave and the deliverance to Madinah. On this view, the hosts are the angels who descended at Badr and Hunayn. And whoever holds that the verse is specific to that story says: the hosts are angels who gave him good news of deliverance and that the disbelievers' efforts would not succeed. In the Mushaf of Hafsa, may Allah be pleased with her, it reads: "Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon both of them and supported both of them." Mujahid recited *wa-ayyadahu* with two *alifs* (*wa-'ayyadahu*), while most read *wa-'ayyadahu* with a shaddah on the *ya'*.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿and made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest﴾ mean: their repulsion, rejection, and humiliation. ﴿And the word of Allah is the highest﴾. It was said: it means "There is no god but Allah." It was also said: it means the Sharia in its entirety. Most reciters read *wa-kalimatu* (and the word) with a *damma* as a nominal beginning (*ibtida'*). Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Ya'qub read *wa-kalimata* with a *fatha*, on the assumption of "and He made the word of." Al-A'mash said: I saw in the Mushaf of Anas ibn Malik, attributed to Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "and He made His word (*kalimatahu*) the highest."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 41–42:

﴿Go forth, light or heavy, and strive with your wealth and your persons in the way of God. That is better for you, if you only knew.﴾ ﴿Had it been a near gain and a moderate journey, they would have followed you. But the distance seemed long to them. They will swear by God, "Had we been able, we would have gone out with you," destroying themselves. God knows that they are liars.﴾

(p. 319) This is a command from God, Exalted is He, to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) to go forth for military campaign. Some people said: this is a general command to all believers, and it was expressed as an obligation upon each individual (fard 'ayn, personal obligation) for that period, then God abrogated it by His saying: ﴿It is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾ [al-Tawba: 122]. This is narrated from al-Hasan and 'Ikrima.

Most people said: rather, this is an exhortation, and the command in itself is limited to a collective obligation (fard al-kifaya, communal obligation), and the verse did not intend its imposition upon each individual.

As for His saying ﴿light or heavy﴾, it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun in His saying "go forth." The meaning of lightness and heaviness here is used figuratively for one who can travel easily and one who can travel with difficulty. As for one who cannot, such as the blind and the like, he is excluded from this. It is narrated that Ibn Umm Maktum came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Is it incumbent upon me to go forth?" He said to him: "Yes," until the revelation: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind﴾ [al-Fath: 17].

People have mentioned various meanings of lightness and heaviness, none of which has a basis for restricting it to one over the others; rather, they are compatible aspects. It was said: the light is the rich, and the heavy is the poor; this was said by Mujahid. It was said: the light is the young, and the heavy is the old; this was said by al-Hasan and a group. It was said: the light is the energetic, and the heavy is the lazy; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada. It was said: the light is the one who is free of occupation, and the heavy is the one who is occupied; this was said by al-Hakam ibn 'Uyayna and Zayd ibn 'Ali. It was said: the one who has property is the heavy, and the one who has no property is the light; this was said by Ibn Zayd. It was said: the brave is the light, and the coward is the heavy; this was related by al-Naqqash. It was said: the infantryman is the heavy, and the horseman is the light; this was said by al-Awza'i.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

These last two views are reversed, and this has been said, but it is according to their weight upon the enemy. So the brave is the heavy, and likewise the horseman; and the coward is the light, and likewise the infantryman. Likewise the poor and the rich are reversed, so the rich is the heavy in the sense of one with occupation. The meaning of this is that people were commanded collectively, and these sayings are only in the sense of examples of heaviness and lightness.

Abu Talha said: "God did not hear the excuse of anyone who went out to Syria and fought until he died." Abu Ayyub said: "I never find myself except heavy or light." It is narrated that some people saw in the campaigns of Syria an old man whose eyebrows had fallen over his eyes due to old age, and he said to him: "O uncle, God has excused you." He said: "O nephew, we have been commanded to go forth light and heavy." Al-Tabari transmitted, from one who saw al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad in Hims, sitting on a money-changer's chest, and he had grown fat beyond the chest from his corpulence while he was preparing for the campaign. He was told: "God has excused you." He said: "There has come upon us the surah of the expeditions: ﴿Go forth light and heavy﴾." It is also narrated as "the surah of the investigations" (al-buhuth).

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿with your wealth and your persons﴾ describes the most complete form of striving and the most precious of its elements with God, Exalted is He. So He urged the most complete qualities. Wealth was mentioned first because it is the first expenditure at the time of preparation. Thus He arranged the matter as it is in itself. Then He informed that this is better for them, for the attainment of God's pleasure, the victory over the enemy, and the inheritance of the land. His saying ﴿if you only knew﴾ is an alert and a stirring of souls.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Had it been a near gain﴾ (to the end of the verse). The apparent meaning of this verse, and what is preserved of the story of Tabuk, is that when God commanded His Messenger to campaign against the Romans, he called the people to go forth. This was in intense heat, and at a time of ripe fruit and shade. The believers went forth, but a group, and especially from the tribes neighboring Medina, inevitably made excuses. This is indicated by His saying, Exalted is He, at the beginning of this passage: ﴿O you who believe, what is wrong with you that when you are told to go forth in the way of God, you cling heavily to the earth?﴾ [al-Tawba: 38], because this address is not only to the hypocrites, but is general. The hypocrites offered false excuses, and they were on a path of excessive laziness and intent to stay behind. The excuses of the believers were slight, but they abandoned the better course of exertion. So the verses preceding this were revealed in rebuke of the believers. Then from this verse onward he begins to mention the hypocrites and expose their inner intentions. So He says: had this campaign been for a gain, that is, for wealth and spoils attainable nearby with an easy, moderate journey, they would have hastened to it, not for the sake of God nor for the manifestation of His word. ﴿But the distance seemed long to them﴾ in the campaign against the Romans, that is, the long distance.

Abu 'Ubayda mentioned that a Bedouin came to Basra who had taken on a burden of debt and was unable to meet it. With him was a son of his named al-Ahwas. Al-Ahwas hurried ahead of his father with speech, saying: "We are those you know, and the sons of the road, and we have come from a long distance, seeking a right, and you give us [something] and God will reward you." Then his father prepared to speak, and he said to him: "Ya, iyyaka (beware), I have already spared you." (p. 320)

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

"Ya" is an interjection to draw attention, and "iyyaka" is a prohibition. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "al-shiqqa" with a kasra on the shin. Al-A'raj read "ba'ida" with a kasra on the ayn. Abu Hatim related that this is the dialect of the Banu Tamim in both words.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And they will swear by God﴾ refers to the hypocrites, and this is a report of the unseen. His saying ﴿destroying themselves﴾ means that at the time of their staying behind, they openly show their disbelief. So it is as if they impose upon themselves the certainty of God's punishment. Then He informed that God, who is the most just of witnesses, knows their lie, and that they were able to go out, but they abandoned it out of disbelief and hypocrisy. All of this is in general, not with the designation of a specific person. Had a person been designated, he would have been killed by the Shari'a.

Al-A'mash read, in the manner of assimilation with the wawa of the plural pronoun: "lawu istata'na" with a damma on the waw. Ibn Jinni mentioned this, and gave as an example His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They had sought sedition﴾ [al-Tawba: 48], ﴿so wish for death﴾ [al-Baqara: 94], and ﴿They have bought error﴾ [al-Baqara: 16], and what is similar to it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verse 43–44:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿May Allah pardon you. Why did you grant them permission until those who were truthful became evident to you and you knew the liars?﴾ ﴿Those who believe in Allah and the Last Day do not ask your permission to strive with their wealth and their lives. And Allah is Knowing of the righteous.﴾

This verse concerns a category extreme in hypocrisy, who asked for permission without any excuse. Among them were 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy, al-Jadd ibn Qays, Rifa'a ibn al-Tabut, and those who followed them. Some of them said: "Grant me permission and do not tempt me," and some said: "Grant us permission to stay behind." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) granted them permission, out of mercy toward them, taking the easier of the matters, and relying upon Allah. Mujahid said: some of them said, "We will ask his permission; if he permits us to sit, we will sit, and if not, we will sit," so the verse was revealed concerning that. A group said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) granted them permission without being commanded to do so, so he was pardoned for what befell him from this. He mentioned the pardon before the rebuke out of honour for him (ﷺ). 'Amr ibn Maymun al-Awdi said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) decided by his own opinion in two matters without being commanded concerning them: this one, and the matter of the captives of Badr, so Allah rebuked him concerning both. A group said: rather, His saying, glorified is He, in this verse, ﴿May Allah pardon you﴾, is an opening of speech, as you say: "May Allah make you righteous, may Allah honour you," and there was no sin from him (ﷺ) for which he needed pardon, because the form of seeking permission and accepting excuses is left to his own ijtihad (independent judgment). As for His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Why did you grant them permission﴾, it is in the sense of confirmation (taqrir).

His saying: ﴿those who were truthful﴾ means: in their asking permission, and that if you had not granted them permission they would have gone out with you. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verse 45–47:

The words of the Most High:

﴿Only those ask your permission who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day, and whose hearts are in doubt, so they waver in their doubt.﴾ ﴿Had they intended to go out, they would have made preparation for it, but Allah disliked their setting out, so He held them back, and it was said: "Sit with those who sit."﴾ ﴿Had they gone out with you, they would have added nothing to you but corruption, and they would have hastened about among you, seeking to cause you trouble, and among you there are listeners to them. And Allah knows the wrongdoers.﴾

This verse explicitly states that those who ask for permission are only those devoted to hypocrisy. "And their hearts were in doubt" means: they were in doubt (shakka). Ar-rayb (suspicion/misgiving) is close to shakk (doubt). "Yataraddadun" means: they are bewildered and no guidance is clear to them. From this verse the theologians (ahl al-kalam) derived the definition of doubt (shakk) as "hesitation between two matters" (taraddud bayna amrayn). The correct definition, however, is that it is "suspension between two matters" (tawaqquf bayna amrayn). The hesitation in the verse refers only to the suspicion of these hypocrites, since at times the truth of the Prophet's (ﷺ) affair would occur to them, and at other times its untruth would occur to them. They were not doubters seeking the truth, for it would have become clear to them had they sought it. Rather, they were wavering, belonging neither to these nor to those, like the sheep wandering between two flocks. Moreover, there is a distinction between shakk and rayb. The true meaning of rayb is a matter about which the observer becomes suspicious, so that it confuses his belief; it may lead to doubt and bewilderment, and it may lead to knowledge of the affair in which he is. Do you not see that the verse of the Hudhali poet:

"As if I had made him suspicious with suspicion"

cannot be interpreted as meaning doubt?

Al-Tabari said: A group of the people of knowledge held that these two verses are abrogated by the verse we mentioned in Surah al-Nur. He reported from al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah that they said regarding the words of the Most High: ﴿Only those who believe...﴾ [al-Tawba: 44] up to His words: ﴿so they waver in their doubt﴾ — it is abrogated by the verse of al-Nur: ﴿The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Nur: 62] up to ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nur: 62].

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an error, and its mention has already preceded.

The words of the Most High: ﴿Had they intended to go out﴾ — the verse is a proof against the hypocrites, meaning: had they intended to go out with their intentions, they would have considered the matter and prepared for it before it occurred. The "'uddah" is what is prepared for the affair and made ready from things.

The majority of readers read "'uddatan" with a damma on the ʿayn and a feminine tāʾ. Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan and his son Mu'awiya ibn Muhammad read "'uddahu" with a damma on the ʿayn and a pronominal hāʾ, meaning "'uddatahu," the tāʾ of feminization being dropped when it was made into an annexed construction, as in His words "wa iqam as-salat," meaning "wa iqamat as-salat." This is the view of al-Farra'; Abu al-Fath weakened it and said: he dropped the tāʾ of feminization and made the hāʾ of the pronoun a substitute for it. Abu Hatim said: it is the plural of "'uddah" on the pattern "'udd," like burrah and burr, durrah and durr, and the proper form would be "'udad," but this does not agree with the orthography of the Mushaf. ʿĀṣim, as transmitted from him by Aban, and Zirr ibn Hubaysh read "'iddahu" with a kasra on the ʿayn and a pronominal hāʾ. In my view, it is a noun for what is prepared, like "dhibh" (slaughtering) and "qitl" (killing), because the enemy was named "qitl" since it is his due to be killed; this is according to the belief of the Arabs when they named it so.

"Inba'athahum" means their setting out for this expedition. "Tathbit" means discouragement and breaking resolve. The words "wa qila" may be understood as a report from Allah, the Most High, meaning: Allah said in His previous decree: ﴿and it was said: "Sit with those who sit"﴾. It may also be understood as a report about them, meaning: this was the saying of some of them to others, either verbally or in meaning, and so it is reported in these words which imply blame for them, since those who sit are women and children. It may also be an expression of the permission of Muhammad (ﷺ) to sit, meaning: when Allah disliked their going out, He facilitated that you say to them: ﴿Sit with those who sit﴾. "Qu'ud" here is an expression for staying behind and delay, as in the words of the poet:

"...............................  and sit, for you are the one who eats and clothes"

In all of this there is no room for the outward form (al-hay'ah), and Allah's disliking of their setting out is an act of kindness toward the believers.

The words of the Most High: ﴿Had they gone out with you﴾ — the verse... is a report that had they gone out, their going out would have been a harm, and His words "illa khabalan" (but corruption) are an exceptive construction of a non-continuous kind (istithna' munqati'). This is the view of those who assumed there was no corruption in the army of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for the hypocrites to increase; so the meaning is: they would add to you neither strength nor vigour, but only corruption. It is also possible that the exception is continuous (ghayr munqati'), because the army of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at the expedition of Tabuk had many hypocrites in it, and for them there is undoubtedly corruption; so had these gone out, they would have mixed with those who went out, and corruption would have increased. "Khabal" is corruption in things that are joined and bound together, such as friendships and some bodily members. From it is the verse of the poet:

"O sons of Lubayna, you are not a hand except a hand whose upper arm is corrupted"

Ibn Abi 'Abla read "ma zadakum" without a waw.

The majority of readers read "la-awda'u," and its meaning is: they would have hastened the pace. "Khilalakum" means: between you, from here to here, to fill the gap between the two men. "Al-iyda'" is hastening the pace. Al-Zajjaj said: "khilalakum" means: in what causes discord among you.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak, and what would he say regarding the words of the Most High: ﴿So they penetrated between the dwellings﴾ [al-Isra': 5]? Mujahid read, as transmitted by al-Naqqash from him: "wa la-awfadu," which has the meaning of hastening, and from it is the words of the Most High: ﴿to a idol they rush﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 43]. It is reported from al-Zubayr that he read: "wa la-arfadu." Abu al-Fath said: this is from "rafada al-ba'ir" when it hastened in its walk, rafadan and rafadanan. From it is the words of Hassan ibn Thabit:

"With a bottle that spilled what was in its bottom, like the spilling of a she-camel by a hurried rider"

In the Mushaf, "wa la awda'u" is written with an alif after the "la," and likewise in the words of the Most High: ﴿or I will surely slaughter him﴾ [al-Naml: 21]. It is said that this is due to the roughness of the orthography of the early ones. Al-Zajjaj said: they wrote it this way because the fatha in Hebrew and many languages is written as an alif.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is possible that the vowel of the lam is prolonged, so that there arises between the lam and the hamza of "awda'a" [a sound].

The words of the Most High: ﴿seeking to cause you trouble﴾ mean: they seek for you discord. As for the words: ﴿and among you there are listeners to them﴾, Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is: spies who listen to the news and convey it to them. al-Tabari preferred this view, while al-Naqqash said: the intensive form of the pattern weakens this view.

The majority of the commentators said: its meaning is: among you are obedient ones who listen to them. The words of the Most High: ﴿And Allah knows the wrongdoers﴾ are a warning to them and to anyone among the believers who has this characteristic.

It is also possible that the exception is continuous (ghayr munqati'), because the army of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at the expedition of Tabuk had many hypocrites in it, and for them there is undoubtedly corruption; so had these gone out, they would have mixed with those who went out, and corruption would have increased. "Khabal" is corruption in things that are joined and bound together, such as friendships and some bodily members. From it is the verse of the poet:

"O sons of Lubayna, you are not a hand except a hand whose upper arm is corrupted"

Ibn Abi 'Abla read "ma zadakum" without a waw.

The majority of readers read "la-awda'u," and its meaning is: they would have hastened the pace. "Khilalakum" means: between you, from here to here, to fill the gap between the two men. "Al-iyda'" is hastening the pace. Al-Zajjaj said: "khilalakum" means: in what causes discord among you.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak, and what would he say regarding the words of the Most High: ﴿So they penetrated between the dwellings﴾ [al-Isra': 5]? Mujahid read, as transmitted by al-Naqqash from him: "wa la-awfadu," which has the meaning of hastening, and from it is the words of the Most High: ﴿to a idol they rush﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 43]. It is reported from al-Zubayr that he read: "wa la-arfadu." Abu al-Fath said: this is from "rafada al-ba'ir" when it hastened in its walk, rafadan and rafadanan. From it is the words of Hassan ibn Thabit:

"With a bottle that spilled what was in its bottom, like the spilling of a she-camel by a hurried rider"

In the Mushaf, "wa la awda'u" is written with an alif after the "la," and likewise in the words of the Most High: ﴿or I will surely slaughter him﴾ [al-Naml: 21]. It is said that this is due to the roughness of the orthography of the early ones. Al-Zajjaj said: they wrote it this way because the fatha in Hebrew and many languages is written as an alif.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is possible that the vowel of the lam is prolonged, so that there arises between the lam and the hamza of "awda'a" [a sound].

The words of the Most High: ﴿seeking to cause you trouble﴾ mean: they seek for you discord. As for the words: ﴿and among you there are listeners to them﴾, Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is: spies who listen to the news and convey it to them. al-Tabari preferred this view, while al-Naqqash said: the intensive form of the pattern weakens this view.

The majority of the commentators said: its meaning is: among you are obedient ones who listen to them. The words of the Most High: ﴿And Allah knows the wrongdoers﴾ are a warning to them and to anyone among the believers who has this characteristic.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 48–51:

(p-328) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Indeed, they had sought discord before, and they had upset affairs for you until the truth came and the command of Allah prevailed, while they were averse.﴾ ﴿And among them is he who says, "Grant me leave and do not put me into trial." Unquestionably, they have fallen into trial. And indeed, Hell is encompassing the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿If good befalls you, it distresses them; but if a misfortune strikes you, they say, "We had already taken our precaution," and they turn away while rejoicing.﴾ ﴿Say, "Nothing will strike us except what Allah has decreed for us. He is our Protector, and upon Allah let the believers rely."﴾

In this verse there is a belittling of them. It informs that they had, in the past, striven against Islam, and Allah nullified their striving. The meaning of His saying "before" (min qabl) is their condition from the time of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) migration and their turning back from him at Uhud and other occasions. The meaning of ﴿and they upset affairs for you﴾ is that they contrived them, turning them back and front (ẓahran li-baṭn), they examined their aspects and divisions, and they strove with every stratagem. Muslima ibn Muharib recited "wa qalabū" (with the lam lightened) without doubling. "The command of Allah" is Islam and its call.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿And among them is he who says, "Grant me leave"﴾, it was revealed concerning al-Jadd ibn Qays. It is mentioned that "when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded the campaign to the lands of the Romans, he urged the people, and he said to al-Jadd ibn Qays: '(Would you, this year, [take part] in the fighting against the sons of al-Asfar?)', and he said to him and to the people: '(Fight, you will capture the daughters of al-Asfar)'. So al-Jadd ibn Qays said to him: 'Grant me leave to stay behind and do not put me into trial by mentioning the daughters of al-Asfar, for my people know that I cannot restrain myself from women when I see them.'" Ibn Ishaq mentioned something similar to this statement, which contains much slackness and a lack of firmness in the excuse. Al-Tabari transmitted with a chain that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Fight at Tabuk, you will capture the daughters of al-Asfar', so al-Jadd said: 'Grant me leave and do not put us into trial with women'." This is a different line of reasoning when examined, and it is more akin to hypocrisy and hostility. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: al-Jadd said: "But I will help you with my wealth." Some people interpreted his saying "and do not put me into trial" to mean: do not make things difficult for me until I need to commit your disobedience and opposition, so make things easy for me and leave me without being ostracised (ghayr mujallah). This is a good interpretation that keeps to the wording, but the consistent reports of the mention of the daughters of al-Asfar stand as an objection to this interpretation. Ibn 'Umar (sic: 'Isa ibn 'Umar) recited "wa lā tufitnī" with a damma on the first tā'. Abu Hatim said: this is the dialect of the Banu Tamim. Al-Asfar is Rum ibn 'Ays ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Khalil, peace be upon them both, and he was yellow in colour, so the Romans are called "the sons of al-Asfar". From this is the saying of Abu Sufyan: "The affair of the son of Abi Kabsha has become great; indeed the king of the sons of al-Asfar fears him." From this is also the saying of the poet:

Ḥ The noble sons of al-Asfar are the kings of the Romans ∗∗∗ none of them remains mentioned.

Al-Naqqash and al-Mahdawi mentioned that al-Asfar was a man of the Abyssinians who came to the lands of the Romans, married, and begot daughters who had beauty. This is weak. His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿Unquestionably, they have fallen into trial﴾ means: into that which they showed flight from, by what has become clear to you and to the believers of their hypocrisy, and what is established with you of their disbelief, and the relationship between you and them has been corrupted.

And ﴿they have fallen﴾ is an expression indicating the firmness of their falling into it, and from it: "You have fallen upon the one who knows" (a'la al-khabir saqatta). Then He said: ﴿And indeed, Hell is encompassing the disbelievers﴾, and this is a severe threat to them, meaning: it is their destination and their outcome, however they turn about in the world, for to it they will be returned; so it encompasses them in this respect.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿If good befalls you﴾ and the verse, He, the Exalted, informed of their belief and what they were upon. The "good" here, in relation to the campaign, is spoil and victory, and the "misfortune" is defeat and failure. The wording is general thereafter for every loved and disliked thing. The meaning of His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿We had already taken our precaution﴾ is: we exercised caution in our staying behind, and we looked out for ourselves.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿Say, "Nothing will strike us"﴾ and the verse: In this verse Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded His Prophet to respond to the hypocrites and to spoil their joy by informing them that the thing they consider a misfortune is not (p-330) as they believe it to be, but rather all of it is from what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has decreed for the believers: either it is victory and joy in this world, or it is a store for the Hereafter. Talha ibn Musarrif recited "Say: will it strike us?" (qul hal yuṣībunā), reported by Abu Hatim, and in Ibn Jinni's record: Talha ibn Musarrif and A'yan, judge of al-Rayy, recited "qul lan yuṣayyibanā" with the second yā' doubled and kasra. Abu al-Fath mentioned this and explained it, but it is an error, and Allah knows best.

Abu Hatim said: 'Amr ibn Shafiq said: I heard A'yan, judge of al-Rayy, reciting "qul lan yuṣībannā" with the nun doubled. Abu Hatim said: this is not permissible, because the nun does not enter with "lan"; and had it been from Talha ibn Musarrif it would have been permissible, because it is with "hal", as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Will his plot remove that which enrages him?﴾ [al-Hajj: 15]. His saying ﴿Allah has decreed﴾ may mean what He has decided and ordained. It may also mean what Allah has prescribed for us in our Qur'an upon us, that we either achieve victory over our enemy or are martyred, and so enter Paradise.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This possibility returns to the first, and al-Zajjaj mentioned both.

His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾ means: alongside their striving and effort, since there is no power and no strength except through Allah. This is the view of most scholars, and it is the correct one, and it is what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) practised throughout his life, including his wearing two coats of mail. People have been confused about the meaning of reliance (tawakkul) in provision. The clearer and more correct position is that a man who is able to earn lawful, pure livelihood free of any reproach should seek what protects and sustains him, such as gathering firewood and the like, for Allah, Blessed and Exalted, has linked provision to seeking it, as in His saying: ﴿And shake towards you the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you fresh ripe dates﴾ [Maryam: 25].

From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) about the bird: "It goes out hungry in the morning and returns full in the evening..." the hadith. From this is his (ﷺ) saying: "Tie it down and rely [upon Allah]." Some people held that a strong, robust man who reaches such a level of reliance as to enter a cave or a house whose matter he does not know, and remains remembering Allah, relying, saying: "If provision remains for me, Allah will bring it; and if my provision has been completed, I die" — that this is good and reaches a high station according to some people. And my father, may Allah be pleased with him, related to me that there was in the Haram a man who stayed continuously, and from his pocket he would take out a card from time to time, look at it, then put it back, and he remained in that state until he died in that place. When I read the card, I found written on it: ﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord, for indeed you are before Our eyes﴾ [al-Tur: 48].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Most people of knowledge do not accept this path. Rather, a man should strive for his daily sustenance in a fine manner that involves no doubtful matter. If that becomes impossible for him and he reaches the point of necessity, then if he is lenient in asking and eats carrion or whatever is available to him of it, it is permissible for him. If he is patient and seeks reward from Allah, he is in the highest rank according to some people; and among people there are those who hold that it is an obligation upon him to preserve his life-breath.

As for the one who chooses to throw himself into destruction while striving is possible, this was never the conduct of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), nor of the Companions, nor of the scholars. Allah, glory be to Him, is the granter of success to what is right.

Among the arguments of those who uphold reliance is the hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ) in which he said: "Seventy thousand of my community will enter Paradise without reckoning, and they are those who do not seek incantation (ruqya), nor seek to be treated by incantation, nor cauterise, nor seek medical treatment, and upon their Lord they rely." In this hadith, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made supplication for 'Ukkasha ibn Mihsan to (p-332) be among them. It was said: that was because he knew of him that he was so; and he said to another: "'Ukkasha has outstripped you with it," and the supplication was cooled. It was said: that was because he was a hypocrite. It was also said: rather, he knew of him that he would not be sound at this degree of reliance.

Abu Hatim said: this is not permissible, because the nun does not enter with "lan"; and had it been from Talha ibn Musarrif it would have been permissible, because it is with "hal", as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Will his plot remove that which enrages him?﴾ [al-Hajj: 15]. His saying ﴿Allah has decreed﴾ may mean what He has decided and ordained. It may also mean what Allah has prescribed for us in our Qur'an upon us, that we either achieve victory over our enemy or are martyred, and so enter Paradise.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This possibility returns to the first, and al-Zajjaj mentioned both.

His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾ means: alongside their striving and effort, since there is no power and no strength except through Allah. This is the view of most scholars, and it is the correct one, and it is what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) practised throughout his life, including his wearing two coats of mail. People have been confused about the meaning of reliance (tawakkul) in provision. The clearer and more correct position is that a man who is able to earn lawful, pure livelihood free of any reproach should seek what protects and sustains him, such as gathering firewood and the like, for Allah, Blessed and Exalted, has linked provision to seeking it, as in His saying: ﴿And shake towards you the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you fresh ripe dates﴾ [Maryam: 25].

From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) about the bird: "It goes out hungry in the morning and returns full in the evening..." the hadith. From this is his (ﷺ) saying: "Tie it down and rely [upon Allah]." Some people held that a strong, robust man who reaches such a level of reliance as to enter a cave or a house whose matter he does not know, and remains remembering Allah, relying, saying: "If provision remains for me, Allah will bring it; and if my provision has been completed, I die" — that this is good and reaches a high station according to some people. And my father, may Allah be pleased with him, related to me that there was in the Haram a man who stayed continuously, and from his pocket he would take out a card from time to time, look at it, then put it back, and he remained in that state until he died in that place. When I read the card, I found written on it: ﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord, for indeed you are before Our eyes﴾ [al-Tur: 48].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Most people of knowledge do not accept this path. Rather, a man should strive for his daily sustenance in a fine manner that involves no doubtful matter. If that becomes impossible for him and he reaches the point of necessity, then if he is lenient in asking and eats carrion or whatever is available to him of it, it is permissible for him. If he is patient and seeks reward from Allah, he is in the highest rank according to some people; and among people there are those who hold that it is an obligation upon him to preserve his life-breath.

Among the arguments of those who uphold reliance is the hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ) in which he said: "Seventy thousand of my community will enter Paradise without reckoning, and they are those who do not seek incantation (ruqya), nor seek to be treated by incantation, nor cauterise, nor seek medical treatment, and upon their Lord they rely." In this hadith, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made supplication for 'Ukkasha ibn Mihsan to (p-332) be among them. It was said: that was because he knew of him that he was so; and he said to another: "'Ukkasha has outstripped you with it," and the supplication was cooled. It was said: that was because he was a hypocrite. It was also said: rather, he knew of him that he would not be sound at this degree of reliance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 48–51:

﴿Indeed, they had sought discord before, and they had upset affairs for you until the truth came and the command of Allah prevailed, while they were averse.﴾ ﴿And among them is he who says, "Grant me leave and do not put me into trial." Unquestionably, they have fallen into trial. And indeed, Hell is encompassing the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿If good befalls you, it distresses them; but if a misfortune strikes you, they say, "We had already taken our precaution," and they turn away while rejoicing.﴾ ﴿Say, "Nothing will strike us except what Allah has decreed for us. He is our Protector, and upon Allah let the believers rely."﴾

In this verse there is a belittling of them. It informs that they had, in the past, striven against Islam, and Allah nullified their striving. The meaning of His saying "before" (min qabl) is their condition from the time of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) migration and their turning back from him at Uhud and other occasions. The meaning of ﴿and they upset affairs for you﴾ is that they contrived them, turning them back and front (ẓahran li-baṭn), they examined their aspects and divisions, and they strove with every stratagem.
