So al-Jadd ibn Qays said to him: 'Grant me leave to stay behind and do not put me into trial by mentioning the daughters of al-Asfar, for my people know that I cannot restrain myself from women when I see them.'" Ibn Ishaq mentioned something similar to this statement, which contains much slackness and a lack of firmness in the excuse. Al-Tabari transmitted with a chain that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Fight at Tabuk, you will capture the daughters of al-Asfar', so al-Jadd said: 'Grant me leave and do not put us into trial with women'." This is a different line of reasoning when examined, and it is more akin to hypocrisy and hostility. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: al-Jadd said: "But I will help you with my wealth." Some people interpreted his saying "and do not put me into trial" to mean: do not make things difficult for me until I need to commit your disobedience and opposition, so make things easy for me and leave me without being ostracised (ghayr mujallah). This is a good interpretation that keeps to the wording, but the consistent reports of the mention of the daughters of al-Asfar stand as an objection to this interpretation. Ibn 'Umar (sic: 'Isa ibn 'Umar) recited "wa lā tufitnī" with a damma on the first tā'. Abu Hatim said: this is the dialect of the Banu Tamim. Al-Asfar is Rum ibn 'Ays ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Khalil, peace be upon them both, and he was yellow in colour, so the Romans are called "the sons of al-Asfar". From this is the saying of Abu Sufyan: "The affair of the son of Abi Kabsha has become great; indeed the king of the sons of al-Asfar fears him." From this is also the saying of the poet:

Ḥ The noble sons of al-Asfar are the kings of the Romans ∗∗∗ none of them remains mentioned.

Al-Naqqash and al-Mahdawi mentioned that al-Asfar was a man of the Abyssinians who came to the lands of the Romans, married, and begot daughters who had beauty. This is weak. His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿Unquestionably, they have fallen into trial﴾ means: into that which they showed flight from, by what has become clear to you and to the believers of their hypocrisy, and what is established with you of their disbelief, and the relationship between you and them has been corrupted.

And ﴿they have fallen﴾ is an expression indicating the firmness of their falling into it, and from it: "You have fallen upon the one who knows" (a'la al-khabir saqatta). Then He said: ﴿And indeed, Hell is encompassing the disbelievers﴾, and this is a severe threat to them, meaning: it is their destination and their outcome, however they turn about in the world, for to it they will be returned; so it encompasses them in this respect.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿If good befalls you﴾ and the verse, He, the Exalted, informed of their belief and what they were upon. The "good" here, in relation to the campaign, is spoil and victory, and the "misfortune" is defeat and failure. The wording is general thereafter for every loved and disliked thing. The meaning of His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿We had already taken our precaution﴾ is: we exercised caution in our staying behind, and we looked out for ourselves.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿Say, "Nothing will strike us"﴾ and the verse: In this verse Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded His Prophet to respond to the hypocrites and to spoil their joy by informing them that the thing they consider a misfortune is not (p-330) as they believe it to be, but rather all of it is from what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has decreed for the believers: either it is victory and joy in this world, or it is a store for the Hereafter. Talha ibn Musarrif recited "Say: will it strike us?" (qul hal yuṣībunā), reported by Abu Hatim, and in Ibn Jinni's record: Talha ibn Musarrif and A'yan, judge of al-Rayy, recited "qul lan yuṣayyibanā" with the second yā' doubled and kasra. Abu al-Fath mentioned this and explained it, but it is an error, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 52–53:

Allah the Exalted says:

﴿Say, "Do you await for us except one of the two best outcomes (martyrdom or victory)? And we await for you that Allah will afflict you with a punishment from Him or at our hands. So wait; indeed, we are waiting with you."﴾ ﴿Say, "Spend willingly or unwillingly; it will never be accepted from you. Indeed, you have been a defiantly disobedient people."﴾

The meaning of this verse is a refutation of the hypocrites in their belief about the believers, and a removal of their assumption that calamities befall the believers, along with an announcement that these calamities, however they turn out, are good outcomes.

Tarabbasu (تَرَبَّصُونَ) means "you wait." Al-husnayan (الحُسْنَيانِ) are martyrdom and victory. Ibn Muhaysin (ابْنُ مُحَيْصِنٍ) recited "إلّا احْدى الحُسْنَيَيْنِ" with the connecting of the alif of "iḥdā" (إحْدى), i.e., reading it as "illā ḥdā al-ḥusnayayn" with the hamza dropped in connected speech.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a dialectal usage and is not according to analogy (qiyas). This is like the saying of the poet:

"O Mughira, how many a grave matter..."

And the saying of another:

"If I do not fight, then dress me in a veil."

(p-333) His saying, ﴿with a punishment from Him﴾, means death through the causing of grief, and it may be that it is a threat of the punishment of the Hereafter. His saying, ﴿or at our hands﴾, means killing.

It has also been said: ﴿with a punishment from Him﴾ means kinds of calamities and disasters. His saying, ﴿So wait; indeed, we are waiting with you﴾, is a warning and a threat.

As for the saying of the Exalted, ﴿Say, "Spend willingly or unwillingly"﴾, its cause is that Jadd ibn Qays, when he said, ﴿Grant me permission and do not put me into trial﴾ [al-Tawbah: 49], said, "I will help you with wealth," and so this verse was revealed concerning him, and it is general after him. Willingly and unwillingly encompass every kind of spending. Ibn Waththab and al-A'mash recited "أو كُرْهًا" with a dammah on the kaf (كُرْهًا).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Here the discussion connects to the deeds of the disbeliever when they are acts of goodness, such as maintaining ties of kinship, setting broken bones, and aiding the oppressed: does he benefit from them or not? The concise answer on this is that in Sahih Muslim, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "Indeed, the reward of the disbeliever for his good deeds is in the food that he is fed," and similar to that. This is convincing, and no further investigation is needed beyond it. As for whether he benefits from them in the Hereafter, there is no proof. That is because 'Aishah, the Mother of the Believers, said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Messenger of Allah, what about 'Abdullah ibn Ju'dan? Will he benefit from what he used to feed and do of good?" He said: "No, for he never once said: 'My Lord, forgive me my sin on the Day of Judgment.'" Another proof is the saying of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, to his son: "That is al-'As ibn Wa'il; may Allah not reward him with good." And this statement was after the death of al-'As. (This is a long hadith.) A third proof is the hadith of Hakim ibn Hizam according to one of the two interpretations, namely the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "You have embraced Islam with the good that you had previously done." There is no proof in the matter of Abu Talib and his being in shallow fire, because that was by the intercession of Muhammad (ﷺ), and because he found him in a deep part of the Fire and brought him out. Even if we suppose that this was due to his own deeds, he would not have needed intercession.

As for the evil deeds of the disbeliever, they increase his punishment, and by that they differ in the punishment of Hell.

As for the saying of the Exalted, ﴿Spend﴾, it is a command that implicitly contains a condition (shart, i.e., a conditional clause), and this applies to every command that has a response. The implied meaning is: "If you spend, it will not be accepted from you." But when the command is stripped of a response, it does not carry the implication of a conditional clause.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 54–56:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿And nothing prevented their contributions from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger, and they do not come to the prayer except while they are lazy, and they do not spend except while they are unwilling.﴾ ﴿So do not let their wealth or their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them through them in the worldly life, and that their souls should depart while they are disbelievers.﴾ ﴿And they swear by Allah that they are indeed of you, but they are not of you; rather, they are a people who are afraid.﴾

It is possible that the meaning of the verse is: "And Allah did not prevent them from having it accepted except because they disbelieved in Allah." In this case, the first "an" (أنْ) is in a position of genitive, and the verb put it in the accusative once the governing particle was removed. The second "anna" (أنَّ) is in a position of accusative, as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). It is also possible that the meaning is: "And Allah did not prevent them from the acceptance of their contributions except for their disbelief." In this case, the first (أنْ) is in a position of accusative. It is also possible that the meaning is: "And nothing prevented them from the acceptance of their contributions except their disbelief," in which case the second (كُفْرُهُمْ) is in the nominative position as the subject (fa'ilah).

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read: "an tuqbala minhum nafaqatuhum" (أنْ تُقْبَلَ مِنهم نَفَقاتُهُمْ). Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Nafi' (according to what has been transmitted from him) read: "an yuqbala minhum nafaqatuhum" (أنْ يُقْبَلَ مِنهم نَفَقاتُهُمْ) with the ya'. al-A'raj, with a variant reported from him, read: "an tuqbala minhum nafaqatuhum" (أنْ تُقْبَلَ مِنهم نَفَقَتُهُمْ) with the ta' on top and the singular "nafaqah." al-A'mash read: "an yuqbala minhum sadaqatuhum" (أنْ يُقْبَلَ مِنهم صَدَقاتُهُمْ). A group read: "an naqbala minhum nafaqatahum" (أنْ نَقْبَلَ مِنهم نَفَقَتَهُمْ) with the nun and the accusative for "nafaqah."

"Kusala" (كُسالى) is the plural of "kaslan" (كَسْلانَ). When "kaslan" is feminine as "kasla" (كَسْلى), it does not take tanwin in any way. If its feminine is "kaslanah" (كَسْلانَةٍ), then in the indefinite form it takes tanwin.

Then He, blessed and exalted, informed about them that they "do not spend except with reluctance" (إلّا عَلى كَراهِيَةٍ), since they do not intend by it the countenance of Allah nor the love of the believers. Nothing remains but the loss of wealth, and that is undoubtedly one of their displeasing things.

As for His words, the Exalted: ﴿So do not let their wealth impress you⦈ [the verse]: this expression belittles the status of the hypocrites and gives the reason for Allah's granting them wealth and children as His will to punish them through them. Scholars differed about the mode of the punishment. Qatadah said: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, so the meaning is: "So do not let their wealth or their children impress you in the worldly life; Allah only intends to punish them through them in the Hereafter." al-Hasan said: the mode of the punishment is that He obligated them, through them, to pay zakat and to spend in the way of Allah.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The pronoun in His words "through them" (بِها) refers, in this view, to the wealth alone.

Ibn Zayd and others said: the punishment is the calamities of the world, and its misfortunes are a punishment for them, since they are not rewarded for them. Although this view encompasses the view of al-Hasan, the view of al-Hasan is strengthened by specifying it, since their punishment through the imposition of the Shari'ah is greater than their punishment through the other misfortunes, because humiliation and defeat accompany the commands of the Shari'ah for them.

His words: ﴿and that their souls should depart﴾ may mean: "and they die in disbelief." It may also mean: "and their souls depart from the severity of the punishment that befalls them."

His words: ﴿while they are disbelievers﴾ are a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) according to the first interpretation, and this is not necessarily so according to the second interpretation.

As for His words, the Exalted: ﴿And they swear﴾ [the verse]: Allah, the Exalted, informed about the hypocrites that they swear that they are of the believers in religion and the Shari'ah. Then He, the Exalted, informed about them, in general terms and not specifically, that they are not of the believers; rather, they fear them, so they show faith while concealing hypocrisy. "Al-faraq" (الفَرَقُ) is fear, and "al-faruqah" (الفَرُوقَةُ) is a coward. In the proverb: "Fear is better than two loves" (وَفَرَقٌ خَيْرٌ مِن حُبَّيْنِ).

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

In this case, the first "an" (أنْ) is in a position of genitive, and the verb put it in the accusative once the governing particle was removed. The second "anna" (أنَّ) is in a position of accusative, as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). It is also possible that the meaning is: "And Allah did not prevent them from the acceptance of their contributions except for their disbelief." In this case, the first (أنْ) is in a position of accusative. It is also possible that the meaning is: "And nothing prevented them from the acceptance of their contributions except their disbelief," in which case the second (كُفْرُهُمْ) is in the nominative position as the subject (fa'ilah).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The pronoun in His words "through them" (بِها) refers, in this view, to the wealth alone.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verse 57–59:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Were they to find a refuge, or caves, or a place to enter, they would turn to it while rushing headlong.﴾ ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities. If they are given from them, they are pleased; but if they are not given from them, behold, they become angry.﴾ ﴿And if only they had been pleased with what Allah and His Messenger gave them, and said, "Allah is sufficient for us; Allah will give us from His bounty, and so will His Messenger. Indeed, we are toward Allah desirous."﴾

Al-malja' (refuge): from laja'a yaljau, meaning to take shelter and seek protection. The majority of readers recited "aw maghaarat" with a fatha on the mim, while Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf recited "aw mughaarat" with a damma on the mim. These are the hollows in the flanks of mountains. The fatha on the mim derives from "ghaara al-shay'" (the thing entered), as in "ghaarat al-'ayn" (the eye sank into its sockets), i.e. it entered into the orbits. The damma on the mim derives from "aghaara al-shay' ghayrahu" (he caused the thing to enter something else), i.e. made it enter. This is one way of deriving the word. It is also said that the Arabs say "ghaara al-rajul wa-aghaara" with one meaning, namely "entered." Al-Zajjaj said: when he enters the depression (al-ghawr), so the word may also be derived from this.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also valid, in the reading with a damma on the mim, that it derives from the expression "habl mughaar," meaning twisted rope; then this is borrowed for a matter that is firmly and tightly bound. The interpretation then becomes: "Were they to find a fortified stronghold or tightly bound affairs that would protect them from you."

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿or a place to enter, they would turn to it﴾. The majority of readers recited "mudkhalan," whose root is muftaʿal, a form of emphasis and intensification, and its meaning is a tunnel or passage into the earth. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, explained it in accordance with what we have mentioned regarding "al-malja' wa-l-maghaarat wa-l-mudkhal." Al-Zajjaj said: the mudkhal means: a people who would admit them into their group. Maslama ibn Muharib, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn Muhaysin, and Ibn Kathir, according to a variant from him, recited "aw madkhalan," which is from dakhala. Qatada, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, and al-A'mash recited "aw mudda&khalan" with the doubling of both letters. Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited "mundakhalan" with a nun; Abu al-Fath said: this is like the saying of the poet:

"... and my hand does not slip into the hot ghee."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Abu Hatim said: the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b is "mutdakhalan" with an open ta', and it is narrated from al-A'mash and 'Isa: "mudkhalan" with a damma on the mim, which is from adkhala (to cause to enter).

The people recited "lawallaw," and the grandfather of Abu 'Ubayda ibn Qarmal recited "lawalaw" from al-muwalah (alliance). Sa'id ibn Muslim rejected it and said: I think it is "lawa'alaw" meaning "lajau" (they sought refuge). The majority of readers recited "yajmahuna," meaning they rush forward, determined and not turning back. From it is the saying of Muhalhil:

"Indeed I have charged headlong into their blood... until I saw the men of their lineage lying still."

Anas ibn Malik recited "yajmazuna," meaning they flee. From it is their saying in the hadith of stoning: "When the stones struck him painfully, he jamaza (fled)."

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you﴾, the verse. The pronoun in His saying "wa-minhum" refers to the hypocrites. Al-Tabari transmitted from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that he said: «The son of Dhu al-Khuwaysira al-Tamimi came while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was dividing a division, and said: "Be just, O Muhammad,"» the well-known long hadith, and in it: Abu Sa'id said: so this verse was revealed concerning that: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities﴾. Dawud ibn Abi 'Asim narrated that «the Prophet ﷺ was brought some charity and he divided it, and behind him was a man from the Ansar who said: "This is not justice,"» and then the verse was revealed.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the tendency of a hypocrite. Likewise it has been narrated through more than one chain that the verse was revealed because of the speech of the hypocrites when they were not given according to the excess of their desires.

And ﴿yalmizuka﴾ means: he criticises you and takes from you behind your back (al-ghayba). From it is the saying of the poet:

"When I meet you, you show me flattery, but if I am absent, you are the one who defames and slanders."

From it is the saying of Ru'ba:

"... in the shade of my two ages of falsehood and my blaming."

Al-hamz also has the same sense, and from it is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Woe to every slanderer, backbiter﴾ [al-Humazah: 1]. It was said to one of the Arabs: "Does the mouse get bitten (yuhmaz)?" He said: "Indeed the cat bites it." Abu 'Ali said: he made eating (al-akl) into hamz, and this is a metaphor, just as Hassan ibn Thabit borrowed ghart (hunger) in his saying:

"... and she becomes hungry from the flesh of the heedless."

(p-340) constructed upon borrowing eating for backbiting.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The Bedouin did not make hamz mean eating; he only meant striking it with the fang and the claw. The majority of readers recited "yalmizuka" with a kasra on the mim. Ibn Kathir, as narrated from him by Hammad ibn Salama, recited "yalmuzuka" with a damma on the mim; this is the reading of the people of Makkah, and the reading of al-Hasan, Abu Raja', and others. Al-A'mash recited "yulammizuka," and Hammad ibn Salama also narrated from Ibn Kathir: "yulamizuka," which is the form of mufa'ala from one party, because it is an act that did not come from the Prophet ﷺ.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And if only they had been pleased with what Allah and His Messenger gave them﴾, the verse.

It is a description of the state in which the upright should be. Allah, the Exalted, says: "And if these hypocrites had been pleased with Allah's division of provision for them and what He gave them through the hands of His Messenger, and had hoped in Allah's bounty and His Messenger's, and had acknowledged their desire toward Allah, it would have been better for them and more excellent than what they are in." The response (jawab) is omitted from the verse because the apparent sense of the speech indicates it, and this is from the eloquence and conciseness of the discourse.

"Indeed I have charged headlong into their blood... until I saw the men of their lineage lying still."

Anas ibn Malik recited "yajmazuna," meaning they flee. From it is their saying in the hadith of stoning: "When the stones struck him painfully, he jamaza (fled)."

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you﴾, the verse. The pronoun in His saying "wa-minhum" refers to the hypocrites. Al-Tabari transmitted from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that he said: «The son of Dhu al-Khuwaysira al-Tamimi came while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was dividing a division, and said: "Be just, O Muhammad,"» the well-known long hadith, and in it: Abu Sa'id said: so this verse was revealed concerning that: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities﴾. Dawud ibn Abi 'Asim narrated that «the Prophet ﷺ was brought some charity and he divided it, and behind him was a man from the Ansar who said: "This is not justice,"» and then the verse was revealed.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the tendency of a hypocrite. Likewise it has been narrated through more than one chain that the verse was revealed because of the speech of the hypocrites when they were not given according to the excess of their desires.

And ﴿yalmizuka﴾ means: he criticises you and takes from you behind your back (al-ghayba). From it is the saying of the poet:

"When I meet you, you show me flattery, but if I am absent, you are the one who defames and slanders."

From it is the saying of Ru'ba:

"... in the shade of my two ages of falsehood and my blaming."

Al-hamz also has the same sense, and from it is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Woe to every slanderer, backbiter﴾ [al-Humazah: 1]. It was said to one of the Arabs: "Does the mouse get bitten (yuhmaz)?" He said: "Indeed the cat bites it." Abu 'Ali said: he made eating (al-akl) into hamz, and this is a metaphor, just as Hassan ibn Thabit borrowed ghart (hunger) in his saying:

"... and she becomes hungry from the flesh of the heedless."

(p-340) constructed upon borrowing eating for backbiting.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The Bedouin did not make hamz mean eating; he only meant striking it with the fang and the claw. The majority of readers recited "yalmizuka" with a kasra on the mim. Ibn Kathir, as narrated from him by Hammad ibn Salama, recited "yalmuzuka" with a damma on the mim; this is the reading of the people of Makkah, and the reading of al-Hasan, Abu Raja', and others. Al-A'mash recited "yulammizuka," and Hammad ibn Salama also narrated from Ibn Kathir: "yulamizuka," which is the form of mufa'ala from one party, because it is an act that did not come from the Prophet ﷺ.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And if only they had been pleased with what Allah and His Messenger gave them﴾, the verse.

It is a description of the state in which the upright should be. Allah, the Exalted, says: "And if these hypocrites had been pleased with Allah's division of provision for them and what He gave them through the hands of His Messenger, and had hoped in Allah's bounty and His Messenger's, and had acknowledged their desire toward Allah, it would have been better for them and more excellent than what they are in." The response (jawab) is omitted from the verse because the apparent sense of the speech indicates it, and this is from the eloquence and conciseness of the discourse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verse 60 (part 1 of 2):

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:
﴿Charity is only for the poor and the needy, and those employed to collect it, and those whose hearts are to be reconciled, and for freeing captives, and for those in debt, and for the cause of God, and for the wayfarer; an obligation from God. And God is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾

"Innama" (إنَّما) in this verse is restrictive (ḥāṣira), requiring that charity be confined to the eight categories. Scholars differed over the manner of distribution. Mālik and others said that it depends on the discretion of the imam (ijtihād al-imām) and according to the needs of those in need. Al-Shāfiʿī, may God have mercy on him, said: it is eight shares for eight categories, and none of them may be omitted, except that those whose hearts are to be reconciled have ceased to exist.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:
The proponent of this view says that it is not sufficient for the giver or the divider to give to each category less than three [persons].

(p-341) As for the faqīr and the miskīn, al-Aṣmaʿī and others said: the faqīr is more extreme in need (afqar fāqa). Others said: the miskīn is more extreme in need.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:
There is no way to resolve this difference or to prefer one view except by examining the evidence of the Qur'an and by examining the speech and poetry of the Arabs. Among the arguments of the first group is God's saying, Exalted is He: ﴿As for the ship, it belonged to needy men who worked on the sea﴾ [al-Kahf: 79].
This evidence has been objected to on several grounds. Among them: it is possible that He called them "needy" (masākīn) in relation to the usurper, even though they were wealthy in terms of the right of pre-emption (shuf'a), as you would say of a group: "He oppresses helpless needy people," though they may be well-off. Among them also: it was read as "li-massākīn" with a doubled sīn, meaning tanners who work with hides (al-musūk), as al-Naqqāsh and others said. Among them: their being attributed to them (idāfa) is not an attribution of ownership; rather, they were working with them, so it is like your saying "the saddle of the horse" and "the door of the house."

Among the argument of the others is the saying of the shepherd-poet:
"As for the faqīr whose milk-camel was
Enough for his dependents, and nothing of his livestock was left to him"

This evidence has been objected to on the grounds that he called him faqīr only after he no longer had a milk-camel, and that he only mentioned the milk-camel in the past tense. But this objection is refuted by the meaning of the poem. The poet's aim is to describe a raid that consumed the entire wealth of the tribe. He said: "As for the faqīr, his property was wiped out; so how about the wealthy in this situation?"

Those who say that the miskīn is more extreme in need went on to say that it derives from sukūn (stillness/rest), and that the faqīr derives from faqār al-ẓahr (the spine), as if his spine had been struck. Those who say that the faqīr is more extreme in need went on to say that it derives from faqartu al-bi'r, when you have drawn out everything in the well, and that the miskīn derives from sakan (dwelling/settlement).

(p-342) The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:
Despite this difference, the two are categories that share poverty and destitution. We should therefore investigate the reason for which God made them two, when their meaning is one. People have been confused about this. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim said: the fuqarā' are from among the Emigrants (muhājirūn), and the masākīn are those who did not emigrate. Al-Nakhaʿī said something similar. Sufyān said: the poor Bedouins are not given any of it.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:
The miskīn is the one who asks, and he is given in Medina and elsewhere. This statement describes the situation at the time the verse was revealed. But since the emigration ceased, people have been equal, and zakat is given to everyone who is characterized by poverty. ʿIkrima said: the fuqarā' are from among the Muslims, and the masākīn are from among the People of the Covenant (ahl al-dhimma), and do not call the poor among the Muslims "masākīn." Al-Shāfiʿī said in the Kitāb of Ibn al-Mundhir: the faqīr is one who has no property and no craft, whether he asks or is discreet; and the miskīn is one who has a craft or property, but it does not suffice him, whether he asks or does not ask. Qatāda ibn Di'āma said: the faqīr is the disabled needy person, and the miskīn is the healthy needy person. Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, al-Zuhrī, Ibn Zayd, Jābir ibn Zayd and Muḥammad ibn Maslama said: the masākīn are those who strive and ask, and the fuqarā' are those who keep themselves from asking. This last statement, when it is summarized and clarified, is the best that has been said on this matter.

Its clarification is that the faqīr is the one who has no property, but who does not humiliate himself nor expose his face (to ask), and this is either due to extreme abstention, or due to a bare subsistence he has, such as a milk-camel and the like. The miskīn is the one whose poverty is accompanied by humility, submission and begging. This is the state of maskana (meekness/destitution). Thus every miskīn is a faqīr, but not every faqīr is a miskīn. This is strengthened by the fact that God described the Children of Israel with maskana and linked it with dhilla (abasement), despite their wealth. When you reflect on what we have said, it becomes clear that they are two categories that exist among the Muslims. This is further strengthened by His, the Blessed and Exalted, saying: ﴿For the poor who are confined to the cause of God, who cannot travel about the land. The ignorant consider them wealthy because of their modesty﴾ [al-Baqara: 273]. It was said to a Bedouin: (p-343) "Are you a faqīr?" He said: "By God, I am a miskīn." The Prophet ﷺ said: "The miskīn is not the one who goes around and is turned away by a morsel or two morsels. Rather, the miskīn is the one who does not find sufficient wealth to suffice him, and whose need is not noticed so that he may be given charity." Recite if you wish: ﴿They do not ask people persistently﴾ [al-Baqara: 273]. This hadith indicates that the miskīn, linguistically, is the one who goes around. The Prophet's ﷺ attention in this hadith to the one who keeps himself from asking follows the pattern of the placing of the fuqarā' first in the verse, for the sake of concern, since if they are not attended to, they perish; whereas the miskīn presses and draws attention to himself.

As for the ʿāmil (collector), he is the man whom the imam appoints to go around to the people and gather their charity. Anyone who performs a task that is indispensable is among the ʿāmilīn, because he gathers the people for the collector. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: the ʿāmilīn are paid the price of what they did, according to the division of the Qur'an. The majority said: they are given the amount of their effort and expenses, as Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī in the Kitāb of Ibn al-Mundhir said. If that exceeds the value of the charity, there is disagreement. It was said: it is completed for them from the other shares. It was also said: rather, it is completed for them from one-fifth of the spoils (khums al-ghanīma). It is also disputed if a Hāshimite (member of the Prophet's clan) works with charity: it was said that he is given his wage from it, and it was said that rather he is given it from the one-fifth. It is not permissible for the collector to accept a gift or to court favor from the one he is collecting from. If he does so, it is returned to the public treasury (bayt al-māl), as the Prophet ﷺ did with Ibn al-Lutbiyya when he appointed him over the charity. He said: "This is for you, and this was given to me as a gift." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Why did you not sit in the house of your father and mother until you knew what would be given to you?" He took all of it from him.

(p-344) The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:
One should consider whether the collector's wage is taken before the work or after it, whether it is a hire (ijāra) or a reward (juʿl), whether the work is known or is pursued and its amount is only known after completion.

As for those whose hearts are to be reconciled, they were of two kinds: Muslims, and concealed unbelievers. Yaḥyā ibn Kathīr said: among them were Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb ibn Umayya, al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām, Ṣafwān ibn Umayya, Suhayl ibn ʿAmr, Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām, Abū Sufyān ibn al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, ʿUyayna, al-Aqraʿ, Mālik ibn ʿAwf, al-ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās, and al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Jāriya al-Thaqafī.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:
Most of these were from among the Ṭulaqāʾ (those freed at the conquest), whose apparent condition on the Day of the Conquest was disbelief. Then they remained displaying Islam, until reconciliation (istiʾlāf) strengthened it in most of them. Their reconciliation was either to bring a benefit to Islam or to ward off a harm from it. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may God be pleased with him, al-Ḥasan, al-Shaʿbī, and a group of the people of knowledge said: this category ended with the might and dominance of Islam. This is the well-known position of the school of Mālik, may God have mercy on him. ʿAbd al-Wahhāb said: if they are needed at some time, they are given from the charity.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:
In my view, ʿUmar's saying, may God be pleased with him, applies to specific individuals. He said to Abū Sufyān when he wanted to take his old stipend: "You take like a man from among the Muslims, for God has made you and your like independent." He meant: in reconciliation. As for ʿUmar denying reconciliation entirely, and on the frontiers of (p-345) Islam, that is far-fetched. Many of the people of knowledge said: those whose hearts are to be reconciled exist until the Day of Resurrection.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:
When the frontiers are considered, the need for reconciliation is found there.

Al-Zuhrī said: those whose hearts are to be reconciled are whoever embraces Islam from among a Jew or a Christian, even if he is wealthy.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:
He means: so that his soul may be softened and the religion of Islam may be made beloved to him.

As for al-riqāb (the captives/slaves), Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Mālik and others said: it is the beginning of manumission (ʿitq) and aiding the mukātab (a slave contracted to buy his freedom) with what will achieve his freedom. It is disputed whether the mukātab may be aided during the course of his installments, with prohibition or permission. And, on the view of permitting that if he fails, it was said: it is returned from the master's share. It was said: it stands, because at the time it was given he was in a valid state. Al-Shāfiʿī said: the meaning of ﴿and for the captives﴾ is: the mukātabīn, and manumission of a slave is not begun from it. This was also said by al-Layth, Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, and Ibn Jubayr. The reason is that these categories are given either for the benefit of the Muslims or for a need in themselves, and the slave has neither of these two reasons, whereas the mukātab has become one of those in need. Al-Zuhrī said: the share of the captives is in two halves: one half for the mukātabīn, and one half from which Muslim slaves who prayed are freed, and from which Muslim captives are ransomed. Others prevented this.

As for the gharim (one in debt), he is a man whose debt has overwhelmed him, not due to disobedience or foolishness. The scholars said: this man has his debt paid on his behalf, even if he has goods that sustain his life and provide for his dependents. Likewise the man who takes on a guarantee (ḥamāla) (p-346) in blood-money (diya) or in reconciling between tribes, and the like. He is one of the five about whom the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Charity is not lawful for a wealthy person except for five: one who collects it, or one who fights in the cause of God, or a man who has taken on a guarantee, or one to whom it is given as a gift, or one who buys it with his own wealth."

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:
The "those whose hearts are to be reconciled" have dropped out of this hadith. The debt of a deceased person is not paid from charity, and it is not given to one who owes a kaffāra (expiation) or similar rights of God. The gharim is only one who owes a debt for which he is imprisoned. It has been said in our school and others that the debt of the deceased is paid from charities, as Abū Thawr said.

As for fī sabīl Allāh (in the cause of God), it refers to the mujāhid (one who fights in jihad). He may take from the charity to spend on his campaign, even if he is wealthy. Ibn Ḥabīb said: pilgrims are not given from it unless they are poor, in which case they are given because of their poverty. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, Aḥmad and Isḥāq said: pilgrims are given from it even if they are wealthy, since the pilgrimage is in the cause of God. It is not given for the building of a mosque, a bridge, the purchase of a copy of the Qur'an, or the like.

As for ibn al-sabīl (the wayfarer), he is the man who is in a foreign land and on a journey, and has run out of resources. He is given from zakat even if he is wealthy in his own land. The traveler is called ibn al-sabīl because he constantly stays on the road (sabīl), just as the bird is called "son of water" because it constantly remains by it. From this, in my view, is their saying "ibn jalā" (son of clarity), and other things have been said about it. From it also is their saying: "the sons of war and the sons of glory."

Ibn al-Majishun, Mutarrif, Asbagh and Ibn Habib said: Neither are the Banu Hashim given from the obligatory alms (ṣadaqa mafrūḍa), nor from voluntary charity (taṭawwu‘), and their clients (mawālī) are not given either, because the client of a people is one of them. Ibn al-Qasim said: The Banu Hashim may be given from voluntary charity, and their clients may be given from both kinds of alms.

If someone asks for alms and claims that he is poor, one group said: he is given without being required to produce evidence of his poverty. This is unlike the rights of human beings, where a poor claimant must produce evidence, because these are the rights of people, and so the most cautious course is taken with them. Also, people who are assumed to have rights owed to other humans are presumed to be wealthy until their lack of means is established. This is shown by God's words: ﴿And if the debtor is in hardship﴾ (2:280), meaning: if hardship occurs, then (give him) respite. This indicates that the default assumption is wealth; if hardship arises, then there is a delay.

Another group said: a healthy man whose poverty is not known is not given, unless his poverty is known. As for someone who claims to be a debtor (gharim), a mukatab (one contracting to buy his freedom), a wayfarer (ibn al-sabil), one in God's way, or something similar, of which nothing is known, he is not given except with evidence, by unanimous agreement. It has been said regarding the debtor that his goods and all that he owns are to be sold, and then he is given on the basis of poverty. A man gives to his poor relatives, who have the greatest right over others. If his relative is absent in a place where prayer is shortened (qasr) when travelling to it, then his poor neighbour has priority. If the absence is not such that prayer is shortened to reach him, then it has been said: the relative has priority over the poor neighbour; and it has been said: the neighbour has priority.

A man gives to his relatives whose maintenance is not obligatory upon him. A woman may give to her husband. Some people said: this is so long as he has not been supporting her with it. A man may give to his wife if she is among the debtors.

There was disagreement concerning the walāʾ (right of patronage) of one who is freed from the alms. Malik said: his walāʾ belongs to the community of Muslims. Abu ‘Ubayd said: his walāʾ belongs to the one who freed him. ‘Ubayd Allah ibn al-Hasan said: his property is placed in the treasury of alms. Al-Hasan, Ahmad and Ishaq said: slaves are freed from his property.

If a man is owed a debt by one in difficulty, it has been said: he may forgive it for him and count that as part of his alms. It has also been said: this is not permissible at all. And it has been said: if he is someone whom, if he were brought before the judge, it would be possible for him to pay, then it is permissible; otherwise it is not permissible, because he has died.

As for the wayfarer (sabīl), it is the category we mentioned earlier. A man in God's way is given even if he is wealthy. Ashab al-Ra'y (the followers of personal opinion) said: one in God's way is not given except if he is cut off from his means. Ibn al-Mundhir said: this contradicts the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and the hadith of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). As for the Qur'an, it is His words: ﴿and in the way of God﴾ (9:60). As for the hadith, it is his saying: "It is not permissible except for five: for one who collects it, or for one who fights in the way of God..."

As for the manner of distribution, Malik and others said: according to need and the judgment of the imam, he places it in whichever category he sees fit. The same applies to the one who gives charity himself. This was also said by Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, Sa‘id ibn Jubayr, Ibrahim and Abu al-‘Aliya. Al-Tabari said: some later scholars said: when the giver distributes it himself, he distributes it among six categories, because there is no collector (‘amil) and because those whose hearts are to be reconciled (mu’allafa qulubuhum) have ceased. If the imam distributes it, then it is among seven categories. Al-Shafi‘i, ‘Ikrima and al-Zuhri said: it is eight divisions for eight categories, and none of them may be omitted. Al-Shafi‘i argued with the words of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to the man who asked him: "God, Exalted is He, was not content regarding the alms with the division of a prophet or anyone else until He Himself divided them, making them eight parts for eight categories. So if you are one of them, I will give to you."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The hadith is in the Musannaf of Abu Dawud. Abu Thawr said: if the imam distributes it, he does not omit any category; and if a man gives his charity to one category rather than another, that suffices for him. Al-Nakha‘i said: if the wealth is large, it is divided among all the categories; if it is small, he gives it to one category. A group of scholars said: one who has fifty dirhams is not given from zakat. Al-Hasan and Abu ‘Ubayd said: one who has an uqiyya, which is forty dirhams, is not given. Al-Hasan said: he is wealthy.

Al-Shafi‘i said: sometimes a man who has no fixed amount is wealthy through a dirham because of his effort and resourcefulness, and sometimes a man who has a fixed amount and dependants is weak in spirit and resourcefulness, so thousands do not make him wealthy. Abu Hanifa said: one who has two hundred dirhams should not take charity, and one who has less than that may take it without harm. Sufyan al-Thawri said: no more than fifty dirhams should be given to anyone from zakat, unless he is a debtor. Ashab al-Ra'y said: if one who is needy is given a thousand, it suffices. Abu Thawr said: he is given from charity until he becomes wealthy and the name of destitution is removed from him, and there is no harm in giving a poor man a thousand or more. Ibn al-Mundhir said: most of those from the people of knowledge whose views are preserved agreed that one who has a house and a servant, without which he cannot manage, may take from zakat, and the giver may give him. Malik said: if there is no surplus in the price of the house or the servant beyond what he needs, it is permissible for him to take; otherwise it is not.

As for a man who gives to another, thinking him poor, and then he turns out to be wealthy: if this happens repeatedly, he takes it back from him. If it has been consumed, then it is examined: if the recipient was wealthy and took it knowing that it is not lawful for him, he is liable for it in every case. If he was not deceived, but believed it was lawful for him, or the giver's intention was not clear, then it is examined: if he wore or ate it, he is liable; if it perished, he is not liable.

It was disagreed whether it counts for the giver. Al-Hasan and Abu ‘Ubayda said: it counts for him. Al-Thawri and others said: it does not count for him. The people of the locality of the alms have the greatest right to it, unless a surplus remains, in which case it is transferred to other places according to the judgment of the imam. Ibn Habib said in al-Wadiha: as for those whose hearts are to be reconciled, their share has ended. As for the way of God, there is no harm in the imam giving to the fighters when the fay’ in the public treasury is small.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This condition is open to question. Ibn Habib said: the imam should instruct the collectors to distribute it in the places from which it was collected, and nothing of it should be carried to the imam except if he sees fit to do so because of need or hardship that has befallen a people; this was said by Malik.

One who has a farm, or something whose price, if sold, would suffice him, is not permitted to take charity.

This is a sufficient portion of the jurisprudence of the verse, given our condition of brevity, and God is the Granter of success by His mercy.

As for His words: ﴿an obligation from God﴾ (9:60), meaning: a binding and defined duty. It is derived from the sense of "cutting" or "severing" (al-farḍ fī al-shay’, meaning incision and cutting), because of its firmness and permanence, like the rulings that are prescribed (yufraḍu). The word "farīḍa" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar). Then He described Himself, blessed and exalted, with two attributes suited to the ruling of this verse: because it proceeds from His knowledge of His creation, and from His wisdom in the division among them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 61–63:

The Almighty's saying:

﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet and say, "He is an ear." Say, "An ear of good for you: he believes in Allah, and believes the believers, and is a mercy for those of you who have believed. But those who harm the Messenger of Allah will have a painful punishment."﴾ ﴿They swear to you by Allah in order to please you, but Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him, if they were believers.﴾ ﴿Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger will have the fire of Hell, to abide therein forever? That is the great disgrace.﴾

The pronoun in His saying "And among them" refers to the hypocrites (munafiqun). "Yu'dhunna" (they harm) is a term that encompasses all the harmful acts and words they directed at the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). After that, it singles out from their words "he is an ear" (huwa udhun). It is narrated that the one who said this expression was Nabtal ibn al-Harith, who was one of the rebellious hypocrites, and he is the one about whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wishes to look at a devil, let him look at Nabtal ibn al-Harith." He had wild hair, frizzled locks, red eyes, scorched cheeks, and a disfigured appearance.

It is narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri and Mujahid that they interpreted their saying "he is an ear" to mean that he hears our excuses and our apologies and accepts them, that is, we do not care about his harm or about falling into it, since he listens to everything said in the way of excuses and the like. This is a disparagement of him for lack of prudence and for being easily deceived. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and a group with him, that they meant by their saying "he is an ear" that he hears everything conveyed to him about us, gives ear to it, and accepts it. This is a suspicion on their part and a description of him as one who accepts falsehoods and tale-bearing.

The meaning of "udhun" is a listener (sammaʿ). A man who listens to every saying is called "udhun" when the use of the ear becomes frequent for him. This is naming a thing by another thing when it is connected to it by a cause, as one says of a sentinel: "ʿayn" (eye), and as one says of a fat she-camel whose tooth has come out: "nab" (tooth). Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 64–66:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿The hypocrites are wary lest a surah be sent down about them, informing them of what is in their hearts. Say: "Mock on; surely Allah will bring forth what you are wary of."﴾ ﴿And if you ask them, they will surely say, "We were only chatting and playing." Say: "Was it Allah, His verses, and His Messenger that you were mocking?"﴾ ﴿Make no excuses; you have disbelieved after your belief. If We pardon a group of you, We will punish another group, because they were criminals.﴾

His, the Exalted, saying: "yahdharu" (they are wary) is a report about the state of their hearts, and their wariness is only that a surah be recited. Whether it is sent down or not is not explicit in the verse but is apparent. If it is taken to mean that, in accordance with the requirement of their hypocrisy and their belief that it is not from Allah, then the meaning is clear. If it is said that they believe it is sent down from Allah and yet they are hypocrites nonetheless, then this is disbelief and obstinacy. Al-Zajjaj and some who went to avoid this possibility said: the meaning of "yahdharu" is a command, even though its wording is that of a report, as if he were saying: "let them be wary" (liyahdhar). (p-355) Abu 'Amr and a group with him read "an tanzila" with a sukun on the nun and a light zay. Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, 'Asim, al-A'mash and 'Isa read it with a fatha on the nun and a shadda on the zay. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verse 67–69:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women are of one another. They enjoin what is evil and forbid what is good, and they withhold their hands. They have forgotten Allah, so He has forgotten them. Indeed, the hypocrites are the defiantly disobedient.﴾ ﴿Allah has promised the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women and the disbelievers the fire of Hell, abiding therein. It is sufficient for them. And Allah has cursed them, and for them is a lasting punishment.﴾ ﴿Like those before you, they were stronger than you in power and greater in wealth and children. They enjoyed their portion, so you have enjoyed your portion as those before you enjoyed their portion, and you have plunged as they plunged. Those—their deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the losers.﴾

This is the beginning of an informative statement about them, and a ruling from Allah the Exalted upon them concerning what this verse contains.

As for His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿of one another﴾, it means: in the ruling and in the status of disbelief. This is like the saying of people: "The two ears are from the head," meaning: in the ruling of wiping (over them in ablution); otherwise it is known that they are from the head. And since "They are not of you" was mentioned earlier, this statement is apt.

And His saying: ﴿They enjoin what is evil﴾ means: disbelief and the worship of other than Allah. The rest of the verse is of the same kind, because the hypocrites about whom these verses were revealed were not people of power or of apparent actions, due to the manifestation of Islam and the word of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. "Withholding" (qabd) refers to withholding from charity and doing good. As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿They have forgotten Allah, so He has forgotten them﴾, it means: they abandoned Him when they abandoned His Prophet and his law, so He abandoned them when He did not guide them nor spared them the punishment of the Fire. Forgetting is expressed as a figure for abandoning only for emphasis, since the most intensive forms of abandonment are those accompanied by forgetting. On this basis comes ﴿And do not forget graciousness among yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237] and ﴿And do not forget your share of this world﴾ [al-Qasas: 77]. Then the Mighty and Majestic judged them as defiantly disobedient (fasiq), which is the defiance of disbelief that necessitates eternal abiding in the Fire. Qatadah used to say: "So He forgot them" means: from good, and He did not forget them from evil.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Allah has promised the hypocrite men﴾ and the rest of the verse: when the promise is restricted by explicit mention of evil, that is correct and apt, even though it is a verse of pure threat. The "disbelievers" in this verse are those who openly declare (their disbelief). His saying: ﴿It is sufficient for them﴾ means: it suffices them, and suffices for their crime and their disbelief as retribution and recompense. So if anyone wished a punishment for them greater than this, it would be sufficient for them in his estimation. ﴿And Allah has cursed them﴾ means: He removed them far from His mercy. And ﴿a lasting punishment﴾ means: perpetual, with no removal from it.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Like those before you﴾ and the rest of the verse: Allah commanded His Prophet to address the hypocrites with it, saying to them: "Like those before you." The meaning is: you are like those, or your likeness is the likeness of those before you. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: a promise as Allah promised those before you, so it is connected to "promised."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In this there is some difficulty. Then he said: they were stronger than you and greater, yet they disobeyed and were destroyed; so you are more deserving of destruction for your disobedience and your weakness.

Al-khalaq: the share of worth, of religion, and of the whole condition of a person; and the khalaq of a person is the thing by which he is worthy. The meaning: they hastened their share in their worldly life and abandoned the gate of the Hereafter, so you followed them.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Al-Tabari cited in the interpretation of this verse the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "You will certainly follow the ways of those before you, span by span and cubit by cubit, so that even if they entered a lizard's burrow, you would enter it." And what resembles this hadith of what requires the following of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) of all other nations is a meaning very unfitting for the verse, since the verse addresses hypocrites who are disbelievers whose deeds are void, whereas the hadith addresses monotheists who follow the ways of those who passed in worldly matters that do not take them out of the religion.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And you have plunged as those plunged﴾: meaning, you immersed yourselves as they immersed themselves. It is a metaphor taken from plunging into liquids, and it is not used except for falsehood, because dealing with realities is according to order and system, whereas the affairs of falsehood are merely plunging. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Many a one who plunges into the wealth of Allah will have the Fire on the Day of Resurrection."

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Those—their deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter﴾. It is possible that "those" refers to the people described with strength, abundance of wealth, and enjoyment of their share, the meaning being: you too, by your turning away from the truth, will be afflicted likewise. It is also possible that "those" refers to the hypocrites contemporary with Muhammad (ﷺ), and the address is to Muhammad (ﷺ); in that case there is a shift from one address to a different one than the first. "Deeds became worthless" and what is similar to it: it becomes void (habata, yahbutu, habatan) when it is nullified after toil. "Habita al-batn" (the belly became bloated/ailing) with a fatha on the ba' is a disease of the stomach; from this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, of what spring produces is that which kills by bloating (habat) or causes illness." As for His saying "in this world," its meaning, if it refers to the hypocrites: what afflicts them in this world of hatred from the believers and the corruption of their deeds, and in the Hereafter that it benefits them not and no reward falls upon them. What strengthens that the reference of "those" is to the hypocrites is His, the Exalted, saying in the following verse: ﴿Has there not come to them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 70]. So reflect on it.

This is the beginning of an informative statement about them, and a ruling from Allah the Exalted upon them concerning what this verse contains.

On this basis comes ﴿And do not forget graciousness among yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237] and ﴿And do not forget your share of this world﴾ [al-Qasas: 77]. The "disbelievers" in this verse are those who openly declare (their disbelief). His saying: ﴿It is sufficient for them﴾ means: it suffices them, and suffices for their crime and their disbelief as retribution and recompense. So if anyone wished a punishment for them greater than this, it would be sufficient for them in his estimation. ﴿And Allah has cursed them﴾ means: He removed them far from His mercy. And ﴿a lasting punishment﴾ means: perpetual, with no removal from it.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Like those before you﴾ and the rest of the verse: Allah commanded His Prophet to address the hypocrites with it, saying to them: "Like those before you." The meaning is: you are like those, or your likeness is the likeness of those before you. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: a promise as Allah promised those before you, so it is connected to "promised."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In this there is some difficulty. Then he said: they were stronger than you and greater, yet they disobeyed and were destroyed; so you are more deserving of destruction for your disobedience and your weakness.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 70–72:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿Has there not come to them the news of those before them: the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Abraham, the companions of Madyan, and the overturned cities? Their messengers came to them with clear proofs. It was not Allah who wronged them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ ﴿The believing men and believing women are allies of one another. They enjoin what is good and forbid what is evil, establish the prayer, give the zakat, and obey Allah and His Messenger. Those, Allah will have mercy upon them. Indeed, Allah is Mighty and Wise.﴾ ﴿Allah has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence. And the pleasure of Allah is greater. That is the great triumph.﴾

Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, says to His Prophet (ﷺ): Has there not come to these hypocrites the report of the earlier nations who disobeyed Allah by denying His messengers, so that He destroyed them? 'Ad and Thamud were two tribes. The people of Abraham were Nimrod and his companions and the followers of his rule. The companions of Madyan were the people of Shu'ayb. The overturned cities were the people of the four towns; it is said they were the seven whom Lot (ﷺ) was sent to. The meaning of al-mu'tafikat (the overturned cities) is "those turned away and overturned." It is said: afikat, fa-'ta-fakat, because He made their upper parts their lower parts. In the Qur'an the word appears in the singular while indicating the plural. From this word is the verse of 'Imran ibn Hattan:

"With a speech clear and free of confusion, by which the tongue is guided, and I am not one who is turned away (mu'tafik)."

That is: not one who is turned, diverted, or disturbed. From it the wind is called mu'tafikah because of its shifting. From it also is the verse: ﴿How are they turned away?﴾ And ifk is turning speech from truth to falsehood. The pronoun in His words ﴿their messengers came to them﴾ refers to these mentioned nations. It is also said that it refers only to the overturned cities. He gave them messengers, though their prophet was one, because he would send to every town a messenger calling to it, so they were the messengers of the Messenger of Allah. This was mentioned by al-Tabari. The first interpretation, in which the pronoun refers to all the nations, is clearer. His words ﴿with clear proofs﴾ mean with miracles, which are clear in themselves relative to the truth, not relative to those who denied them.

When He finished mentioning the hypocrites, with the things that should turn one away from hypocrisy and restrain one from it, He followed that with mention of the believers, with the things that encourage belief and stir one toward it, as a gentleness from Him, blessed and exalted is He, toward His servants, there being no lord other than Him. Here allegiance (wilayah) is mentioned, since there is no allegiance among the hypocrites, no intercession for them, and none of them calls upon another. It seems that the allegiance intended here is allegiance in Allah specifically. His words ﴿what is good﴾ mean the worship of Allah, His Oneness, and all that follows from that. His words ﴿what is evil﴾ mean turning from the worship of idols and all that follows from that. al-Tabari reported from Abu al-'Aliya that he said: Everything Allah mentions in the Qur'an regarding enjoining what is good is a call from polytheism to Islam, and everything mentioned regarding forbidding what is evil is a prohibition of worshipping idols and devils. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said regarding His words ﴿and establish the prayer﴾ that they are the five daily prayers.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

According to this, the zakat intended is the obligatory zakat. In my view, praise for the voluntary acts is more eloquent, since one who establishes the voluntary acts is more deserving of establishing the obligatory. His words ﴿and obey Allah and His Messenger﴾ encompass the recommended acts (mandubat). The sin in His words ﴿Allah will have mercy upon them (sa-yarhamuhumu)﴾ enters into the promise as a delay, so that souls may delight in hoping for it. And His grace, exalted is He, is a guarantor of fulfilment.

As for His words ﴿Allah has promised the believers﴾ and the rest of the verse, His promise in this verse is explicit and clear regarding good. His words ﴿beneath which﴾ may mean beneath their trees, or beneath their upper rooms, or beneath their gathering places, relative to this. This is like saying of two adjacent houses of equal space: "this one is beneath that one."

al-Tabari reported regarding His words ﴿and pleasant dwellings﴾, from al-Hasan, that he said: I asked 'Imran ibn al-Husayn and Abu Hurayra about it, and they said: "You have fallen upon one who knows. We asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and he said: 'A palace in Paradise of pearl, in which are seventy houses of red ruby, in each house seventy chambers of green emerald, in each chamber seventy couches.'" A similar report, close to these wordings or resembling them, I have abridged, seeking brevity.

As for His words ﴿in gardens of 'Adn﴾, its meaning is: in gardens of residence and permanence. It is said: 'adana al-shay' fi al-makan when it stayed in a place and remained there. From it comes al-ma'dan (the mine), that is, the place where a thing remains. From it is the verse of al-A'sha:

"And if they seek hospitality for his forbearance, they are received by one of weight who has stayed (qad 'adan)."

This is the linguistic discussion. Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "Jannat 'Adn" in Persian means "gardens of vines and grapes."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

I think this is a mistake, mixed up with al-Firdaws. al-Dahhak said: Jannat 'Adn is the city of Paradise and its greatest part. In it are the prophets, scholars, martyrs, and leaders of justice, and people are around them afterward, and the gardens around it. Ibn Mas'ud said: 'Adn is the innermost part of Paradise and its navel. 'Ata' said: 'Adn is a river in Paradise, its gardens upon its banks. al-Hasan said: 'Adn is a palace in Paradise that none enters except a prophet, a truthful one, a martyr, or a just judge; and he prolonged his voice with it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The verse rejects this restriction, since Allah has promised it to the whole body of believers.

As for His words ﴿and the pleasure of Allah is greater﴾, it is reported concerning it that "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says to His servants when they have settled in Paradise: 'Are you pleased?' They say: 'And how would we not be pleased, our Lord?' He says: 'I will give you better than all of this: My pleasure. I am pleased with you, so I shall never be angry with you again.'" The hadith continues. His words ﴿greater﴾ mean greater than everything previously mentioned, and the meaning of the verse and the hadith agree.

al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: The pleasure of Allah reaches their hearts with a delight and joy that is more pleasant to them and more consoling to their eyes than anything of the delights of Paradise they have received.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It appears that His words ﴿and the pleasure of Allah is greater﴾ point to the dwellings of those brought near (al-muqarrabun), who drink from Tasnim, who are seen as a fading star is seen on the horizon. All who are in Paradise are content, while the dwellings differ, and the grace of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, is vast. Al-fawz (triumph) means salvation and deliverance: ﴿Whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has triumphed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 185]. Those brought near are in the great triumph. In my view, the expression of their state as "joy and perfection" is better than expressing it as "delight," though delight is also used in this sense.

As for His words ﴿in gardens of 'Adn﴾, its meaning is: in gardens of residence and permanence. It is said: 'adana al-shay' fi al-makan when it stayed in a place and remained there. From it comes al-ma'dan (the mine), that is, the place where a thing remains. From it is the verse of al-A'sha:

"And if they seek hospitality for his forbearance, they are received by one of weight who has stayed (qad 'adan)."

This is the linguistic discussion. Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "Jannat 'Adn" in Persian means "gardens of vines and grapes."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

I think this is a mistake, mixed up with al-Firdaws. al-Dahhak said: Jannat 'Adn is the city of Paradise and its greatest part. In it are the prophets, scholars, martyrs, and leaders of justice, and people are around them afterward, and the gardens around it. Ibn Mas'ud said: 'Adn is the innermost part of Paradise and its navel. 'Ata' said: 'Adn is a river in Paradise, its gardens upon its banks. al-Hasan said: 'Adn is a palace in Paradise that none enters except a prophet, a truthful one, a martyr, or a just judge; and he prolonged his voice with it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The verse rejects this restriction, since Allah has promised it to the whole body of believers.

As for His words ﴿and the pleasure of Allah is greater﴾, it is reported concerning it that "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says to His servants when they have settled in Paradise: 'Are you pleased?' They say: 'And how would we not be pleased, our Lord?' He says: 'I will give you better than all of this: My pleasure. I am pleased with you, so I shall never be angry with you again.'" The hadith continues. His words ﴿greater﴾ mean greater than everything previously mentioned, and the meaning of the verse and the hadith agree.

al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: The pleasure of Allah reaches their hearts with a delight and joy that is more pleasant to them and more consoling to their eyes than anything of the delights of Paradise they have received.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It appears that His words ﴿and the pleasure of Allah is greater﴾ point to the dwellings of those brought near (al-muqarrabun), who drink from Tasnim, who are seen as a fading star is seen on the horizon. All who are in Paradise are content, while the dwellings differ, and the grace of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, is vast. Al-fawz (triumph) means salvation and deliverance: ﴿Whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has triumphed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 185]. Those brought near are in the great triumph. In my view, the expression of their state as "joy and perfection" is better than expressing it as "delight," though delight is also used in this sense.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 73–74:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them. Their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾ ﴿They swear by Allah that they said nothing, but they had indeed uttered the word of disbelief and disbelieved after their submission (Islam), and they resolved upon what they could not attain. They found fault with nothing except that Allah and His Messenger had enriched them out of His bounty. So if they repent, it will be better for them; but if they turn away, Allah will punish them with a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no protector or helper on earth.﴾

His saying "jahid" (strive) is derived from "bulugh al-jahd" (exerting one's utmost effort). What is intended by it is confronting and opposing, and it varies according to the one who strives. The striving against the open disbeliever is by the sword, and the striving against the hypocrite who conceals himself is by the tongue, by rebuke, and by displaying a stern countenance toward him, and the like.

Do you not see that among the expressions of the Sharia is his saying (ﷺ): "The one who strives is the one who strives against his own self in obedience to Allah." The striving of the self is only its persistence in following the truth and abandoning desires. This is what is fitting for the meaning of this verse. However, we shall cite the words of the exegetes verbatim so that they may be open to examination. Al-Zajjaj said (and he relies in this on the words of Ibn Mas'ud): "In this verse He commanded the striving against the disbelievers and the hypocrites by the sword, and it was permitted to him in it to kill the hypocrites." Ibn Mas'ud said: "If he is able, then by the sword; if not, then by the tongue; and if not, then by the heart and by a stern countenance."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Killing does not occur except with clear proof (tajlih), and whoever is clearly proven (in his disbelief) has left the rank of hypocrisy. Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning is: strive against the hypocrites by the tongue. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: the meaning is: strive against the hypocrites by enforcing the prescribed punishments (hudud) upon them. He said: and most of the prescribed punishments in that day used to fall upon the hypocrites.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The reason the Prophet (ﷺ) left the hypocrites in Madina is that they were not clearly proven; rather, every one who was suspected, when confronted, claimed Islam. So in leaving them there was preservation and protection of Islam, and fear that the Arabs would be repelled if they heard that Muhammad (ﷺ) kills those who manifest Islam. I have fully explained this meaning at the beginning of Surat al-Baqara. The view of al-Tabari is that the Prophet (ﷺ) knew them and concealed them.

As for His saying, "and be harsh with them" (waghlud 'alayhim), it is a general expression that applies to actions, words, and glances. From it is His saying: ﴿And if you had been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have dispersed from around you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159]. From it is also the saying of the women to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him: "You are more severe and harsher than the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." The meaning of ghilaz (harshness) is roughness of side, so it is the opposite of His saying: ﴿And lower your wing to those who follow you of the believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 215]. Then the verse, after the command, informed of their abode: that they are in Hell. The meaning is: they are deserving of everything you are commanded to do to them. And al-Ma'wa (refuge) is where a person takes shelter and settles.

As for His saying: ﴿They swear by Allah that they said nothing﴾, the verse was revealed concerning al-Jullas ibn Suwayd ibn al-Samit. That was because he was coming from Quba', and with him was the stepson of his wife, 'Umayr ibn Sa'd, according to what Ibn Ishaq said. 'Urwa said: his name was Mus'ab. Others said: they were both on donkeys. "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had named a people among those he accused of hypocrisy, and said: 'They are filth.' Al-Jullas said to the one who was traveling with him: 'By Allah, those whom Muhammad named are none but our elders and our masters. If what Muhammad says is true, then we are worse than these donkeys of ours.' His stepson, or the other man, said to him: 'By Allah, it is indeed true, and you are worse than your donkey.' Then the man feared that a consequence would befall him in his religion, so he went out and informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of the matter. The Prophet (ﷺ) sent after al-Jullas and confronted him, and he swore by Allah that he had not said it. So this verse was revealed."

The reference of "the word of disbelief" is to his saying: "If what Muhammad says is true, then we are worse than the donkeys," because denial is implicit in the force of this statement. Mujahid said: When his companion said to him, "I will inform the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of your words," al-Jullas resolved to kill him, but then did not do it, out of inability to do so. So to this is the reference in His saying: ﴿and they resolved upon what they could not attain﴾. Qatada ibn Di'ama said: this verse was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, and that was because Sinan ibn Wabara al-Ansari and al-Jahjah al-Ghifari, one of them struck the other's foot during the expedition of al-Muraysi'. They then rose up; al-Jahjah cried out to the Ansar, and Sinan cried out to the Muhajirun. The people rose, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) calmed them. 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul said: "I see these people have only gathered against us. Our likeness and theirs is only as the first one said: 'Fatten your dog and it will devour you.' If we return to Madina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it." This reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who confronted him, and he swore that he had not said that. So the verse was revealed refuting him." The reference of "the word of disbelief" is to his parable: "Fatten your dog and it will devour you." Qatada said: the reference of "they resolved" is to His saying: ﴿If we return to Madina﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. Al-Hasan said: they are the hypocrites, through displaying polytheism and obstinacy against the Prophet (ﷺ), "with what they could not attain." He, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿after their submission﴾ and did not say: "after their faith," because that (submission) had not passed beyond their tongues.

As for His saying: ﴿They found fault with nothing except that Allah and His Messenger had enriched them﴾, its meaning is: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul a blood-money (diya) which had been suspended for him. 'Ikrima mentioned that it was twelve thousand, and it was said: rather, it was for al-Jullas.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is in accordance with the earlier disagreement about whom the verse was revealed concerning from its beginning. The disagreement of the reciters (qurra') concerning "naqamu" was mentioned in Surat al-A'raf. Abu Haywa and Ibn Abi 'Abla read it with a kasra on the qaf, and this is a dialect (lugha). As for His saying: ﴿except that Allah had enriched them﴾, it is an exception from something other than the first (i.e., a munqati' exception). As al-Nabigha said:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords / are notched from the clashing of the battalions."

So the sense is: "They found fault with nothing except what deserves to be thanked."

Mujahid said, concerning His saying: ﴿and they resolved upon what they could not attain﴾: it was revealed concerning a group of Quraysh who intended to kill the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This does not fit the verse. A group said: al-Jullas was the one who resolved to kill the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This resembles the verse, except that its chain (sanad) is not strong. Al-Zajjaj related that twelve of the hypocrites resolved upon that, and Allah made it known to them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is mentioned in regard to their enrichment, in that their wealth increased from the spoils of war; so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the cause of that. And in this same sense the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the Ansar: "You were poor, and Allah enriched you through me." Then, may He be mighty and majestic, opened the door of repentance for them out of gentleness and kindness, in His saying: ﴿So if they repent, it will be better for them.﴾ It is related that al-Jullas repented from hypocrisy and said: "Indeed Allah has left for me the door of repentance," so he confessed and sincerely purified himself, and his repentance was good. And the painful punishment that befalls them in this world is contempt, fear, and disgrace in the eyes of the believers.
