Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 75–78:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with God: "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and we will surely be among the righteous."﴾ ﴿But when He gave them of His bounty, they became stingy with it and turned away while they were refusing.﴾ ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him, because they broke their promise to God and because they used to lie.﴾ ﴿Do they not know that God knows their secret and their private talk, and that God is the Knower of the unseen?﴾

This verse was revealed concerning Tha'laba ibn Hatib al-Ansari. Al-Hasan said: "And concerning Mu'tab ibn Qushayr along with him." The summary of what al-Tabari and others mention about his affair is that "he came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of God, pray to God that He makes wealth mine, for if I had wealth I would surely fulfill its rights and do good with it.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) turned him away and said: 'A little that you can thank for is better than a lot that you cannot bear.' He returned again, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'Do you not wish to be like the Messenger of God? If I prayed to God to make the mountains move with me as gold, they would move!' He kept pressing him until the Messenger of God (ﷺ) supplicated for him with that. So he acquired sheep, and they multiplied as worms multiply, until Medina became too small for him, so he moved away from it, and his sheep increased until he withdrew far away, and his hypocrisy appeared. During this time the obligation of zakat was revealed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), so he sent collectors with his letter regarding taking the zakat of sheep. When they reached Tha'laba and he read the letter, he said: 'This is the sister of the jizya.' Then he said to them: 'Leave me until I consider my opinion.' When they came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and informed him, he said: 'Woe to Tha'laba!' three times, and the verse was revealed concerning him. A relative of Tha'laba who had witnessed the affair went out to him and said: 'Attend to your matter, for such and such has been revealed.' So Tha'laba went out until he came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and begged to pay his zakat, but the Messenger of God (ﷺ) turned away from him and said: 'God has commanded me not to accept your zakat.' He remained in this state until the Messenger of God (ﷺ) died. Then Tha'laba came to Abu Bakr, then to 'Umar, then to 'Uthman, desiring from each of them that he take zakat from him, but all of them rejected that and refused it, following the example of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Tha'laba remained so until he perished in the days of 'Uthman."

Regarding His saying, ﴿So He caused to follow﴾ (fa-a'qabahum): it is explicit that the punishment for the sin is with something worse than it. His saying, ﴿until the Day they meet Him﴾, requires that they die upon hypocrisy. For this reason the caliphs, may God be pleased with them, did not accept Tha'laba's return, since the Qur'an testifies against him that he died in that state. Were it not for the possibility that it was hypocrisy of disobedience, his killing would have been obligatory.

al-A'mash recited "li-nassaddaqanna" with the heavy nun like the majority, and "wa-lanakunanna" with a light nun.

The pronoun in His saying "fa-a'qabahum" refers to God, the Exalted and Majestic, and it may refer to the stinginess implied in the verse, though that pronoun in "yalqawnahu" would be weakened by this. His saying ﴿hypocrisy in their hearts﴾ may be hypocrisy of disbelief, and Tha'laba's continuance after this text and his being left alone would be due to his outward display of Islam and his attachment to what has a possibility (of acceptability). It may also be that His saying ﴿hypocrisy﴾ means hypocrisy of disobedience and weakness of uprightness, in which case its affirmation is sound, and he was left at the beginning of zakat as a punishment and deterrent to him. This is similar to what is related: an official wrote to 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may God be pleased with him, that a certain person withholds zakat, and he wrote back to him: "Leave him, and make his punishment that he does not pay zakat with the Muslims," meaning: because of the abhorrence that will reach him in that.

al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Nafi' and the rest read "yakdhibun" lightly. Abu Raja' read "yukadhdhibun" with shadda.

al-Tabari mentions in this verse what is suitable to it from the hadith of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Three whoever has them is a pure hypocrite: when he promises he breaks it, when he speaks he lies, and when he is entrusted he betrays." And in another hadith: "And when he makes a covenant he betrays, and when he disputes he transgresses." And similar hadiths. It appears from the view of al-Bukhari and others among the people of knowledge that these blameworthy traits make one a hypocrite until the Day of Resurrection for whoever is characterized by them. It is related that 'Amr ibn al-'As, when he was dying, said: "Marry so-and-so, for I have promised him; I do not want to meet God with a third of hypocrisy." This is the apparent meaning of the words of al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: "The brothers of Yusuf did these traits, and they were not hypocrites, rather they were prophets." These hadiths are only about the hypocrites in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), whom God testified about, and these traits among the rest of the Ummah are acts of disobedience, not hypocrisy. al-Tabari mentions that al-Hasan returned to this view.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Undoubtedly these were acts of disobedience alongside monotheism and faith in Muhammad (ﷺ), but they are of the kind of linguistic hypocrisy (nifaq lughawi). al-Tabari mentions from a group that they said: the covenant which these hypocrites made with God was something they intended in their souls and did not speak it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is open to question.

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Do they not know﴾ and the rest of the verse, is a wording which those who said in the previous verse that the covenant was from the hypocrites by intention and not by speech cling to. The majority read "ya'lamu" with the yaa below; Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and al-Hasan read "ta'lamu" with the taa above. This verse suits their state, for it includes the encompassment of God's knowledge of them and His enumeration of them, and in it is their rebuke for what they were doing of speaking within themselves, gathering to disparage Islam, and comforting one another concerning the Prophet (ﷺ) and his law. So it covers all the hypocrites, while the speaker of the aforementioned statement went to the view that it is specific to the group that made the covenant.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrah al-Tawbah, verses 79–80:**

The Most High said:

﴿Those who find fault with the volunteers among the believers regarding charity, and with those who find nothing to give except their effort, and they mock them: God mocks them, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿Ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them. Even if you ask forgiveness for them seventy times, God will not forgive them, because they disbelieved in God and His Messenger. God does not guide the defiant people.﴾

His words, "Those who find fault" (*alladhīna yalmizūna*), refer back to the pronouns in His words, "they swear falsely" [9:77], "Do they not know" [9:78], and "their secret and their private talk" [9:78]. *Yalmizūna* means: they attack with their tongues. The seven readers recited *yalmizūna* with a kasrah on the *mīm*. Al-Ḥasan, Abū Rajāʾ, Yaʿqūb, and Ibn Kathīr (according to what is narrated from him) recited *yalmuzūna* with a ḍammah on the *mīm*.

"The volunteers" (*al-muṭṭawwiʿīn*) is a word of general meaning, applying to every giver of charity, but what is intended by it is a specific group: those who gave a great deal. This is shown by His words, coordinated with *al-muṭṭawwiʿīn*: "and those who find nothing" (*wa-alladhīna lā yajidūna*). Had "those who find nothing" been included among "the volunteers," the coordination of a thing with itself would not be sound. This is the view of Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī regarding the words of the Most High: "Whoever is an enemy to God and His angels and His messengers, and Jibrīl and Mīkāl" [2:98]; he said that what is meant by "the angels" is those other than these two. He said the same regarding His words: "In them are fruit, palm trees, and pomegranates" [55:68]. Yet all of this is open to question, because repetition for the sake of honour permits this, together with the Arabs' latitude in their speech. The original form of *al-muṭṭawwiʿīn* is *al-mutaṭawwiʿīn*; the *tāʾ* was changed to *ṭāʾ* and assimilated.

As for the giver of much charity who was the occasion of the verse, most reports say he was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, who gave four thousand and kept back the same amount. The Prophet ﷺ said to him: "May God bless you in what you kept back and in what you spent." It is also said that he was ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may God be pleased with him, who gave half of his wealth. It is also said that he was ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAdī, who gave a hundred *wasq*. As for the giver of little, he was Abū ʿAqīl Ḥabḥāb al-Arāshī, who gave a *ṣāʿ* of dates and said: "O Messenger of God, last night I carried water with a yoke and earned two *ṣāʿ*s. I left one for my dependents and brought the other as charity." The hypocrites said: "God is not in need of the charity of this man." Some of them said: "God is not in need of the *ṣāʿ* of Abū ʿAqīl." It is also said that the one who found fault regarding the small amount was Abū Khaythama, and this was said by Kaʿb ibn Mālik, a companion of the Prophet ﷺ. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf gave four thousand. It is also said he gave four hundred *ūqiyya* of silver, and it is also said that it was less than this. The hypocrites said: "This is nothing but showing off." So the verse was revealed concerning all of this.

His words, "they mock them" (*fa-yaskharūna*), mean: they ridicule and belittle. It is coordinated with *yalmizūna*. This was objected to on the ground that what is coordinated with a relative clause (*ṣila*) belongs to the relative clause, and between this coordinated element and what it is coordinated with, His words "and those who find nothing" have intervened. But this is not a problem, because (p-371) His words "wa-alladhīna" (and those who) are the object of the agent of "al-muṭṭawwiʿīn," so it is in the position of the saying: "The one who struck Zayd and ʿAmr came to me, and he killed them both." His words, "God mocks them" (*sakhira Allāhu minhum*), are the naming of the punishment by the name of the sin. It refers to what befell them of abhorrence and humiliation in their souls. His words, "and for them is a painful punishment" (*wa-lahum ʿadhābun alīm*), mean: a punishing one. This is a verse of pure threat.

The majority of readers recited *juhdahum* with a ḍammah on the *jīm*. Al-Aʿraj and a group with him recited *jahdahum* with a fatḥah. It is said that the two have the same meaning, and this was said by Abū ʿUbayda. It is also said that the two have different meanings: the ḍammah refers to wealth, and the fatḥah to bodily exertion. This was reported similarly from al-Shaʿbī.

His words, "those who find fault" (*alladhīna yalmizūna*), may be the predicate of a subject, its estimated form being: "They are those who..." It may also be a subject whose predicate is "mocked" (*sakhira*), and in "sakhira" there is the sense of a curse upon them. It may be a plain predicate without the sense of a curse. It may also be that "alladhīna" is a descriptive modifier continuing what precedes it, as I mentioned at the beginning of the translation.

His words, "Ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them" (*istaghfir lahum aw lā tastaghfir lahum*), admit of two meanings. The first: it is in the form of a command, but its meaning is a condition, as if to say: "Whether you ask forgiveness for them or you do not, God will not forgive them." This is like His words: "Say: Spend willingly or unwillingly; it will not be accepted from you" [9:53], and like the saying of the poet:

*Be harsh to us or be kind; there is no blame upon us from you, nor are you hated by us, if you should depart.*

This meaning was adopted by al-Ṭabarī and others regarding the meaning of the verse. The second meaning the wording admits of is that it is an option, as if He said to him: "If you wish, ask forgiveness, and if you wish, do not ask forgiveness." Then He informed him that He will not forgive them even if he asks forgiveness seventy times. This is the sound meaning, because of the saying of the Messenger of God ﷺ and his clarification of this. It is narrated that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may God be pleased with him, heard him after the revelation of this verse asking forgiveness for them, and said: "O Messenger of God, do you ask forgiveness for the polytheists when God has informed you that He will not forgive them?" He said to him: "O ʿUmar, God has given me the choice and I have chosen. Had I known that if I exceeded the seventy He would forgive them, I would have exceeded it." Similar to this is the exchange with ʿUmar at the time the Prophet ﷺ intended to pray over ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl. The apparent meaning of his praying over him is that his disbelief was not certain to him, and it is impossible that he would pray over an unbeliever. But he regarded his outward profession, and entrusted his inner state to God, the Mighty and Majestic. On this basis was the concealment of the hypocrites, because of the non-determination of their disbelief.

In these words of the Messenger of God ﷺ there is a rejection of binding by *dalīl al-khiṭāb* (the argument from the implication of speech). That is because *dalīl al-khiṭāb* requires that beyond seventy, forgiveness would be attained with it. But the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Had I known," and thus made that something he does not know, and something that ought to be learned and whose knowledge is sought from God, the Mighty and Majestic. So in this there is a great proof for the view that *dalīl al-khiṭāb* is to be rejected. If, as we have said, the option is established in this verse, then it is sound that this option is what was abrogated (*nusikha*, i.e., annulled by later revelation) by His words in Sūrat al-Munāfiqūn: "It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them; God will not forgive them. God does not guide the defiant people" [63:6].

Mālik, may God have mercy on him, has issues that require the acceptance of *dalīl al-khiṭāb*. Among them is his saying that one who catches only the *tashahhud* (the final sitting) is not bound by the rulings of the imam, because the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever catches one rakʿa of the prayer has caught the prayer." The implication (*dalīl al-khiṭāb*) requires that whoever does not catch one rakʿa has not caught it. He also has issues that require rejecting *dalīl al-khiṭāb*. Among them is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "In animals grazing freely, there is zakāt." The implication is that there is no zakāt in other than grazing animals, while Mālik holds that there is zakāt in other than grazing animals (p-372). Among them is that God, the Mighty and Majestic, says regarding game: "And whoever of you kills it intentionally" [5:95]. Mālik said: the ruling for one who kills by mistake and one who kills intentionally is the same, while the implication requires otherwise.

As for his giving the example of seventy rather than other numbers, it is because it is a number that often comes as a limit and as conclusive in multitude. Do you not see the people whom Mūsā chose, and the companions of the ʿAqaba? Some philologists have said that the *taṣrīf* (morphological derivation) formed from *sīn*, *bāʾ*, and *ʿayn* signifies severity of matter. It also appears in the arrows of the game of chance, in the climes, and other things. Among that are *al-sabʿ* (the beast), *al-ʿubūs* (sternness), *al-ʿanbas* (lion), and similar words.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrah al-Tawbah, verses 79–80:**

The Most High said:

﴿Those who find fault with the volunteers among the believers regarding charity, and with those who find nothing to give except their effort, and they mock them: God mocks them, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿Ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them. Even if you ask forgiveness for them seventy times, God will not forgive them, because they disbelieved in God and His Messenger. God does not guide the defiant people.﴾

His words, "Those who find fault" (*alladhīna yalmizūna*), refer back to the pronouns in His words, "they swear falsely" [9:77], "Do they not know" [9:78], and "their secret and their private talk" [9:78]. *Yalmizūna* means: they attack with their tongues. The seven readers recited *yalmizūna* with a kasrah on the *mīm*. Al-Ḥasan, Abū Rajāʾ, Yaʿqūb, and Ibn Kathīr (according to what is narrated from him) recited *yalmuzūna* with a ḍammah on the *mīm*.

"The volunteers" (*al-muṭṭawwiʿīn*) is a word of general meaning, applying to every giver of charity, but what is intended by it is a specific group: those who gave a great deal. This is shown by His words, coordinated with *al-muṭṭawwiʿīn*: "and those who find nothing" (*wa-alladhīna lā yajidūna*). Had "those who find nothing" been included among "the volunteers," the coordination of a thing with itself would not be sound. This is the view of Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī regarding the words of the Most High: "Whoever is an enemy to God and His angels and His messengers, and Jibrīl and Mīkāl" [2:98]; he said that what is meant by "the angels" is those other than these two. He said the same regarding His words: "In them are fruit, palm trees, and pomegranates" [55:68]. Yet all of this is open to question, because repetition for the sake of honour permits this, together with the Arabs' latitude in their speech. The original form of *al-muṭṭawwiʿīn* is *al-mutaṭawwiʿīn*; the *tāʾ* was changed to *ṭāʾ* and assimilated.

As for the giver of much charity who was the occasion of the verse, most reports say he was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, who gave four thousand and kept back the same amount. The Prophet ﷺ said to him: "May God bless you in what you kept back and in what you spent." It is also said that he was ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may God be pleased with him, who gave half of his wealth. It is also said that he was ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAdī, who gave a hundred *wasq*. As for the giver of little, he was Abū ʿAqīl Ḥabḥāb al-Arāshī, who gave a *ṣāʿ* of dates and said: "O Messenger of God, last night I carried water with a yoke and earned two *ṣāʿ*s. I left one for my dependents and brought the other as charity." The hypocrites said: "God is not in need of the charity of this man." Some of them said: "God is not in need of the *ṣāʿ* of Abū ʿAqīl." It is also said that the one who found fault regarding the small amount was Abū Khaythama, and this was said by Kaʿb ibn Mālik, a companion of the Prophet ﷺ. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf gave four thousand. It is also said he gave four hundred *ūqiyya* of silver, and it is also said that it was less than this. The hypocrites said: "This is nothing but showing off." So the verse was revealed concerning all of this.

His words, "they mock them" (*fa-yaskharūna*), mean: they ridicule and belittle. It is coordinated with *yalmizūna*. This was objected to on the ground that what is coordinated with a relative clause (*ṣila*) belongs to the relative clause, and between this coordinated element and what it is coordinated with, His words "and those who find nothing" have intervened. But this is not a problem, because (p-371) His words "wa-alladhīna" (and those who) are the object of the agent of "al-muṭṭawwiʿīn," so it is in the position of the saying: "The one who struck Zayd and ʿAmr came to me, and he killed them both." His words, "God mocks them" (*sakhira Allāhu minhum*), are the naming of the punishment by the name of the sin. It refers to what befell them of abhorrence and humiliation in their souls. His words, "and for them is a painful punishment" (*wa-lahum ʿadhābun alīm*), mean: a punishing one. This is a verse of pure threat.

The majority of readers recited *juhdahum* with a ḍammah on the *jīm*. Al-Aʿraj and a group with him recited *jahdahum* with a fatḥah. It is said that the two have the same meaning, and this was said by Abū ʿUbayda. It is also said that the two have different meanings: the ḍammah refers to wealth, and the fatḥah to bodily exertion. This was reported similarly from al-Shaʿbī.

His words, "those who find fault" (*alladhīna yalmizūna*), may be the predicate of a subject, its estimated form being: "They are those who..." It may also be a subject whose predicate is "mocked" (*sakhira*), and in "sakhira" there is the sense of a curse upon them. It may be a plain predicate without the sense of a curse. It may also be that "alladhīna" is a descriptive modifier continuing what precedes it, as I mentioned at the beginning of the translation.

His words, "Ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them" (*istaghfir lahum aw lā tastaghfir lahum*), admit of two meanings. The first: it is in the form of a command, but its meaning is a condition, as if to say: "Whether you ask forgiveness for them or you do not, God will not forgive them." This is like His words: "Say: Spend willingly or unwillingly; it will not be accepted from you" [9:53], and like the saying of the poet:

*Be harsh to us or be kind; there is no blame upon us from you, nor are you hated by us, if you should depart.*

This meaning was adopted by al-Ṭabarī and others regarding the meaning of the verse. The second meaning the wording admits of is that it is an option, as if He said to him: "If you wish, ask forgiveness, and if you wish, do not ask forgiveness." Then He informed him that He will not forgive them even if he asks forgiveness seventy times. This is the sound meaning, because of the saying of the Messenger of God ﷺ and his clarification of this. It is narrated that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may God be pleased with him, heard him after the revelation of this verse asking forgiveness for them, and said: "O Messenger of God, do you ask forgiveness for the polytheists when God has informed you that He will not forgive them?" He said to him: "O ʿUmar, God has given me the choice and I have chosen. Had I known that if I exceeded the seventy He would forgive them, I would have exceeded it." Similar to this is the exchange with ʿUmar at the time the Prophet ﷺ intended to pray over ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl. The apparent meaning of his praying over him is that his disbelief was not certain to him, and it is impossible that he would pray over an unbeliever. But he regarded his outward profession, and entrusted his inner state to God, the Mighty and Majestic. On this basis was the concealment of the hypocrites, because of the non-determination of their disbelief.

That is because *dalīl al-khiṭāb* requires that beyond seventy, forgiveness would be attained with it. But the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Had I known," and thus made that something he does not know, and something that ought to be learned and whose knowledge is sought from God, the Mighty and Majestic. So in this there is a great proof for the view that *dalīl al-khiṭāb* is to be rejected. If, as we have said, the option is established in this verse, then it is sound that this option is what was abrogated (*nusikha*, i.e., annulled by later revelation) by His words in Sūrat al-Munāfiqūn: "It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them; God will not forgive them. God does not guide the defiant people" [63:6].

Among them is his saying that one who catches only the *tashahhud* (the final sitting) is not bound by the rulings of the imam, because the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever catches one rakʿa of the prayer has caught the prayer." The implication (*dalīl al-khiṭāb*) requires that whoever does not catch one rakʿa has not caught it. He also has issues that require rejecting *dalīl al-khiṭāb*. Among them is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "In animals grazing freely, there is zakāt." The implication is that there is no zakāt in other than grazing animals, while Mālik holds that there is zakāt in other than grazing animals (p-372). Among them is that God, the Mighty and Majestic, says regarding game: "And whoever of you kills it intentionally" [5:95]. Mālik said: the ruling for one who kills by mistake and one who kills intentionally is the same, while the implication requires otherwise.

As for his giving the example of seventy rather than other numbers, it is because it is a number that often comes as a limit and as conclusive in multitude. Do you not see the people whom Mūsā chose, and the companions of the ʿAqaba? Some philologists have said that the *taṣrīf* (morphological derivation) formed from *sīn*, *bāʾ*, and *ʿayn* signifies severity of matter. It also appears in the arrows of the game of chance, in the climes, and other things. Among that are *al-sabʿ* (the beast), *al-ʿubūs* (sternness), *al-ʿanbas* (lion), and similar words.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 81–83:

His, the Mighty and Majestic's, saying:

﴿Those who were left behind rejoiced in their sitting [at home] contrary to the Messenger of God, and they disliked to strive with their wealth and their selves in the way of God, and they said: "Do not go forth in the heat." Say: "The Fire of Hell is more intense in heat, if only they understood."﴾ ﴿So let them laugh a little, and let them weep much, as a recompense for what they used to earn.﴾ ﴿So if God returns you to a group of them and they ask your permission to go out, then say: "You will never go out with me, nor will you fight an enemy with me. You were content with sitting the first time, so sit with those who stay behind."﴾

This verse describes their condition in a manner of rebuke, and within it there is a threat. His saying "those who were left behind" (al-mukhallafun) is a term that implies their contempt, and that they are those whom God has removed from His pleasure. This is more fitting for this context than saying "those who lagged behind" (al-mutakhallifun). No one rejoices except a hypocrite, so the three [who were left behind] are excluded from this, as are those with valid excuses. "Maq'ad" is a verbal noun with the meaning of "sitting," and similar to it is the saying:

[Poetry] "Whoever was glad at the killing of Malik..." [rest of the line]

His saying "khilafa" means "after," and Abu 'Ubayda cited in this regard:

"The spring came after them (khilafahum), as though the palm-fronds had spread a mat between them."

He means: after them. From this is the saying of the poet:

"So say to the one who remains after (khilafa) the one who has passed: 'Prepare for another like it, as if it were already here.'"

Al-Tabari said: it is a verbal noun of "khalafa, yukhalifu" (to oppose).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Based on this, it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and the meaning is: "Those who were left behind rejoiced in their sitting because of opposing the Messenger of God ﷺ." Or it is a verbal noun, and its accusative case in the first opinion is as if it were an adverb of time (zarf). Their disliking of what was mentioned is avarice, since they do not believe in the reward for striving in the way of God; they think only of the worldly life. Their saying: "Do not go forth in the heat" was because the expedition of Tabuk took place at a time of intense heat and the ripeness of fruits and shade. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ka'b ibn Malik, and the people. Thus the proof was established against them, by saying to them: "If you dread the heat of summer, then the Fire of Hell, which is more intense, is more fitting for you to dread, if you understood."

Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Hayawa read "khalfa" (behind). Ya'qub mentioned it without attributing it to anyone. It was also read "khulfa" with a dammah on the kha'. What strengthens the opinion of al-Tabari that the word khilaf is a verbal noun from "khalafa" is what the reports have widely transmitted: that the Messenger of God ﷺ commanded them to go forth, but they disobeyed, opposed him, and remained behind seeking permission. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "Do not go forth in the heat" was said by a man from the Banu Salama. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: a man said, "O Messenger of God, the heat is intense, so do not go forth in the heat." An-Naqqash said: in the recitation of 'Abdullah, "ya'lamun" (they know) is read instead of "yafqahun" (they understand).

Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Razin, al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd said: His saying "So let them laugh a little" refers to the duration of life in the world, and His saying "and let them weep much" refers to the perpetuity of eternal abiding in the Fire. It came in the form of a command but its meaning is a report of their condition. It may also be understood as a description of their state: they, because of the peril they are in with God and the evil of their condition, should laugh little and weep much on account of it. This implies that the time of laughter and weeping is in this world, in the manner of His saying ﷺ to his community: "If you knew what I know, you would weep much and laugh little." It is narrated that when the Messenger of God ﷺ said this statement, God revealed to him: "O Muhammad, do not make My servants despair."

His saying "as a recompense" (jaza'an) is connected to the meaning whose implied sense is: "and let them weep much, since they are punished as a recompense." His saying "they used to earn" (yaksibun) is an explicit text that earning is what reward and punishment depend upon.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿So if God returns you to a group of them﴾ and the rest of the verse: "returned" (raja'a) is transitive in its meaning. His saying "in" (in), exalted, indicates that the Prophet ﷺ does not know the future outcomes of his affair, including the term of life or other things. Also, it is possible that they may die before his return. God's command to His Prophet ﷺ to say to them ﴿You will never go out with me﴾ is a punishment for them, and a demonstration of the baseness of their rank and the evil of their condition. This is the intended point in the story of Tha'laba ibn Hatib, which was mentioned earlier regarding the refusal to accept his charity. There is no greater disgrace (p-377) than for a person to be rejected and turned away by the Shari'a, like a mangy camel.

His saying: ﴿to a group﴾ implies, in my view, that what is meant is their leaders and those who are followed. Upon them fell the severity, in that they will not go out nor fight an enemy. He repeated the meaning of fighting the enemy because it is the greatest part of striving and the place of the flashing of swords, under which is Paradise. Were it not for the specification of the group, the statement would have been: "If God returns you to them." It seems that this group had been decreed by God to die upon hypocrisy, and they were identified to the Prophet ﷺ; otherwise, how could the prohibition of praying over their dead be justified if God had not identified them? His saying: ﴿and they die while they are defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Tawba: 84] is an explicit text on their dying in that state. Among what supports this is what is narrated: "that the Prophet ﷺ identified them to Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, and whenever the Companions saw Hudhayfa abstain from the funeral prayer over a man, they too would abstain from it." It is also narrated from Hudhayfa that one day he said: "Such-and-such number of hypocrites remain." 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, said to him: "I beseech you by God, am I one of them?" He said: "No, and by God, I will not grant immunity from this to anyone after you."

The majority of readers recited "ma'iya" with a sukun on the yā' in both places. 'Asim, according to what al-Mufaddal reported, recited "ma'iya" with a fatha on the yā' in both places. His saying "awwal" is in the genitive by being in construct with the time of seeking permission.

Al-Khalifun (those who remain behind) refers to all who stayed behind, including women, children, and people with excuses. The masculine was given precedence, so it takes the masculine sound plural with the yā' and nūn, even if there are women among them. It is a sound plural of khalif.

Qatada said: al-Khalifun are the women. This is rejected. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: they are the men. Al-Tabari said: His saying ﴿with those who remain behind﴾ may intend: "with the corrupt," so that it would be derived from "khalafa al-shay'" (the thing spoiled) when it becomes corrupt, and from it: "khulufu fami's-sa'im" (the bad breath of the fasting person).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation is forced, and the first is more eloquent and more consistent with the word. Malik ibn Dinar and 'Ikrima read "ma'a al-khalifin" (with the khalifin), which is a shortened form of "al-khalifin," as in the saying: "'aridan wa baridan" meaning "'aridan wa baridan" (p-378)... (the poet's line): "Like the sand-hill, its ground is cool in the shadows," meaning: "al-zilal" (the shades).

Say: "The Fire of Hell is more intense in heat, if only they understood."﴾ ﴿So let them laugh a little, and let them weep much, as a recompense for what they used to earn.﴾ ﴿So if God returns you to a group of them and they ask your permission to go out, then say: "You will never go out with me, nor will you fight an enemy with me. You were content with sitting the first time, so sit with those who stay behind."﴾

This verse describes their condition in a manner of rebuke, and within it there is a threat. His saying "those who were left behind" (al-mukhallafun) is a term that implies their contempt, and that they are those whom God has removed from His pleasure. This is more fitting for this context than saying "those who lagged behind" (al-mutakhallifun). No one rejoices except a hypocrite, so the three [who were left behind] are excluded from this, as are those with valid excuses. "Maq'ad" is a verbal noun with the meaning of "sitting," and similar to it is the saying:

[Poetry] "Whoever was glad at the killing of Malik..." [rest of the line]

His saying "khilafa" means "after," and Abu 'Ubayda cited in this regard:

"The spring came after them (khilafahum), as though the palm-fronds had spread a mat between them."

He means: after them. From this is the saying of the poet:

"So say to the one who remains after (khilafa) the one who has passed: 'Prepare for another like it, as if it were already here.'"

Al-Tabari said: it is a verbal noun of "khalafa, yukhalifu" (to oppose).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Based on this, it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and the meaning is: "Those who were left behind rejoiced in their sitting because of opposing the Messenger of God ﷺ." Or it is a verbal noun, and its accusative case in the first opinion is as if it were an adverb of time (zarf). Their disliking of what was mentioned is avarice, since they do not believe in the reward for striving in the way of God; they think only of the worldly life. Their saying: "Do not go forth in the heat" was because the expedition of Tabuk took place at a time of intense heat and the ripeness of fruits and shade. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ka'b ibn Malik, and the people. Thus the proof was established against them, by saying to them: "If you dread the heat of summer, then the Fire of Hell, which is more intense, is more fitting for you to dread, if you understood."

Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Hayawa read "khalfa" (behind). Ya'qub mentioned it without attributing it to anyone. It was also read "khulfa" with a dammah on the kha'. What strengthens the opinion of al-Tabari that the word khilaf is a verbal noun from "khalafa" is what the reports have widely transmitted: that the Messenger of God ﷺ commanded them to go forth, but they disobeyed, opposed him, and remained behind seeking permission. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "Do not go forth in the heat" was said by a man from the Banu Salama. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: a man said, "O Messenger of God, the heat is intense, so do not go forth in the heat." An-Naqqash said: in the recitation of 'Abdullah, "ya'lamun" (they know) is read instead of "yafqahun" (they understand).

Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Razin, al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd said: His saying "So let them laugh a little" refers to the duration of life in the world, and His saying "and let them weep much" refers to the perpetuity of eternal abiding in the Fire. It came in the form of a command but its meaning is a report of their condition. It may also be understood as a description of their state: they, because of the peril they are in with God and the evil of their condition, should laugh little and weep much on account of it. This implies that the time of laughter and weeping is in this world, in the manner of His saying ﷺ to his community: "If you knew what I know, you would weep much and laugh little." It is narrated that when the Messenger of God ﷺ said this statement, God revealed to him: "O Muhammad, do not make My servants despair."

His saying "as a recompense" (jaza'an) is connected to the meaning whose implied sense is: "and let them weep much, since they are punished as a recompense." His saying "they used to earn" (yaksibun) is an explicit text that earning is what reward and punishment depend upon.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿So if God returns you to a group of them﴾ and the rest of the verse: "returned" (raja'a) is transitive in its meaning. His saying "in" (in), exalted, indicates that the Prophet ﷺ does not know the future outcomes of his affair, including the term of life or other things. Also, it is possible that they may die before his return. God's command to His Prophet ﷺ to say to them ﴿You will never go out with me﴾ is a punishment for them, and a demonstration of the baseness of their rank and the evil of their condition. This is the intended point in the story of Tha'laba ibn Hatib, which was mentioned earlier regarding the refusal to accept his charity. There is no greater disgrace (p-377) than for a person to be rejected and turned away by the Shari'a, like a mangy camel.

His saying: ﴿to a group﴾ implies, in my view, that what is meant is their leaders and those who are followed. Upon them fell the severity, in that they will not go out nor fight an enemy. He repeated the meaning of fighting the enemy because it is the greatest part of striving and the place of the flashing of swords, under which is Paradise. Were it not for the specification of the group, the statement would have been: "If God returns you to them." It seems that this group had been decreed by God to die upon hypocrisy, and they were identified to the Prophet ﷺ; otherwise, how could the prohibition of praying over their dead be justified if God had not identified them? His saying: ﴿and they die while they are defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Tawba: 84] is an explicit text on their dying in that state. Among what supports this is what is narrated: "that the Prophet ﷺ identified them to Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, and whenever the Companions saw Hudhayfa abstain from the funeral prayer over a man, they too would abstain from it." It is also narrated from Hudhayfa that one day he said: "Such-and-such number of hypocrites remain." 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, said to him: "I beseech you by God, am I one of them?" He said: "No, and by God, I will not grant immunity from this to anyone after you."

The majority of readers recited "ma'iya" with a sukun on the yā' in both places. 'Asim, according to what al-Mufaddal reported, recited "ma'iya" with a fatha on the yā' in both places. His saying "awwal" is in the genitive by being in construct with the time of seeking permission.

Al-Khalifun (those who remain behind) refers to all who stayed behind, including women, children, and people with excuses. The masculine was given precedence, so it takes the masculine sound plural with the yā' and nūn, even if there are women among them. It is a sound plural of khalif.

Qatada said: al-Khalifun are the women. This is rejected. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: they are the men. Al-Tabari said: His saying ﴿with those who remain behind﴾ may intend: "with the corrupt," so that it would be derived from "khalafa al-shay'" (the thing spoiled) when it becomes corrupt, and from it: "khulufu fami's-sa'im" (the bad breath of the fasting person).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation is forced, and the first is more eloquent and more consistent with the word. Malik ibn Dinar and 'Ikrima read "ma'a al-khalifin" (with the khalifin), which is a shortened form of "al-khalifin," as in the saying: "'aridan wa baridan" meaning "'aridan wa baridan" (p-378)... (the poet's line): "Like the sand-hill, its ground is cool in the shadows," meaning: "al-zilal" (the shades).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 84–87:**

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, nor stand at his grave. Indeed, they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger, and they died while defiantly disobedient.﴾ ﴿And do not let their wealth and their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them with them in this world, and that their souls should depart while they are disbelievers.﴾ ﴿And when a surah (chapter) is sent down, [saying], "Believe in Allah and strive alongside His Messenger," those of wealth among them ask your permission and say, "Leave us, that we may be with those who sit [at home]."﴾ ﴿They are content to be with those who remain behind (the khawalif), and their hearts have been sealed, so they do not understand.﴾

This verse was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, and the prayer of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) over him. Anas ibn Malik narrated that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) moved forward to pray over him, Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him, seized him by his garment, and recited to him this verse: "And do not pray over any of them who has died," through to the end of the verse. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned away and did not pray over him.

The reports are consistent that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did pray over him, and that the verse was revealed after that. In the Book of Funerals of al-Bukhari, on the authority of Jabir, he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy after he had been placed in his grave. He ordered that he be brought out, placed him on his knees, breathed upon him from his saliva, and clothed him in his shirt."

It is also related in this regard that 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy sent to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) during his illness, desiring that he ask forgiveness for him and pray over him.

It is also related that his son, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah, came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after his father's death, and desired that he do this, and that he clothe his father in the shirt that was next to the Prophet's body. He did so. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to pray over him, 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) rose to him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, will you pray over him when Allah has forbidden you from seeking forgiveness for them?" And he began to enumerate the deeds of 'Abd Allah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Step back from me, O 'Umar, for I have been given a choice. And if I knew that by exceeding seventy [times] he would be forgiven, I would exceed it."

In another narration: "Indeed, my shirt will not avail him anything against Allah. And indeed I hope that by this act of mine a thousand men of my people will embrace Islam." This is what is found in some narrations, meaning [men] of the hypocrite Arabs. The correct version is that he said, "men of his people." 'Umar then fell silent. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed over 'Abd Allah, and after that this verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed over him because of the outward display of faith, and it is impossible that he would pray over him while knowing his disbelief. After this, and Allah knows best, he was specified as one over whom he should not pray.

It occurs in the Maghazi of Abu Ishaq, and in some books of tafsir: "Because of this act from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the desire from 'Abd Allah, a thousand men of the Khazraj embraced Islam and repented."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is weak; it was said by one who did not know the number of the Ansar.

As for His statement, "So do not let their wealth impress you" [al-Tawbah 9:55], and the verse, the tafsir of a similar verse has already preceded. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), but what is meant is his community, since by consensus he is someone whom the adornments of this world do not tempt. It is possible that the meaning of the verse is: "And do not let it impress you, O human being," with the intended meaning being the category of humankind. The reason for its repetition is to emphasise and clarify this meaning, because people were tempted by the good condition of the hypocrites in their worldly life.

(p-380) As for His statement, "And when a surah is sent down," the verse: the governing element of "idha" (when) is "asta'dhanaka" (they ask your permission). The surah referred to is, according to some, Bara'ah (al-Tawbah). It is possible that it refers to every surah containing the command to believe and to strive alongside the Messenger (ﷺ). As for the word "surah" of the Qur'an, there is consensus on omitting the hamzah in its usage, but it has been disputed whether its original form contains a hamzah or not. It was said: its original form has a hamzah, so it derives from "as'ar," meaning when a portion of something remains for someone; thus the surah is a portion of the Qur'an. It was also said: its original form has no hamzah, so it is like the "surah" of a building, which is what is built up piece by piece; thus it is a rank after a rank. From this is the statement of al-Nabigha:

> Have you not seen that Allah has given you a surah (eminence),
> Every king below it wavers?

All of this has been covered comprehensively at the beginning of this book.

As for "an" in His statement, "an amminu" (that believe): it is possible that it is explanatory, in the sense of "i.e.," in which case it has no grammatical position (i'rab). It is possible that the intended construction is "bi-an" (with "an"), in which case it is in the accusative position. "Al-tawl" (ability/means) in this verse means wealth; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Ishaq, and others. The reference of this verse is to Jadd ibn Qays, 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, and their likes.

"Al-qa'idun" (those who sit): these are the disabled and those with excuses in general, and those who were left to guard Madinah, because that is an excuse. As for His statement, "They are content to be with the khawalif," the verse is a rebuke and a display of disgrace, as one says in a tone of reproach: "Are you content with such-and-such, O so-and-so?" The "khawalif" are the women, the plural of khalifah. This is the view of the majority of the mufassirun. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: "A man in whom there is no good is called khalifah, so this is its plural according to the wording, and what is meant is the lowliest of people and their inferiors." Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said in the book of al-Naqqash: "The khawalif are those in whom there is no good." Another group said: "The khawalif are the plural of khalif, and it follows the pattern of fawaris, nawakis, and hawalik."

"Utiba" (sealed) in this verse is a metaphor. Since sealing upon a stone or a book prevents and protects what is inside, the heart that has been covered by disbelief and misguidance, to the point that faith and guidance are barred from it, is likened to the stone sealed upon it. From this is the metaphorical use of "ghufl" (uncovered/unmarked) and "kinan" (covering) for the heart. "La yafqahun" (they do not understand) means: they do not comprehend.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 84–87:**

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, nor stand at his grave. Indeed, they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger, and they died while defiantly disobedient.﴾ ﴿And do not let their wealth and their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them with them in this world, and that their souls should depart while they are disbelievers.﴾ ﴿And when a surah (chapter) is sent down, [saying], "Believe in Allah and strive alongside His Messenger," those of wealth among them ask your permission and say, "Leave us, that we may be with those who sit [at home]."﴾ ﴿They are content to be with those who remain behind (the khawalif), and their hearts have been sealed, so they do not understand.﴾

This verse was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, and the prayer of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) over him. Anas ibn Malik narrated that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) moved forward to pray over him, Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him, seized him by his garment, and recited to him this verse: "And do not pray over any of them who has died," through to the end of the verse. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned away and did not pray over him.

The reports are consistent that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did pray over him, and that the verse was revealed after that. In the Book of Funerals of al-Bukhari, on the authority of Jabir, he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy after he had been placed in his grave. He ordered that he be brought out, placed him on his knees, breathed upon him from his saliva, and clothed him in his shirt."

It is also related in this regard that 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy sent to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) during his illness, desiring that he ask forgiveness for him and pray over him.

It is also related that his son, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah, came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after his father's death, and desired that he do this, and that he clothe his father in the shirt that was next to the Prophet's body. He did so. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to pray over him, 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) rose to him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, will you pray over him when Allah has forbidden you from seeking forgiveness for them?" And he began to enumerate the deeds of 'Abd Allah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Step back from me, O 'Umar, for I have been given a choice. And if I knew that by exceeding seventy [times] he would be forgiven, I would exceed it."

In another narration: "Indeed, my shirt will not avail him anything against Allah. And indeed I hope that by this act of mine a thousand men of my people will embrace Islam." This is what is found in some narrations, meaning [men] of the hypocrite Arabs. The correct version is that he said, "men of his people." 'Umar then fell silent. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed over 'Abd Allah, and after that this verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed over him because of the outward display of faith, and it is impossible that he would pray over him while knowing his disbelief. After this, and Allah knows best, he was specified as one over whom he should not pray.

It occurs in the Maghazi of Abu Ishaq, and in some books of tafsir: "Because of this act from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the desire from 'Abd Allah, a thousand men of the Khazraj embraced Islam and repented."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is weak; it was said by one who did not know the number of the Ansar.

As for His statement, "So do not let their wealth impress you" [al-Tawbah 9:55], and the verse, the tafsir of a similar verse has already preceded. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), but what is meant is his community, since by consensus he is someone whom the adornments of this world do not tempt. It is possible that the meaning of the verse is: "And do not let it impress you, O human being," with the intended meaning being the category of humankind. The reason for its repetition is to emphasise and clarify this meaning, because people were tempted by the good condition of the hypocrites in their worldly life.

(p-380) As for His statement, "And when a surah is sent down," the verse: the governing element of "idha" (when) is "asta'dhanaka" (they ask your permission). The surah referred to is, according to some, Bara'ah (al-Tawbah). It is possible that it refers to every surah containing the command to believe and to strive alongside the Messenger (ﷺ). As for the word "surah" of the Qur'an, there is consensus on omitting the hamzah in its usage, but it has been disputed whether its original form contains a hamzah or not. It was said: its original form has a hamzah, so it derives from "as'ar," meaning when a portion of something remains for someone; thus the surah is a portion of the Qur'an. It was also said: its original form has no hamzah, so it is like the "surah" of a building, which is what is built up piece by piece; thus it is a rank after a rank. From this is the statement of al-Nabigha:

> Have you not seen that Allah has given you a surah (eminence),
> Every king below it wavers?

All of this has been covered comprehensively at the beginning of this book.

As for "an" in His statement, "an amminu" (that believe): it is possible that it is explanatory, in the sense of "i.e.," in which case it has no grammatical position (i'rab). It is possible that the intended construction is "bi-an" (with "an"), in which case it is in the accusative position. "Al-tawl" (ability/means) in this verse means wealth; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Ishaq, and others. The reference of this verse is to Jadd ibn Qays, 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, and their likes.

"Al-qa'idun" (those who sit): these are the disabled and those with excuses in general, and those who were left to guard Madinah, because that is an excuse. As for His statement, "They are content to be with the khawalif," the verse is a rebuke and a display of disgrace, as one says in a tone of reproach: "Are you content with such-and-such, O so-and-so?" The "khawalif" are the women, the plural of khalifah. This is the view of the majority of the mufassirun. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: "A man in whom there is no good is called khalifah, so this is its plural according to the wording, and what is meant is the lowliest of people and their inferiors." Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said in the book of al-Naqqash: "The khawalif are those in whom there is no good." Another group said: "The khawalif are the plural of khalif, and it follows the pattern of fawaris, nawakis, and hawalik."

"Utiba" (sealed) in this verse is a metaphor. Since sealing upon a stone or a book prevents and protects what is inside, the heart that has been covered by disbelief and misguidance, to the point that faith and guidance are barred from it, is likened to the stone sealed upon it. From this is the metaphorical use of "ghufl" (uncovered/unmarked) and "kinan" (covering) for the heart. "La yafqahun" (they do not understand) means: they do not comprehend.

(p-381) His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿But the Messenger and those who believed with him strove with their wealth and their lives. For them are the good things, and they are the successful ones.﴾ ﴿Allah has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great triumph.﴾ ﴿And those who had excuses among the Bedouins came seeking permission, while those who lied to Allah and His Messenger sat back. Those of them who disbelieve will be struck by a painful punishment.﴾

The most common use of "lakin" (but) is that it comes after a negation, and here the negation is implicit in the meaning. The preceding verse means that the hypocrites did not strive, so after it there is good sense in saying: "But the Messenger and the believers strove." "Al-khayrat" is the plural of "khayrah," which means the best of anything. Its use is most common for women. From this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Therein are good, beautiful women﴾ [al-Rahman: 70]. From this also is the verse of the poet, related by al-Tabari:

"Indeed I stabbed the joints of the calves... the calves of Hind, the choicest of queens."

"Al-muflihun" (the successful) are those who attained their desired goal of Paradise. "Al-falah" (success) comes to mean attaining one's aim. From this is the verse of Labid:

"Prosper by whatever you wish, for the weak may be made to reach it, and the clever may be deceived."

It also comes to mean survival, as in the verse of the poet:

"For every sorrow among the sorrows there is a respite, and with the evening and the morning there is no falah (lasting prosperity)."

That is, there is no survival.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Attaining one's aim covers the word "falah" wherever it occurs, so reflect upon it.

"A'adda" means he made easy and prepared. His saying "from beneath them" means from beneath their buildings and their upper parts. "Al-fawz" (triumph) is a person's attaining his hope and gaining his aim. From this is the triumph of the arrows of the al-aysar (the game of chance).

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who had excuses among the Bedouins came﴾, the verse... the scholars differed about these who came: were they believers or disbelievers? Ibn 'Abbas and a group with him, among them Mujahid, said: they were believers and their excuses were true. He recited "wa jā'a al-mu'dhirūn" with a sukun on the 'ayn, and this is the recitation (qira'a) of al-Dahhak, Hamid al-A'raj, Abu Salih and Isa ibn Hilal. Some of those who held this view recited "al-mu'adhdhirūn" with a shaddah on the dhal, and they said its origin is "al-mutaʿadhdhirūn," so the taʾ was changed into a dhal and assimilated. In this view, "al-mu'tadhirūn" could have two meanings: first, those who make excuses on genuine grounds; second, those who have reached the limit of their excuse by striving to join the expedition with you but were unable, so it is like the verse of Labid:

"... and whoever weeps for a full year has made his excuse."

Qatada and a group with him said: rather, those who came were disbelievers, and their words and excuses were lies. All of this group recited "al-mu'adhdhirūn" with a shaddah on the dhal. Some of them said its origin is "al-mutaʿadhdhirūn," the vowel of the taʾ was moved to the ʿayn, and the taʾ was assimilated into the dhal, and the meaning is: those making excuses with a lie. Others said it is from al-taʿdhīr, that is, those who make excuses to avoid the expedition and push against the Law. In this view, the verse up to its end describes one category, a disbelieving category, which divides into Bedouin and townsman. According to the first view, it describes two categories: a believer and a disbeliever.

Abu Hatim said: Some of them said: I asked Muslima, and he said: "al-mu'adhdhirūn" with a shaddah on the ʿayn and the dhal. Abu Hatim said: he meant "al-mu'tadhirīn," and the taʾ is not assimilated into the ʿayn because the places of articulation are far apart, and this is an error from him or upon him.

Abu 'Amr said: Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited "al-mu'tadhirūn" with an added taʾ. Al-Hasan (in a variant reported from him), Abu 'Amr, Nafi' and the people recited "kadhabū" with a light dhal. Al-Hasan (and this is what is well known from him), Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Nuh and Isma'il recited "kadhdhabū" with a heavy dhal. The meaning is: they did not believe in Him, the Exalted, nor in His Messenger, and they rejected His command. Then at the end of the verse He threatened the disbelievers with a painful punishment. It may mean punishment in this world by killing and capture, and it may mean punishment in the Hereafter by the Fire.

His saying "minhum" (among them) means that the excusers were believers. Some preponderance supports this, so reflect upon it. Al-Tabari weakened the view of those who said that "al-mu'adhdhirūn" comes from al-taʿdhīr, and he inclined against it. The view is explicitly stated, its reasoning is clear, and Allah is the Helper.

Ibn Ishaq said: "al-mu'adhdhirūn" were a group from the Banu Ghifar, among them Khafaf ibn Ima' ibn Ruhdah.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This requires that they were believers.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 91–92:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿There is no blame upon the weak, nor upon the sick, nor upon those who find nothing to spend, when they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger. There is no cause for blame against the good-doers. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿Nor is there blame upon those who came to you that you might provide them with mounts, and you said, "I cannot find anything to mount you upon." They turned back while their eyes overflowed with tears from grief that they could not find anything to spend.﴾

He, exalted is He, says: There is no sin upon the people of valid excuses, whether weakness of body, sickness, chronic disability, or lack of means to spend. Al-haraj (blame) means sin. His words ﴿when they are sincere﴾ mean: in their intentions and their words, privately and publicly. Abu Hayawa recited, "nasahu Allaha wa rasulahu" (they were sincere to Allah and His Messenger) without the lam and with the final ha' written in the mushaf pronounced in the accusative (nasb). His words, blessed and exalted is He, ﴿there is no cause for blame against the good-doers﴾ (the verse), mean there is no reproach directed at them, nor any censure or punishment. Then he affirmed the hope with His words: ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, recited, "Wa Allahu li-ahli al-isa'a ghafurun rahim" (And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful to the people of wrongdoing).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This reading is more fitting as an explanation (tafsir) than as a recitation (tilawa), because it contradicts the mushaf.

Scholars differed about who is meant by His words, glorified is He: ﴿those who find nothing to spend﴾.

One group said: it was revealed concerning the Banu Muqarrin.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The Banu Muqarrin were six brothers who accompanied the Prophet (ﷺ), and there are no six brothers among the Companions other than them. It was also said that they were seven.

It was said: it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Mughaffal al-Muzani. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said this.

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿Nor upon those who came to you﴾ (the verse), scholars differed about who this verse was revealed concerning. It was said: it was revealed concerning 'Irbad ibn Sariya. It was said: it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Mughaffal. It was said: concerning 'A'idh ibn 'Amr. It was said: concerning Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and his people. It was said: concerning the Banu Muqarrin, and this is the view of the majority of commentators (mufassirun). It was also said: it was revealed concerning seven men from various clans, who are known as "the weepers" (al-bakka'un). They are: Salim ibn 'Umayr from the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf; Harami ibn 'Amr from the Banu Waqif; Abu Layla 'Abd al-Rahman from the Banu Mazin ibn al-Najjar; Sulayman ibn Sakhr from the Banu al-Mu'alla; Abu Ra'ila 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd from the Banu Haritha, who is the one who gave his honour in charity, and Allah accepted it from him; 'Amr ibn Ghanama from the Banu Salama; and 'A'idh ibn 'Amr al-Muzani. It was also said that he was 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr al-Muzani. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said all of this. Mujahid said: the weepers are the Banu Bakr from Muzayna.

The meaning of His words, "li-tahmilahum" (that you might provide them with mounts) is: upon a beast that is ridden and on which furnishings are carried. Some people said: they only asked him for sandals (al-ni'al). This was mentioned by al-Naqqash from al-Hasan ibn Salih, but this view is far-fetched and anomalous (shadhdh).

The element governing "idha" (when) may be "qulta" (you said), in which case His words "tawallaw" (they turned back) are a new sentence (maqta', i.e., disconnected from what precedes). It may also be that the governing element is "tawallaw", and the sense of the sentence is then "fa-qulta" (so you said). Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 91–92:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿There is no blame upon the weak, nor upon the sick, nor upon those who find nothing to spend, when they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger. There is no cause for blame against the good-doers. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿Nor is there blame upon those who came to you that you might provide them with mounts, and you said, "I cannot find anything to mount you upon." They turned back while their eyes overflowed with tears from grief that they could not find anything to spend.﴾

He, exalted is He, says: There is no sin upon the people of valid excuses, whether weakness of body, sickness, chronic disability, or lack of means to spend. Al-haraj (blame) means sin. His words ﴿when they are sincere﴾ mean: in their intentions and their words, privately and publicly. Abu Hayawa recited, "nasahu Allaha wa rasulahu" (they were sincere to Allah and His Messenger) without the lam and with the final ha' written in the mushaf pronounced in the accusative (nasb). His words, blessed and exalted is He, ﴿there is no cause for blame against the good-doers﴾ (the verse), mean there is no reproach directed at them, nor any censure or punishment. Then he affirmed the hope with His words: ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, recited, "Wa Allahu li-ahli al-isa'a ghafurun rahim" (And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful to the people of wrongdoing).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This reading is more fitting as an explanation (tafsir) than as a recitation (tilawa), because it contradicts the mushaf.

Scholars differed about who is meant by His words, glorified is He: ﴿those who find nothing to spend﴾.

One group said: it was revealed concerning the Banu Muqarrin.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The Banu Muqarrin were six brothers who accompanied the Prophet (ﷺ), and there are no six brothers among the Companions other than them. It was also said that they were seven.

It was said: it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Mughaffal al-Muzani. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said this.

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿Nor upon those who came to you﴾ (the verse), scholars differed about who this verse was revealed concerning. It was said: it was revealed concerning 'Irbad ibn Sariya. It was said: it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Mughaffal. It was said: concerning 'A'idh ibn 'Amr. It was said: concerning Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and his people. It was said: concerning the Banu Muqarrin, and this is the view of the majority of commentators (mufassirun). It was also said: it was revealed concerning seven men from various clans, who are known as "the weepers" (al-bakka'un). They are: Salim ibn 'Umayr from the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf; Harami ibn 'Amr from the Banu Waqif; Abu Layla 'Abd al-Rahman from the Banu Mazin ibn al-Najjar; Sulayman ibn Sakhr from the Banu al-Mu'alla; Abu Ra'ila 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd from the Banu Haritha, who is the one who gave his honour in charity, and Allah accepted it from him; 'Amr ibn Ghanama from the Banu Salama; and 'A'idh ibn 'Amr al-Muzani. It was also said that he was 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr al-Muzani. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said all of this. Mujahid said: the weepers are the Banu Bakr from Muzayna.

The Qur'an, the Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 93–94:

Almighty and Majestic is He, said:

﴿The blame is only upon those who ask your permission to stay behind while they are wealthy. They are content to be with the women who stay behind (al-khawalif), and Allah has sealed their hearts, so they do not know.﴾ ﴿They will make excuses to you when you return to them. Say: "Do not make excuses; we will not believe you. Allah has already informed us of your news. Allah will see your deeds, and so will His Messenger, and then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do."﴾

His saying in this verse, "innama" (only), is not restrictive. It is used for emphasis on what he wishes to establish, like your saying: "Innama al-shuja'u 'Antara" ("The brave man is only 'Antara"). This is supported by the fact that we find "al-sabil" (the way, i.e., grounds for blame) existing in the Sharia regarding other than this group. The word "sabil" may be followed by "'ala" (upon) and by "ila" (to). You say: "la sabila 'ala fulan" (there is no way against so-and-so) and "la sabila ila fulan" (there is no way to so-and-so). However, its connection with "'ala" sometimes implies the weakness of the one reached and the paucity of his protection, and therefore it is appropriate in this verse. That is not the case with "ila." Do you not see that you say: "Fulan la sabila lahu ila al-amr wa la ila ta'at Allah" (So-and-so has no access to the matter nor to obedience to Allah), and "'ala" is not appropriate in the like of this? The "sabil" in this verse is the way of punishment. This verse was revealed concerning the hypocrites mentioned earlier: 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, al-Jadd ibn Qays, Mu'tib, and others. A similar explanation of this verse has already been given.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They will make excuses to you﴾, the verse. This address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Muslims share in part of it, because the hypocrites used to make excuses also to the believers, and because the news from Allah is also obtained by the believers. His saying: ﴿when you return﴾ means: from the expedition of Tabuk. His saying: ﴿we will not believe you﴾ means: we will not trust you. However, the verb "nu'minu" is sometimes connected with the preposition "li" (lam), as has been mentioned earlier in his saying: (yu'minu lil-mu'minin) ("He believes the believers"). As for "nabba'a" in this verse, it has been said that it has the meaning of "'arrafa" (to inform), which requires no more than two objects. So the pronoun is the first object, and His saying ﴿of your news﴾ is the second object according to the view of Abu al-Hasan (al-Akhfash) concerning the addition of "min" in an affirmative sentence. The construction is: "qad nabba'ana Allahu akhbarakum" (Allah has informed us of your news). According to the view of Sibawayh, it is an adjective of an omitted noun which is the second object; its estimate is: "qad nabba'ana Allahu jaliyyatan min akhbarikum" (Allah has informed us of a clear matter from your news). It has also been said that "nabba'a" has the meaning of "a'lama" (to make known), which requires three objects. Then the pronoun is one, and ﴿of your news﴾ is the second according to the two views mentioned, and the third is omitted, which the speech indicates by its estimate: "qad nabba'ana Allahu min akhbarikum kadhiban aw nahwahu" (Allah has informed us of your news as a lie or the like). The omission of this object while being indicated by context is permissible, unlike the restriction to fewer objects. That is because the restriction (iqtisar, leaving out complements) is permissible only in two ways: either on the first object, with the two others dropped, since they are the subject and the predicate; or on the last two, with the first dropped; or else restricting oneself to the first two objects while dropping the third without any indication of it, and that is not permissible. Omitting it with an indication of it is permissible.

The reference in His glorified saying: ﴿Allah has informed us﴾ is to His saying: ﴿They would have added nothing to you but confusion, and they would have hurried about among you, seeking to cause you discord﴾ [al-Tawba: 47], and similar. His saying: ﴿And Allah will see﴾ is a threat; its meaning: He will see it while it exists, and the requital will come from Him upon it: if good, then good; if evil, then evil. His saying: ﴿then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen﴾ means the resurrection from the graves. "The unseen" and "the witnessed" encompass all things. His saying: ﴿and He will inform you﴾ means: a warning from One from whom nothing is hidden.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 95–97:

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿They will swear to Allah to you when you return to them, that you may turn away from them. So turn away from them. Indeed, they are impure, and their refuge is Hell as recompense for what they used to earn.﴾ ﴿They swear to you that you may be pleased with them. But if you are pleased with them, indeed Allah is not pleased with the defiantly disobedient people.﴾ ﴿The Bedouins are most severe in disbelief and hypocrisy and most likely not to know the limits of what Allah has revealed to His Messenger. And Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾

It has been said: this verse is among the first revealed concerning the hypocrites at the Battle of Tabuk. This is because some of the hypocrites sought excuses from the Prophet ﷺ and asked his permission to stay behind before his departure, and he granted them permission. They left his presence, and one of them said: "By Allah, he is nothing but fat for the first one who eats it." When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ departed, the Qur'an was revealed concerning them. A man from the people returned and said to the hypocrites in one of their gatherings: "By Allah, a Qur'an has been revealed to Muhammad ﷺ concerning you." They said to him: "And what is that?" He said: "I do not remember, except that I heard your description in it as impure." Makhshi said to them: "By Allah, I would love to be lashed a hundred lashes and not be with you." He left and caught up with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said to him: "What brought you?" He said: "The face of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the wind battering it while I am in shelter." It is narrated that he was among those who repented.

As for His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, we were commanded to rebuke them and to punish them by turning away and by branding them with hypocrisy. This was in general terms, not with an explicit specification from Allah or from His Messenger; rather, each one of them had a wide field for deception. As for His saying ﴿impure﴾, it means filthy and foul. And consider this description a worldly station; then he connected it to the station of the Hereafter, saying: ﴿and their refuge is Hell﴾, meaning their dwelling. Then He made that a recompense for their earning of sins and disbelief, although that is among what Allah has decreed and decided, there being no lord other than Him and no deity besides Him.

Al-Tabari narrated, "from Ka'b ibn Malik that he said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned from Tabuk, he sat down for the people, and those who had stayed behind came to him, apologizing and swearing oaths. They were about eighty-some men. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ accepted from them their outward profession, pledged allegiance to them, asked forgiveness for them, and left their inner states to Allah, Most High."

As for His saying, Most High: ﴿They swear to you that you may be pleased with them﴾, this verse and the one before it address the believers together with the Messenger. The meaning: they swear to you falsely, and their aim is that you be pleased, not that they do this for the sake of Allah or for righteousness.

As for His saying: ﴿But if you are pleased﴾ up to the end of the verse, it is a conditional clause that includes a prohibition against being pleased with them. The ruling of this verse continues to apply to everyone who is censured for an innovation or the like, for the believer should hate him and not be pleased with him for any worldly reason.

As for His saying, Most High: ﴿The Bedouins are most severe in disbelief and hypocrisy and most likely not to know the limits of what Allah has revealed﴾ — the verse. "The Bedouins" (al-A'rab) is a general term, and its meaning is particular to those whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, excepted; this is known by observation and however the matter stands. This description applied to them only in accordance with their distance from the cities and the places of knowledge, rulings and the Law. This verse was revealed concerning hypocrites who were in the desert, and there is no doubt that their fear there was less than the fear of the hypocrites of Madinah, so their tongues were unrestrained and their hypocrisy more brazen.

Al-Tabari narrated that Zayd ibn Suhan used to teach knowledge to his companions while a Bedouin was present. Zayd's left hand had been struck on the day of Nahawand. The Bedouin said: "By Allah, your speech pleases me, but your hand unsettles me." Zayd said: "And what about my hand unsettles you, when it is the left?" The Bedouin said: "By Allah, I do not know whether you cut off the right or the left." Zayd said: "Allah has spoken the truth: ﴿The Bedouins are most severe in disbelief and hypocrisy and most likely not to know the limits of what Allah has revealed to His Messenger.﴾" And "most likely" (ajdar) means more fitting and more deserving. The "limits" (hudud) here means the sunan, the rulings, and the landmarks of the Shari'ah.
