Al-Tabari narrated that Zayd ibn Suhan used to teach knowledge to his companions while a Bedouin was present. Zayd's left hand had been struck on the day of Nahawand. The Bedouin said: "By Allah, your speech pleases me, but your hand unsettles me." Zayd said: "And what about my hand unsettles you, when it is the left?" The Bedouin said: "By Allah, I do not know whether you cut off the right or the left." Zayd said: "Allah has spoken the truth: ﴿The Bedouins are most severe in disbelief and hypocrisy and most likely not to know the limits of what Allah has revealed to His Messenger.﴾" And "most likely" (ajdar) means more fitting and more deserving. The "limits" (hudud) here means the sunan, the rulings, and the landmarks of the Shari'ah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verse 98–99:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And among the Bedouins are those who take what they spend as a loss, and they wait for misfortunes to befall you. Upon them is the circle of evil; and Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And among the Bedouins are those who believe in Allah and the Last Day, and take what they spend as means of nearness to Allah and as prayers of the Messenger. Indeed, it is a means of nearness for them. Allah will admit them into His mercy. Indeed, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.﴾

This is a statement about the hypocrites among them. The meaning of "yattakhidh" (takes) in these verses is: he makes it his aim, and intends nothing else by it. The root of "maghram" (loss) is debt, and from it the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sought refuge from "maghram" and "ma'thim" (sin). However, the use of "maghram" became common for what a person pays that he is not obligated to pay in truth. The word carries the meaning of obligation (luzum), and from it is the saying of the Blessed and Exalted: ﴿Indeed, its torment was a constant loss﴾ [al-Furqan: 65], meaning: a disliked, inescapable thing. And "al-dawa'ir" (the circles, i.e., calamities) are the misfortunes from which a person has no escape, so they encompass him as a circle encompasses. It is also possible that it is derived from the turning of time (dawr al-zaman), and the meaning is: he awaits for you what the days bring and turn with. Then He said, in the form of supplication: ﴿Upon them is the circle of evil﴾. Everything that comes in the form of a supplication from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, means in fact the necessity of the thing, because Allah does not invoke curses upon His creatures while they are in His grasp. From this is His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿Woe to every slanderer, backbiter﴾ [al-Humazah: 1], ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 1]. All of these are complete rulings contained in His statement, the Blessed and Exalted.

The majority of the Seven and others read "dā'iratu as-sū'" with a fatha on the sin, while Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn Muhaysin in one transmission, and 'Asim and al-A'mash in one transmission from them read "dā'iratu as-sūʾ" with a damma on the sin. There is a difference narrated from Ibn Kathir. It has been said: the fatha is the verbal noun (masdar) and the damma is the noun (ism). People differed concerning both, and this is a difference that comes close to one another. The fatha on the sin entails describing the circle as evil. Abu 'Ali said: the meaning of "circle" entails the meaning of "sū'," so it is an idafa of explanation and emphasis, as they say "shamsu an-nahar" (the sun of the day) and "laḥyā ra'sihi" (the jawbone of his head).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"Rajulu sū'" is not said except with a fatha on the sin; this is the view of most of them. It has been reported as "rajulu sūʾ" with a damma, and the poet has said:

"And I was like the wolf of evil when he saw blood, with his companion one day, and turned toward the blood."

The reciters did not differ on the fatha of the sin in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Your father was not a man of evil﴾ [Maryam: 28].

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And among the Bedouins are those who believe in Allah﴾ and so on, Qatadah said: "This is Allah's exception among the Bedouins." And "yattakhidh" in this verse also means: he makes it his aim, and the meaning is: he intends by his spending in the way of Allah nearness to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and seeking the supplication of the Messenger (ﷺ). In his supplication for them is good of the Hereafter in salvation from the Fire, and good of this world in their provisions and the bounties Allah grants them. So "ṣalawāt" (prayers) on this reading is coordinated with "qurubāt" (means of nearness). It is also possible that it is coordinated with "mā yunfiq" (what they spend), meaning: and he takes, by righteous deeds, the Messenger's prayers as a means of nearness. The first is clearer.

"Qurubāt" is the plural of "qurba" or "qurba," with sukun or damma on the ra', and these are two dialects. The ṣalāh in this verse is supplication, by consensus. Some scholars said: ṣalāh from Allah is mercy, from the Prophet and the angels is supplication, and from people is worship. The pronoun in His saying "innahā" (indeed it) may refer to the spending, and this is in the case of "ṣalawāt" being coordinated with "qurubāt"; it may refer to the prayers, and this is in the case of its being coordinated with "mā yunfiq." Nafi' read "qurubatan" with a damma on the ra', with a difference narrated from him, from 'Asim, and from al-A'mash; the rest read "qurbatan" with sukun on the ra'. There is no difference regarding "qurubāt." Then the Blessed and Exalted promised by His saying: ﴿Allah will admit them into His mercy﴾, and so on. It is narrated that this verse was revealed concerning the sons of Muqarrin of Muzaynah, and Mujahid said so. Al-Tabari transmitted through 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mughaffal ibn Muqarrin that he said: "We were ten, the sons of Muqarrin, and this verse was revealed about us: ﴿And among the Bedouins are those who believe in Allah﴾ to the end of the verse."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

His saying "ten, the sons of Muqarrin" means six sons of Muqarrin by his loins, or seven according to what is in al-Istiab from the saying of Suwayd ibn Muqarrin, along with their sons, because this is what is in the well-known registers of the people of knowledge.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 9, verses 100–101:**

His Exalted and Majestic Lord said:

﴿The foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them in goodness: Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. And He has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great triumph.﴾ ﴿And among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites, and among the people of Madinah are those who have become hardened in hypocrisy. You do not know them; We know them. We will punish them twice, then they will be returned to a great punishment.﴾

Abu Musa al-Ashʿari, Ibn al-Musayyib, Ibn Sirin and Qatadah said: "The foremost, the first" are those who prayed toward both qiblas. ʿAtaʾ said: "The foremost, the first" are those who witnessed Badr.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The qiblah was changed two months before Badr.

Amir ibn Sharahil al-Shaʿbi said: "The foremost, the first" are those who attained the Pledge of al-Ridwan. "And those who followed them in goodness" refers to the rest of the Companions. This wording also includes the Successors (al-tabiʿun) and the rest of the Ummah, but on the condition of goodness. This designation has become specific to the generation that saw those who saw the Prophet (ﷺ). If someone said that "the foremost, the first" are all who emigrated until emigration ended, that would be a view the wording supports, with "min" (from) being used to specify the category, and "alladhina" (those who) in this verse being coordinated with His saying "al-sabiqun" (the foremost).

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Qatadah, Salam, Saʿid, Yaʿqub ibn Talha and Isa al-Kufi recited: "wal-sabiqunal-awwalun min al-muhajirin wal-ansar" with the letter ra (in al-ansar) in the nominative case, coordinating it with "al-sabiqun." Likewise, in both readings, His saying "wal-ladhina ittaba'uhum bi-ihsan" is coordinated, making following (ittiba') equivalent to the Helpers.

Al-Tabari transmitted that Zayd ibn Thabit heard it and rejected it, so ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, sent for Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and asked him. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb said: "The foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them in goodness." ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "We thought we had been elevated to a rank that no one with us could attain." Ubayy said: "The confirmation of this is in the Book of Allah, in the beginning of Surah al-Jumuʿah: ﴿and others from among them who have not yet joined them﴾ [62:3]; in Surah al-Hashr: ﴿and those who came after them say: Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith﴾ [59:10]; and in Surah al-Anfal in His saying: ﴿and those who believed afterwards and emigrated and struggled alongside you, they are of you﴾ [8:75]." ʿUmar then returned to Ubayy's view.

This verse points to the Successors, who met the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), just as the one who mentioned them pointed out the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Allah, have mercy on the Helpers, the sons of the Helpers, and the sons of the sons of the Helpers." So reflect upon it.

Ibn Kathir recited "min tahtiha al-anhar" (with min), while the rest recited "tahtaha" without min. The meaning of this verse is the judgment of Allah's pleasure with them through admitting them to Paradise and forgiving their sins, and the judgment of their pleasure with Him through their gratitude, praise for His blessings, their faith in Him, and their obedience to Him. May Allah make us among those who triumph through His mercy and bounty.

As for His saying: ﴿And among those around you of the Bedouins﴾, the verse is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), though his Ummah shares in part of it. The reference in ﴿among those around you of the Bedouins﴾ is to Juhaynah, Muzaynah, Aslam, Ghifar, ʿUsayyah, Lihyan and others among the tribes neighboring Madinah. Allah informed about their hypocrites. The estimated sense of the verse is: "And from the people of Madinah there are people who are hypocrites." This is the best meaning the wording bears.

As for "marradu" (they became hardened): Abu ʿUbayda said its meaning is: they were trained in it and persisted in it. Others said other things close to this. Ibn Zayd said: they remained upon it and did not repent as the others repented.

The apparent meaning of the word is that "tamarrud" in something, or "marud" upon it, is only obstinacy, becoming reckless with it, defiance toward the one who restrains, and insisting on it, and it is used for evil, not good. From this comes the saying "a rebellious devil" (shaytan marid and marid). From this, the name Murad was given because they rebelled. Some people said: it is said "tamarrada al-rajul fi amr kadha" (the man became hardened in such-and-such matter) meaning he stripped himself for it, and this derives from their saying "shajarah marda'" (a bare tree) when it has no leaves. From it comes His saying: ﴿a smooth palace﴾ [27:44]. From it also comes the saying "tamarrada marid wa ʿazza al-ablaq" (the rebel became hardened and the piebald became mighty). From it also comes "al-amrad" (the beardless), who has no beard. So the meaning of "marradu" in this verse is: they persisted in it, became reckless with it, and defied those who restrained them.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, negated His Prophet's knowledge of them individually. Al-Tabari transmitted from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿You do not know them; We know them﴾, that he said: "What is the matter with people who burden themselves with knowing the affairs of others: so-and-so is in Paradise, so-and-so is in the Fire? When you ask one of them about himself, he says: 'I do not know.' By my life, you know yourself better than you know the deeds of people. You have burdened yourself with something the Messengers were never burdened with. The Prophet of Allah Nuh (ﷺ) said: ﴿And what is my knowledge of what they used to do?﴾ [26:112]. And the Prophet of Allah Shuʿayb said: ﴿What remains from Allah is better for you, if you are believers. And I am not a guardian over you﴾ [11:86]." And Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿You do not know them; We know them.﴾

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

As for His saying: ﴿We will punish them twice, then they will be returned to a great punishment.﴾ In the codex (mushaf) of Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads "sa-yuʿadhdhibuhum" with the letter ya. The statement, in both readings, is a warning. The wording implies three stages of punishment. There is no disagreement among the interpreters that the great punishment to which they are returned is the punishment of the Hereafter. Most people hold that the intermediate punishment is the punishment of the grave. Scholars differed regarding the first punishment. Mujahid and others said it is their punishment by killing and hunger. This is far-fetched, because some of them were not afflicted with this. Ibn ʿAbbas also said it is their punishment through the enforcement of the legal punishments of the Sharia upon them despite their dislike of it. Ibn Ishaq said it is their anxiety over the manifestation of Islam and the elevation of its word. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said, and this is the most well-known from him: their punishment is their disgrace and their being branded with hypocrisy. In this interpretation it was transmitted that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave a sermon on a Friday, denouncing the hypocrites and speaking openly, and said: 'Go out, O so-and-so, from the mosque, for you are a hypocrite. Go out, you, O so-and-so. Go out, you, O so-and-so,' until he expelled a group of them. ʿUmar saw them leaving the mosque while he was coming to the Friday prayer, so he thought the people had dispersed and the Friday prayer had passed him by, so he hid from them out of shame. Then he reached the mosque and saw that the prayer had not been concluded, and he understood the matter."

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The Prophet's (ﷺ) action toward them was by way of discipline, based on his own judgment regarding them. It did not strip them of Islam. Rather, it was like the expulsion of sinners and suspects. There is no punishment greater than this. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would often speak about them in general terms without specifying individuals, and this too is a form of punishment. Qatadah and others said: the first punishment is illnesses and afflictions which Allah, Blessed and Exalted, informed His Prophet (ﷺ) that He would afflict them with. Al-Tabari transmitted on this authority from Qatadah that he said: "It was mentioned to us that the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) confided to Hudhayfah the names of twelve men among the hypocrites, and said: 'Six of them, the Dubaylah will suffice against them: a flame of the Fire of Hell that takes hold of one of their shoulders until it reaches his chest. And six will die a natural death.'" It was mentioned to us that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, whenever a man died whom he suspected to be among them, would look at Hudhayfah. If he prayed over him, ʿUmar would pray over him too; otherwise he would leave him. It was also mentioned to us that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said to Hudhayfah: "I adjure you by Allah, am I one of them?" He said: "No, by Allah, and I will not vouch for anyone after you." Ibn Zayd, regarding His saying ﴿We will punish them twice﴾, said: "As for the punishment of this world, it is wealth and children; each category has a punishment, so that makes two." He recited the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿So do not let their wealth and their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them thereby in the life of this world﴾ [9:55]. Ibn Zayd also said: the two punishments are in this world: the first is killing, hunger and calamities, and the second is death, since for the disbelievers it is a punishment. Al-Hasan said: the first is the taking of zakah from their wealth, and the great punishment is everything after death. I think al-Zajjaj pointed to this.

Al-Tabari transmitted from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿You do not know them; We know them﴾, that he said: "What is the matter with people who burden themselves with knowing the affairs of others: so-and-so is in Paradise, so-and-so is in the Fire? When you ask one of them about himself, he says: 'I do not know.' By my life, you know yourself better than you know the deeds of people. You have burdened yourself with something the Messengers were never burdened with. The Prophet of Allah Nuh (ﷺ) said: ﴿And what is my knowledge of what they used to do?﴾ [26:112]. And the Prophet of Allah Shuʿayb said: ﴿What remains from Allah is better for you, if you are believers. And I am not a guardian over you﴾ [11:86]." And Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿You do not know them; We know them.﴾

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

As for His saying: ﴿We will punish them twice, then they will be returned to a great punishment.﴾ In the codex (mushaf) of Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads "sa-yuʿadhdhibuhum" with the letter ya. The statement, in both readings, is a warning. The wording implies three stages of punishment. There is no disagreement among the interpreters that the great punishment to which they are returned is the punishment of the Hereafter. Most people hold that the intermediate punishment is the punishment of the grave. Scholars differed regarding the first punishment. Mujahid and others said it is their punishment by killing and hunger. This is far-fetched, because some of them were not afflicted with this. Ibn ʿAbbas also said it is their punishment through the enforcement of the legal punishments of the Sharia upon them despite their dislike of it. Ibn Ishaq said it is their anxiety over the manifestation of Islam and the elevation of its word. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said, and this is the most well-known from him: their punishment is their disgrace and their being branded with hypocrisy. In this interpretation it was transmitted that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave a sermon on a Friday, denouncing the hypocrites and speaking openly, and said: 'Go out, O so-and-so, from the mosque, for you are a hypocrite. Go out, you, O so-and-so. Go out, you, O so-and-so,' until he expelled a group of them. ʿUmar saw them leaving the mosque while he was coming to the Friday prayer, so he thought the people had dispersed and the Friday prayer had passed him by, so he hid from them out of shame. Then he reached the mosque and saw that the prayer had not been concluded, and he understood the matter."

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The Prophet's (ﷺ) action toward them was by way of discipline, based on his own judgment regarding them. It did not strip them of Islam. Rather, it was like the expulsion of sinners and suspects. There is no punishment greater than this. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would often speak about them in general terms without specifying individuals, and this too is a form of punishment. Qatadah and others said: the first punishment is illnesses and afflictions which Allah, Blessed and Exalted, informed His Prophet (ﷺ) that He would afflict them with. Al-Tabari transmitted on this authority from Qatadah that he said: "It was mentioned to us that the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) confided to Hudhayfah the names of twelve men among the hypocrites, and said: 'Six of them, the Dubaylah will suffice against them: a flame of the Fire of Hell that takes hold of one of their shoulders until it reaches his chest. And six will die a natural death.'" It was mentioned to us that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, whenever a man died whom he suspected to be among them, would look at Hudhayfah. If he prayed over him, ʿUmar would pray over him too; otherwise he would leave him. It was also mentioned to us that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said to Hudhayfah: "I adjure you by Allah, am I one of them?" He said: "No, by Allah, and I will not vouch for anyone after you." Ibn Zayd, regarding His saying ﴿We will punish them twice﴾, said: "As for the punishment of this world, it is wealth and children; each category has a punishment, so that makes two." He recited the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿So do not let their wealth and their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them thereby in the life of this world﴾ [9:55]. Ibn Zayd also said: the two punishments are in this world: the first is killing, hunger and calamities, and the second is death, since for the disbelievers it is a punishment. Al-Hasan said: the first is the taking of zakah from their wealth, and the great punishment is everything after death. I think al-Zajjaj pointed to this.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 102–103:

His Exalted Majesty said:

﴿And others have acknowledged their sins; they had mixed a righteous deed with another that was evil. Perhaps Allah will turn to them in forgiveness. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow, and invoke blessings upon them. Indeed, your invocation is a comfort for them. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾

The meaning: Among these groups are others who acknowledged their sins. The interpretation of this verse has been disputed (p-396). Ibn 'Abbas, according to what has been related from him, and Abu 'Uthman said: it concerns the Bedouins, but it is general for the Ummah until the Day of Resurrection, concerning whoever has both righteous and evil deeds; so it is a verse of hope in this sense. Al-Tabari transmitted this from Hajjaj ibn Abi Zaynab, who said: I heard Abu 'Uthman say: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more hopeful to me for this Ummah than His saying: ﴿And others have acknowledged their sins.﴾" Qatada said: rather, this verse was revealed specifically concerning Abu Lubaba al-Ansari, regarding his matter with the Banu Qurayza. That is because he spoke to them about coming down under the judgment of Allah and His Messenger, and he gestured to them with his throat, meaning that the Prophet ﷺ would slaughter them if they came down. When he was exposed, he repented and regretted it, and he tied himself to one of the pillars of the mosque, and he swore that he would neither eat nor drink until Allah forgave him or he died. He remained so until Allah forgave him, and this verse was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered that he be untied. Al-Tabari related this from Mujahid, and Ibn Ishaq mentioned it in the Book of Biographies (al-Sira), more comprehensively and precisely.

A large group said: rather, this verse was revealed concerning those who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk. Thus, "their evil deed" was staying behind, by the consensus of the adherents of this view, and they differed concerning the "righteous" deed. Al-Tabari and others said: it is acknowledgment, repentance and regret (p-397). Another group said: rather, the "righteous" deed is their earlier participation in the expeditions of the Prophet ﷺ. Then the adherents of this view differed on the number of the people intended by this verse. Ibn 'Abbas radiyallahu 'anhu said: they were ten men, seven of whom tied themselves up, and the three who had been left behind without tying themselves up remained, as mentioned after this. Zayd ibn Aslam said: they were eight, among them Kardam, Mirdas, Abu Qays, and Abu Lubaba. Qatada said: they were seven. Ibn 'Abbas also said, and a group said: they were five, and all of them said that Abu Lubaba was among them. Qatada mentioned among them al-Jadd ibn Qays, and this, to my knowledge, is a mistake, because no repentance has been related for al-Jadd.

As for His saying Exalted: "wa-akhar," it means "bi-akhar," and the two are close in meaning. "'Asa" from Allah is binding.

It is related in the report about those who tied themselves up that "when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered the mosque and saw them, he said: 'What is the matter with these?' It was said to him: 'They have repented and sworn not to untie themselves until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ unties them and excuses them.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'By Allah, I will not untie them nor excuse them unless Allah commands me to do so, for they stayed behind from me and abandoned striving against the disbelievers alongside the believers.'"

As for His saying Exalted: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ — the verse. It is related that "Abu Lubaba and the repentant group who tied themselves up, and who are the ones intended by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿they had mixed a righteous deed with another that was evil﴾, came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when their repentance had been accepted, and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we wish to give our wealth in charity in addition to our repentance.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'I am not to take your wealth except by a command from Allah,' and he left them until this verse was revealed." They are the ones intended by it. It is related that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took one third of their wealth, observing His saying Exalted: ﴿from their wealth﴾. This is what the views of the interpreters, Ibn 'Abbas radiyallahu 'anhuma and others, have converged upon.

(p-389) A group of jurists said: the intended meaning of this verse is the obligatory zakat. Thus, His saying, on this view: ﴿Take from their wealth﴾, its pronoun refers to all people, and this is a general expression intended in a specific sense, since types of wealth in which there is no zakat, such as clothing, real estate and the like, are excluded from it. The pronoun in "their wealth" is likewise a general expression intended in a specific sense, since slaves and others are excluded from it. His saying "charity" (ṣadaqa) is unspecified and requires explanation. This implies that the imam takes charge of collecting the charities and considers them. And "min" in this verse is partitive; this is the strongest of its readings.

His saying Exalted: ﴿by which you purify them and cause them to grow﴾. The most likely possibility is that these verbs are attributed to the pronoun of the Prophet ﷺ. It may also be that they are in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "Take" (khudh). It may also be that they describe the charity; this is preferred according to the raising of the verb. The phrase "bihā" means "by itself," i.e., their purification from their sins occurs through it. It may also be that "tuṭahhiruhum" is a description of "ṣadaqa," and "tuzakkīhim" is attributed to the Prophet ﷺ. It may also be that it is a circumstantial clause from ṣadaqa, but that is weak because it is a circumstance of an indefinite noun. Makki related that "tuṭahhiruhum" may be a description of ṣadaqa, and "wa-tuzakkīhim" is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "khudh."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is rejected because of the presence of the conjunctive waw, for that would be construed as: "Take from their wealth a charity purifying and a purifier of them by it," and this is corrupt in meaning; were there no conjunctive waw in the sentence, it would be permissible. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "tuṭhhirhum" with a sukun on the ṭa'.

His saying Exalted: ﴿and invoke blessings upon them﴾ means: pray for them, for in your supplication for them there is tranquility for their souls (p-399), serenity and dignity; this is an expression for the soundness of belief. Makki, al-Nahhas and others related that it was said that this verse is abrogated by His saying Exalted: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever﴾ [al-Tawba: 84].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a distant error, because that verse concerns the hypocrites who have the ruling of disbelievers, whereas this verse concerns those who repented from staying behind, who have the ruling of believers; so there is no abrogation between the two verses.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "inna ṣalawātika" in the plural, and likewise in Hud and in al-Mu'minun. Hafs from 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "inna ṣalātaka" in the singular, and likewise Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it in the singular in Hud and in al-Mu'minun. 'Asim read it in the plural in al-Mu'minun alone. They did not differ in surah al-An'am and "Sa'ala sa'il." It is a verbal noun (maṣdar), which one group treated as singular and another treated as plural.

His saying Exalted: ﴿Hearing﴾ means: of your supplication; ﴿Knowing﴾ means: of whom He guides and whom He accepts repentance from, and other matters required by these two attributes. It is related that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did what he was commanded, namely supplication and seeking forgiveness for them. Ibn 'Abbas radiyallahu 'anhuma said: ﴿a comfort for them﴾ means mercy for them. Qatada said: ﴿a comfort for them﴾ means dignity for them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Its meaning is rather that the one for whom the Prophet ﷺ prays, his soul is at ease and his hope is strengthened; and it is related that his means of access to Allah the Exalted has been made sound (p-400). This is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verse 104–105:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿Do they not know that it is Allah who accepts repentance from His servants and takes charities, and that Allah is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful?﴾ ﴿And say: "Work, for Allah will see your work, and so will His Messenger and the believers. And you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do."﴾

The majority of readers recited "ألَمْ يَعْلَمُوا" (alam ya'lamu, "Do they not know?") in the third person (addressing the absent). Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan (in one of the transmissions from him) recited "ألَمْ تَعْلَمُوا" (alam ta'lamu, "Do you not know?"), meaning: say to them, O Muhammad, "Do you not know?" It is likewise written in the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b with the "ta" at the top. As for the pronoun in "يَعْلَمُوا", Ibn Zayd said: it is intended to refer to those among the people who stayed behind and did not repent, because when repentance was granted to some of them, others said: "What is this special privilege that these have been singled out for?" So this verse was revealed. It is also possible that the pronoun in "يَعْلَمُوا" refers to those who repented and tied themselves (to the pillars of the mosque).

His saying "huwa" (He) is an emphasis confirming that these matters belong to Allah alone and a securing of that. For if He had said "Allah accepts repentance," it could have been understood that the acceptance of His Messenger is an acceptance from Him; so the verse makes clear that this is something no prophet or angel can reach. His saying ﴿and takes charities﴾ means: He commands them and legislates them, as when you say: "The ruler took such-and-such from the people," meaning he compelled them to pay it. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "and accepts the charities." Traditions have been related about Allah taking charity from His servants, among them the saying of the Prophet ﷺ narrated by Abdullah ibn Abi Qatada al-Muharibi from Ibn Mas'ud, from him (ﷺ): "Indeed, when a servant gives a charity, it falls into the hand of Allah before it falls into the hand of the beggar." And among them his saying narrated by Abu Hurayra: "Indeed, charity, even the size of a morsel, is taken by Allah in His right hand, and He nurtures it for one of you just as one of you nurtures his foal or his young camel, until it becomes like a mountain." Other traditions besides these are expressions of the acceptance and nurturing of the servant's charity, so it may be possible to interpret the word "wa-ya'khudhu" ("and takes") in this light.

(p-401) Connected to this verse is the discussion about the acceptance of repentance, and the summary of that is: the acceptance of repentance from disbelief is definitively (qat'an) affirmed to be by Allah, the Exalted, by consensus (ijma'), and this is the occasion of revelation of this verse, and this group that repented from hypocrisy repented from disbelief. As for the acceptance of repentance from sins, it is definitively affirmed that Allah, the Exalted, accepts the repentance of a group from the community, and it has been disputed whether the repentance of all is accepted. As for when a specific person is named as repentant, the acceptance of his repentance is hoped for and it is not affirmed definitively concerning Allah. And if we posit an unspecified repentant whose repentance is valid, is it definitively affirmed that Allah accepts his repentance or not? There is disagreement. One group, among whom are the jurists and traditionists, and this was the school of my father, may Allah be pleased with him, held: it is definitively affirmed concerning Allah that He accepts his repentance, because He, the Exalted, has informed of this concerning Himself; and according to this it follows that the repentance of all repentant people must be accepted. Abu al-Ma'ali and other imams held that this is not definitively affirmed concerning Allah, the Exalted; rather hope is strengthened in it. Among their proofs is that when a person says in general: "I will not forgive anyone who wronged me," and then someone who has insulted and harmed him comes, he has the right to pursue his due; and forgiveness is for a people whose promise is true, and he is not obliged to forgive every wrongdoer.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Something similar to this is said, and the first view is more preponderant, and Allah is the Granter of success to what is correct.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿from His servants﴾: "ʿan" here has the meaning of "min" (from). Often in one place both this and that are used: you say "lā ṣadaqata illā ʿan ghinan" and "min ghinan" (there is no charity except from wealth), and "fa'ala fulanun dhalika min asharihi wa-batarihi" and "ʿan asharihi wa-batarihi" (so-and-so did that out of his insolence and arrogance).

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do they not know?﴾ is an affirmation, meaning: it is right for them to know. His saying ﴿And say: "Work"﴾ and the rest of the verse is a command-form whose implication is a warning. Al-Tabari said: what is meant by it are those who offered excuses from among those who stayed behind and repented.

(p-402) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning is that what is meant by it are those who offered excuses and did not repent, and they are the ones threatened, and they are the ones referred to in the pronoun of His saying ﴿Do they not know?﴾ — except according to the second possibility, that the verses as a whole concern those who mixed a righteous deed with another wicked one. The meaning of ﴿Allah will see﴾ is: existing, [and] His reckoning of the recompense for it, with good or evil. As for the Messenger and the believers, their "seeing" is a true seeing, not a metaphorical one. Ibn al-Mubarak said: the seeing of the believers is their testimony about a person after his death, and it is their praise of him at funerals. Al-Hasan said, in meaning, that they warned against the discernment of the believer, concerning which the Prophet ﷺ said: "Beware the discernment of the believer, for he looks with the light of Allah."

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do﴾ refers to the resurrection from the graves. The meaning of "the unseen and the witnessed" is what is hidden and what is observed; these are two states that encompass everything. His saying "fa-yunabbi'ukum" ("and He will inform you") is an expression for the presence of the deeds and their being made manifest for recompense, and this is a warning.

As for the pronoun in "يَعْلَمُوا", Ibn Zayd said: it is intended to refer to those among the people who stayed behind and did not repent, because when repentance was granted to some of them, others said: "What is this special privilege that these have been singled out for?" So this verse was revealed. It is also possible that the pronoun in "يَعْلَمُوا" refers to those who repented and tied themselves (to the pillars of the mosque).

His saying "huwa" (He) is an emphasis confirming that these matters belong to Allah alone and a securing of that. For if He had said "Allah accepts repentance," it could have been understood that the acceptance of His Messenger is an acceptance from Him; so the verse makes clear that this is something no prophet or angel can reach. His saying ﴿and takes charities﴾ means: He commands them and legislates them, as when you say: "The ruler took such-and-such from the people," meaning he compelled them to pay it. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "and accepts the charities." Traditions have been related about Allah taking charity from His servants, among them the saying of the Prophet ﷺ narrated by Abdullah ibn Abi Qatada al-Muharibi from Ibn Mas'ud, from him (ﷺ): "Indeed, when a servant gives a charity, it falls into the hand of Allah before it falls into the hand of the beggar." And among them his saying narrated by Abu Hurayra: "Indeed, charity, even the size of a morsel, is taken by Allah in His right hand, and He nurtures it for one of you just as one of you nurtures his foal or his young camel, until it becomes like a mountain." Other traditions besides these are expressions of the acceptance and nurturing of the servant's charity, so it may be possible to interpret the word "wa-ya'khudhu" ("and takes") in this light.

(p-401) Connected to this verse is the discussion about the acceptance of repentance, and the summary of that is: the acceptance of repentance from disbelief is definitively (qat'an) affirmed to be by Allah, the Exalted, by consensus (ijma'), and this is the occasion of revelation of this verse, and this group that repented from hypocrisy repented from disbelief. As for the acceptance of repentance from sins, it is definitively affirmed that Allah, the Exalted, accepts the repentance of a group from the community, and it has been disputed whether the repentance of all is accepted. As for when a specific person is named as repentant, the acceptance of his repentance is hoped for and it is not affirmed definitively concerning Allah. And if we posit an unspecified repentant whose repentance is valid, is it definitively affirmed that Allah accepts his repentance or not? There is disagreement. One group, among whom are the jurists and traditionists, and this was the school of my father, may Allah be pleased with him, held: it is definitively affirmed concerning Allah that He accepts his repentance, because He, the Exalted, has informed of this concerning Himself; and according to this it follows that the repentance of all repentant people must be accepted. Abu al-Ma'ali and other imams held that this is not definitively affirmed concerning Allah, the Exalted; rather hope is strengthened in it. Among their proofs is that when a person says in general: "I will not forgive anyone who wronged me," and then someone who has insulted and harmed him comes, he has the right to pursue his due; and forgiveness is for a people whose promise is true, and he is not obliged to forgive every wrongdoer.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Something similar to this is said, and the first view is more preponderant, and Allah is the Granter of success to what is correct.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿from His servants﴾: "ʿan" here has the meaning of "min" (from). Often in one place both this and that are used: you say "lā ṣadaqata illā ʿan ghinan" and "min ghinan" (there is no charity except from wealth), and "fa'ala fulanun dhalika min asharihi wa-batarihi" and "ʿan asharihi wa-batarihi" (so-and-so did that out of his insolence and arrogance).

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do they not know?﴾ is an affirmation, meaning: it is right for them to know. His saying ﴿And say: "Work"﴾ and the rest of the verse is a command-form whose implication is a warning. Al-Tabari said: what is meant by it are those who offered excuses from among those who stayed behind and repented.

(p-402) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning is that what is meant by it are those who offered excuses and did not repent, and they are the ones threatened, and they are the ones referred to in the pronoun of His saying ﴿Do they not know?﴾ — except according to the second possibility, that the verses as a whole concern those who mixed a righteous deed with another wicked one. The meaning of ﴿Allah will see﴾ is: existing, [and] His reckoning of the recompense for it, with good or evil. As for the Messenger and the believers, their "seeing" is a true seeing, not a metaphorical one. Ibn al-Mubarak said: the seeing of the believers is their testimony about a person after his death, and it is their praise of him at funerals. Al-Hasan said, in meaning, that they warned against the discernment of the believer, concerning which the Prophet ﷺ said: "Beware the discernment of the believer, for he looks with the light of Allah."

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do﴾ refers to the resurrection from the graves. The meaning of "the unseen and the witnessed" is what is hidden and what is observed; these are two states that encompass everything. His saying "fa-yunabbi'ukum" ("and He will inform you") is an expression for the presence of the deeds and their being made manifest for recompense, and this is a warning.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 9, verses 106–107:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And others are deferred to the command of Allah: either He will punish them, or He will turn to them in forgiveness. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿And those who took a mosque for harm and disbelief and division among the believers, and as a station of ambush for those who had warred against Allah and His Messenger before. And they will surely swear, "We intended nothing but good." And Allah testifies that they are liars.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: "And others" is conjoined to His earlier saying "and others." Nafi', al-A'raj, Ibn Nassah, Abu Ja'far, Talha, al-Hasan, and the people of the Hijaz recited *murjawna* (مُرْجَوْنَ) from *arjaa*, *yurji*, without a hamza. Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and the people of Basra recited *murji'un* (مُرْجَؤُونَ) from *arja'a*, *yurji'u*, with a hamza, and there is a difference of report from 'Asim. Both are dialectal forms (*lughatan*), and their meaning is delay (al-ta'khir). From this comes the term *al-Murji'a* (the Murji'a, a theological school), because they deferred the works, meaning they deferred their ruling and rank. Al-Mubarrad denied that dropping the hamza carries the meaning of delay, but he was not correct in what he said.

The intended people of this verse, according to what Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, 'Ikrima, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatada, and Ibn Ishaq said, are the three who were left behind: Hilal ibn Umayya al-Waqifi, Marara ibn al-Rabi', and Ka'b ibn Malik. This verse was revealed before their repentance was accepted. It was also said that it was revealed about others among the hypocrites who were exposed to repentance together with their building of the Mosque of Harm. On this view, "those who took" (﴿والَّذِينَ اتَّخَذُوا﴾) is either a substitute (badal) for "others" (﴿آخَرُونَ﴾) without the conjunction *waw*, or it is the predicate of a new subject, with the implied meaning "they are those who." According to this, the verse contains an expectation of their return and an invitation to faith and repentance. *'Alim* (All-Knowing) means: knowing of whoever is guided to right conduct. *Hakim* (All-Wise) means: in what He carries out, granting bliss to whom He wills and punishing whom He wills. There is no lord other than Him and no deity besides Him.

'Asim, the majority of the readers, and the common people in every region except Medina recited "wa-alladhina ittakhadhu" (وَالَّذِينَ اتَّخَذُوا) with the *waw*. The people of Medina, Nafi', Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and others recited "alladhina ittakhadhu" (الَّذِينَ اتَّخَذُوا) without the *waw*. It is likewise so in their *mushaf* (copy of the Qur'an), as Abu Hatim said. Al-Zahrawi said it is the recitation of Ibn 'Amir, and it is in the *masahif* (copies) of the people of Syria without a *waw*. As for the one who recites with the *waw*, it is a conjunction to His saying "and others," meaning: and among them are those who took. As for the one who recites without it, he makes "alladhina" (الَّذِينَ) the subject of a nominal sentence. The predicate has been disputed. It was said the predicate is "do not stand in it ever" (﴿لا تَقُمْ فِيهِ أبَدًا﴾), as al-Kisa'i said. This is possible with an implied element either at the beginning of the verse or at its end, with the meaning "do not stand in their mosque." It was also said the predicate is "their building will not cease" (لا يَزالُ بُنْيانُهُمْ), as al-Nahhas said, and this is more eloquent. I have already mentioned that "alladhina" is a substitute for "others" a moment ago. Al-Mahdawi said the predicate is omitted, with the meaning "they will be punished" or something similar.

As for the group intended by "alladhina ittakhadhu," they are the hypocrites of Banu Ghanm ibn 'Awf and Banu Salim ibn 'Awf. Al-Tabari narrated with a chain (isnad) from Ibn Ishaq, from al-Zuhri and others, that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came back from the expedition of Tabuk until he halted at Dhu Awan, a place between it and Medina about an hour into the day. The people of the Mosque of Harm had come to him while he was preparing for Tabuk and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we have built a mosque for the one with an excuse, the one in need, and the rainy night, and we love that you come to us and pray for us in it.' He said: 'I am on the verge of a journey and in a state of preoccupation. If we return, Allah willing, we will come to you and pray for you in it.' When he came back and halted at Dhu Awan, the Qur'an was revealed to him concerning the Mosque of Harm. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called Malik ibn al-Dukhshum and Ma'n ibn 'Adi, or his brother 'Asim ibn 'Adi, and said: 'Go to this mosque whose people are wrongdoers, demolish it and burn it.' So they went quickly and did so, and they burned it with fire on palm fronds." Al-Naqqash mentioned that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent 'Ammar ibn Yasir and Wahshi, the freedman of al-Mut'im ibn 'Adi, to demolish it and burn it." Its builders were twelve men: Khudhām ibn Khalid, from whose house the Mosque of Division (Masjid al-Shiqaq) was brought out; Tha'laba ibn Hatib; Mut'ab ibn Qushayr; Abu Habiba ibn al-Azar; 'Abbad ibn Hanif, the brother of Sahl ibn Hanif; Jariya ibn 'Amr, and his two sons, Majma' ibn Jariya, who was their imam, and he swore to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, during his caliphate, that he had not known of their affair; Zayd ibn Jariya; Nabtal ibn al-Harith; Bahzaj from Banu Dubay'a; Bijad ibn 'Uthman; and Wadi'a ibn Thabit. Bahzaj, among them, is the one who swore to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I intended nothing but good and ease for us and for whoever is unable or weak to travel to the Mosque of Quba'."

Ibn Abi 'Abla recited: "ma aradna illa al-husna" (مَا أرَدْنا إلّا الحُسْنى).

The verse requires an explanation of something about the matter of these mosques. It is narrated that "when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived in Medina at the time of the Hijra, he built a mosque among Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf, which is the Mosque of Quba'." It was also said he found it already built before his arrival. It was said he found it a place of prayer and built it, and the people were honored by this, so men from their paternal cousins, from Banu Ghanm ibn 'Awf and Banu Salim ibn 'Awf, envied them from that time, and hypocrisy arose among them. The site of the Mosque of Quba' had been a tethering place for the donkey of a woman of the Ansar named Liya. The hypocrites would say: "By Allah, we will not endure praying in the tethering place of Liya's donkey," and similar statements. Abu 'Amir, whose name was 'Abd 'Amr and who was known as al-Rahib (the monk), was among them. His mother was from the Romans, and he used to worship in the pre-Islamic era, so he was called al-Rahib. He is Abu Handhala, "the one washed by the angels." He was a leader, an unequaled figure, and close to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul. When Allah, blessed and exalted, brought Islam, he became a hypocrite and continued to openly profess this. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named him "the wicked" (al-Fasiq). Then he went out with a group of hypocrites and gathered the factions (al-ahzab) against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When Allah repelled them in their rage, Abu 'Amir remained in Mecca openly displaying his enmity. When Allah conquered Mecca, he fled to al-Ta'if. When the people of al-Ta'if embraced Islam, he left fleeing to Syria, seeking Caesar, asking him for support against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He wrote to his hypocritical people, instructing them to build a mosque in opposition to the Mosque of Quba' and to belittle it, saying: "I will come with an army of Romans with which I will expel Muhammad and his companions from Medina." They built it, and they said: "Abu 'Amir will come and pray in it, take it as a place of worship, and be delighted by it." Then Abu 'Amir died with Caesar. The Qur'an was revealed concerning the matter of the Mosque of Harm. That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and as an outpost for one who had warred against Allah and His Messenger﴾, meaning Abu 'Amir, and their saying: "Abu 'Amir will come." Al-A'mash recited "li-alladhina harabu Allah" (لِلَّذِينِ حارَبُوا اللهَ).

His saying: ﴿harm﴾ (ضِرارًا) means: a call to mutual harm between two groups. Therefore He said "dirar" (ضِرارًا). It is, in origin, a verbal noun of what occurs between two parties, although the verbal noun that is constantly used for this is *mufa'ala*, as Sibawayh said. "Dirar" and what follows it are in the accusative as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). It is also permissible that it be an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi). His saying: ﴿among the believers﴾ means: among the community that used to pray in the Mosque of Quba'. Whoever passed by their mosque would be turned away toward it, and that was a call to turn him away from faith. It was also said: by His saying "among the believers," He meant the community of the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This depends on the disagreement concerning the mosque "founded upon piety," which will be discussed later. Al-Naqqash said: "It follows from this that prayer should not be performed in a church or similar place, because it was built upon an evil greater than all of this." It has been said concerning this: ﴿Do not stand in it ever﴾ (Surat al-Tawba: 108).

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"This is a jurisprudential inference that is not strong."

*Al-irsad* (the lying in ambush, the preparing) means: preparing and readying. "The one who warred against Allah and His Messenger" is Abu 'Amir the wicked. His saying: ﴿before﴾ (min qabl) means: at the battle of the Confederates and others. The one who swears intended in His saying: ﴿and they will surely swear﴾ is Bahzaj and whoever swore among his companions. The *alif* in His saying "innahum la-kadhibun" (إنَّهم لَكاذِبُونَ) is pronounced with a kasra because testimony (al-shahada) carries the meaning of saying.

Al-Tabari narrated from Shaqiq that he came to pray in a mosque built in Ghadira, but found that the prayer had already passed him. He was told: "The mosque of so-and-so has not yet been prayed in." He said: "I do not like to pray in it, for it was built upon harm." Every mosque built for harm, ostentation, and reputation is under the ruling of the Mosque of Harm. It was also narrated that when the Mosque of Harm was demolished and burned, it was made into a dunghill where filth and refuse were thrown.

Al-Tabari narrated from Shaqiq that he came to pray in a mosque built in Ghadira, but found that the prayer had already passed him. He was told: "The mosque of so-and-so has not yet been prayed in." He said: "I do not like to pray in it, for it was built upon harm." Every mosque built for harm, ostentation, and reputation is under the ruling of the Mosque of Harm. It was also narrated that when the Mosque of Harm was demolished and burned, it was made into a dunghill where filth and refuse were thrown.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 108–109 (part 1 of 2):

(p-407) His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:
﴿Do not stand in it ever. A mosque founded on righteousness from the first day is more worthy that you stand in it. In it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves.﴾ ﴿Is one who founded his building on God-consciousness from Allah and good pleasure better, or one who founded his building on the edge of a crumbling cliff, so that it collapsed with him into the fire of Hell? And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

It is narrated that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was revealed: ﴿Do not stand in it ever﴾, he would not pass along the road on which the mosque was. This prohibition was only because the builders of the mosque of harm had deceived the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "We have built a mosque for the needy and for the rainy night, and what separates us from our people. We want you to pray for us in it and invoke blessing." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) resolved to walk with them to that, and called for his shirt to rise, and then the verse was revealed: ﴿Do not stand in it ever﴾. As for his saying ﴿la-masjidun﴾ (indeed a mosque), it has been said that the lam is the lam of oath, and it has been said that it is the lam of initiation, as you say: "la-Zaydun is the best of people in conduct," and it entails emphasis.

Ibn 'Abbas and a group of the Companions and the Successors (may Allah be pleased with them) said: the mosque that was founded on righteousness is the mosque of Quba. It is narrated from 'Umar, Abu Sa'id, and Zayd ibn Thabit that it is the mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Medina. The first view fits the narrative, but the second view is narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and there is no consideration against a hadith. Al-Tabari cited, concerning this, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that he said: "A man from Banu Khudra and a man from Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf disputed, and the Khudri said: it is the mosque of the Messenger (ﷺ), and the other said: it is the mosque of Quba. So they both came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him, and he said: 'It is my mosque here, and in the other is much good.'" And there are many reports on this from Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Sahl ibn Sa'd.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:
The mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was on a site that had palm trees, graves of polytheists, and a drying-yard of two orphans who were under the guardianship of As'ad ibn Zurara. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) built it three times: the first time with al-samit, which is one brick in front of another brick; the second time with al-sa'ida, which is a brick and a half across the width of the wall; and the third time with the female and the male, which are two bricks over which two bricks are laid. Its length was seventy cubits. Its pillars were of palm trunks, and it was a shelter that kept off the rain. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was shown its building and elevation, and he said: "No, rather let it be a shelter like the shelter of my brother Musa, who, when he stood, struck his head against its roof." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to carry the bricks on his chest in it. It is said that the first to place a stone in its foundation was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then Abu Bakr placed a stone, then 'Umar placed a stone, then 'Uthman placed a stone, then the people threw stones, and some of the Companions took this as an omen that it was the caliphate, and his omen was true.

His saying ﴿min awwali yawm﴾ (from the first day): it has been said its meaning is "since the first day," and it has been said its meaning is "from the founding of the first day." What prompted this disagreement is that among the principles of the grammarians is that "min" does not govern time-periods; rather time-periods are governed by "mundhu," as you say: "I have not seen him since two days or a year or a day," and you do not say "min shahr" (from a month), nor "min sana" (from a year), nor "min yawm" (from a day). So when "min" occurs in speech and is followed by a period of time, a suitable implied word is supposed that "min" can govern, as in the saying of the poet:
"To whom are the abodes, like the summit of al-Hijr, / weathered by years and by ages?"
And "min shahr" is a variant reading; they supposed it to be "min marri hijajin wa min marri dahr" (from the passing of years and from the passing of an age). And since His saying ﴿awwali yawm﴾ is a day, and it is a noun of time, they needed to suppose "min ta'sis" (from the founding). In my view it would be good (p-409) to dispense with a supposition in this verse, and for "min" to govern the word "awwal," because it carries the sense of beginning, as if He said: "from the starting-point of days." Here it takes the place of "al-marr" in the verse above, and it is like your saying: "I came from before you and from after you," and you indicate by these two words only time. This which I have chosen has been related to me from some of the imams of grammar.

The meaning of ﴿an taqūma fīhi﴾ (that you stand in it) is: with your prayer and worship. The majority of people read: "an taqūma fīhi fīhi rijālun" with a kasra on the ha'. 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd read: "an taqūma fīhi, fīhu" with a damma on the second ha', according to the original form, and what makes it better is avoiding the repetition of a single word. Qatada and others said: the pronoun refers to the mosque of the Messenger (ﷺ), and "the men" are the group of the Ansar.

It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "O assembly of the Ansar, I have seen that Allah praised you for purification; what do you do?" They said: "O Messenger of Allah, we have seen our Jewish neighbours purify themselves with water" (the Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: he means cleansing oneself with water after relieving oneself), "so we did likewise, and when Islam came we did not abandon it." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Then never abandon it."

'Abd Allah ibn Salam and others said, in substance, that the pronoun refers to the mosque of Quba, and the intended people are Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf. It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) only said the aforementioned statement to Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf. The first view is more common. The scholars differed on which is better: cleansing with water or with stones. Some said this and some said that, and a group of the scholars saw combining the two, so one cleans with stones and then follows with water. Abu (my father, may Allah be pleased with him) related to me that he had been informed that some scholars of Qayrawan used to keep stones in dust in their washing places, with which they cleansed and then washed with water, taking according to this view.

(p-410) The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:
The disagreement can only be conceived in regions where it is possible to clean with stones. Ibn Habib does not permit cleansing with stones where water is available, and this is a view in which he stands alone.

The majority of people read: "yatatahharū." Talha ibn Musarrif and al-A'mash read: "yattahharū" with assimilation. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) read: "al-mutatahhirīn" with a ta'. Al-Tabari cited from 'Ata' that he said: some people of Quba introduced cleansing with water, so the verse was revealed concerning them. And it is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Among them is 'Uwaym ibn Sa'ida." And no one else among them was named except 'Uwaym.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and a group read: "assassa bunyānahu" with the verb in the active form and "bunyān" in the accusative in both places. 'Imara ibn Damma (transmitted by Ya'qub) read the first in the passive and the second in the active. The verse contains an equation between two things, either between the two constructions or between the two builders. The first equation is by supposition: "Whose construction is it of the one who founded?" Nasr ibn 'Asim also read: "ussus bunyānihi" on the pattern fu'ul with damma on the fa' and the 'ayn, which is the plural of asās, like qadhāl and qudhul; Abu al-Fath related this. Abu Hatim mentioned that this reading of Nasr is actually "asas," with a fatha on the hamza, a fatha on the sin, and a damma on the second sin. On both reports the annexation is to bunyān. Nasr ibn 'Ali also read: "asās," as the plural of "ass." The word bunyān is a verbal noun; it is said: banā yabnī binā'an and bunyānan, like ghufrān and ṭughyān, and so the built structure is named by it, like khalq when you mean the created thing. It has also been said that it is a plural whose singular is bunyānah, and Abu 'Ali cited in this:
"Like the bunyānah of the reciter, where the place of her foot / and the traces of her two ropes from the drum are spotted."

The majority read: "ʿalā taqwā," and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read: "ʿalā taqwan" with tanwin on the waw. Sibawayh related this reading and people rejected it. Abu al-Fath said: its analysis is that the alif is for extension, like arṭā and the like.

As for the meaning of the building founded on righteousness and good pleasure, it is — in the apparent wording and the view of the majority — the mosque mentioned before, and the previous disagreement applies to it. It is narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said: the intended mosque founded on righteousness is the mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the intended by "founded on God-consciousness from Allah and good pleasure" is the mosque of Quba. As for the building founded on the edge of a crumbling cliff, it is by consensus the mosque of harm.

(p-412) Al-shafa is the edge and the brink. Al-jurf is the pit around a well and the like, of what the torrents have eroded, and the crumbling and decay. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, and a group read: "jurufin" with a damma on the ra'. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamza, and a group read: "jurfin" with a sukun on the ra'. The report from 'Asim varies. They are two dialects. It has been said the original is with a damma on the ra' and that lightening it afterwards is in use. Hari means crumbling and collapsing, from hara yahuru. It is also said: hara yahiru and yahar. Its origin is hayir or hawir. It has been said its ra' was moved before the weak letter, so it became hari or hari, and it was treated as qadin and ghazin were treated. On this view, in the accusative one says hariyan. Similar is "fī yawmin rāḥin" (on a windy day), originally rā'iḥin. Similar is "shākī al-silāḥ" (armed with weapons), originally shā'ik. Similar is the saying of al-'Ajjaj:
"Entwined around it are the acacia and the 'ubri,"
originally lā'ith. Similar is the saying of the poet:
"......................... they lowered their spear-points, so every one of them is nā'i"
on one of the two readings, for it may be from "na'a ya'nī" (to lament), and the meaning is that they say: "O vengeance of so-and-so!" It may also be intended: "so all of them are nā'i'," that is, thirsty, as 'Umayr ibn Shiyyam said:
"......................... and the lances thirsty"
It has been said of "hārin": its weak letter was entirely deleted, so on this view it follows the declensions of case, and you say: jurfun hārun, and ra'aytu jurfan hāran, and marartu bi-jurfin hārin. The readers differed on the imala of "hārin" and "inhāra."

The founding on the edge of a crumbling cliff is only by corrupt intention and seeking display and dividing among the believers. These are sound and brilliant comparisons. The word "khayr" in this verse is a comparative, and there is no sharing of the two matters in goodness except according to the belief of the builder of the mosque of harm; by that belief the comparison is valid.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿so that it collapsed with him into the fire of Hell﴾. The apparent meaning of it, and what is established of their report and the demolition by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of their mosque, is that it is given in the form of a parable, meaning: the likeness of these harmful hypocrites in their intention of disobeying Allah, and their earning from that His wrath, is like one whose building collapses into the fire of Hell. Then the speech was abridged in a manner indicated by its apparent meaning. It has been said: rather, this is literal, and that very mosque collapsed into the fire of Hell; this was said by Qatada and Ibn Jurayj. It is narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and others that he said: "I saw smoke coming out of it in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." It is related in some books that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw it when it collapsed until it reached the seventh earth, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was alarmed by that. It is also narrated that they did not pray in it more than three days: they completed it on Friday, prayed in it on Friday and the night of Saturday, and it collapsed on Monday.

(p-414) The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:
All of this is with a weak chain, and what we have presented before is more correct and sound. Likewise its affair remained, and prayer in it, from before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)'s journey to Tabuk until he returned from it.

"And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is a rebuke of these hypocrites and an indication of them. The meaning is: He does not guide them insofar as they are wrongdoers. Or the intended meaning is particular, referring to those who die upon their wrongdoing. Al-Tabari transmitted, via Khalaf ibn Yasin, that he said: 'I saw the mosque of the hypocrites whom Allah mentioned in the Qur'an, and I saw in it a place from which smoke emerges, and that was in the time of Abu Ja'far al-Mansur.' Something similar to this, or close to it, is also related from Ibn Jurayj, which al-Tabari transmitted with a chain of narration."

The apparent meaning of it, and what is established of their report and the demolition by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of their mosque, is that it is given in the form of a parable, meaning: the likeness of these harmful hypocrites in their intention of disobeying Allah, and their earning from that His wrath, is like one whose building collapses into the fire of Hell. Then the speech was abridged in a manner indicated by its apparent meaning. It has been said: rather, this is literal, and that very mosque collapsed into the fire of Hell; this was said by Qatada and Ibn Jurayj. It is narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and others that he said: "I saw smoke coming out of it in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." It is related in some books that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw it when it collapsed until it reached the seventh earth, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was alarmed by that. It is also narrated that they did not pray in it more than three days: they completed it on Friday, prayed in it on Friday and the night of Saturday, and it collapsed on Monday.

(p-414) The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:
All of this is with a weak chain, and what we have presented before is more correct and sound. Likewise its affair remained, and prayer in it, from before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)'s journey to Tabuk until he returned from it.

"And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is a rebuke of these hypocrites and an indication of them. The meaning is: He does not guide them insofar as they are wrongdoers. Or the intended meaning is particular, referring to those who die upon their wrongdoing. Al-Tabari transmitted, via Khalaf ibn Yasin, that he said: 'I saw the mosque of the hypocrites whom Allah mentioned in the Qur'an, and I saw in it a place from which smoke emerges, and that was in the time of Abu Ja'far al-Mansur.' Something similar to this, or close to it, is also related from Ibn Jurayj, which al-Tabari transmitted with a chain of narration."

﴿Their building which they built will not cease to be a source of doubt in their hearts, unless their hearts are cut to pieces. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties, in return for which they shall have Paradise. They fight in the cause of Allah, so they kill and are killed. It is a true promise binding upon Him in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an. And who is more faithful to his covenant than Allah? So rejoice in the bargain you have made. That is the great triumph.﴾

The pronoun in *bunyanuhum* (their building) refers to the hypocrites who built the mosque and those who shared their aim. His saying *alladhi banaw* (which they built) is an emphasis and a clear identification of the matter of the mosque, removing any ambiguity. *Ribah* (doubt) means uncertainty. It may also be used for corruption of belief, its disorder, objection to a matter, confusion regarding it, and resentment arising from it, even if it is not outright doubt. A person may feel doubt without actually doubting, but in ordinary usage *ribah* is associated with doubt. The meaning of *ribah* in this verse is a matter that encompasses rage and fury, and encompasses the belief that their action was correct, and similar things, all of which lead to doubt about Islam. Thus the purpose of the statement is: this building, which was demolished for them, will continue to leave in their hearts resentment and an evil effect. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) interpreted *ribah* here as doubt, while al-Suddi interpreted it as disbelief. It was said to him: "Did Majma' ibn Jariyah disbelieve?" He said: "No, but it was resentment."

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Majma' (may Allah have mercy on him) swore to 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) that he did not know the inner state of the people and did not intend any evil. The verse refers only to those who concealed evil, so Majma' is not among them. It is possible that the meaning is: they will continue to be in doubt because of their building, in which their hypocrisy became clear. The sum of this is that *ribah* in the verse encompasses many meanings, each hypocrite taking from them according to his degree of hypocrisy.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and al-Kisa'i read *illa an tuqatta'a qulubuhum* (unless their hearts are cut to pieces) with a *damma* on the *ta'* and the verb in the passive voice. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and 'Asim (with a variant from him) read *illa an taqatta'a* with a *fatha* on the *ta'*, taking the verb as active with the heart as subject. al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ya'qub read *ila an taqatta'a* (until their hearts are cut to pieces), meaning *ila an yamutu* (until they die). Some read *ila an taqta'a*. Abu Hayawah read *illa an yuqti'a* with *ya'* vowelled with a *damma*, the *ta'* with a *kasra*, and *qulub* in the accusative, meaning: by killing. As for the first reading, it was said that it means by death, as Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, and others said. It was also said that it means by repentance, but this is not the apparent meaning, unless it is interpreted as: or they repent a sincere repentance, accompanied by such remorse and regret for the sin that it cuts the hearts with grief and anxious thought. In the *mushaf* (codex, written copy) of Ibn Mas'ud it reads *wa-law qutti'at qulubuhum* (even if their hearts were cut to pieces), and his companions read it thus, and Abu 'Amr related it. There is also *wa-in qutti'at* with the *ta'* lightened. In the *mushaf* of Ubayy it reads *hatta al-mamat* (until death), and in it also *tuqta'* (is cut).

His saying, exalted is He: *Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives...* This verse was revealed concerning the third pledge, which is the Pledge of 'Aqabah the Greater, in which the men of the Ansar, numbering seventy, pledged allegiance, the youngest of them in age being 'Uqbah ibn 'Amr. They gathered with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at 'Aqabah and said: "Stipulate for yourself and for your Lord." The one who spoke was 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stipulated his protection from what they protect themselves from, and stipulated for his Lord the commitment to the Shari'ah and fighting the red and the black (all people) in defending the sacred territory. They said: "What do we get in return for that?" He said: "Paradise." They said: "Yes, the sale is profitable; we will neither cancel it nor request its cancellation." In some reports: "nor will we ask to be released from it." So the verse was revealed concerning that. Then the verse, after that, is general in its application to everyone who strives in the cause of Allah from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) until the Day of Resurrection. Some scholars said: every Muslim has this pledge upon his neck to Allah; whether he fulfils it or does not. It is in a *hadith*: "Indeed, above every act of righteousness there is another act of righteousness, until the servant gives his blood; when he does that, there is no righteousness above it." This is a beautiful analogy from Allah, exalted and mighty is He, using the imagery of a sale (*mubaya'ah*, pledge). The reality of a *mubaya'ah* is that it takes place between two parties by their intention and valid ownership. In this narrative, Allah granted His servants their lives and their properties, then commanded them to expend them in His cause, and promised them in return something better than them. This is the utmost of grace. Then He likened the matter to a *mubaya'ah*. Al-Tabari transmitted, through a chain citing many scholars, that they said: Allah, exalted is He, in this verse made a bargain with His servants and so exalted them. This was also said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan. Ibn 'Uyaynah said: the meaning of the verse is: He purchased from them their lives, that they would not employ them except in obedience to Allah, and their properties, that they would not spend them except in the cause of Allah.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

According to this, the verse is more general than killing in the cause of Allah. The allegiance to the caliphs is derived from this verse. People would give the caliphs their obedience, sincere counsel, and exertion, and the caliphs would give them justice, consideration, and the management of their affairs. My father (may Allah be pleased with him) related to me that he heard the preacher Abu al-Fadl ibn al-Jawhari say from the pulpit in Egypt: "Enough of a transaction in which the Seller is the Lord of the Most High, the price is the Abode of Paradise, and the intermediary is Muhammad the Chosen (ﷺ)."

His saying, exalted is He: *They fight in the cause of Allah* is a separate, new sentence, according to the interpretation of Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah. As for the interpretation of the majority, that the buying and selling is with those who strive, then it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Abu Raja', and others read *fa-yaqtuluna* (so they kill) in the active voice, and *wa-yuqtaluna* (and are killed) in the passive voice. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Wuthab, Talhah, and al-A'mash read the reverse of that. The meaning is one, since the point is that the believers fight, so among them there is one who kills, among them one who is killed, among them one for whom both occur, and among them one for whom neither happens. The purpose is not that each one must have both. When this is considered, it becomes clear.

His saying, exalted is He: *a promise binding upon Him* (*wa'dan 'alayhi haqqan*) is an emphatic verbal noun (*masdar mu'akkid*), because what precedes in the verse has the sense of a promise, so this clause comes as an emphasis of what came before in His saying: *that they shall have Paradise*. The commentators said: from His saying, exalted is He: *in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an*, it becomes apparent that every community that was commanded to strive and was promised reward for it.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It is possible that the promise to the community of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was mentioned in these books.

His saying, exalted is He: *And who is more faithful to his covenant than Allah?* is a rhetorical question in the form of an affirmation, meaning: no one is more faithful to his covenant than Allah. His saying: *So rejoice* (*fastabshiru*) is a verb in which *istaf'ala* carries the meaning of *af'ala* (to make happy), and this is not the sense of requesting something, as one says *istawqada naran* (he kindled a fire), *istahda mala* (he asked for wealth as a gift), *istad'a nasran* (he sought victory). Rather it is like *'ajiba* and *ista'jaba* (to be amazed). Then Allah, blessed and exalted is He, described that transaction as *the great triumph*, meaning that it is the attainment of the most desirable portion, namely the erasure of sins and entry into Paradise without reckoning.
