Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 112–113:

Allah the Exalted said:

﴿Those who repent, who worship, who praise, who travel (for the cause of Allah), who bow, who prostrate, who enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and who observe the limits set by Allah. And give good tidings to the believers.﴾ ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were close relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾

These attributes are among the attributes of the believers whom Allah said He purchased from them their selves. These attributes are in the nominative case because they came unattached (to the preceding words) at the beginning of a verse, meaning: "They are the repentant ones." The meaning of the verse, according to what the views of the scholars and the Sharia require, is that these are the attributes of the perfect among the believers, which Allah the Exalted mentioned so that the people of monotheism would race toward them until they reach the highest rank. The first verse stands on its own: every monotheist who fought in the path of Allah, so that the word of Allah may be supreme, falls under that pledge, even if he does not possess these attributes, or most of them, that are in this verse. One group said: "Rather, these attributes came in the form of a condition, and the two verses are linked, so only the believers who have these attributes and who give themselves in the path of Allah enter the pledge." Al-Tabari narrated, through al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, that a man asked him about the saying of Allah the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased﴾ [al-Tawba: 111], the verse, and the man said: "Shall I not charge against the polytheists and fight until I am killed?" Al-Dahhak said: "Woe to you, where is the condition: ﴿those who repent, who worship﴾, the verse?" This view is a constraint and a restriction, and Allah knows best. The first view is more correct. Martyrdom erases every sin except the wrongs done to people. It has been narrated that Allah the Exalted bears on behalf of the martyr the wrongs done to people and recompenses them on his behalf. May Allah conclude our lives with goodness.

Another group said: The nominative case of "al-tai'buna" (the repentant ones) is by way of the inchoative (mubtada'), and what follows it are attributes, except His saying "al-amirun" (those who enjoin), for it is the predicate of the inchoative, as if He had said: "They are those who enjoin." This is good, except that the meaning of the verse becomes separated from the meaning of the one before it, and that is unsound, so consider it carefully. In the codex of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, the reading is: "al-tai'bina, al-'abidina" to the end of it. For this there are two possibilities: first, that it is an attribute of the believers, following the wording; second, that it is in the accusative case by way of praise.

"Al-tai'buna" encompasses returning from evil to good, whether that was from disbelief or sin, and returning from one state to what is better than it, even if the first state was not evil but good. Thus was the repentance of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his seeking forgiveness seventy times a day. The penitent (al-tai'b) is one who abandons sin, resolves to persist in abandoning it, and regrets what has passed. Whoever repents from one sin is called penitent, even if he persists in another, unless it is of the same kind, in which case he is not a penitent. Repentance, and its repeated breaking and renewal, is better than persistence. Whoever repents, then breaks his repentance and dies in that breaking, his earlier sins remain upon him, because Allah knew that his repentance from them was broken. The matter may admit of other than this, and Allah knows best.

Al-Hasan said in explaining the verse: "Al-tai'buna" means: from polytheism.

"Al-'abidun" is a word that encompasses the performance of the worship of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, the adherence to His Sharia, the constancy in that, persevering in it, and continuing in it. The worshipper (al-'abid) is the one who does good, which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained in his saying: "That you worship Allah as though you see Him." With the least worship that a Muslim performs, the name "worshipper" falls upon him and he attains the lowest rank of it, and according to his increase in worship the attribute is attained.

"Al-hamidun" means: those who remember Allah with His beautiful attributes in every state, in times of ease and hardship, and their praise is because He is worthy of it. It is more general than gratitude, since gratitude is only for the blessings specific to the one who is grateful.

"Al-sa'ihun" means: those who fast. It is narrated from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "The travelling (siyaha) of this Ummah is fasting." Al-Tabari traced it, and it is narrated that it is from the words of the Prophet (ﷺ). In a hadith: "Indeed, Allah has angels who travel and walk through the horizons, conveying to me the prayers of my Ummah upon me." The hadith is also narrated as "sayyahin" with the letter sad (meaning those who shout), from "sihah" (outcry). Travelling in the earth (al-siyaha fi al-ard) is derived from "al-say'h", which is water flowing over the earth without a destination. Some people said, and it is in the book of al-Naqqash: "Al-sa'ihun" are those who wander with their thoughts in the power of Allah and His dominion. This is a good view, and it is among the most excellent acts of worship. Among this is the saying of Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him: "Sit with us, let us believe for an hour." It is also narrated that one of the worshippers took the cup to perform ablution for the night prayer, and inserted his finger into the handle of the cup and began to reflect until dawn broke. He was asked about this, and he said: "I inserted my finger into the handle of the cup, and I remembered the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿When the shackles are on their necks and the chains﴾ [Ghafir: 71], and I reflected on how I would receive the shackle, and I remained in that all night."

﴿Those who bow and those who prostrate﴾ are those who perform the five prayers, as the people of knowledge said. However, there is no disagreement that one who increases voluntary prayers is more fitting for the name and more immersed in the attribute.

His saying: ﴿those who enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ is a command of obligation upon the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) collectively; then people differ concerning it in its specific application. As for the rulers and leaders, it is an obligation upon them in every state. As for the rest of the people, it is an obligation upon them subject to conditions, among them: that no harm befalls him, and that he knows his word will be heard and acted upon, and the like. Then whoever bears hardship for the sake of Allah beyond that is greater in reward. Al-Tabari narrated from some scholars that he said: Wherever Allah mentions the enjoining of good and forbidding of evil, it means enjoining Islam and forbidding disbelief.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no doubt that this includes that, and it is more fitting to include what is less than it, so generalising the wording is preferable. As for this "wa" (and) in His saying ﴿and those who forbid﴾, when no attribute has preceded it previously, it has been said: its meaning is linking these two attributes, namely enjoining good and forbidding evil, since they are not of the same kind as the earlier attributes.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Because the earlier attributes concern the person himself, while these two concern between him and others. Linking them was necessary due to their mutual necessity and their correspondence. It has been said that the "wa" is superfluous, but this is a weak view with no meaning. It has also been said that it is the "wa" of eight (wāw al-thamāniya), because this attribute came eighth in rank. From this is His saying the Exalted concerning the gates of Paradise: ﴿and its gates are opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], and His saying: ﴿and the eighth of them is their dog﴾ [al-Kahf: 22], and from this His saying: ﴿previously married and virgins﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5].

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Yet this is objected to, so that it does not follow that it is a "wa" of eight, for it separates two sections which together encompass all women, and it cannot be "previously married and virgins", so it is necessarily a separator. The "wa" of eight was mentioned by Ibn Khalawayh in his debate with Abu 'Ali al-Farisi concerning the meaning of His saying: ﴿and its gates are opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], and Abu 'Ali denied it. My father, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated to me from the grammarian teacher Abu 'Abd Allah al-Kafif al-Malik̲i, who was among those who settled in Granada and taught there during the period of Ibn Habus, that he said: "It is an eloquent dialect of some Arabs. Their custom, when they count, is to say: wahid, ithnan, thalatha, arba'a, khamsa, sitta, sab'a, wa-thamaniya, tis'a, 'ashara. Thus is their dialect, and whenever the matter of eight comes up in their speech, they insert the 'wa'."

His saying the Exalted: ﴿and those who observe the limits of Allah﴾ is a general term under which falls the binding of the Sharia and abstaining from what Allah has forbidden in every matter and every field. His saying: ﴿and give good tidings to the believers﴾: it has been said that it is a general term which the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to use to give good tidings to all his Ummah of goodness from Allah. It has also been said: rather, these words are specific to the one who has not fought; that is, since the promise and virtue of the fighters were mentioned earlier in the verse, he was commanded to give good tidings to the rest of the people who have not fought, that faith is a deliverance from the Fire. And all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿It is not for the Prophet﴾ (the verse) requires reproach and prohibition of seeking forgiveness for the polytheists while despairing of their faith, either by their dying upon disbelief, and from this is the saying of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il: "May Allah not reward him with good"; or by an explicit text from Allah the Exalted concerning a specific person, such as Abu Lahab and others, so seeking forgiveness for him while he is alive is forbidden.

The exegetes differed concerning the occasion of this verse. The majority said, and its basis is on Ibn al-Musayyab and 'Amr ibn Dinar: it was revealed concerning Abu Talib. That was because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon him when he was dying, admonished him, and said: "O uncle, say: there is no god but Allah, a word by which I may argue on your behalf before Allah the Exalted." Present there were Abu Jahl and 'Abd Allah ibn Umayya, and they said to him: "O Abu Talib, do you turn away from the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib?" Abu Talib said: "O Muhammad, by Allah, were it not that I fear my son would be reproached with it after me, I would have made you happy by it." Then he said: "I am upon the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib," and he died upon that, since the Prophet (ﷺ) did not hear from him what he had said to al-'Abbas. Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [al-Qasas: 56]. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Allah, I will seek forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden from you." So he kept seeking forgiveness for him until this verse was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ceased seeking forgiveness for Abu Talib. It is also narrated that when the believers saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) seeking forgiveness for Abu Talib, they began to seek forgiveness for their dead, so they were included in the reproach and prohibition. And the verse, according to this, abrogates the action of the Prophet (ﷺ), since his actions carry the weight of established Sharia.

Fudayl ibn 'Iyad and others said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Makkah, he came to the grave of his mother, stood by it until the sun heated upon it, and began to long to be permitted to seek forgiveness for her, but he was not permitted. He informed his companions that he had been permitted to visit her grave but was forbidden from seeking forgiveness for her. He was never seen weeping more than on that day, and the verse was revealed concerning that. Another group said: It was revealed only because of the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning the hypocrites: "By Allah, I will add to the seventy." Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, and others said: The verse was revealed because of a group of believers who said: "We will seek forgiveness for our dead, just as Ibrahim (ﷺ) sought forgiveness for his father," so the verse was revealed concerning that. In any case, the prohibition of seeking forgiveness for the polytheists carries an objection regarding the story of Ibrahim (ﷺ), upon our Prophet and upon him, and the revelation of the following verse removed that objection.

Seeking forgiveness for a living polytheist is permissible, since his Islam is hoped for. From this is the saying of Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him: "May Allah have mercy on a man who sought forgiveness for Abu Hurayra and his mother." It was said to him: "And for his father?" He said: "No, my father died a disbeliever." 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: The verse concerns the prohibition of praying over the polytheists, and seeking forgiveness here means prayer.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 112–113:

Allah the Exalted said:

﴿Those who repent, who worship, who praise, who travel (for the cause of Allah), who bow, who prostrate, who enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and who observe the limits set by Allah. And give good tidings to the believers.﴾ ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were close relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾

These attributes are among the attributes of the believers whom Allah said He purchased from them their selves. These attributes are in the nominative case because they came unattached (to the preceding words) at the beginning of a verse, meaning: "They are the repentant ones." The meaning of the verse, according to what the views of the scholars and the Sharia require, is that these are the attributes of the perfect among the believers, which Allah the Exalted mentioned so that the people of monotheism would race toward them until they reach the highest rank. The first verse stands on its own: every monotheist who fought in the path of Allah, so that the word of Allah may be supreme, falls under that pledge, even if he does not possess these attributes, or most of them, that are in this verse. One group said: "Rather, these attributes came in the form of a condition, and the two verses are linked, so only the believers who have these attributes and who give themselves in the path of Allah enter the pledge." Al-Tabari narrated, through al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, that a man asked him about the saying of Allah the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased﴾ [al-Tawba: 111], the verse, and the man said: "Shall I not charge against the polytheists and fight until I am killed?" Al-Dahhak said: "Woe to you, where is the condition: ﴿those who repent, who worship﴾, the verse?" This view is a constraint and a restriction, and Allah knows best. The first view is more correct. Martyrdom erases every sin except the wrongs done to people. It has been narrated that Allah the Exalted bears on behalf of the martyr the wrongs done to people and recompenses them on his behalf. May Allah conclude our lives with goodness.

Another group said: The nominative case of "al-tai'buna" (the repentant ones) is by way of the inchoative (mubtada'), and what follows it are attributes, except His saying "al-amirun" (those who enjoin), for it is the predicate of the inchoative, as if He had said: "They are those who enjoin." This is good, except that the meaning of the verse becomes separated from the meaning of the one before it, and that is unsound, so consider it carefully. In the codex of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, the reading is: "al-tai'bina, al-'abidina" to the end of it. For this there are two possibilities: first, that it is an attribute of the believers, following the wording; second, that it is in the accusative case by way of praise.

"Al-tai'buna" encompasses returning from evil to good, whether that was from disbelief or sin, and returning from one state to what is better than it, even if the first state was not evil but good. Thus was the repentance of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his seeking forgiveness seventy times a day. The penitent (al-tai'b) is one who abandons sin, resolves to persist in abandoning it, and regrets what has passed. Whoever repents from one sin is called penitent, even if he persists in another, unless it is of the same kind, in which case he is not a penitent. Repentance, and its repeated breaking and renewal, is better than persistence. Whoever repents, then breaks his repentance and dies in that breaking, his earlier sins remain upon him, because Allah knew that his repentance from them was broken. The matter may admit of other than this, and Allah knows best.

Al-Hasan said in explaining the verse: "Al-tai'buna" means: from polytheism.

"Al-'abidun" is a word that encompasses the performance of the worship of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, the adherence to His Sharia, the constancy in that, persevering in it, and continuing in it. The worshipper (al-'abid) is the one who does good, which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained in his saying: "That you worship Allah as though you see Him." With the least worship that a Muslim performs, the name "worshipper" falls upon him and he attains the lowest rank of it, and according to his increase in worship the attribute is attained.

"Al-hamidun" means: those who remember Allah with His beautiful attributes in every state, in times of ease and hardship, and their praise is because He is worthy of it. It is more general than gratitude, since gratitude is only for the blessings specific to the one who is grateful.

"Al-sa'ihun" means: those who fast. It is narrated from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "The travelling (siyaha) of this Ummah is fasting." Al-Tabari traced it, and it is narrated that it is from the words of the Prophet (ﷺ). In a hadith: "Indeed, Allah has angels who travel and walk through the horizons, conveying to me the prayers of my Ummah upon me." The hadith is also narrated as "sayyahin" with the letter sad (meaning those who shout), from "sihah" (outcry). Travelling in the earth (al-siyaha fi al-ard) is derived from "al-say'h", which is water flowing over the earth without a destination. Some people said, and it is in the book of al-Naqqash: "Al-sa'ihun" are those who wander with their thoughts in the power of Allah and His dominion. This is a good view, and it is among the most excellent acts of worship. Among this is the saying of Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him: "Sit with us, let us believe for an hour." It is also narrated that one of the worshippers took the cup to perform ablution for the night prayer, and inserted his finger into the handle of the cup and began to reflect until dawn broke. He was asked about this, and he said: "I inserted my finger into the handle of the cup, and I remembered the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿When the shackles are on their necks and the chains﴾ [Ghafir: 71], and I reflected on how I would receive the shackle, and I remained in that all night."

﴿Those who bow and those who prostrate﴾ are those who perform the five prayers, as the people of knowledge said. However, there is no disagreement that one who increases voluntary prayers is more fitting for the name and more immersed in the attribute.

His saying: ﴿those who enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ is a command of obligation upon the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) collectively; then people differ concerning it in its specific application. As for the rulers and leaders, it is an obligation upon them in every state. As for the rest of the people, it is an obligation upon them subject to conditions, among them: that no harm befalls him, and that he knows his word will be heard and acted upon, and the like. Then whoever bears hardship for the sake of Allah beyond that is greater in reward. Al-Tabari narrated from some scholars that he said: Wherever Allah mentions the enjoining of good and forbidding of evil, it means enjoining Islam and forbidding disbelief.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no doubt that this includes that, and it is more fitting to include what is less than it, so generalising the wording is preferable. As for this "wa" (and) in His saying ﴿and those who forbid﴾, when no attribute has preceded it previously, it has been said: its meaning is linking these two attributes, namely enjoining good and forbidding evil, since they are not of the same kind as the earlier attributes.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Because the earlier attributes concern the person himself, while these two concern between him and others. Linking them was necessary due to their mutual necessity and their correspondence. It has been said that the "wa" is superfluous, but this is a weak view with no meaning. It has also been said that it is the "wa" of eight (wāw al-thamāniya), because this attribute came eighth in rank. From this is His saying the Exalted concerning the gates of Paradise: ﴿and its gates are opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], and His saying: ﴿and the eighth of them is their dog﴾ [al-Kahf: 22], and from this His saying: ﴿previously married and virgins﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5].

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Yet this is objected to, so that it does not follow that it is a "wa" of eight, for it separates two sections which together encompass all women, and it cannot be "previously married and virgins", so it is necessarily a separator. The "wa" of eight was mentioned by Ibn Khalawayh in his debate with Abu 'Ali al-Farisi concerning the meaning of His saying: ﴿and its gates are opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], and Abu 'Ali denied it. My father, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated to me from the grammarian teacher Abu 'Abd Allah al-Kafif al-Malik̲i, who was among those who settled in Granada and taught there during the period of Ibn Habus, that he said: "It is an eloquent dialect of some Arabs. Their custom, when they count, is to say: wahid, ithnan, thalatha, arba'a, khamsa, sitta, sab'a, wa-thamaniya, tis'a, 'ashara. Thus is their dialect, and whenever the matter of eight comes up in their speech, they insert the 'wa'."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 114–116:

His Exalted and Majestic words:

﴿The plea for forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, he disassociated himself from him. Indeed, Abraham was compassionate and forbearing.﴾ ﴿And Allah would never misguide a people after He had guided them until He makes clear to them what they should avoid. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾ ﴿Indeed, to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He gives life and causes death. And you have not, other than Allah, any protector or helper.﴾

The meaning: There is no proof, O believers, in Abraham the Friend's (al-Khalil) plea for forgiveness for his father, for that did not happen (p-424) except because of a promise. Scholars differ on this. It is said: it was a promise from Abraham that he would seek forgiveness for his father, and this is His saying: ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord. Indeed, He has ever been gracious to me﴾ [Maryam: 47]. It is also said: it was a promise from his father to him that he would believe, so Abraham's hope in his faith grew strong, which led him to plead forgiveness for him until he was forbidden from it. Talha recited: "And Abraham did not seek forgiveness," and it is narrated from him: "And Abraham did not seek forgiveness." "Mawidah" is a form (mafʿilah) from the root "wa'd" (promise). As for his becoming clear that he was an enemy of Allah, it is said: by the death of Azar in disbelief; and it is said: it was that he was forbidden from it while he was still alive. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: all of that will be on the Day of Resurrection, for in a hadith it is related that Abraham, peace be upon him, will meet his father, recognise him, and remember his saying: "I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord." He will say to him: "Hold on to my loins, for I will not leave you today for anything." He will cling to him until they reach the Bridge (al-Sirat), then he will turn to him and find that he has been transformed into a filthy, striped hyena, and then he will disassociate himself from him.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Tying the matter of the plea for forgiveness to the Hereafter is weak.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was compassionate and forbearing﴾ is praise from Allah, the Exalted, for Abraham. "Awwah": Ibn Mas'ud said it means one who supplicates much. It is said: one who calls out with humility. It is said: one who is certain, as Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said. It is said: it means merciful, also said by Ibn Mas'ud. It is said: it means one who is repentant and turns back to Allah. It is said: one who glorifies (Allah). It is said: one who remembers Allah, Mighty and Majestic, much. It is said: one who recites the Qur'an (al-tallah li-l-Qur'an). It is said: one who, out of fear of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, constantly says "Awwah" and repeats it. It is narrated that "Abu Dharr heard a man repeatedly saying this during his circumambulation, so he complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'Leave him, for he is an awwah.'" Ta'awwuh is a lamentation of grief that increases until a person utters "awh" along with it. The author said: it is also said "awwah." From the first form is the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to Bilal regarding a sale or purchase which he disapproved of: "Awh, that is exactly usury." From the second form is the saying of the poet:

"Fa-awhin li-dhikraha idha ma dhakartuha / wa-min bu'di ardin baynana wa-sama'"

And from this meaning is the saying of al-Muthaqqab al-'Abdi:

"Idha ma qumtu arhaluha bi-laylin / ... ta'awwaha ahata al-rajuli al-hazeen"

It is also narrated as "ahhatan." From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Awwah for the chicks of Muhammad." Halim means: patient, forbearing, of great intellect; and hilm means intellect.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah would never misguide a people﴾ and the rest of the verse, its meaning is: reassurance for the believers. It is said: some of them feared for themselves because of seeking forgiveness for the polytheists without a command from Allah, Blessed and Exalted, so the verse was revealed as reassurance, i.e.: Allah would never—after He guided them to Islam and rescued them from the Fire—nullify that and misguide its people for having committed a sin which had not previously been prohibited to them. But when He has made clear to them what they should avoid of matters and what they should shun of things, then whoever commits (a sin) after the prohibition deserves punishment. It is also said: this verse was revealed because of a group of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who were absent when the qibla was changed and so prayed—before the news reached them—towards Bayt al-Maqdis, and others who drank wine after its prohibition before the news reached them, so they feared for themselves and spoke about it, and the verse was revealed. The first view is more correct and more fitting to the verse.

Al-Tabari held that His saying, glorified is He: ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ is an indication that, O believers, you must not be fearful of an enemy, however numerous, nor fear anyone, for the feared death and the beloved life are only in the hand of Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning he stated is sound in itself, but his statement that "the intended purpose of the verse is indeed this" is a far-fetched view. The apparent purpose of the verse is, rather, that since in the preceding verse He mentioned His blessing and favour upon His servants in that when He bestows guidance upon them, His grace is more abundant than that He would turn them away and misguide them before they commit disobedience or violate a command, He followed that with attributes that contain the glorification and magnification of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the stirring of souls to persist in thanking Him and acknowledging their servitude to Him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 114–116:

Indeed, Abraham was compassionate and forbearing.﴾ ﴿And Allah would never misguide a people after He had guided them until He makes clear to them what they should avoid. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾ ﴿Indeed, to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He gives life and causes death. Indeed, He has ever been gracious to me﴾ [Maryam: 47]. It is also said: it was a promise from his father to him that he would believe, so Abraham's hope in his faith grew strong, which led him to plead forgiveness for him until he was forbidden from it. Talha recited: "And Abraham did not seek forgiveness," and it is narrated from him: "And Abraham did not seek forgiveness." "Mawidah" is a form (mafʿilah) from the root "wa'd" (promise). As for his becoming clear that he was an enemy of Allah, it is said: by the death of Azar in disbelief; and it is said: it was that he was forbidden from it while he was still alive. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: all of that will be on the Day of Resurrection, for in a hadith it is related that Abraham, peace be upon him, will meet his father, recognise him, and remember his saying: "I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord." He will say to him: "Hold on to my loins, for I will not leave you today for anything." He will cling to him until they reach the Bridge (al-Sirat), then he will turn to him and find that he has been transformed into a filthy, striped hyena, and then he will disassociate himself from him.

Tying the matter of the plea for forgiveness to the Hereafter is weak.

It is said: one who calls out with humility. It is said: one who is certain, as Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said. It is said: it means merciful, also said by Ibn Mas'ud. It is said: it means one who is repentant and turns back to Allah. It is said: one who glorifies (Allah). It is said: one who remembers Allah, Mighty and Majestic, much. It is said: one who recites the Qur'an (al-tallah li-l-Qur'an). It is said: one who, out of fear of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, constantly says "Awwah" and repeats it. It is narrated that "Abu Dharr heard a man repeatedly saying this during his circumambulation, so he complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'Leave him, for he is an awwah.'" "Fa-awhin li-dhikraha idha ma dhakartuha / wa-min bu'di ardin baynana wa-sama'"

And from this meaning is the saying of al-Muthaqqab al-'Abdi:

"Idha ma qumtu arhaluha bi-laylin / ... ta'awwaha ahata al-rajuli al-hazeen"

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 117–119:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Certainly Allah turned in forgiveness toward the Prophet, the Emigrants and the Helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship, after the hearts of a party of them had nearly swerved. Then He turned toward them in forgiveness. Indeed, He is Kind and Merciful to them.﴾ ﴿And toward the three who were left behind, until the earth, for all its vastness, became constricted for them, and their souls became constricted for them, and they thought that there was no refuge from Allah except in Him. Then He turned toward them that they might repent. Indeed, Allah is the Accepter of repentance, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with the truthful.﴾

Repentance from Allah means His returning His servant from one state to a higher one. It is, for the most part, a return from the state of disobedience to the state of obedience, and it may be a return from a state of obedience to one more perfect than it. His repentance toward the Prophet (ﷺ) in this verse is of the latter kind, because He returned him from his condition before achieving the military campaign, its reward, and bearing its hardships, to his condition after all of that. As for His repentance toward the Emigrants and the Helpers, their state was liable to be a move from shortcoming to obedience and earnestness in the campaign and in supporting the religion. As for His repentance toward the party that had nearly swerved, it was a return from a state of being brought low to a state of forgiveness and good pleasure.

His saying "who followed him" means: they entered into his command and his mobilization, and they did not turn away from his person with their own selves. His saying, glorified is He, "in the hour of hardship" means: "at the time of hardship." He placed "hour" in the position of a period, a time and an age, although the usual meaning of "hour" in the language is a small portion of time, like a segment of the day. Do you not see his saying (ﷺ) concerning the going out on Friday: "in the first hour and in the second hour" (the hadith)? So it is figurative here. It is possible that by his saying "in the hour of hardship" he means the hour in which their resolve and their submission to bearing the hardship occurred, since the whole journey follows that hour, and by it and in it the reward with Allah is realized and the intention is bound. So whoever resolved on the campaign while in hardship, has followed in the hour of hardship. And if it happened that wealth came to them during the rest of their journey, that would not undermine their being followers in the hour of hardship. Hardship (al-'usra) means adversity, straitened circumstances and destitution. From it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if someone is in hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 280]. This is the "army of hardship" concerning which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever equips the army of hardship, for him is Paradise." So 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, equipped it with a thousand camels and a thousand dinars. It is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned the dinars over in his hand and said: "What harm can come to 'Uthman from what he does after this?" And a man from the Helpers also came with seven hundred wasqs of dates. Mujahid and Qatadah said: the hardship reached them in that campaign, which was the Campaign of Tabuk, to the extent that they divided a date between two men. Then a group would take one date and one of them would chew it and drink water over it, and then all of them would do the same with it. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: during part of it a severe thirst afflicted them, until they began slaughtering camels and drinking what was in their stomachs of water, and squeezing the dung, until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked for water for them. He raised his hands in supplication, and he did not lower them until a cloud poured down. They drank, stored water, and then departed. Then the cloud had not gone beyond the camp. At that point a man from the hypocrites said: "Is this anything but a passing cloud?" The campaign took place in the extreme of heat, and the people were numerous while the mounts were few, so hardship came to them from every direction. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reached the first parts of the enemy's land, and the people of Adhruh and Aylah, and others, made peace with him on the basis of the jizya (poll tax) and the like, and he turned back.

As for the swerving that the hearts of a party of them nearly fell into, it was said: a group intended to withdraw when they met with the hardship and difficulty. This was said by al-Hasan. It was also said: their swerving was only due to suspicions that befell them concerning the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) resolve on that campaign, because of what they saw of the severity of the hardship, the scarcity of provisions, the length of the difficulty, and the strength of the enemy targeted.

Jumhur al-Sab'a (the majority of the seven reciters), and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, read "tazigh" with a "ta" above (feminine), agreeing with the word "hearts." It is related from Abu 'Amr that he used to perform idgham (assimilation, merging one letter into another) of the "dal" into the "ta." Hamzah, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, al-A'mash, and al-Jahdari read "yazigh" with a "ya," in accordance with the meaning of the plural "hearts." Ibn Mas'ud read: "min ba'di ma zaghat qulubu fariqin" (after the hearts of a party had swerved). Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: "min ba'di ma kadat tazigh" (after it had nearly swerved).

As for "kada" (nearly), three things may be considered as its subject. The first and strongest is the "story" or the "matter" (al-qissa wa'l-sha'n, the dummy subject), which is the view of Sibawayh. On this view, "hearts" is governed by "tazigh." The second is that the subject is what the mention of the Emigrants and Helpers at the beginning requires, and it is taken as "the people," so it is as though he said: "after the people had nearly swerved, the hearts of a party of them." The third is that the subject is "the hearts," and the pronoun in "tazigh" refers to "the hearts." This is permissible by analogy with "kana" in His saying: ﴿And it was an obligation upon Us to help the believers﴾ [al-Rum: 47]. Also, this fronting of the predicate is intended to mean postponement. "Kada" was likened to "kana" because its predicate is obligatory for it. Abu 'Ali said: this is not permissible with "'asa" (perhaps).

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed that He also turned in forgiveness toward this party and returned to them, and He was pleased to inform the community that He is Kind and Merciful.

The three are: Ka'b ibn Malik, Hilal ibn Umayyah al-Waqifi, and Murarah ibn al-Rabi' al-'Amiri. It is said: Ibn Rabi'ah, and it is said: Ibn Ribi'i. Their account has been transmitted in full by al-Bukhari and Muslim, and it is in the biographical literature (al-siyar), so we have abridged its telling. They are the ones concerning whom it was said earlier: ﴿and others are deferred﴾ [al-Tawbah: 106]. The meaning of "khullifu" (were left behind) is: they were held back, their matter was left pending, their excuse was not accepted, and it was not returned to them. It is as though they were left behind from those who made excuses. It was said: the meaning of ﴿khullifu﴾ is that they were left behind from the Campaign of Tabuk. This was said by Qatadah, but it is weak, and Ka'b ibn Malik himself rejected it and said: the meaning of "khullifu" is that they were left aside from accepting the excuse, and it is not about our staying behind from the campaign. What strengthens this is that he made ﴿until when the earth became constricted﴾ a limit for the staying behind, and that was not because of their being left behind from the campaign, but rather the earth became constricted for them because of their being left aside from accepting the excuse.

Jumhur read "khullifu" with a damma on the "kha" and a shaddah on the "lam" (kasra). 'Ikrimah ibn Harun al-Makhzumi, Zirr ibn Hubaysh, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, and also Abu 'Amr read "khalafu" with a fatha on the "kha" and the "lam" not doubled. Abu Malik read "khalifu" with a damma on the "kha" and a light "lam" with a kasra. Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, Ja'far ibn Muhammad, and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read "khalafu" (with the letter "kha" and "alif", as "khalafu"), and the meaning is close to the previous reading. Abu Ja'far said: if they had been left behind, they would have had no sin. Al-A'mash read: "wa 'ala al-thalathati al-mukhallafina" (the left-behind ones).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿for all its vastness﴾ means: with its breadth, as though He said: "despite what it is in itself, being wide." So "ma" is a verbal (masdariyya) particle. ﴿And their souls became constricted for them﴾ is a metaphor (isti'ara), because worry and grief filled them. ﴿And they thought﴾ in this verse means: they became certain, and knowledge came to them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then He turned toward them that they might repent﴾. Since this statement was in the enumeration of His blessings, its ordering appeared with reference to the direction that is from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so that this would alert to receiving the blessing from Him, there being no lord other than Him. Had the statement been an enumeration of a sin, the beginning would have been with the direction that is from the sinner, as Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿So when they swerved, Allah caused their hearts to swerve﴾ [al-Saff: 5], so that this would be a stronger confirmation of the sin against them. This is among the eloquence of the Qur'an, the wondrous arrangement of its composition, and its inimitable coherence. The explanation of this verse and the placement of its words (maqa'i al-alfaz) is only complete along with reading the account of the three who were left behind in the books we mentioned. Their sin was great, and they deserved that because the Law requires them to be earnest in it according to their ranks and their precedence in it, since they were an example and a proof for the hypocrites and the detractors, as Ka'b was from the people of 'Aqabah, and his two companions were from the people of Badr. In this is an indication that the learned man and the one who is followed has less excuse for falling short than others. Al-Awza'i, may Allah have mercy on him, wrote to al-Mansur Abu Ja'far in the closing part of a letter: "Know that your kinship with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) will only increase the right of Allah upon you in greatness, and His obedience only in obligation, and people will only increase their denunciation of you in what opposes that. Peace." And al-Qadi al-Tanukhi spoke well in his saying:

"And blame attaches to the great, as the great is (blamed)."

In some transmissions of the hadith of the three, it is said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was, on the night their repentance was revealed, in the house of Umm Salamah, and she was righteous with them. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to her: 'O Umm Salamah, repentance has been accepted for Ka'b ibn Malik and his two companions.' She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall I not send to them?' He said: 'If you do, the people will trample you all night long and keep you from sleep.'"

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with the truthful﴾. This command to be with the people of truthfulness is fine after the story of the three, when truthfulness benefited them and carried them away from the stations of the hypocrites. So this command came as an interjection in the midst of the speech, since in the narrative there arose something whose compliance must be alerted to. Ibn Jurayj and others said: truthfulness in this verse is truthfulness of speech. Nafi' and al-Dahhak said something to the effect that the wording is more general than truthfulness of speech, and it has the meaning of soundness in religion and firmness in goodness, as the Arabs say: "a true return (ʿawd sidq) and a true man (rajul sidq)." This group said: be with Muhammad (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, 'Umar, and the best of the Emigrants who were truthful to Allah in Islam. The "ma'a" (with) in this verse requires companionship in the state and sharing in the attribute that calls for praise. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas read: "wa kunu min al-sadiqin" (and be among the truthful). It is also reported from the Prophet (ﷺ), and Ibn Mas'ud used to interpret it as truthfulness of speech. It is related from him that he said: "Lying is not fit for anyone, neither in earnest nor in jest. Recite, if you wish: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with the truthful﴾."

In this is an indication that the learned man and the one who is followed has less excuse for falling short than others. Al-Awza'i, may Allah have mercy on him, wrote to al-Mansur Abu Ja'far in the closing part of a letter: "Know that your kinship with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) will only increase the right of Allah upon you in greatness, and His obedience only in obligation, and people will only increase their denunciation of you in what opposes that. Peace." And al-Qadi al-Tanukhi spoke well in his saying:

"And blame attaches to the great, as the great is (blamed)."

In some transmissions of the hadith of the three, it is said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was, on the night their repentance was revealed, in the house of Umm Salamah, and she was righteous with them. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to her: 'O Umm Salamah, repentance has been accepted for Ka'b ibn Malik and his two companions.' She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall I not send to them?' He said: 'If you do, the people will trample you all night long and keep you from sleep.'"

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with the truthful﴾. This command to be with the people of truthfulness is fine after the story of the three, when truthfulness benefited them and carried them away from the stations of the hypocrites. So this command came as an interjection in the midst of the speech, since in the narrative there arose something whose compliance must be alerted to. Ibn Jurayj and others said: truthfulness in this verse is truthfulness of speech. Nafi' and al-Dahhak said something to the effect that the wording is more general than truthfulness of speech, and it has the meaning of soundness in religion and firmness in goodness, as the Arabs say: "a true return (ʿawd sidq) and a true man (rajul sidq)." This group said: be with Muhammad (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, 'Umar, and the best of the Emigrants who were truthful to Allah in Islam. The "ma'a" (with) in this verse requires companionship in the state and sharing in the attribute that calls for praise. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas read: "wa kunu min al-sadiqin" (and be among the truthful). It is also reported from the Prophet (ﷺ), and Ibn Mas'ud used to interpret it as truthfulness of speech. It is related from him that he said: "Lying is not fit for anyone, neither in earnest nor in jest. Recite, if you wish: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with the truthful﴾."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 117–119:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Certainly Allah turned in forgiveness toward the Prophet, the Emigrants and the Helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship, after the hearts of a party of them had nearly swerved. Then He turned toward them in forgiveness. Indeed, He is Kind and Merciful to them.﴾ ﴿And toward the three who were left behind, until the earth, for all its vastness, became constricted for them, and their souls became constricted for them, and they thought that there was no refuge from Allah except in Him. Then He turned toward them that they might repent. Indeed, Allah is the Accepter of repentance, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with the truthful.﴾

Repentance from Allah means His returning His servant from one state to a higher one. It is, for the most part, a return from the state of disobedience to the state of obedience, and it may be a return from a state of obedience to one more perfect than it. His repentance toward the Prophet (ﷺ) in this verse is of the latter kind, because He returned him from his condition before achieving the military campaign, its reward, and bearing its hardships, to his condition after all of that. As for His repentance toward the Emigrants and the Helpers, their state was liable to be a move from shortcoming to obedience and earnestness in the campaign and in supporting the religion. As for His repentance toward the party that had nearly swerved, it was a return from a state of being brought low to a state of forgiveness and good pleasure.

His saying "who followed him" means: they entered into his command and his mobilization, and they did not turn away from his person with their own selves. His saying, glorified is He, "in the hour of hardship" means: "at the time of hardship." He placed "hour" in the position of a period, a time and an age, although the usual meaning of "hour" in the language is a small portion of time, like a segment of the day. Do you not see his saying (ﷺ) concerning the going out on Friday: "in the first hour and in the second hour" (the hadith)? So it is figurative here. It is possible that by his saying "in the hour of hardship" he means the hour in which their resolve and their submission to bearing the hardship occurred, since the whole journey follows that hour, and by it and in it the reward with Allah is realized and the intention is bound. So whoever resolved on the campaign while in hardship, has followed in the hour of hardship. And if it happened that wealth came to them during the rest of their journey, that would not undermine their being followers in the hour of hardship. Hardship (al-'usra) means adversity, straitened circumstances and destitution. From it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if someone is in hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 280]. This is the "army of hardship" concerning which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever equips the army of hardship, for him is Paradise." So 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, equipped it with a thousand camels and a thousand dinars. It is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned the dinars over in his hand and said: "What harm can come to 'Uthman from what he does after this?" And a man from the Helpers also came with seven hundred wasqs of dates. Mujahid and Qatadah said: the hardship reached them in that campaign, which was the Campaign of Tabuk, to the extent that they divided a date between two men. Then a group would take one date and one of them would chew it and drink water over it, and then all of them would do the same with it. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: during part of it a severe thirst afflicted them, until they began slaughtering camels and drinking what was in their stomachs of water, and squeezing the dung, until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked for water for them. He raised his hands in supplication, and he did not lower them until a cloud poured down. They drank, stored water, and then departed. Then the cloud had not gone beyond the camp. At that point a man from the hypocrites said: "Is this anything but a passing cloud?" The campaign took place in the extreme of heat, and the people were numerous while the mounts were few, so hardship came to them from every direction. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reached the first parts of the enemy's land, and the people of Adhruh and Aylah, and others, made peace with him on the basis of the jizya (poll tax) and the like, and he turned back.

As for the swerving that the hearts of a party of them nearly fell into, it was said: a group intended to withdraw when they met with the hardship and difficulty. This was said by al-Hasan. It was also said: their swerving was only due to suspicions that befell them concerning the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) resolve on that campaign, because of what they saw of the severity of the hardship, the scarcity of provisions, the length of the difficulty, and the strength of the enemy targeted.

Jumhur al-Sab'a (the majority of the seven reciters), and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, read "tazigh" with a "ta" above (feminine), agreeing with the word "hearts." It is related from Abu 'Amr that he used to perform idgham (assimilation, merging one letter into another) of the "dal" into the "ta." Hamzah, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, al-A'mash, and al-Jahdari read "yazigh" with a "ya," in accordance with the meaning of the plural "hearts." Ibn Mas'ud read: "min ba'di ma zaghat qulubu fariqin" (after the hearts of a party had swerved). Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: "min ba'di ma kadat tazigh" (after it had nearly swerved).

As for "kada" (nearly), three things may be considered as its subject. The first and strongest is the "story" or the "matter" (al-qissa wa'l-sha'n, the dummy subject), which is the view of Sibawayh. On this view, "hearts" is governed by "tazigh." The second is that the subject is what the mention of the Emigrants and Helpers at the beginning requires, and it is taken as "the people," so it is as though he said: "after the people had nearly swerved, the hearts of a party of them." The third is that the subject is "the hearts," and the pronoun in "tazigh" refers to "the hearts." This is permissible by analogy with "kana" in His saying: ﴿And it was an obligation upon Us to help the believers﴾ [al-Rum: 47]. Also, this fronting of the predicate is intended to mean postponement. "Kada" was likened to "kana" because its predicate is obligatory for it. Abu 'Ali said: this is not permissible with "'asa" (perhaps).

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed that He also turned in forgiveness toward this party and returned to them, and He was pleased to inform the community that He is Kind and Merciful.

The three are: Ka'b ibn Malik, Hilal ibn Umayyah al-Waqifi, and Murarah ibn al-Rabi' al-'Amiri. It is said: Ibn Rabi'ah, and it is said: Ibn Ribi'i. Their account has been transmitted in full by al-Bukhari and Muslim, and it is in the biographical literature (al-siyar), so we have abridged its telling. They are the ones concerning whom it was said earlier: ﴿and others are deferred﴾ [al-Tawbah: 106]. The meaning of "khullifu" (were left behind) is: they were held back, their matter was left pending, their excuse was not accepted, and it was not returned to them. It is as though they were left behind from those who made excuses. It was said: the meaning of ﴿khullifu﴾ is that they were left behind from the Campaign of Tabuk. This was said by Qatadah, but it is weak, and Ka'b ibn Malik himself rejected it and said: the meaning of "khullifu" is that they were left aside from accepting the excuse, and it is not about our staying behind from the campaign. What strengthens this is that he made ﴿until when the earth became constricted﴾ a limit for the staying behind, and that was not because of their being left behind from the campaign, but rather the earth became constricted for them because of their being left aside from accepting the excuse.

Jumhur read "khullifu" with a damma on the "kha" and a shaddah on the "lam" (kasra). 'Ikrimah ibn Harun al-Makhzumi, Zirr ibn Hubaysh, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, and also Abu 'Amr read "khalafu" with a fatha on the "kha" and the "lam" not doubled. Abu Malik read "khalifu" with a damma on the "kha" and a light "lam" with a kasra. Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, Ja'far ibn Muhammad, and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read "khalafu" (with the letter "kha" and "alif", as "khalafu"), and the meaning is close to the previous reading. Abu Ja'far said: if they had been left behind, they would have had no sin. Al-A'mash read: "wa 'ala al-thalathati al-mukhallafina" (the left-behind ones).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿for all its vastness﴾ means: with its breadth, as though He said: "despite what it is in itself, being wide." So "ma" is a verbal (masdariyya) particle. ﴿And their souls became constricted for them﴾ is a metaphor (isti'ara), because worry and grief filled them. ﴿And they thought﴾ in this verse means: they became certain, and knowledge came to them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then He turned toward them that they might repent﴾. Since this statement was in the enumeration of His blessings, its ordering appeared with reference to the direction that is from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so that this would alert to receiving the blessing from Him, there being no lord other than Him. Had the statement been an enumeration of a sin, the beginning would have been with the direction that is from the sinner, as Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿So when they swerved, Allah caused their hearts to swerve﴾ [al-Saff: 5], so that this would be a stronger confirmation of the sin against them. This is among the eloquence of the Qur'an, the wondrous arrangement of its composition, and its inimitable coherence. The explanation of this verse and the placement of its words (maqa'i al-alfaz) is only complete along with reading the account of the three who were left behind in the books we mentioned. Their sin was great, and they deserved that because the Law requires them to be earnest in it according to their ranks and their precedence in it, since they were an example and a proof for the hypocrites and the detractors, as Ka'b was from the people of 'Aqabah, and his two companions were from the people of Badr. In this is an indication that the learned man and the one who is followed has less excuse for falling short than others. Al-Awza'i, may Allah have mercy on him, wrote to al-Mansur Abu Ja'far in the closing part of a letter: "Know that your kinship with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) will only increase the right of Allah upon you in greatness, and His obedience only in obligation, and people will only increase their denunciation of you in what opposes that. Peace." And al-Qadi al-Tanukhi spoke well in his saying:

"And blame attaches to the great, as the great is (blamed)."

In some transmissions of the hadith of the three, it is said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was, on the night their repentance was revealed, in the house of Umm Salamah, and she was righteous with them. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to her: 'O Umm Salamah, repentance has been accepted for Ka'b ibn Malik and his two companions.' She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall I not send to them?' He said: 'If you do, the people will trample you all night long and keep you from sleep.'"

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with the truthful﴾. This command to be with the people of truthfulness is fine after the story of the three, when truthfulness benefited them and carried them away from the stations of the hypocrites. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 120–121:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿It was not for the people of Medina, nor for those of the Bedouins around them, to remain behind from the Messenger of Allah, or to prefer their own selves over his self. That is because they are not afflicted by thirst, nor fatigue, nor hunger in the way of Allah, nor do they tread any path that enrages the disbelievers, nor do they gain anything from an enemy, but that a righteous deed is written for them thereby. Indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Nor do they spend any expenditure, small or large, nor do they cross a valley, but it is written for them, that Allah may reward them with the best of what they used to do.﴾

This is a rebuke to the believers among the people of Yathrib and the tribes of the Arabs neighbouring it for staying behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his campaign. The force of the speech implies a command to accompany him when he sets out as a warrior and to give up their souls in his cause. The commentators differed. Qatadah said: this obligation was specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the duty to go forth to battle when he himself went out was binding; this ruling did not remain for anyone else among the caliphs. Zayd ibn Aslam said: this command and obligation applied when Islam was small and there was a need for the joining of hands; then it was abrogated when Islam became strong, by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this concerns setting out to fight an enemy in order to bring them into Islam. As for when the enemy attacks a region, then it becomes obligatory upon every individual to repel and confront it.

As for His saying, ﴿nor to prefer their own selves﴾, its meaning is that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) should not bear hardship for the sake of Allah and give up his self in the way of Allah, while they hold back, being miserly with their own selves, and refrain from what he has entered into. Then He, Exalted is He, mentioned why it was not permissible for them to remain behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by His saying: ﴿That is because they...﴾, to the end of the verse. Al-Nasab means fatigue. From it is the saying of al-Nabigha:

"Leave me, O Umayma, to a sorrow that wearies..." ...........................

meaning: one possessed of nasab (fatigue). From it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed we have met with fatigue from this journey of ours﴾ [al-Kahf: 62].

Al-Makhmasa is a maf'ala from khamasa al-batn, which means its emptiness (its shrinking), and this is borrowed for the state of hunger, since emptiness of the belly is inseparable from it. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"You spend the winter with your bellies full, while your neighbouring women spend the night hungry, lean in their bellies."

From it also: "akhmas al-qadam" (the arch of the foot), and khumsana (a slender woman).

As for His saying, ﴿nor do they tread any path﴾, that is: nor do they reach any point of the earth that is harmful to the disbelievers, and that is what enrages them. From it, in the Mudawwana, is the saying: "We would not perform ablution because of a treading (mawti')," from the statement of Ibn Mas'ud. And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿nor do they gain anything from an enemy﴾ is a general expression covering both the little and the much that the believers do to the disbelievers, such as taking wealth or inflicting humiliation. Al-Nayl is the verbal noun of nala yanal; it is not from the expression niltu anwiluhu nawlan wa nawalan. It has been said that it derives from that, with the waw changed to ya' for lightness here, but this is weak, and al-Tabari mentioned something similar and weakened it, saying: that is not the known usage of the Arabs.

As for His saying, ﴿nor do they spend﴾, the verse, He placed "small" first for emphasis, meaning: if the small is written, then the large is more deserving. Al-Wadi is what lies between two mountains, whether or not it has water in it, and its plural is awdiya. In the speech of the Arabs there is no pattern fa'il with af'ila except in this word alone. And in the hadith: "No people increase in distance from Allah by being distant from their families in the way of Allah except that they increase in nearness to Allah."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 122–123:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿It was not for the believers to go forth all together. Why should not a group from every section of them go forth, that they may gain understanding in the religion and warn their people when they return to them, so that they may beware?﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, fight those adjacent to you of the disbelievers, and let them find in you harshness. And know that Allah is with the righteous.﴾

One group said: the cause of this verse was that the believers who were dwellers of the desert, and who were sent to teach the Sharia, when they heard the saying of Allah, the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿It was not for the people of Medina and those around them of the bedouins﴾ [al-Tawba: 120], were concerned by it, so they went forth to Medina, to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, fearing that they might be sinful for staying behind from the expedition. So this verse was revealed concerning their going forth.

Another group said: when the verses concerning those who stayed behind were revealed, the hypocrites said, "The people of the desert have perished." So this verse was revealed establishing the excuse of the people of the desert.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So the saying of the Exalted, ﴿It was not for the people of Medina and those around them﴾ [al-Tawba: 120], comes general in wording, while what is meant in meaning is the majority and most of them. This verse comes explaining that, consistent in its wording and connected in meaning, from His saying, blessed and exalted, ﴿It was not for the people of Medina﴾ [al-Tawba: 120] to His saying, exalted, ﴿that they may beware﴾. At the end of the verse it clarifies the generality that is at its beginning, since it is liable to be interpreted as meaning that no human being should stay behind. The gaining of understanding (tafaqquh) is from those who go forth, and the warning (indhar) is from them too, and the pronoun in "rajaʿu" (they returned) refers to them as well. Another group said: this verse is not about the expedition; its cause is that some tribes of the Arabs, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ invoked against Mudar with years of drought, were struck by famine and hardship, so they went forth to Medina seeking sustenance (ma'ash), and they nearly corrupted it. Most of them were not sound in faith; hunger had only humbled them. So the verse was revealed concerning that, and He said: "It was not of the attributes of one who has faith to go forth in such a mass departure," meaning: these are not the believers.

Ibn 'Abbas said, in substance: this verse is specific to the dispatched detachments (bu'uth) and expeditions (saraya), while the preceding verse remains in force regarding the Messenger of Allah ﷺ going out on campaign, and this verse remains in force regarding his staying behind. That is, when he stays behind, it is required that the people not all go forth so that he is left alone; rather it is appropriate that one group go forth and another remain, so that those who remain may gain understanding in the religion and warn those who went forth when they return to them. Another group said: this verse abrogates everything that enjoined on all the obligation to go forth and fight. The pronoun in His saying, ﴿that they may gain understanding﴾, according to this interpretation, refers also to the group that stayed behind with the Prophet ﷺ. The first view in our arrangement refers it to the group that went forth; and in accordance with this arrangement, its reference is ordered in some views upon this, and in some upon that.

The majority hold that gaining understanding is only through witnessing the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and companionship with him. Another group said: it is likely that the gaining of understanding occurs in the expedition, in the detachments, through what they see of Allah's support of His religion and His manifesting of a small number of believers over a large number of disbelievers, and their knowledge through that of the soundness of the religion of Islam and its station with Allah, the Exalted. al-Tabari preferred and strengthened this view, and the other is also strong. The pronoun in His saying, glorified is He, ( liyundhirû ) refers to those who gain understanding, according to the difference of opinion; and warning is general to disbelief and sins, and beware of them likewise.

As for the saying of the Exalted, ﴿O you who have believed, fight those adjacent to you of the disbelievers﴾, the verse. It was said: this verse was revealed before the command to fight all the disbelievers, so it belongs to the gradual stages that existed at the beginning of Islam.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This view is weakened by the fact that this verse is among the last of what was revealed. Another group said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would sometimes pass by a people of the disbelievers while raiding another people further away than them, so Allah, the Exalted, commanded the fighting of the nearer, then the nearer, relative to Medina. Another group said: the verse clarifies the form of fighting as a whole, and it is connected to the command to fight all the disbelievers. Its meaning is that Allah, the Exalted, commanded in it the believers that each section of them should fight the kind of disbelievers adjoining it. This is the fighting for the word of Allah and the returning of people to Islam. As for when the enemy inclines towards a region of the lands of the Muslims, it is an obligation upon those Muslims connected with it to suffice against the enemy of that region, even if the abode is far and the lands distant. The proponents of this view said: the verse was revealed indicating the fighting of the Romans in al-Sham, because they were at that time the enemy that is near and close, since the Arabs had been overspread by Islam while Iraq was far away. Then, when the scope of Islam widened, the obligation turned to fighting the Persians, the Daylam and other nations. He means in that time. This was also said by 'Ali ibn al-Husayn. Some of the Companions have said: "You fight people only by your deeds." Its people are those who strive earnestly on the paths of truth, so Allah, the Exalted, promised that He is with the people of piety, and whomever Allah is with will never be defeated.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 122–123:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿It was not for the believers to go forth all together. Why should not a group from every section of them go forth, that they may gain understanding in the religion and warn their people when they return to them, so that they may beware?﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, fight those adjacent to you of the disbelievers, and let them find in you harshness. And know that Allah is with the righteous.﴾

One group said: the cause of this verse was that the believers who were dwellers of the desert, and who were sent to teach the Sharia, when they heard the saying of Allah, the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿It was not for the people of Medina and those around them of the bedouins﴾ [al-Tawba: 120], were concerned by it, so they went forth to Medina, to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, fearing that they might be sinful for staying behind from the expedition. So this verse was revealed concerning their going forth.

Another group said: when the verses concerning those who stayed behind were revealed, the hypocrites said, "The people of the desert have perished." So this verse was revealed establishing the excuse of the people of the desert.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So the saying of the Exalted, ﴿It was not for the people of Medina and those around them﴾ [al-Tawba: 120], comes general in wording, while what is meant in meaning is the majority and most of them. This verse comes explaining that, consistent in its wording and connected in meaning, from His saying, blessed and exalted, ﴿It was not for the people of Medina﴾ [al-Tawba: 120] to His saying, exalted, ﴿that they may beware﴾. At the end of the verse it clarifies the generality that is at its beginning, since it is liable to be interpreted as meaning that no human being should stay behind. The gaining of understanding (tafaqquh) is from those who go forth, and the warning (indhar) is from them too, and the pronoun in "rajaʿu" (they returned) refers to them as well. Another group said: this verse is not about the expedition; its cause is that some tribes of the Arabs, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ invoked against Mudar with years of drought, were struck by famine and hardship, so they went forth to Medina seeking sustenance (ma'ash), and they nearly corrupted it. Most of them were not sound in faith; hunger had only humbled them. So the verse was revealed concerning that, and He said: "It was not of the attributes of one who has faith to go forth in such a mass departure," meaning: these are not the believers.

That is, when he stays behind, it is required that the people not all go forth so that he is left alone; rather it is appropriate that one group go forth and another remain, so that those who remain may gain understanding in the religion and warn those who went forth when they return to them. Another group said: this verse abrogates everything that enjoined on all the obligation to go forth and fight. The pronoun in His saying, ﴿that they may gain understanding﴾, according to this interpretation, refers also to the group that stayed behind with the Prophet ﷺ. The first view in our arrangement refers it to the group that went forth; and in accordance with this arrangement, its reference is ordered in some views upon this, and in some upon that.

The majority hold that gaining understanding is only through witnessing the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and companionship with him. Another group said: it is likely that the gaining of understanding occurs in the expedition, in the detachments, through what they see of Allah's support of His religion and His manifesting of a small number of believers over a large number of disbelievers, and their knowledge through that of the soundness of the religion of Islam and its station with Allah, the Exalted. al-Tabari preferred and strengthened this view, and the other is also strong. The pronoun in His saying, glorified is He, ( liyundhirû ) refers to those who gain understanding, according to the difference of opinion; and warning is general to disbelief and sins, and beware of them likewise.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This view is weakened by the fact that this verse is among the last of what was revealed.
