Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verse 124–126:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He:

﴿And when a surah is revealed, some of them say, "Which of you has had its faith increased by this?" As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice.﴾ ﴿But as for those in whose hearts is a disease, it has added to their filth the filth [of their own], and they died while they were disbelievers.﴾ ﴿Do they not see that they are tested once or twice every year? Yet they do not repent, nor do they take heed.﴾

This verse was revealed concerning the hypocrites. The pronoun in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿some of them﴾, refers back to the hypocrites. His saying, blessed and exalted is He, ﴿Which of you has had its faith increased by this?﴾ may be understood as referring to hypocrites like them, and it may be understood as referring to a group of their relatives among the believers who lean towards them, trust in their concealing [of their hypocrisy], and hope to return them to hypocrisy. The meaning of ﴿Which of you has had its faith increased by this?﴾ is belittling and disparagement of the status of the surah, as you would say, "What strangeness is there in this? Or what proof is there?"

Then, exalted and majestic is He, began the refutation of them and the ruling that demolishes their confusion. He informed that the believers have had their faith increased, and that they rejoice, from its words and meanings, in the mercy of Allah and His good pleasure. The increase in faith is a point of much confusion and prolixity among people, and the summary of the matter is that faith, which is the very assent (taṣdīq), does not in itself accept increase and decrease; rather, the increase occurs in the one who assents to it. So when a surah from Allah, blessed and exalted is He, is revealed, there occurs for the believers through it a specific assent that did not exist before. Thus their assent to what the surah contains of reports, commands and prohibitions is an additional matter beyond what they had before. This is one aspect of the increase of faith. Another aspect is that the surah may contain a proof or an alert to it, so the believer has known Allah through several proofs, and when the surah is revealed it adds to his proofs. This too is another aspect of increase, and all of these lie outside the very assent when it is complete, for then no place for increase remains in it. Another aspect of increase is that a man may have a slight doubt or a disturbing misgiving come to him, and when the surah is revealed that misgiving is removed and he is relieved of it. This too is an increase in faith, since his belief rises from the level of contesting that misgiving to being free of it. As for the view of those who call acts of obedience faith—and that is metaphorical according to the People of the Sunnah—the increase is brought about by the surah, since it contains commands, prohibitions and rulings. This is the ruling for one who seeks knowledge, regarding the meaning of the increase and decrease of faith until the Day of Resurrection, for a person's learning of knowledge is in the position of the revelation of a surah of the Qur'an.

And ﴿those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ are the hypocrites, and this is a figure of speech: the one whose belief is sound and whose breast is expanded with faith is likened to the healthy, and the one whose belief is corrupt is likened to the sick. So there is an eloquent metaphor in the expression, for health and sickness are properly qualities of the organs, and in beliefs they are metaphorical. The word "filth" (rijs) in this verse is an expression for their state which combines the meanings of rijs in the language, for rijs in the language comes with the meaning of uncleanliness and also with the meaning of punishment. The state of these hypocrites is uncleanliness, and it is a hastened punishment that entails a deferred one. The increase of filth to their filth is their wandering in disbelief and their floundering in misguidance; Allah punishes them for disbelief and aversion by sealing their hearts and sealing them into the Fire. And since they disbelieved in a surah, their disbelief increased, and that is the increase of filth to their filth.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do they not see that they are tested...﴾ the verse. The majority read "Do they not see" with the yā’ (ya-), meaning: "Do the hypocrites not see?" Ḥamzah read "Do you not see" with the tā’ (ta-), meaning: "Do you not see, O believers?"—so this is an admonition to the believers. Ibn Mas'ūd, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and al-A'mash read "Do you not see" (tará), meaning: "Do you not see, O Muhammad?" It is also related from al-A'mash: "Do you not see?" (plural). Abu Ḥātim mentioned from him: "Have they not seen?" Mujāhid said: "they are tested" (yuftanūn) means: they are tested by drought and hunger. Al-Naqqāsh related from him that he said: "a sickness or two sicknesses." al-Ḥasan ibn Abi al-Ḥasan and Qatādah said: its meaning is: they are tested by the command to jihad. What appears from what precedes the verse and from what follows it is that the trial and testing are only by Allah, exalted is He, disclosing their secrets and exposing their beliefs. This is the testing upon which the proof is established, by their seeing it and their not repenting. As for jihad or hunger, what we have mentioned is not anticipated along with them. So the meaning of the verse on this basis is: Will these people not be restrained, whose inner secrets are exposed once or twice every year, each one according to his state, and who know that this is from Allah, so that they repent and remember the promise and threat of Allah? As for the testing by sickness, it concerns the believers. al-Ḥasan used to recite:

"Every year a sickness, then a convalescence—
How long, how long, and until when?"

A group said: the meaning is: they are tested by what the polytheists spread against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of lies, so those in whose hearts is a disease are tested in that. Al-Ṭabarī related this view from Ḥudhayfah, and it is a strange meaning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 9, verses 127–129:

The pronoun in the words of the Exalted, ﴿بَعْضُهم﴾ (some of them), refers to the hypocrites. The meaning is: "And whenever a surah is revealed in which their secrets are exposed, some of them look at others with a glance that signals a question, [a glance] from which one understands the question: 'Is there anyone with you who conveys what you say? Does anyone see you while you are plotting your affairs?'" The saying of the Exalted, ﴿ثُمَّ انْصَرَفُوا﴾ (then they turned away), means: away from the path of guidance. This is because, when the disclosure of their secrets and the announcement of the hidden matters of their affairs is made clear to them, they inevitably experience astonishment, hesitation and reflection. Had they been guided, that moment would have been the occasion for this. But since they insist on disbelief and become entangled in it, it is as if they had turned away from that state, which was the occasion for correct reflection and guidance. He began with the verb attributed to them because it is a enumeration of a sin, as we have explained. The saying: ﴿صَرَفَ اللهُ قُلُوبَهُمْ﴾ (Allah turned their hearts away) may be an invocation against them, and it may be a statement of fact, meaning: they deserved that, ﴿بِأنَّهم قَوْمٌ لا يَفْقَهُونَ﴾ (because they are a people who do not understand), that is, they do not comprehend from Allah or from His Messenger. Al-Tabari, in his tafsir of this verse, related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him both) that he said: "Do not say, 'We have turned away from the prayer,' for indeed a people turned away and Allah turned their hearts away; rather, say, 'We have completed the prayer.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This glance mentioned in this verse is a gesture, and al-Tabari related from some of them that he said: "nazara" (glanced) in this verse is in the place of "qala" (said).

The saying of the Exalted, ﴿لَقَدْ جاءَكُمْ﴾ (There has certainly come to you), is addressed to the Arabs according to the view of the majority. This is a enumeration of the favour bestowed upon them in this, for [the Messenger] came in their own tongue and with what they understand of the aims and eloquence, and they were honoured by him for the remainder of time. Al-Zajjaj said: it is addressed to the entire world, and the meaning is: "There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among mankind." The first view is more correct. The saying: ﴿مِن أنْفُسِكُمْ﴾ (from among yourselves) implies praise for the lineage of the Prophet (ﷺ), that he is of the pure stock and most noble of the Arabs. In line with this meaning is his (ﷺ) saying: "Indeed Allah chose Kinana from among the descendants of Isma'il, chose Quraysh from Kinana, chose Banu Hashim from Quraysh, and chose me from Banu Hashim." And from it is his (ﷺ) saying: "I am from a legitimate marriage, not from illegitimate union." The meaning is that his (ﷺ) lineage back to Adam (peace be upon him) contained no offspring except from marriage, and there was no fornication in it.

Abdullah ibn Qusayt al-Makki read ﴿مِن أنْفَسِكُمْ﴾ with a fatha on the fa', from nafasa (preciousness/nobility), and this was related from the Prophet (ﷺ) and from Fatima (may Allah be pleased with her). Abu 'Amr mentioned that Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) related it from the Prophet (ﷺ).

The saying: ﴿ما عَنِتُّمْ﴾ (what you suffer) means: your suffering, so "ma" is a verbal-source particle (masdariyya), and it is the subject; "'azizun" (grievous) is the predicate that precedes. It is also permissible that "ma 'anittum" be the agent of "'azizun", and "'azizun" be an attribute of the Messenger (ﷺ); this is more correct than the first. Al-'anat means hardship. Here the word is general, meaning: whatever hardship befalls you from disbelief and error according to what is right, and from killing, captivity and trial because of the truth and your belief along with it. Qatada also said: the meaning is the suffering of your believers.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Generalizing the suffering to all is more apt.

The saying of the Exalted, ﴿حَرِيصٌ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ (desirous of you), means: desirous of your faith and your guidance. As for His saying ﴿رَءُوفٌ﴾ (kind), its meaning is: exceedingly compassionate. Abu 'Ubayda said: ra'fa is more tender than rahma (mercy). Al-A'mash, the people of Kufa, and Abu 'Amr read ﴿رَؤُفٌ﴾ without the elongation (madd).

Then, after establishing this favour upon them, He addressed the Prophet (ﷺ) saying: ﴿فَإنْ تَوَلَّوْا﴾ (But if they turn away), O Muhammad, that is, they turn away after this established state with which Allah, blessed and exalted is He, has favoured them. ﴿فَقُلْ حَسْبِيَ اللهُ﴾ (then say: Allah is sufficient for me). Its meaning is: and your deeds are according to your words of committing the matter to Allah, relying upon Him, and striving earnestly in fighting them. This is not a verse of truce, because it is among the last to be revealed. The Throne is singled out for mention because it is the greatest of created things. Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿الْعَظِيمُ﴾ (the Mighty) with a damma on the mim, as an attribute of the Lord, and this was related from Ibn Kathir.

These two verses were not found when the Mushaf was compiled, except in the memory of Khuzayma ibn Thabit, and in al-Bukhari it occurs as: "or Abu Khuzayma." When he brought them, many of the Companions remembered them. Zayd had known them, and for this reason he said: "I lost two verses from the end of Surat al-Tawba." Had he not known them, he would not have known whether he had lost something or not. The verse was established by consensus (ijma'), not by Khuzayma alone. Al-Tabari related in his book: 'Umar would not establish a verse in the Mushaf unless two men testified to it. When Khuzayma brought these two verses, he said: "By Allah, I will never ask you for a proof concerning them," for it was thus that the Prophet (ﷺ) acted.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

He means the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) contained in the verse. This, Allah knows best, was said by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) during the caliphate of Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), at the time of the first compilation. At that time the two verses were missing, and nothing of the Qur'an was compiled during the caliphate of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). Khuzayma ibn Thabit is the one known as Dhu al-Shahadatayn (the one of the two testimonies), and he was known by this because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) allowed his testimony alone in the purchase of a horse and ruled by it for himself (ﷺ), and this is a specific privilege of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). al-Naqqash mentioned from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he said: "The closest of the Qur'an to Allah in its revelation are these two verses: ﴿لَقَدْ جاءَكم رَسُولٌ﴾ (There has certainly come to you a Messenger) to the end of the surah."

Completed, by the help and success of Allah the Exalted, is Surat al-Tawba. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
